The Government Will Not Allow Further Lay-offs in the Coal Mines of Zagłębie / In Today's Issue, No. 1, of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“

[Zagłębie — economy; the coal mines, lay-offs.]
On Wednesday a conference took place at the Ministry of Social Welfare [Ministerstwo Opieki Społecznej], at which the decision of the industrialists to lay off 4 thousand workers of „Renard“, „Milowice“ and „Reden“ was dealt with.
The industrialists declared that the reduction must be carried out because coal exports have fallen considerably.
To this the deputies Dr. Madeyski and Konieczki[?] replied, showing that the lay-off proposals are due only to the egoism of the foreign capitalists, who chase only after large profits and do not want to reckon with the actual situation.
The Sosnowiec labour inspector, Mr. Federowicz, declared that new lay-offs in Zagłębie would lead to catastrophic results.
After the discussion the chief inspector, engineer Klott, chairman of the conference, declared that the government will not allow any new lay-offs. Moreover, that the government will endeavour that the working time in the Zagłębie coal mines be maintained as it has been until now.
—o—

The Young Shochtim Strike and the Old Ones Do Not Want to Do the Inspection / „Huta Bankowa“ in Dąbrowa Has Laid Off 315 Workers / Lay-offs in Upper Silesia / Summary Court to Sit on the 16th of This Month in Sosnowiec / 11 Groszy the Tax — and 3 Złoty Execution Costs / A Man Found Hanged at the „Społem“ Cooperative in Ząbkowice

[Będzin — kehilla; ritual slaughter.]
This week the kehilla „gemoyzekhts“ [the muddle, the „mice's nest“] in Będzin heaved itself up, and to the surface there rose once again the young shochtim („shokhtimlekh“), who on Monday threw down their work in the slaughterhouse and went on strike.
On Wednesday at midday the shu"b [slaughterer and inspector] R' Berish Makower announced that, because R' Shlomo shu"b has fallen ill and R' Avraham shu"b slaughters poultry, he is not able to deal with the slaughtering in the slaughterhouse alone.
After R' Berie [sic; = R' Berish] shu"b had announced this, he went off home after the slaughtering, and in the slaughterhouse there was not a single shochet to carry out the inspection (bedika).
The butchers, seeing that there was none of the shochtim to inspect the large number of cattle and calves, went off to the Rabbi with the threat that in such a situation they would bring in meat from elsewhere.
In connection with this the kehilla administration held an urgent meeting, at which it came to a sharp exchange of words between the dozors[?] [kehilla board members] Rinski and Liwer.
Several butchers were also present at the meeting, who simply threatened to throw chairs at those who had brought about such lawlessness in the slaughterhouse.
At last the matter was settled, after R' Avraham shu"b was prevailed upon to do the inspecting, and the young shochtim — they are to be employed at the poultry slaughter.
—o—

11 Groszy the Tax — and 3 Złoty Execution Costs
[Szczekociny — taxes; Rubinlicht's intervention.]
Last Tuesday a delegation from Szczekociny turned to Mr. Rubinlicht and handed over to him a series of wrongs which the Jewish population in Szczekociny suffers from the tax bailiffs (sequestrators) there.
Among other things the delegation reported the following fact:
A Jewish woman trader in Szczekociny remained owing, through a mistake, 11 (eleven) groszy of tax. A sequestrator came in to her, who snatched 3 złoty and 11 groszy out of the drawer and left a receipt stating that the 3 złoty are for execution costs...
Mr. Rubinlicht intervened with this material with the vice-president of the Chamber of Commerce, Mr. Szykański[?] [שיקאנסקי], who promised that he will forward the unheard-of facts to the Izba Skarbowa [Treasury Chamber] in Kielce.

An Open Letter to the Board of the Jewish Hospital in Sosnowiec

[Sosnowiec — letter to the editor.]
Visiting this week the large general ward of the hospital, I saw the memorial plaque of the late benefactor Reb Ayzik Ber Wolfson, of blessed memory, who has in this way been commemorated by the hospital board. But how astonished I was when I became convinced that to this very day, after a period of 4½ years, there is still no memorial plaque in the hospital for the late Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory, who over the course of 20 years gave his energy and his whole life to the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec.
Did the deceased, as chief physician (ordinator) of many years' standing, not deserve that his name be commemorated by such a memorial plaque?
I believe and hope that the Jewish public in Sosnowiec, among whom the name of our dear and unforgettable leader Dr. Abraham Perlman, of blessed memory, always remains in memory, will demand of the hospital board that it fulfil its duty and commemorate the great communal worker in all Jewish social and national institutions.
Respectfully,
Jakub Szymon Feldman.

A Divorce on Account of New Year's Eve.

[Sosnowiec — from life.]
The first divorce of the new year has come about precisely because of New Year's Eve (Sylvester night). The story is a hackneyed one.
A young wife, a year after the wedding, left home and told her husband that she was going to acquaintances to play cards.
When the clock struck 3 and she was still not back, the husband, from a main street in Sosnowiec, went off to look for her at the acquaintances'; it turned out, however, that she had not been there at all.
He therefore no longer lay down to sleep, but walked about near the house and waited for his spouse. He strolled thus until 5 before dawn, when a droshky drove up to his gate and out of it stepped his young wife with an elegant gentleman, both half drunk.
The epilogue will shortly be played out at the rabbinate.
"The Danger of Assimilation".

[Będzin — Mizrachi, lecture.]
Under this title Rabbi Dr. Chameides of Katowice gave a lecture on Sunday evening in the premises of the Będzin "Mizrachi".
The lecturer, making use of various sayings of the Sages, argued that Judaism has an existence only when thought is bound together with deed; thinking and acting must be closely joined.
As the main foundation of the danger of assimilation is, in the lecturer's opinion, to speak the Holy Tongue...
After the lecture, over a glass of tea, topical questions were touched upon, among them also that the Mizrachi organisations in Zagłębie should publish a monthly periodical devoted to spiritual matters.
Penalties for Failing to Report Liquidated Businesses.

[Commerce — notice to merchants.]
According to the existing commercial laws every merchant is obliged to report when a business is opened or liquidated.
Insofar as the merchants who open new businesses still remember this, the same merchants nevertheless forget to report when they liquidate their enterprises.
Attention is therefore drawn to the fact that for failure to comply with the binding regulations there is a penalty of up to 2000 zł, 2 weeks' arrest, or both penalties together. The penalties are imposed by administrative procedure.

On Guard Before a Catastrophe. XVII. (The Crisis and Antisemitism. — The Positions We Have Been Pushed Out Of — We Must Create New Branches of Livelihood)

L. Szpigelman.
(XVII. The crisis and antisemitism. — The positions we have been pushed out of — We must create new branches of livelihood.)
In one of the previous chapters we thus came to the conclusion that we have neglected ourselves. We have neglected all our trades, professions and specialities and have held them cheap, and that is the reason why, at the very beginning of the terrible crisis, which has already entered a chronic stage, we were the first to bring the greatest sacrifices. Thanks to our disdain we did not come to our senses at the proper time, we did not orient ourselves in the twinkling of an eye, and therefore the road became slippery and catastrophic for the Jewish community with a rare speed, so that none of the masses managed to keep up with the momentum and save himself from the catastrophe, which at the first moment was not foreseen as so terrible, so cruel.
Apart from the hard times in which we live, apart from the prevailing crisis, we as Jews have lost our possibilities of existence. When it is a matter of supply contracts, we are the second-rank ones, if we are considered at all. There is a stubborn front against us, which does not let the Jew get near the factory. Our antisemites incite on the right and on the left. The "Rozwój" slogans and the antisemitic articles, which are printed constantly in the antisemitic sheets, incite without cease and instil in the Polish people poison and hatred towards the Jewish citizens. They invent whatever can be thought up, just to make loathsome in the eyes of the Pole the "superfluous ones" of society, who consist of Jewish elements. Had so much poison and hatred not been sown, Jews would have lived quite peacefully with the Polish inhabitants, we would always have got along with one another and the unity would truly have been a harmony between Jews and Christians; no one would have taken anything from the other; on the contrary, each would have given to the other.
As soon as they see an article of trade that is in Jewish hands, they become eager for it and throw themselves upon it with enthusiasm, to tear it out of the Jewish hands. It happens very often that the Jew has been driven out of this or that line of business and they themselves have achieved nothing whatsoever by it. The end is that the Jew has been ruined, broken, and the Christian competitor has become a pauper. Such phenomena occur quite often in our life. But the end is that we are pushed out of our positions and later there is no more strength to catch up with them again; we then become lower, more fallen, more dispirited, and there is nothing to take hold of.
In order that we should not lose our positions, in order that we should not fall to the bottom, we must be firm as a rock, we must have immense patience and unusual endurance; otherwise we would long ago have been lost, otherwise we would already have vanished and been erased from every human existence.
We must therefore not lose heart, we must not lose courage, we must strengthen our powers, we must keep ourselves on the surface; we do have our specific, distinctive Jewish qualities, of which we can truly be proud. We can often work wonders in every field of our activity thanks to our abilities. It does not matter if we say that we must not fool ourselves, that we must not live with fantasies and dreams — we must nevertheless hold ourselves bravely, thanks to the rock-firm energy that we possess; and if one position is snatched away, from which we draw our livelihood with honour, we are at once understanding enough to be able to switch over quickly and discover new sources of livelihood, fresh positions, from which no one has yet profited at all.
In addition one more thing must not be forgotten: we have neglected many branches, neglected them because perhaps we had no need of them and perhaps paid them no attention; we are not of those who force their way in, we let ourselves be content with what we had, we were the true "he who is happy with his lot". But today, when everything has run out, when the Jewish citizen is impoverished and helpless, one must not stand with folded hands; we must begin to think how to continue the thread of our life.
Many positions have been torn away from us entirely, many have disappeared of themselves, both because of the bitter times on the one hand and because of the pouring of pitch and brimstone on Jewish heads on the other; therefore we too ought to look for fresh sources of income, not stopping short even at minimally satisfactory results, for whatever elements it may be.
In the big European cities there exist laundries which come to every house to collect the washing from the housewife; it is washed, it is mangled, it is pressed, and it is brought back in the best order to the house from which it was taken. This is done quickly, nicely and cheaply. The housewife is content: she does not have the burden on her head, she does not need to watch the washerwoman in the kitchen lest she take something from her, and she does not need to tremble, as long as the washing hangs in the attic, lest thieves "take pity" on it. The washing that she hands over is thus insured, and the firm is responsible for everything. It seems that this means a great deal to a housewife, for after all the washing costs money at home too, it causes disorder and crowding, and moreover the family is in fear: now one is not sure whether the washing will come out well, and now one is afraid of a theft. So that such an undertaking means a great deal; every housewife would gladly hand over her washing into safe hands, where she could be sure that it will not be damaged. Moreover one must know that specialists in this field can achieve much, both in convenience and in economy.
By the way, among us there are no washerwomen at all for whom this is a profession and who could support themselves from it with honour.
The same is the case among us with maidservants. People among us are altogether ashamed of this occupation; they quite forget that today's maidservant is not the one of 20 years ago, who was enslaved and worn out with toil and never had any rest. Today, after all, the occupation is no worse than that of any clerk. Why then should one be ashamed of it? Altogether, it is a line of work that is classified. Thus, for example, there are professional cooks, who hire themselves out only for cooking and, incidentally, with everything provided for them, earn very well. Then there are those who are not for the kitchen alone and can also obtain posts; besides that, girls or women can also find employment by taking on houses to tidy up, which should take 2–3 hours a day. Then there is a category of nursemaids, who are needed especially to bring up children; that too can be quite a respectable profession. But unfortunately people among us are ashamed of these occupations, which have risen to quite a respectable level and pay not badly; and as for those who are not ashamed of their occupation, it is altogether impossible to approach them, so high are their prices.
We have only mentioned in passing a few occupations from which many women could support themselves, and among us no attention is paid to this. If people took an interest in this or that line of work, we would have many, many fewer "respectable ones", and this would, by the way, bring the Jewish people more honour, true honour.
People among us are accustomed to imitate one another. Hardly does Shimon see that Berl has opened a little shop, and that people are seen going in to him, be it only for a few groszy's worth of pepper, than the shopkeeper is already envied and they seek to open the very same little shop opposite him. To seek out something new, to invent something fresh, to do that which is not yet so "current with the merchant" — of that no one wants to think.
Shmerl is of the opinion: better let Berl rack his brains and invent something new, and then he will copy the same thing. On the other hand the sense, the train of thought, is lacking for introducing something fresh and positive, which can bring the proper benefit to the Jewish population and from which one could support oneself with honour.
It would truly be only right to give it some thought and to set about intensively seeking out new lines of business, on which we have not yet cast a glance.
With our abilities we could possibly still achieve much, we could still take hold in various insignificant branches from which a livelihood could be drawn. The main thing, however, is that one should not lose heart and should not be ashamed of anything; we should forget that we are a "Thou hast chosen us" people. After all, our troubles ought already to have trained us not to hold anything cheap. Schnorrers we have already raised enough; now we need to have only productive people, and if we are pushed out of various branches, we must be courageous and bold to fight for our existence. Only we must not forget in what period and in what century we live, when it is altogether hard to struggle for a respectable and honest existence.

Seeing Off 1932

[Feuilleton — a look back at 1932.]
You can imagine that the year which has just taken itself off was very busy packing and getting ready for the road.
Such is the nature of the years: when the new one comes into power, the old one is already gone and has become a piece of history.
From this it follows that the old year must be packed up and ready to go before the new one shows itself.
And the time needed for getting ready and packing depends on the baggage one has to take along, on the number of packs one has with one.
Well, as far as packs and bundles are concerned, 1932 has nothing to be ashamed of.
Such a year with bundles is one of those one does not ask about, one of those that make themselves remembered, though one would sooner have wished to forget them.
And it is hard to understand how he will be able to manage with such a large amount of baggage.
Should he want to travel by railway, that will positively not do: he will make such a hole in the till that we shall never be able to pay it off.
So he will presumably go on travelling fourth class, according to Sholem Aleichem's famous classification. Fourth class is when one rides under the bench and, on top of that, drags off the neighbours' bundles.
Passenger 1932 is a master[?] at such journeys. One really feels like counting him as a separate class all of his own — shall we call it the fifth class? Quite a fine idea. In the fifth class one presumably behaves like this: one strips all the passengers and lays them all out under the bench, then one empties their pockets, clears out their bundles and makes off.
Yes, he is already on his way.
Just reckon up what concerns the bit of business that he wiped away and took: such a thing can be achieved only by extraordinary strength; millions of horses could not have budged it. Houses and estates — people had them and have them no more. 1932 rode through and took them.
Banks stood there looking like fortresses, strong as iron; 1932 ran through, shook them apart[?], scattered them and dragged them away.
1932 burst into the very centre of the mountain of securities and wrought destruction there; he penetrated into the hindmost positions and set upon everything; he ruined everything and dragged it along with him.
He broke into the British Empire and cleared out the bit of gold; the crisis with the unemployment he did leave behind, but the gold he dragged out. He has no consideration for anyone; because of him even a royal palace must suffer. The budget for the holiday ceremonies was terribly cut there. One has to make do with fewer flowers and less luxury.
While he was at it he also dropped in on Japan and seized the bit of gold there too. But the rifles and cannons he did not take, and one can understand why.
When people fight with greater relish, one can meanwhile drag the bit of wealth out of the country more quickly.
In China the field is so large that it was necessary to introduce several measures there so that the work of 1932 could proceed as it ought to. There is room enough there for hunger, revolution and wars all together.
In Poland he worked upon the Endek [National Democratic] youth so that they would commit the excesses and the boycott; the crisis alone is too little. It has to be helped along with extra means. And all so that it should become leaner and more ruined.
In Germany he woke up the “Nazis”. The Germans are a strong people and cannot be overcome so easily. All the earlier years of war, revolution and reparations had not yet broken them. So 1932 came with the “Nazis” to finish the job.
The year that has taken itself off also wound in a novelty, a kind of bundle that is called: moratorium. A new headache from which one cannot wriggle out. It is supposed to be the opposite of demanding reparations; since nowadays nothing can be achieved by pressing the debtor, the plan was created not to press him but to wait.
That was a plan to end the crisis — and do you know when a crisis ends? When a new one begins; and a moratorium looks like quite a fine instrument for such a purpose — go on, say that it isn't.
One cannot collect the debts because one cannot get the money out; that alone is already a sufficient explanation. So what can a moratorium do for us here? You can call it “one doesn't pay”, and you spare yourself the use of words that stir up tempers and lead to scandals.
What does a moratorium mean? The creditor says to his debtor: you need not pay me now, you will pay later; if you cannot pay later, your children will pay; if they cannot, the grandchildren will pay; we shall wait for the great-grandchildren; some day we shall settle accounts.
Well, the question arises: what are the great-grandchildren guilty of? Why must one already prepare for them a soil for wars and revolutions? And why at all must one quarrel about it now? The fact remains the same: one does not pay, and one will not pay so soon, positively not so soon, whether you call it a moratorium or do not call it a moratorium.
The excuse is that this is, after all, 1932 — he has to leave something behind. Well, so he fattened up the crisis and the unemployment, brought out a few excesses, a boycott, and in the end a moratorium.
In return he cleared away the little bit of good that still remained, and now he has gone off on his way. He took a fair lot of bundles with him.
An important passenger of the fifth class was 1932.
H. Lazarson.
On the Border Between Two Years

[Article — world politics; a balance of the year 1932.] The World War did not introduce a new reckoning of time, as the great French Revolution did — and without success. But the war of the nations cut so deeply into the life of mankind in every field that it is impossible to draw up any summing-up of the past or any forecast for the future without returning to the two great dates: the dates of the beginning and of the end of the war.
The year we have entered will in this respect be a jubilee year: 15 years will have passed since the war was ended. Every month, every day will bring back to memory events and occurrences that had a world-historic significance: the grey, hopeless days of the German occupation; the January unrest in Germany, when the patient, worn-out German people tried to put to its rulers the terrible question: why, whither and how long? The mighty attempts of German militarism, through enormous sacrifices, to bring the situation on the fronts to such a state that the sword would be able to dictate its will to the nations, just as that will was dictated to the Russian people at Brest-Litovsk. America's entry into the war, which was a turning point and tipped the scales — decided them on the side of the Allies. Foch's mighty counter-offensive, the “black day” of the German army in the month of August, when the fortune of war turns finally away from Germany and passes over to the side of the Allies, when German military power begins to roll downhill, down to the terrible catastrophe of the autumn, to the dreadful armistice which puts an end to the war, calling forth in the countries of the victorious states a wild frenzy of joy and lust for revenge, which will soon pass over into the heavy, leaden worries of liquidating the war and its enormous damages and sacrifices.
From that moment begins the phenomenon that can be compared with Homer's poetic image in the “Odyssey”: like Penelope, who sits and waits for the return of her husband Odysseus and each time unravels the garment she has knitted, in order to take up again the laborious work of knitting on — so the world sits and waits impatiently for the coming of its redeemer, for the longed-for rest and peace, and does its Sisyphean labour, which is each time undone as useless and unsuccessful. How many times and in what ways have attempts not already been made to bring the world back, politically and economically, to an equilibrium; but every time new, enormous difficulties grow up and one turns back again to the starting point, establishing that the efforts undertaken have not led to the goal.
The same was to be observed in the past year 1932 as well. The political-economic problems were concentrated last year as if in three foci, in three phases: the disarmament conference, the reparations, the war debts.
The three problems, which are so bound and knotted one with another that without their solution no progress whatever, no way out of the world crisis whatever, is possible — the three problems were raised, moved one jolt forward, only to remain standing further in their entangled and unsolved form. Without disarmament, without relieving the state budgets and the consuming war expenditures, any restoration of the economy to health is impossible, it is impossible to tear oneself out of the claws of the crisis; but the disarmament conference, for which preparations had been made for months and years, brought no results.
The greatest hopes were placed in Lausanne. Lausanne was to have created the great economic programme for the world, and the first point was the liquidation of the German reparations, the source of perpetual political-moral ferment and of financial-economic collapse in Germany. Lausanne created no programme. The German reparations were in fact abolished, but at the very end of the year came the surprise from America: America's refusal to renounce the war monies in Europe, the ruthless demand that the debts be paid — and thereby what had been achieved in Lausanne was placed under a question mark: Europe turns back again to its starting points.
Just at the end of the old year all the wounds from which Europe suffers were laid bare anew.
The economic and political crisis has sharpened everywhere; even France, which until now had suffered least from the crisis, has been drawn into its iron arms — the resignation of Herriot's government is the outward symptom of it. Unemployment, want and misery do not recede; bitterness and disappointment have built themselves nests in such places as were until now held to be secured against upheavals. The events in the city of peace, Geneva, were a very telling memento for the whole world, and some threatening political symptoms are receding. Yet the economic devastations remain in their full force; this can be seen in Germany: in the great struggle between democracy and the wildest fascism, sound common sense is, it seems, nevertheless beginning to gain the upper hand; the phenomenon of political madness, Hitlerism, is beginning to lose its tension — but unemployment is not growing milder, and in the last days of the departed year we had the great “hunger march” on Berlin.
Just as last year, as two years ago and so on further back, the world today too, standing on the border between the departed and the arrived year, yearns for peace, rest, security; the community yearns for it, the individual yearns and longs for it, but there is no peace, no rest and no security. The past year is symbolised by an event that did not happen: in the year 1932 all the prizes of Nobel's foundation were distributed; only one prize there was no one to give to, just as in the dark years of the war: it was the prize for peace — for it no candidate was found.
P. B.
Is It Really Getting Better Already?

[World economy — letter from Leipzig.]
From our Leipzig correspondent Z. Haber.
Today, rising up and lying down, we have only one worry: have we already nearly come through the great economic crisis that is choking our whole life; is a spark of improvement already showing itself to us from somewhere, which might bring us new hopes in the sad situation in which we now find ourselves.
And therefore it is worth leafing through the various reports that arrive from the four corners of the world at the Leipzig Fair Office (Messeamt).
Since the Leipzig Fair opens as early as the 5th of March, the Fair Office is now receiving exact information about the situation of all countries in the whole world.
In general almost all the reports are not good. Everywhere the situation is bad; only in individual countries does a bit of improvement show itself.
It is interesting that precisely in the Orient the biggest business is to be done today.
In Eretz Israel the whole of industry is quite well employed. Not only is there a market in the country itself — all kinds of goods are bought and sold — but the surrounding countries too, Syria, Egypt and Iraq, are literally flooded with goods produced in Eretz Israel.
In Egypt, for example, people look only for Palestinian goods. Even in the articles which are produced in Egypt itself and on which there is a high customs duty, one can do the best business with Eretz-Israel products; the things from Eretz Israel are nicer and better than the Egyptian ones and the population buys them gladly.
Especially the embroidery works and linen factories of Tel Aviv, ready-made clothes, soap, crockery and many other articles from Palestine literally flood the Egyptian market.
Not to speak of Syria, where there is not a single industry. There the goods from Palestine arrive duty-free and are snatched out of one's hands. Only razor blades are now manufactured in Syria itself, and the government plans to introduce a duty on razor blades, because in the country itself two and a half million blades a year are produced.
In Iraq all kinds of goods are needed: electrical articles, automobiles, ironware, paints, jewellery, etc. Germany delivers very many goods there; lately Czechoslovakia (Bata) has flooded the market with shoes and has pushed out all the German and English shoe factories. Eretz Israel supplies all kinds of knitwear there and could do quite big business there if the factories in Eretz Israel had more capital and could export more.
In Turkey too many goods of all branches are needed, and the Turkish government has now founded an industry office of its own with a bank of its own, which is to occupy itself with building up various industries in the country, which are very urgently needed there.
Textile goods are especially badly needed there now. Japan and Russia flood Turkey with textile goods and depress the price so strongly that other countries cannot compete there. Especially cheap are the Japanese, who sell there at any price whatever that they are given.
In Greece too goods are needed, especially in those parts that were destroyed by the earthquake; it is also expected that building will soon begin there again, and with that all kinds of building materials will be needed there. For the time being, however, the Greek government does not yet have the money necessary to rebuild the ruined places.
In Brazil things have now begun to get a little better; the foodstuffs branch has revived, rubber articles and ironware are much sought after, and England has begun to import all kinds of goods there, which they throw on the market for next to nothing. It appears that England wants to drive out all the competition there, for they sell as cheaply as is at all possible; meanwhile business has improved a little.
In Denmark there is a great demand for all kinds of chemical-technical articles. Germany and England are beginning to deliver there: zinc, potash, natron, soda, saltpetre, carbide and other chemicals, which are needed in large quantities.
In Yugoslavia there is a great shortage of radio articles. In a country of thirteen million people there are only sixty thousand radio listeners; Holland, America, France, Germany and Austria have begun to deliver radio sets and all kinds of radio articles there, which are bought there in great numbers.
In Morocco too a bit of improvement is showing; the population is afraid that the money may fall in value, and therefore people there buy whatever they possibly can.
From the remaining countries the news is such that in the last months the situation has become still more serious. The import restrictions have become stronger, the foreign-currency regulations have become still stricter, and trade in the whole world is so bad that for the time being no clear answer can yet be given to the question whether things really are already getting better in economic life.
The Strongman [Der Takif]

[Feuilleton — a satire on a kehilla president.]
(Such a tale).
What is told here is a true, not an invented story. I heard it myself from my grandfather, of blessed memory — a true story in a town in Congress Poland.
* * *
His first name and family name I do not remember. Instead I remember quite exactly his nickname, with which he was endowed — "Takif" [the Strongman, the overbearing one] they called him. He was a Jew, a simple one, but to make up for it a rich man, an owner of houses and of a big business.
But this Jew was not content with his great wealth, and as was the way in those times — it was then pre-war times — he dreamed of becoming something of a communal worker. And indeed, why not? This world he already has, so one must begin to take care of the world to come as well. Of charity he did not exactly think much, because charity — he used to say — diminishes his share of this world... Through communal activity, through becoming a public worker "not for the sake of receiving a reward" — now that is the way to a portion in the world to come. When he comes there after a hundred and twenty years, when he is dispatched to that world...
The Takif was elected president of the kehilla.
He came home to his wife and, full of joy, addressed her and spoke to her thus:
— "Be it known to you, my dear little wife, that from today on you are 'pani prezesowa' [Madam President]. I, your husband, have been elected 'jako pan prezes gminy wyznania mojżeszowego' [as the honourable president of the community of the Mosaic faith]."
In the town the Takif's election made no particular impression; only among his own gang did people whisper and boast:
— Ay-ay, is that a president... can you imagine!...
In point of fact, the Takif was no politician. Politics — he said — is a matter for idlers. Nor was he a party man; he did not meddle in any matters at all. A plain Jew. A non-party one.
The jesters of the generation even used to say that he was no party man because 1) a party demands money from a person, and all the more from a rich man such as the Takif is, and there they will not be content with honey-cake and brandy; and secondly, he is not one of those people who would let themselves be led by the nose by presidents — he himself can, thank God, lead himself and lead others.
— What am I, a horse, that I should let myself be led, and what do I need a coachman over me for? — when he was once asked why he does not occupy himself with parties at all.
This holding himself aloof from political life made him very popular among his "amkho" [common-folk] Jews of the gang, for he gave all his free time to the kehilla's affairs, had a new hearse made to carry the dead to their eternal rest, and many, many more good things, until the kehilla elections came.
Day follows day. Day after day went by. The term of office of the gmina [the community board] came to an end.
Those were then quite hard times for Jews. The demoralisation in the Jewish street had reached the highest degree; the atmosphere was stifling as in a sweat-bath. It was not ideas that then ruled the Jewish street. On the contrary: lack of ideas, high-handedness and strong fists ran riot there. Men close to the authorities, intercessors [shtadlanim], then schemed on all fronts, promised to be good and pious.
Those were then bitter times, when on account of a petty rabbinical post somewhere in a godforsaken little Polish town a Hasidic Jew fired a shot at his opponent in the synagogue on the Sabbath... (Łuków).
And to just this type of communal worker the Takif too belonged. A man close to the authorities, he made common cause with the dark element, the radical-clericalist element, and rode[?] his little horse in the kehilla.
As it happened, the town in its overwhelming majority was nationally minded, with a national tradition.
National parnasim [board members] were elected and brought in. The national dozors [members of the kehilla board] elected national presidents, and the Takif with his clique were sent packing. The Takif, however, did not sit still[?]; he laid down his "veto" — I do not permit it — and banged hastily on the table, and from the high windows, where they were sitting in deliberation[?], a heavenly voice went forth:
— No, we do not accept!...
The national majority wanted to go on conducting the work, but the Takif shouted:
— I want it so, I am the president and I will do as I want.
* * *
The end of the story I do not remember. And may the readers forgive me for having wearied them with such a long tale, but because the story is a true one and not an invented one, I have told it to you.
Y. M. Biderman.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayigash)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayigash
The Portion
—o—
a) "And let not your eye have pity on your belongings" (Gen. 45:20)
"Your eye" [ve-einkhem] — in the singular, not "your eyes" [ve-eineikhem].
For however a man may look away from his money and property, however much he may want to turn his gaze from it, he still casts his eye back... Only with one eye does one look away from it...
After "Or Pnei Moshe".
—o—
b) "Of the good things of Egypt" (ibid., 23)
"He sent him old wine, in which the mind of the elderly finds contentment." Rashi.
By way of a jest:
The chief disgrace of Egypt, the basest Egyptian trait, was their pride, and in Isaiah (30:7) Egypt is therefore called "Rahab" [arrogance]. And the Gemara says (Bava Batra 98) that "whoever is haughty, his wine turns sour".
Therefore Joseph sent the old wine, to show that he had not learned Egyptian pride — the proof: his wine is good, not sour...
Rabbi Avraham Abele of Vilna.
—o—
c) "All the souls of the house of Jacob that came [sic, plural] into Egypt" (46:27)
1.
"All the soul" [singular] — all the sons of Jacob held themselves as one soul, because "they came into Egypt": for coming to Egypt, being in a time of trouble, the only salvation is to feel as one.
Orach Chaim.
* * *
Rabbi Mendele of Kotzk was once in Pinsk and stayed with one of his Hasidim, a great contractor [podryadchik], who had many warehouses of goods around Sevastopol.
On the Sabbath the Hasid receives a telegram that many warehouses in Sevastopol have burnt down. The Hasid nevertheless felt in good spirits; the Rebbe says to him:
— I assure you that your warehouses have not burnt down.
And so it was. It later turned out so.
Says the Kotzker Rebbe: This is no holy spirit; I understood it simply: for a man bears his own sorrow with difficulty, whereas another's sorrow he bears easily... And if you were in a good mood after the news, I understood that the troubles were not yours but someone else's, for other people's troubles one bears easily...
* * *
A person should make light of his own troubles and think highly of the other's honour, make light of his own honour and feel for the other's troubles.
Unfortunately it is the reverse: people think highly of their own honour and make light of the other's troubles... Imrei Chen.
2.
R' Yosef Shaul Nathanson cites in his book "Divrei Shaul", in the name of a "wise gentile"...
It is better when Jews hold together as one and are united in one religion. For if they do not hold to religion and are splintered, one has to fight each one separately; but if all are united in religion, one can strike them all together through the religion. .
—o—
d) "Then make them rulers over cattle" [ve-samtam sarei mikneh] (47:6)
A Masoretic note:
"Ve-samtam sarei mikneh" [and you shall set them as rulers over cattle].
And:
"Ve-samtam ba-aron" [and you shall set them in the coffin/ark].
Mostly, when it comes to "ve-samtam ba-aron", when one is already being laid in the coffin, on the bier — then "ve-samtam sarei mikneh": the deceased is made out to be a shepherd of the flock, a ruler over cattle; but in life they were persecuted...
Ma'adanei Melekh.
—o—
e) "And Israel dwelt in the land of Egypt, in the land of Goshen, and they took possession of it" [va-ye'achazu vah].
"Va-ye'achazu vah — an expression of achuzah [holding, possession][?]." Rashi.
What does Rashi mean by these words?
Only that according to the vowel-pointing "va-ye'achazu" is a nif'al [passive] form, and it could have been rendered: the children of Israel were seized by the land — for that is how it is: when Israel already wants to leave a country, the country holds him back. . Rashi remarks on this that with the first children of Israel it was not so, and the meaning of "va-ye'achazu" is an expression of possession [achuzah][?]. On the contrary[?] — not held back; for the time being they were not yet bound to Egypt, but later...
Tekhelet Mordechai.
—o—
f) "Now that I have seen your face" (46:30)
For from a person's face one recognises what he is. From Joseph's face alone Jacob recognised that he had not sinned, that he was still the Joseph of old.
The Rebbe R' Hershele.

Haftarah
g) "And all the house of Israel his companions" (Ezekiel 37)
The written form [ketiv] is "chavero" [his companion] and the read form [qeri] is "chaverav" [his companions].
It is indeed a commandment, "Love your neighbour as yourself", to love all Jews equally; yet it cannot be that a person should not love his close friends more than Jews in general. But this must be only outward (therefore the qeri, the outward sound[?]: "chaverav" — his friends, his close ones), whereas deep in the heart, inwardly, every Jew must be as dear to the other as his most intimate friend (therefore the ketiv: "chavero" — all as one friend). Ahavat Yehonatan.

h) "And they all shall have one shepherd" (ibid.)
A Jewish leader is never described in the Bible as a warrior, a fighter. Fighting for the Jews — God already does that. The leader need only be a shepherd, who must guard his sheep so that they may graze in peace...
R' Yehonatan Eybeschütz.

New enforcement regulations.
[Law — a new statute.] On 1 January [stycznia] the new law on enforcement (execution of judgments) came into force.
The basis of every enforcement will be the "tytuł wykonawczy" [enforcement title], which must be furnished with an enforcement clause.
The enforcement will be carried out — as until now — by the komornik [court bailiff], who must, at his first action, hand the debtor a notice of the commencement of the enforcement and state the content of the "tytuł wykonawczy". The bailiff has the right to open all receptacles and to search the things in the dwelling as well as the pockets and clothing of the debtor.
The enforcement does not extend to: the most necessary household goods, linen, everyday clothing, food for 1 month, raw materials needed for work for 1 month, as well as objects needed for professional work, teaching aids, subsidies and the like. From those who receive a fixed salary, the part that is needed until the next pay date cannot be taken. Those who do not receive a fixed salary must be left money equal to 2 weeks' pay.
The regulations on enforcement comprise over 350 articles (from 508 onward) and introduce very important changes in the enforcement system used until now. R.

He made a mistake, poor fellow.
[Sosnowiec — feuilleton.] (A true fact, which happened last Saturday night in Sosnowiec.)
It happens that a fast is "postponed" [nidcheh]; it is also conceivable that a celebration, a day of leisure, be put off; but that there should be one "brought forward" [mukdam] — that has never yet been heard of. Here in Sosnowiec, where everything is possible and the most outlandish things can happen, where the rich men are, Heaven preserve us, the spokesmen... where one is a "fine Jew" and at the same time an informer, where people preach morals and do every forbidden thing — such a thing too has now occurred, and indeed here, not long ago.
Now to the main story: last Saturday night, on account of the Sylvester [New Year's Eve] holiday, which among certain Jewish societies has acquired the name — "Hanukkah evenings"... a Jew came to grief, a respectable Sosnowiec householder and a father of children (his name we shall of course not mention; he has already had enough public shaming), who, poor fellow, said the blessing over Hanukkah candles as late as the ninth day...
And the story went like this: everywhere people were talking about the holy Sylvester holiday; in our hero's home too his children were making great preparations, and since the man's head, poor fellow, is in a spin — may it not befall us — from today's "good" business dealings, he completely lost count, and — why should we spin it out for you — while the children were dancing the "rumba" in the theatre, our protagonist too said the blessing over Hanukkah candles at home, at the window... But he had not yet finished the blessing when on the threshold of his home there suddenly appeared a neighbour of his, who, seeing the "scene", cried out: Stop! — why, yesterday the eighth candle was lit... — — —
And it is from this very neighbour that we learned of the whole affair; he asked us, however, to keep it secret and tell no one about it. We are obliging him, as you see, and we merely describe it — word for word. Of you, dear readers, we too ask the same: tell no one. Moshe'l.
The Silesian Righteous Convert — Yosef son of R' Avraham (Józef Steblicki)

[Serialised historical tale — Upper Silesia.]
Yosef son of R' Avraham (Józef Steblicki).
A historical tale by Y. Azuren[?].
The trial.
In the month of October of the year 1785 the Oberamt government (Oberamtsregierung) in Brieg [Brzeg] charged the judicial commissioner's office (Justizkommissariat), Mr. Kastelli in Pless (Pszczyna), with interrogating a certain Józef Steblicki, a resident of Nikolai [Mikołów] (Upper Silesia).
On this Józef Steblicki, a town councillor (Ratmann) in Nikolai, there lay a sufficient suspicion that he had gone over from the Catholic faith to Judaism.
The investigating judge was instructed to do this at once and in general outline. From the investigation a report was to be compiled for Berlin, and the extraordinary case was to be submitted at the session of the very highest council (Beirat).
According to the Josephine criminal code, which was then in force in Silesia although it belonged to Prussia, such a flagrant heresy — passing from Catholicism to Judaism — carried corporal punishment.
In such a case the judges were completely at a loss, for such a punishment did not suit at all the general spirit of Enlightenment that prevailed at that time. Here, therefore, they wanted a "cabinet justice" (Kabinettsjustiz), one of the famous rulings of Frederick the Great, who took no account of formal law.
The witnesses.
Only the most necessary witnesses were summoned to the investigation. These were the wife of the accused Steblicki, his son, the owner of the synagogue Mr. Avraham Samson, and a number of officials of the magistrate in Nikolai.
At the investigation Marianna, the wife of the accused, declared that she had been living with the accused for thirty years already and had had four children by him.
To the judge's question whether her husband had become a Jew, the witness declared that she did not know for certain whether he had become a Jew, but she inferred it from the fact that since Michaelmas he would not partake of anything at home; he does not eat the prepared dishes, except milk and coffee, and he goes every day to eat at the widow of Rabbi Salomon.
His beard — she went on to say — he does not shave, but cuts it with scissors. On the Sabbath he goes to the synagogue, where he performs prayers together with all the Jews. Every day in the morning he prays at home with his head covered and with straps (tefillin); during the ceremony he lets no one into the room. Many times he goes out in the morning, but I do not know whether he goes to the synagogue for the morning prayer. It is some time now, already a few years before the Michaelmas holiday, that he has separated himself from me and does not touch me. Earlier, too, he used to perform his morning prayer, as I have already related, but without straps (tefillin). Whether he circumcised himself? — I do not know; I can only say that a short time before Michaelmas he went away, for three days he was away from home, and afterwards, when he came back, he lay ill for several days. The main suspicion fell on him because the local burghers Eisenhacker and Kozak noticed him on Yom Kippur in the synagogue, wrapped in a kittel...
— Did he read the Bible?
— Yes, his favourite thing was to read the Holy Scripture of the Old Testament.
— His conduct at home?
— Of his behaviour towards me during the whole time since the wedding I cannot complain; he was a decent man, an enemy of drinking alcohol, and in my opinion the main reason why he came to have religious doubts and to leave the Catholic Church is that he read the Bible very diligently, and his melancholy temperament.
— Do you want to divorce him?
— No, I and my husband are already old, I do not want to divorce him; although the charm of youth and married love are already gone, I still want to spend with him the years that are left to us to live. More than that, Your Honour, my husband's circumstances are not known to me, because he revealed to me very little of the plan that he intends to carry out.
The second witness, the accused's son, a young man 28 years old, confirms his mother's words: "reading the Bible, tefillin, board at the rabbi's" and the like. As regards the main cause, I can only say that my father has for a long time had an inclination to melancholy; he devoted himself with great assiduity to the Bible and many times expressed himself that Judaism is better than the Christian religion.
— Do you know anything about your father's Jewishness?
— For a long time now I have not been in Nikolai; also when he went away to have himself circumcised I was then in Rybnik. On coming back I found him ill; he did not want to say what was wrong with him, but the people of the household and acquaintances held that his illness came from his having circumcised himself.
On the Sabbath he is seldom at home; on that day he does no work whatsoever. This and other conduct prove that he has gone over to Judaism, but he has thereby done harm neither to me nor to my mother; I have nothing to complain of in my father, and I beg you, honourable judges, to treat the fault my father has committed with grace and compassion. More I do not know of my father's offence.
The floor is given to the third witness, the owner of the synagogue, Mr. Avraham Samson.
(To be continued).
What Does the Yiddish Book Look Like in Zagłębie?

[Zagłębie — culture and books.] Staying [?] in Zagłębie for a short time with the aim of organising the "Month of the Yiddish Book", I was surprised by the warm reception I met with here. Not knowing the region, and contenting myself merely with information about the better Yiddish reader in Zagłębie, I believed in a colossal success of the campaign.
But things are not always as one imagines them. I have indeed met here a good Yiddish reader, who knows what he ought to buy. In every house you find a smaller or larger library. The trouble, however, is that the region used to be visited by a number of agents, distributors of the Yiddish book, who have so confused the reader here — one by selling books that have not the slightest literary value, just to make "takings", another by taking money and not sending any books at all — that at times it is simply unpleasant to explain to the customer that "that one was not in order, but I shall be a righteous man".
In all other trades one knows of theft and robbery, one takes from the other, that is "commerce"; but in this region I also ran into such unpleasant things that one feels very dejected.
When visiting Upper Silesia one must travel to Königshütte [Królewska Huta], where there is a community of 2000 Jews, all of them elements who for the most part have come from elsewhere — not German "Yahudim", but Jews who know that a Yiddish book exists.
Seeking contact with the buyer of the Yiddish book, I came upon a Zionist who had a good attitude to the Yiddish book, and to my great regret I was quickly convinced that one must give up on selling books here: there had been an "agent" who sold Yiddish books, but the buyers were left only with the order slips and without their money; the money was taken and no books were sent. On top of the already so bad situation of the Yiddish book, all that was lacking was that the small number of Yiddish readers who are ever willing to buy a Yiddish book should be punished like this for their naivety.
Now, with the founding of the new central book depot "Kult-Bukh", around which all the larger publishing houses are concentrated, things will be much more convenient for the reader. All that remains for him is to avoid the back-corner publishers and to stay constantly in contact with the one and only book depot, which cares solely for the distribution of the better Yiddish book.
In this case too it is desirable, when an agent presents himself, to demand an authorisation; only then will the Yiddish reader be certain that he is being dealt with punctually and honestly, and the will and desire will awaken to keep enriching his library with new books.
Both sides — the buyer of the Yiddish book on the one hand and the seller on the other — must draw closer to one another through the common interest in the good Yiddish book. In your [sic] joint forces will give the weakened publishing trade the possibility of budging from the dead point.
In the only Zagłębie organ, the "Zaglembier Tsaytung", the Jewish reader must often be reminded that, just as the various "histories of morals" [Sittengeschichten] lie in his study or in his cupboard, a Yiddish classic or a scholarly book might rather be found there, and his honour will not be diminished by it.
I want to believe that with the energy and will of us all we can easily achieve that Zagłębie together with Upper Silesia can be the takers of a respectable number of copies of every book that appears.
Y. Yatshkovski [J. Jaczkowski].

Arbitration courts in the new civil procedure (by R. Rechtman)

[Law — the new Code of Civil Procedure.] By R. Rechtman.
In no. 112 of the „Dz. Ustaw" [Dziennik Ustaw, the Polish Journal of Laws] the uniform text of the Polish civil procedure has already appeared; it came into force on the 1st of „styczeń" [January] 1933, i.e. a few days ago.
The provisions of the new code will have a very important influence on the economic life of the country, first of all because they speed up court procedure and are better adapted to present-day economic life than the previous procedure of the year 1864. And above all — because of their clarity and simplicity.
Apart from various changes of principle, which we shall shortly treat separately, the new procedure abolishes the[?] [enforcement] clauses on bills of exchange, introduces payment orders, considerably enlarges the competences of the municipal courts and especially underlines the importance of the arbitration courts, the so-called „sądy polubowne", to which the third book of the code is devoted (arts. 479—5[?]5).
Whereas the previous procedure required that the submission to an arbitration court be drawn up at the notary's („rejent"), a written agreement now suffices, in which the questions in dispute are specified.
As until now, each party chooses one arbitrator, and both arbitrators together — an umpire (super-arbiter). But the law provides for exact time-limits, which must be observed.
In case of overstepping or not observing the time-limits or other provisions of the law, the wronged party has the right to demand the intervention of the state courts.
Copies of the award must be handed to each party; the original must be sent to the state court.
There is no appeal against the award of an arbitration court. The award, as well as any settlement concluded before the arbitration court, has the same force as a judgment of a state court; if in issuing the award the laws were not violated, or when the content of the awards does not go against public order or morality, the state court will furnish the awards of the arbitration courts with enforcement clauses.
The awards of the arbitration courts can be annulled, but only in exceptional cases. Art. 503 enumerates 5 cases in all, for example: if there was no written submission („zapis"); if any one of the parties was not given the possibility of defending itself; in case of violation of the laws; in case of unclarity and contradictions in the award. In these cases the interested party has the right to file, within a month, a suit in the state court and to demand the annulment of the award of the arbitration court.
From the content and spirit of the provisions on arbitration courts it is evident that the legislator wants to make these courts an important factor in the economic life of the country.
The slow procedure in force until now was too costly and not adapted to the tempo of today's economic life.
The provisions on arbitration courts give the economic organisations possibilities of reorganising the legal aid and the defence of the property of their members. It is therefore to be expected that the economic organisations will make use, for the benefit of their members, of this very important and highly useful law.
A year has gone (by Y. Rubinlicht)

[Będzin — sketch (feuilleton) for the turn of the civil year.]
A year has gone, a year has come; the last day of last year was in no way different from the first day of the new year.
I walk in the street and think: where can one see how the old year goes away and what it leaves us.
I slip into the „finance cash-office" [the tax office] and I see that here one can indeed live through the true emotions of the change of years.
In the hall it is as noisy as at a fair. All the clerks are writing out „patents" [annual trade licences], and the big new desks are covered with various banknotes and small change.
Behind the barriers stand sweating people who are waiting in line to be issued a new patent.
Every moment a breathless shopkeeper runs in and asks whether the cash-desk is open. He excuses himself for having come so late. It was not so easy for him to scrape together the 40—50 gulden [złoty] for the patent.
And indeed it really is not so easy.
A second visit in honour of the old year I paid to the Jewish cheap kitchen.
Here, without any economic articles and statistical figures, one could convince oneself what kind of inheritance the old year has left us.
For 2 hours on end women went by, wrapped in shawls or in torn coats, carrying little pots in their hands.
These women are the messengers of their households, who wait impatiently for the bit of warm food with the piece of black bread.
Their number in Będzin reaches into the hundreds; they are many, many more than the number of those who rejoiced and revelled on New Year's Eve (Sylvester night).
At night, when I „went" to the Sylvester balls and watched the women in the long silk dresses dancing the „rumba", I could not drive out of my mind the picture that I had seen by day in the kitchen, when I went to see the old year off.
Y. Rubinlicht.
„Der Kokh-lefl" (The Stirring Spoon) in honour of the New Year, by Ben Amotz — For the New Year 1933

[Der Kokh-lefl — humour page; poem.] „Der Kokh-lefl" [„The Stirring Spoon"] in honour of the New Year. By Ben Amotz.
For the New Year 1933
Old years,
new years,
all the years
crawl, fly,
and with the years
we ride away;
every year
brings new wrinkles,
grey hair...
So what is the joy
about the new year?
Years, years,
old years,
new years,
time spits out
days and years.
And life
keeps on riding
uphill
and downhill,
sings along to itself
and groans along to itself.
Years, years,
old years,
new years,
dear years,
gloomy years,
genuine years,
bad years,
years crawl,
years fly,
years wither,
years bloom.
Years, years,
you make [us] wiser,
you make colder,
you make heavier,
you make older...
Economic survey of the past year.

Paper
sold poorly, because fewer promissory notes [veksl — weksle] were written, and the “Moshkes” [nickname for Jews; [?]], instead of writing, did their “talking” by mouth..

Hard leather [sole leather]
was used up in great quantity, since merchants ran about without cease to grab an interest-free loan [gmiles-khesed] somewhere. In general, people wore through a great many soles roaming around the streets...

Snuff
rose sharply, because merchants were sniffing out — at which merchant it smells of a “nadzór” [Polish nadzór sądowy — court supervision of an insolvent firm].

Paint and lip-pomade [lipstick]
sold briskly. Because of the crisis many girls painted themselves. Also, because the old women of the Będzin old-age home took up this craft, these articles rose sharply.

A sharp fall in prices was recorded for

Hats
because last year people went around without heads.

Furniture
was hardly bought at all. People were afraid that the Będzin magistrate [municipality] might seize it.

Lemons
In this article there was a boom [“hossa”]. The female sex gulped down lemons in order to “schudnąć” [Polish: slim down] and to lose “na wadze” [Polish: in weight].
What will happen in the year 1933? (Prophecies of the “Kokh-lefl”).

(Prophecies of the “Kokh-lefl”.)

In 1933, as in previous years, very important events will take place, which can already be foretold on the basis of certain astrological calculations..:

January.
In the month of January 65 peace conferences will be held — in Geneva, The Hague, London and at the vice-president of the Sosnowiec kehilla council...

February.
The League of Nations will publish 20 volumes (splendidly bound) of the speeches delivered by its members over the last years.
The committee of the Sosnowiec “Beit Lechem” [charity for the poor] will hold a series of meetings at which coal for poor people will be discussed — for the year after next...

March.
A Swedish scientist will invent a new cannon which fires simultaneously both 100-pood bombs and peace speeches, from which thousands of people may be suffocated by boredom...

April.
Several thousand scandals [“afery”] will be uncovered.
The president of the Będzin kehilla will begin writing memoirs.

May.
The income of the railways will improve. The womenfolk will travel to doctors, and the men — to rent dachas [summer cottages]...

June — July.
All of Europe will burn with heat. The Polish Endeks [National Democrats] will unite with the German “Nazis” and beat Jews.
In the remaining months it will be the same as in the past year...

What's New in Zagłębie? / Będzin / The First Exhibition by the Land-Knowledge (Touring) Society, Zagłębie Branch / Turnover-Tax Declarations for 1932 / Smuggled Goods Confiscated / Suicide in Police Custody

Friday, 8 Tevet 5693 — piątek, 6 stycznia 1933
Będzin
The First Exhibition
by the Land-Knowledge Society, Zagłębie Branch.
In the premises of the Będzin “Merchants' Association” (Sochrim-Farein), the first touristic exhibition was opened last Saturday night, organised by the Society for Knowledge of the Land, Zagłębie branch.
In the presence of a large number of invited guests, the president of the Society, Dr. Wiederman, delivers the opening address; he greets the town commissioner Mr. Rzeczkowski[?], the chairman of the Będzin “Maccabi” Dr. Rechtschaft, the president of the “Merchants' Association” Mr. Rubinlicht, who helped the Society's development by putting the Association's premises at its disposal, Mr. Pesachson, the press and others.
Then Dr. Wiederman gives a survey of the origin of the Society, which at the beginning counted barely 12 members and today has reached a membership of up to 280.
Our task — says the speaker — is not yet finished; first of all the Society will endeavour to draw in the Jewish working masses as members.
On behalf of the magistrate (town administration) greetings are brought by Commissioner Mr. Rzeczkowski[?], on behalf of “Maccabi” — by Dr. Rechtschaft, on behalf of the elementary schools — by Mr. Rapaport, and on behalf of the Chamber of Commerce — by Councillor Mr. Rubinlicht.
Written greetings were received from: the Central Board and from the following branches: Warsaw, Łódź, Częstochowa and Olkusz.
After the exhibition is declared open, those present view the stands (kiosks) with sport, clothing and equipment, the photographic section, sports literature and various photographs and reproductions made by Messrs. A. Weinberg, engineer Erlich, advocate Teitelbaum and J. Eisenberg.
A meritorious piece of work is the stand executed by Messrs. Waisenfreund, Sternberg, Rotenberg and Eisenberg.
From the individual coloured drawings one gets a clear picture of the Society's origin, its momentum and its activity.
The Society was created with three members in the year 1929 in Sosnowiec; in 1930 the seat of the Society becomes Będzin, where the number of members rises steadily, so that as of today the Society counts 280 members, among them 155 men and 125 women.
90 excursions were made, of which: 81 local, i.e. in the Zagłębie industry, and 18 outside Zagłębie.
The Society has 4 sections: excursions, skiing, photographic, and a lecturers' section.
Of the 10 stands, 2 are from Będzin (Potasz and Żmigród), 1 from Sosnowiec (Manela) and 1 from Katowice (Wik[?]).
Before the close, Mr. Pesachson takes the floor; he greets the initiators of the Society, speaks about the importance of developing tourism among Jews, and expresses the view that in future care should be taken to interest the democratic currents on the Jewish street, and that the Yiddish language should occupy a place of honour in the Society.
On behalf of the tourists' section of the Evening Courses Society, greetings are brought by Mr. A. Weizenberg, who draws attention to the point that in the Society's public announcements the Yiddish language, too, should be given its right.
The exhibition will remain open for several more days.
The Budget Reduced by 800 Thousand Zł.

[Będzin — municipality, budget.]
On Tuesday evening the budget committee held a meeting, at which the municipal budget for the year 1933 was adopted in the second reading.
In the new budget all subventions have been struck out. A series of items for administration and other expenses have also been reduced.
The new budget is to be smaller than the previous one by a sum of 800 thousand zł.
Reduction of Officials in the Magistrate.

[Będzin — municipality.]
In the tax department of the local magistrate (municipality), 16 officials have received notices that in 3 months' time they will be dismissed from their posts.
A Tragic Incident in the “Kapitol” Cinema.

[Będzin — accident.]
On Friday night the following tragic incident occurred in the “Kapitol” cinema:
During the performance of the troupe of acrobats, two of them fell from a height of several metres. One broke an arm and the other was severely battered. In an unconscious state they were taken to the hospital.
A New Tax Statute for Hotels.

[Będzin — municipality, taxes.]
At the last meeting of the council of commissioners a new tax statute for hotels was adopted. The new statute says, among other things, that from persons who stay in a hotel up to 4 weeks a hotel tax of up to 10 per cent will be taken; for more than 4 weeks — 5 per cent.
A “Faithful” Brother...

[Będzin — crime.]
Mrs Rivka Szwarcman has reported to the police that her 17-year-old brother Binyamin took from her flat 3 garments to the value of 1,300 zł. and has disappeared.
The Traditional Ball of the Jewish Furriers.

[Będzin — trade unions, entertainment.]
This Saturday night the traditional ball of the trade union of furrier workers will take place in the “Kapitol” cinema.
The organisers of the ball are preparing a varied programme and many attractions.
A Half-Yearly Report Meeting.

[Będzin — societies, culture.]
The Jewish Song and Music Society is holding today, Friday, at 6[?] in the evening, a half-yearly report meeting in the premises of the Artisans' Association.
Not “An Eye for an Eye” — Only 3 Years in Prison

[Zagłębie — court.]
At the fair in Grabocin a certain peasant was “learning” to shoot, and during the “lesson” a bullet knocked out an eye of Jechiel Glajtman[?].
The shooter stood before the district court, which sentenced him to 3 years in prison.
When the Wife Goes Off to Trade...

[Będzin — town life.]
Zawodzie lane is all astir (“on wheels”) because of a story that happened there last Monday.
A Jewish resident of that street, taking advantage of the moment when his wife had gone away on business matters, invited a “merry lady” to his flat..,
As the devil would have it, several persons noticed this, and they gave the man who wanted to spend a “jolly minute” a warm “reception”...
“HeChalutz” Conference

[Będzin — Zionist movements.]
This Saturday and Sunday a large conference of the “HeChalutz” branches and hachshara kibbutzim of the Kielce and Katowice voivodeships takes place in the premises of “Hitachdut”. 400 members from over 30 towns are to take part.
On the agenda of the conference stand very important and topical problems of the pioneer movement, such as hachshara, aliyah, etc., as well as the situation in Zionism at the present moment.
From the Central Committee the participants are: P.[?] Ben-Dori (Eretz Israel), Ch. L. Fisz and Jona Goldberg.
Grabbed the Upper Part of the Machine and Ran Away

[Czeladź — taxes and hardship.]
A characteristic little scene took place at the home of a poor tailor in Czeladź.
A sequestrator (tax bailiff) came in to the tailor, wanting to take away the machine, from which the whole tailor's family draws its livelihood.
The tailor, with tears in his eyes, begged the sequestrator to leave the machine, the only source of livelihood, and for the tax to take whatever there is of furniture.
When the sequestrator refused the request, the desperate tailor grabbed the upper part of the machine and ran away.
Będzin Thieves Sentenced in Lwów

[Będzin — crime.]
In Lwów (Lemberg) the Będzin residents Gembała and Zygmunt Czesław were arrested, who had robbed several telephone pay-machines there.
The thieves stood before the Lwów court, which sentenced Gembała to 7 and Zygmunt to 6 months in prison.
From “Gordonia”

[Będzin — youth movements, aliyah.]
Of the current allotment of certificates “Gordonia” has received a larger number, and by the end of January 15 members will make aliyah.
But because of the terrible economic crisis, which has taken away from some of the members the material possibility of doing so, and the danger threatens that on that account they will have to remain at home, “Gordonia” has decided to carry out a campaign for the benefit of this purpose, which should enable it to have all the designated members travel. The campaign begins next Sunday.
Sosnowiec: On the Eve of New Kehilla Elections

[Sosnowiec — kehilla.]
Today the election commission is to be set up.
The report in our newspaper that we here stand on the eve of new kehilla elections has proved correct. This Tuesday the deputy starosta, Mr. Izydorczyk[?], officially ordered the kehilla administration that within 5 days an election commission is to be elected.
In connection with the order, a meeting takes place this Friday in the community office (gmina) for the purpose of electing an election commission.
Petition of the “ZUPU” tenants to reduce the rent

[Sosnowiec — housing / rent.]
As we already reported in the previous issue, the directorate of “ZUPU” [Zakład Ubezpieczeń Pracowników Umysłowych — the White-Collar Employees' Insurance Institution] has decided that the tenants of the “ZUPU” houses in Upper Silesia shall, from 1 January [printed: “styczeń”] on, pay 40 per cent less rent.
On this question a meeting of the tenants of the directorate [i.e. of the institution's houses] also took place in Sosnowiec, and it was resolved to address a petition to the directorate, so that the local tenants too may benefit from the same concession of reducing the rent by 40 per cent.
The magistrate must pay an instalment of 17 thousand zł. every month

[Sosnowiec — municipality / finances.]
The local magistrate [municipality] owes the State Treasury a large sum. After many interventions the Ministry of Finance has at last agreed that the debt be paid in instalments, in the amount of 17 thousand zł. every month.
Besides that, the magistrate owes the “Ulen” company [apparently Ulen & Co., the American firm that lent to Polish towns for waterworks and sewerage] a sum of 360 thousand zł...

Campaign for the benefit of the Gemilut Chesed fund.
On Sunday a meeting of the board of the local G"Ch [free-loan] fund took place; representatives of the G"Ch funds of Pogoń and Katarzyna[?] were also present at the meeting.
A committee was elected which is to carry out the campaign together with the board.

Arrested for taking collected monies.

[Zagłębie — taxes.]
Declarations of turnover tax for 1932
By 15 February “declarations” [zeznania] must be filed by all commercial enterprises of the 1st and 2nd commercial category, industrial enterprises of the first 5 categories and the free professions. Smuggled goods confiscated.

Suicide in police custody
On Sunday in the daytime a certain Gazda[?], who has a criminal past behind him, committed suicide in police custody with vinegar essence.
Home-baked bread

[Editorial office — self-promotion / calendar.]
[Home-baked bread] is the best. Therefore do not look for “bargains” by buying foreign, imitation calendars, for which nobody is responsible. Better buy your own home-grown calendar “Di Vokh” [“The Week”], which has long since made a name for itself by its merits.
Reports drawn up for not having new licences

[Sosnowiec — taxes / trade licences.]
As is known, this year the tax office has not extended the deadline for purchasing licences [“patents”].

Life in Zawiercie

A lecture by Prof. Sak.
The local women's society "WIZO" brought down Prof. Dr. Sak of Częstochowa, who lectured on the subject "Shylock in the Light of Literary-Psychological Criticism". The lecture was a successful one and rich in content.

New Year's greeting from the community.
A delegation from the Rabbi, shlita — Messrs. Bornsztajn, Wigdman[?] and Chajc[?] — conveyed New Year's wishes to the starosta [district head]. In Olkusz the secretary of the Zawiercie bailiff [komornik], Mr. Zuch[?], went off in the company of his fiancée into the nearby little wood, where he committed suicide. His fiancée, seeing her bridegroom fall dead, also shot herself and was only wounded.

On Saturday a ping-pong match between "Hakoach 2" and the sports club "Warta 2" took place in the premises of the local sports club "Hakoach". The Jewish sports club came out with a victory of 7:0.
Ben Ir [a native of the town].

From the Hanukkah evening in the "Gan Yeladim" [kindergarten].

Visit of Mr. Gedaliahu Żuchowiecki from Eretz Israel in Będzin.
[Będzin — Jewish National Fund.] In recent days the representative of the JNF [Keren Kayemet] head office in Jerusalem, Mr. Gedaliahu Żuchowiecki of Eretz Israel, stayed in Będzin on JNF business.
In the course of that time various propaganda meetings took place, as well as a ceremonial gathering [akademia] devoted to the Dunam campaign for the benefit of the JNF in our town.
On Saturday a youth meeting took place in the "Kapitol" with the participation of all the youth organisations in Będzin. After the JNF commissioner, Mr. Abraham Liwer, opens the meeting, the floor is given to Mr. Żuchowiecki, who delivers a fine lecture on the task of the JNF, and he calls on the youth to strong and intensive work for the benefit of the JNF.
The festive JNF ceremonial gathering, the next day, Sunday, passed off very impressively. After the lecture the orchestra of "Hakoach" plays with great success, the choir of "Gordonia" sings several beautiful Eretz-Israel songs, and then Mr. Cwi Kurc closes the gathering with an appeal to all to support and to work for the benefit of the JNF.

On making the railway tariff cheaper for the mills in Zagłębie.
[Zagłębie — economy, industry.] The Vice-Minister of Railways received a delegation from Zagłębie, which intervened so that the mills in Zagłębie should receive a reduced tariff for transporting flour from Zagłębie to Warsaw and other industrial areas.

A Peasant Sells a Horse for a Cap
[Wolbrom — everyday life; a market-day tale.]
For the peasant Kędzierski[?] („Kiendshierski“) from a village beyond Wolbrom life, poor man, had become bitter and sour, and the world had grown too narrow for him. Livelihood is ever scarcer, the date when the sequestrator [tax bailiff] will take away his little horse is drawing near, and the main thing: it is cold and one has to buy a cap for the winter.
He therefore decided to get in first: to sell his „only son“, the chestnut, and with the proceeds buy himself a cap.
When he came to the fair in Wolbrom, they were willing to give him no more than 4 złoty for his little horse...
The peasant was beside himself, spat on the whole world and set off into the market.
On the way the peasant hit upon an idea: to give the little horse away for a cap. He went up to a cap-seller and bargained for a cap at 7 gulden [złoty].
After they had come to terms, the peasant told the merchant that he was leaving the horse here for a while, because he wanted to show his wife the cap he had bought, and at the same time he would get money from her.
The merchant agreed to the peasant's proposal, minded the horse and waited for the peasant...
When night fell, the Jewish cap-maker, carrying his wares back home, also led away with him the horse — for 4 gulden...

How a Debt Is Collected by Seizures and Auctions.
[Law — enforcement.] As of 1 January a new code of civil procedure has been introduced, which in legal language is called for short "Kapetse" [K.P.C.] (Kodeks Postępowania Cywilnego). The new "Kapetse" introduces thorough changes in the whole court procedure for collecting debts and legal claims, and in the procedure of seizures ["zajęcia"] and auctions.
First of all, the term "klauzula" [clause] has been abolished,
If one wishes to obtain a fast judgment ["wyrok"] on a bill of exchange, one will have to apply to the court with a request to issue a "tytuł egzekucyjny" [writ of execution], which will be issued within 7 days.
If one wishes to obtain a judgment for a debt without bills of exchange, only on the basis of account books or witnesses, or on the strength of other documents, one will have to apply to the court with a request for a judgment. Such a judgment will be issued only after a trial at which both sides will be heard.
On a fast judgment on a bill of exchange or on a normal judgment one will not yet be able to carry out the seizure. Those who hold judgments and clauses from before the New Year — these are valid now, but they are already subject to the new law, according to which one must obtain for every judgment or clause an enforcement clause (klauzula wykonalności).
The enforcement clause is obtained in the same court where one obtains the judgment. No seizure and no auction whatsoever can take place without such an enforcement clause. If the ruling concerning a seizure comes from the administrative authority or from other instances, they must obtain an enforcement clause from the court.
