About the Lunches in Elementary School No. 2 (A Letter to the Editor)

[Będzin — education, letter to the editor.] Esteemed Mr. Editor!
In number 51 of the „Zaglembier Tsaytung“, in the column „Gehert un gezen“ [„Heard and Seen“], there appeared a report about the lunches in elementary school 2 in Będzin. We wish to point out several inaccuracies that crept into the said report.
It is a fact that in no Jewish elementary school whatsoever in Zagłębie are lunches given out; the campaign in elementary school no. 2 is therefore to be welcomed. At a time when in other elementary schools the children are sent off to householders' homes for lunch, which gives the impression of begging, with us about 250 children are fed daily with breakfast and lunch in a dignified manner for a payment of 5 groszy, and quite poor children for nothing. The campaign is run by a women's committee, which has set the matter up in the best way, as various respected persons have already confirmed, such as the school inspector, householders of the town, and the like.
This women's committee — instead of occupying themselves at home with their housekeeping, they devote much time and effort to this campaign, thanks to which it has indeed been possible to set the campaign up as a model. The expression in the said report, „half a dozen womenfolk“ („a halb tuts vayber“), is therefore out of place and not tactful, for we have already had occasion to see in philanthropic institutions how several women are busy during a lunch, and yet no such expression was thrown out.
As regards the hygienic side, which is touched on in that report, it was established long ago that the hygiene in the premises of the above-mentioned school in general serves as a model for the whole of Zagłębie, and so, naturally, does the dining hall.
As for comfort, the school management endeavours to arrange things as well as possible, but within the limits of what is possible.
In general it is a fact that, from an ordinary onlooker up to the higher school authority, all have expressed their satisfaction and admiration that in such a short time and with our own forces it has been possible to set up such an institution, which in today's crisis brings so much benefit. We expected the same from the press too, which ought to regard it as its task to help in such a campaign, but...
The report of Mr. Ben Amotz was thus not tactful, and we hope that in the future, upon exact observation, such tactless reports will be avoided.
On this occasion we express thanks to the women's committee for their untiring and fruitful work.
Respectfully,
The management and the „Opieka“ [parents' guardianship committee]
at elementary school 2 in Będzin.

"Upomnienia" (Tax Reminders) Will Become Cheaper.

The Council of Ministers resolved at its last session to issue an amendment to the Council of Ministers' ordinance on the enforcement (execution) procedure of the fiscal authorities. The changes concern the fees for the reminders ("upomnienia") that are sent out to the taxpayers.
According to the amendment these fees will be reduced.
If the tax sum amounts to no more than 1.50 zł, 50 groszy will be added for the reminder; if the tax sum amounts to from 1.50 zł up to 5 zł, 1 zł will be added; and to tax sums amounting to more than 5 złoty, 1.50 zł will be added for a reminder.

Before Anything Begins

[Sosnowiec — kehilla elections; opinion article.] (Boxed sub-headline: Approaching the kehilla elections in Sosnowiec. — Is it possible to maintain decent form?)
The starosta has officially informed the Jewish kehilla in Sosnowiec that it must prepare for new kehilla elections. Jewish Sosnowiec must therefore elect new kehilla representatives, who are to represent, and be responsible for, all Jewish affairs in the town.
Once, at the time they came into being and for some time after, we placed great hope in these kehilla representative bodies. We imagined them as local parliaments that would decide and resolve[?] all Jewish affairs; later all of this turned into a legend, a kind of invented fantasy. For the most part this is to be ascribed, unfortunately, to our representatives themselves, who did not understand and did not want to understand the responsible tasks that stood at their disposal. First they made of the sacred mission a kind of political shtibl; afterwards they made altogether light of this communal problem and came there to make sport, until things reached the level of acrobatic tricks. And at such a moment, at such a time, people allow themselves anything in the world.
And since this has become a kind of plaything everywhere, it is no wonder that the institution has reached the same state among us too. What a sad role a handful of kehilla representatives played here at the time of the most important, most decisive moments, Jewish Sosnowiec knows excellently — so that thereby they have stained the Jewish kehilla institution for generations.
Usually people in our town remain cold and indifferent to all Jewish communal problems. Whatever has nothing to do with business, with finances, with livelihood — there nobody likes to get involved, and one relies on the other: let them quarrel there, let them bang their heads against the wall there — the well-situated Jews say to themselves — we entrust everything to them, and let them do as they wish and what they wish and however it pleases them. It goes without saying that such tactics, such a way of settling the most significant matters, lead to everything that one cannot imagine in life.
Thanks to these tactics, to this ice-cold attitude, our kehilla representation has come to what it is now.
But that is not all: Sosnowiec is extraordinarily original, extraordinarily different from all other towns. We are different in this: just as we are cold and neglectful towards everything communal, just so are people here hot-headed and intense — all of it not in a normal state. Here we ruin things with our indifference, and we wreak destruction with our hot-headedness and intensity.
Among us things are not done in time, when one ought to — with deliberation and composure — in order to resolve this or that question logically and practically; rather, either the question is left to float entirely on the water, and let who-knows-who take pity on it, or the child is hugged so tightly that it is smothered, even if out of love
That is roughly how both the neglect and slackness and the activity and intensity look among us, and it comes from the fact that neither the former nor the latter is done with understanding and deliberation, in firm faith, in fruitful activity for the good of the communal interests.
And it is in such conditions and with such baggage that one must this time face the elections and choose kehilla representatives. We do know, after all, for what purpose people are now going into the kehilla, and what an important thing there is to be resolved there, and what has to be decided once and for all.
Naturally, at the first moment one gives oneself no account, and one is drawn in unwillingly and without considering the later results, the future consequences. For the communal game at the present moment is a kind of enchanted wheel that bites in with its teeth right down to the guts; and then, once one has been spun deep into the enchanted wheel, all means become kosher and the riskiest steps permitted.
We would gladly not be half-prophets and foresee what a tragic character the struggle may take on, if the matter of the elections is not approached with full responsibility and decency. And it is precisely for this reason that our attention is turned in good time to the leading elements, those who are beginning to touch the responsible work, which can bring us either honour — if it is done decently, or disgrace and shame — if people conduct themselves in a lawless manner.
The prospects, after all, are of getting into the kehilla in order to resolve the so painful rabbinate question, of which there has for so long been so much to sing and to tell; it is therefore self-evident that each side will want to bring in as many of its representatives as possible. Naturally, everyone is permitted to do such a thing, and even to exploit everything possible, even everything impossible; but one thing must not be forgotten in the process: that this is a communal problem, which demands decency, restraint and responsibility all along the line.
It is self-evident that this is a very weak weapon in today's lawless times; such moral arguments are very, very seldom asked about, and people are no longer afraid of them. In today's times all means are permitted and nobody stops at such words. We know that lawless deeds will not be lacking, and one will without doubt trip up the other. And yet it must be remembered that lawlessness too must have a limit, and one must know how far irresponsibility is to reach.
We would want, first and foremost, that under all conditions a desecration of God's name be avoided. Let those who do not know our innermost life not mock us; and whatever the whole absurdity and tragedy of our most painful affairs, let sanctity at least outwardly not be desecrated.
Among ourselves, in the Jewish camp, among us, let everything be done. Only into the street it must not go out. In the end a modus can be found that will preserve decency in each camp, and a decent, permissible activity can be adopted that will not blacken Jewish Sosnowiec in the eyes of the world, in the eyes of our enemies.
We hold that now, before the hullabaloo has yet begun, before people begin bringing out the caricatures, which grow ever more tragic and ridiculous as time goes on, the course of the elections should be handled with full seriousness, decency and sincerity.
Let the communal question first of all be approached with clean hands, in a clean manner, and let the possibility be given, and efforts be made, to keep it so to the very end.
The main thing and the most important is to seek a contact that will decently bind together the further course of the procedure, which can bring us honour and pride — even if we should not be counting on it.
That is what must be remembered at the very beginning.
Dr. Popuri [“Potpourri” — a pen-name].
Legal Guidance: Fee Schedule for Court Bailiffs (Komorniks)

[Law — the column “Legal Guidance”.] Fees for bailiffs [komornik — court enforcement officer].
In Dz. Ustaw [Dziennik Ustaw, the Polish Journal of Laws] no. 114 an ordinance of the Minister of Justice has been published, which lays down a precise schedule of fees for the various steps in the official activity of a bailiff.
The said ordinance introduces
proportional fees,
which are charged according to the amount of the claim that is to be collected.
On a debt of up to 50 zł the fee is 2 zł, up to 100 zł — 3 zł, up to 200 — 4 zł, up to 400 zł — 6 zł, up to 600 zł — 7 zł, up to 1000 zł — 8 zł; for every further thousand złoty 3 zł is charged.
The full fee is charged for a seizure (“zajęcie”); for an auction (“licytacja”) — even when the creditor himself receives the auctioned goods — the fee is charged on the sum that has come in or on the sale sum; in any case it may not be less than 5 zł.
Half the fee is charged when one creditor joins a seizure already made by another creditor, [and] for checking whether the sequestrated goods are in place.
Fixed fees
are charged for summonses/demands (“wezwania”) at the rate of 80 groszy. For transferring sequestrated goods to another place 3 zł is charged; for taking (attaching) a debt from a third person — 1 zł; for putting [a party] into possession of immovable property a fee is charged according to the amount of the insured sum: on a sum of up to 3 thousand zł — 8 zł, up to 10 thousand zł — 10 zł, up to 20 thousand zł — 13; for an eviction from 1 room — 3 zł, and 2 zł for each further room.
If the bailiff's activity lasts longer than 3 hours, he is due 2 zł for each further hour.
In the case where the bailiff comes to hold an auction but it is stopped by the claimant creditor (“moner”), the bailiff receives half the fee. If for other reasons no auction takes place, the bailiff is due 3 zł.
By contrast, in the cases where a seizure cannot be made for lack of goods, where an auction did not take place for lack of bidders, where an eviction was not carried out — the bailiff is due no more than 2 zł.
If the bailiff has to travel to a point lying further than 2 kilometres from his seat, he is due 40 groszy for each further kilometre.
—L. D. [signed “לד.”]
The Weekly Portion: Eretz Yisrael (A Little Letter to a Friend)

[Feuilleton — Eretz Yisrael.] (A little letter to a friend.)
My friend! If you ask me what weekly portion is being read here in Zagłębie today, I shall answer you at once: the portion of Eretz Yisrael. For wherever you come, wherever you stand, you hear nothing but Eretz Yisrael and Eretz Yisrael. In the synagogues and the study-houses and — forgive the comparison — in all the theatres, everything is taken and hired out for lectures, with reports, with surveys, all about Eretz Yisrael... And one wants to outdo the other with a good word, with a good piece of news, and each one strives to discover some little corner that the other has not noticed and that has not been exploited until now, and to explain the great prospects in every field; in a word, everything that is studied and seen is only “not[?] good and not[?] good”...
And I, my friend, and thousands more like me, who have not merited this — who have not been privileged to be among the travellers[?] (“oysraysers”) and the bringers of tidings — have made our ears like a funnel, we keep our ears pricked up, and we must see and hear out the greetings and the tidings; and the heart swells to see how, from the most extreme Agudist to the most extreme Folkist, all are so enchanted with and enthusiastic about Eretz Yisrael that, willingly or unwillingly, you have to give it a thought: is all this really as they say? Is there really, at the present moment, when the whole world is squeezed and choking and breaking under the burden of the heavy, lasting crisis, when no one creates and no one builds, still a little corner on the globe where people do not go about like the dead, whose only thought is how to choose themselves a fine death, but get up in the morning in order to create and to build and to make a fine, sweet life? — And are not all these good tidings, with all their conclusions, sometimes a product of the “rash people” (ama peziza) who put “we will do” before “we will hear”, and who are always inclined to extremes and fall very quickly (I would put it: fly very quickly) from one extreme to the other in the blink of an eye... each time losing the middle point, the golden mean?
Just try, for example, and ask a Jew: Why are you laughing? He will answer you at once: What then do you want — that I should cry? And when you ask a Jew: Why are you crying? he will at once give you an answer: What then do you want — that I should laugh? Apparently he understands it no other way — either laughing or crying; a middle point does not exist for him at all. And we are the same with regard to Eretz Yisrael.
I still remember the enthusiasm and the urge that prevailed a few years ago, when every Jew of the “Mondzhever” [Modrzejowska Street] had no patience and no time to wait, because that was a time when the speculation in building plots in Tel Aviv was going at full blaze; and however much we warned, and however much we then tried to hold back the urge, nothing helped at all. People ran without order and without calculation, and afterwards, when there came a panic and a running back, going out once onto Modrzejowska Street I meet one such returnee, with lowered eyes. I stop him and ask him: My friend, what happened? Why did you run, and why did you come back? He begins to give me a lecture, so that my eyes ran over. Just like those spies: “Behold, a hard people... and the country is hard”, and very bad and bitter people there. When one asks another for a cigarette, he gets the answer that the smoke he can have, nothing more. So how, he asks me, is it possible that anyone could remain there?
And therefore, my friend, when I draw up the account and make a sum total of all the good tidings and achievements that I hear from all the representatives who have studied the land through its length and breadth, what pleases me best is the assertion of the guest from Eretz Yisrael, who gave me to understand that a kind of “pyatiletka” [five-year plan] must be created in Eretz Yisrael: everything should be calculated and organised in advance under a certain control, because Jews, he says, are a “rash people”, and all behave according to one pattern, as it says in the verse: “If ‘the streaked’ shall be your wages — then all the flock bore streaked; and if ‘the speckled’ shall be your wages — then all the flock bore speckled”... If a Jew sees that there is profit, for example, in an orange grove — “all the flock bore” orange groves; if a Jew sees that someone has made money on a building plot — “all the flock bore” building plots, and so on in order... until there is over-production and the same thing happens as everywhere, where people are choked by the production and there is nowhere to put it. It is different, however, when every enterprise is calculated and organised beforehand, and things are created at such a tempo as is suited to the consumption and the welfare of the country, where there are still now many fields of industry that are entirely unexploited; and it is enough merely to transfer over the enterprises which here stand as wholly superfluous and are on the verge of going under — and there there is room to develop and to expand. And first of all a commission must now be created that could support the transfer of the enterprises. And if we do not do it, other countries will do it, for Eretz Yisrael is becoming a great consumer, and everyone is running after that and doing everything possible in order to find a place for himself.
In any case, my friend, we must come to the conclusion that we are really living in a very, very interesting time, and all the excursionists and all the tourists who are now travelling there are just like Noah's dove, [finding] that “the waters were abated upon the face of the earth”, and not like the earlier ones, “who found no rest for the sole of their foot” and came back like the spies; now we are convinced that “she returned not again unto him any more” — the tourists and the excursionists will not come back any more, and that is indeed just what we want — would that it be so!
From me, your friend, Josef Perlmuter.
The Bloody Tragedy in Nahalal

[Eretz Israel — a letter by Motek Hampel, Rishon LeZion: the murder of Yosef and David Yaakobi in Nahalal.]
(A letter from Eretz Israel).
The Jezreel Valley, the pearl of Eretz Israel and the most beautiful corner of the country, has been shaken by an explosive bomb thrown by an undiscovered hand, on the first night of Hanukkah, at the house of a peaceful young working family in the village of Nahalal. The Valley, and with it the whole Yishuv, are wrapped in mourning, bewailing the 2 innocent bloody victims who perished on the altar of the sanctification of the nation.
From „Tal Yizre'el“ [the Jezreel Valley], from the hills of Nazareth, there drifts the smell of freshly spilled blood, which has drenched the fields of Nahalal that were diligently tilled for 10 years by the tragically killed Jewish farmer, Yosef Yaakobi of blessed memory.
Nahalal: a peaceful workers' village, a settlement that lives on self-labour, on national land, on mutual aid and on cooperative foundations — has been hit hard, very hard, by the loss of one of its most beloved comrades, Yosef, and his 9-year-old child, Dudl, who now remain immortalised in the heavy and bloody book of the Jewish martyrs and holy ones.
Nahalal had been preparing for a Hanukkah celebration; the youth of Nahalal, wholly lost in a dream, was awaiting the illumination procession in honour of the Hasmonean festival; the Jewish home was flooded with the light of the little Hanukkah candles and of the radiant children's faces. Suddenly, however, an explosion was heard, and father and son came to eternal rest.
It was 11 at night. After a hard day's work the village was sunk in sweet sleep; the farmers were gathering fresh strength for the coming morning of work. And at just such an hour a wild beast destroyed a Jewish home. A bomb was thrown through the open window, it exploded, and on the bed there remained, asleep for ever, the 9-year-old boy Dudl Yaakobi, who — dreaming of the heroic Maccabees and of Hannah and her seven sons — barely managed to utter his last word: „Abbale! Immale!“ [Daddy! Mummy!]
The 40-year-old father, Yosef Yaakobi (born in Lithuania, studied agronomy in California and worked for many years in Eretz Israel), wishing to shield his child from the Angel of Death, lost his left hand in the explosion. The unfortunate man was at once taken to „Hadassah“ in Haifa. And Yosef, who for long years had walked behind the ploughshare and had brought a wilderness in the Valley to life — was left without a hand. Language is too poor to express the pain and tragedy of a working man who, lying in hospital, asks in despair:
— Nurse, how shall I work with one hand?
Fate willed that the child should not be parted, even in death, from his father the cripple, who indeed died 2 days after the operation of blood poisoning.
I do not wish to pass over in silence the heavy impression that the bloody event in Nahalal has made throughout the country and no doubt in the lands of the Diaspora as well. The Hebrew press and public opinion are now occupied solely with the problem of the security and protection of the Jewish minority in Eretz Israel. The horror of the incident lies spread over everyone, everything speaks only of this disaster, and people are still not safe from dangers; various functions and entertainments have been called off and postponed, because mourning is poured out over the land from Dan to Beersheba. In the local newspaper „Haaretz“ a proposal was voiced that all boys born this month in Eretz Israel should bear the name — David, so as to immortalise the young martyr in this way.
For some considerable time the northern part of Eretz Israel has been terrorised, and on the part of the authorities no energetic steps whatever have been seen that would put an end to the abnormal situation. The censorship was mild towards the wild incitement carried on in the Arab press against Jews, and the government did not have the courage to come out energetically and react as it has done more than once when the matter concerned a murdered English official.
For over two years mourning has reigned over the quiet Jewish population in the Jezreel Valley; for over 2 years the blood has been shed of defenceless people who came to Eretz Israel with the ideals of culture, labour and peace.
The story began with the three pioneer victims in 1931 at Yazhur [Yajur/Yagur], then Kfar Hasidim, then Kfar Yehezkel, then Balfouria. Now Nahalal, and tomorrow — if the network of the murderers is not soon uncovered — whose turn will it be? The infernal machine that lies in wait for our work, for us, the living, runs well, murders excellently and can show a pretty considerable „success“. Is there, then, another country in the world where murders can be carried out systematically and the authorities are unable to expose the killers? Can one, under such conditions, have confidence in the Palestine government, and can its indifferent attitude to the above-mentioned events help to calm people's minds?
Yes. I shall be objective in saying that this time the police are active enough and are striving at any price to discover the assailants. The police are now mobilised; they are searching for the tracks of the murderers, which led into an Arab district, but they have vanished and hidden themselves, leaving behind a bloody mark, 2 victims and the broken heart of a wife and mother and of a whole people. The authorities have proclaimed a reward of 500 pounds (15 thousand złoty) for the discovery of those who took part in all the murders, and the High Commissioner, Sir Wauchope, a friend of the Jews and a good administrator, has sent the „Jewish Agency“ a letter of condolence in which he expresses his sorrow at the Nahalal tragedy.
The president of the World Zionist Organization, Mr. Nahum Sokolow, who has lately been staying in Eretz Israel, calmed the Jewish public by saying that the Jerusalem Executive and the „Va'ad Leumi“ have taken energetic steps with the central government in the matter of the latest murderous attack.
The Arab press, too, is occupied with the affair, and one newspaper, „Al Islamiya“[?], is able to report that „the bomb in Nahalal did not come from Arabs, and that the Jews are only out to make capital for Zionism from this murder“... This same newspaper advises the government to conduct the investigation only within the bounds of Nahalal, because the laboratory of the explosives is located in that village...
In a eulogy over the fresh graves of the 2 young lives cut short it was said: „Hear, murderers! Your deeds will not lead us off the right path; you will never weaken our will and our diligence to build a land for the Jewish people, for whom Eretz Israel is the last corner in the world. Here not only does our life have content, but death, too, has a meaning here. A house in the people of Israel has been laid waste, but in place of the shattered family there will come new thousands of Jewish families“.
Will Arab terror really frighten us, the Jews of Eretz Israel, away, and will it paralyse our idea of revival? Shall we here, at the front, give up our work for the building of Zion? No and no! The positions we have conquered we shall not abandon, and the blood that has been shed will weld us still more strongly to the soil of Eretz Israel, with which we have concluded an eternal covenant for life and death. Not „an eye for an eye“ will be our answer to all our blood-seeking enemies; rather, the answer of the Diaspora must be: to concentrate around working Eretz Israel, to strengthen the positions and the ranks of „HeHalutz“, to increase the income of our national funds and to prepare a great aliyah to Eretz Israel.
Motek Hampel, Rishon LeZion.
Keeping books. (Monologue of a spice-shopkeeper woman)

[Feuilleton — humour; petty trade and bookkeeping.] ...You can lead a blind horse, an ox, or — forgive the comparison — a town Jew by the nose, but not books.
What does it mean to "keep [lead] books" — how on earth does one "lead" books? May I know as much of it as I know of my enemies' heads! —
With such a complaint my shopkeeper woman, the one who supplies me with potatoes, bread and herring, fell upon me.
Just imagine — she won't let go of me — though you needn't imagine anything at all, you can see it for yourself; as you hope to keep the sight of your eyes, my hands are soaked in herring, so that I told you to put your fifteen groszy into the bowl — so how does one go and keep books with hands like these? I ask you! And where has such a thing ever been heard of, that one should have to write down every herring a madam takes? And what does one do when the madam brings the herring back — she doesn't like it — how does one write it then?
Or imagine that I bought a whole barrel of herring and entered in the book that the barrel holds so-and-so many pieces, and afterwards, in the selling, it turns out there are five herrings left over — so what am I to do with them — bury them?
Or take another article — the bucket of cucumbers standing here on the table. There are five tens [fifty] in it. Before I sell them I will throw ten away; must I then, so to speak, enter it from the very start with ten fewer?
And what does one do with all the spices? When I sell half a deka [5 grams] of pepper for five groszy, I have to go and write it down; a box of matches for 10 groszy — it has to be written; a pair of candles for ten groszy — write, write and write...
All week long it would make no difference to me — I sit over the fire-pot and doze anyway — but what does one do on Friday, when all the women gather here together and I am being torn at from every side? One has her pot standing on the trivet, the second on the Primus stove, a third has to take the challah out of the oven, they all shout "quicker, quicker" — and I am supposed to stand there and keep the books?
Well, I ask you, is there any sense in that, is that fair? It is already twenty-five years that I have been keeping this little bit of a shop here, and I hear of it for the first time. May we be rid of this dark, bitter bread already!
Her.
Heard and seen.

[Będzin and vicinity — weekly feuilleton.] By Ben Amotz.
When figures speak...
The power of figures is very great. States that have behind them gigantic armies, mighty warships, air fleets, are after all powerless when they are shown — figures, figures that unmask their lie.
Were it not for the figures we would surely have had fresh wars already, fresh slaughters of human beings. But as soon as the clanging of the sharp swords is heard, they are shown the number of victims of the last world slaughter — 10 million!... And the fire that has flared up is put out again.
So what was all this leading up to?
— Before me lies the new kehilla budget of the town of Będzin.
A budget! Our great-great-grandfathers never even dreamed that a time would come when the democratic order would reign, when the Będzin kehilla would not be run, as in the "reactionary" times, by 2–3 dozors [board members], but by two and a half dozen representatives — thirty dozors!
And when 30 dozors sit down at the kehilla bowl and begin to divide (in Będzin speech — "taln"...) to the right and to the left, the budget grows high and wide, up to 363,517.60 zł...
With great respect I "study" the new budget of the Będzin kehilla, look at every "dział" [section] with its items; then come subsidies for all sorts of institutions and societies, among them such as nobody knows and nobody knows whether they exist — except the 30 dozors who allotted them shares...
And I see:
150 zł for "Bnos Agudas Yisroel".
500 zł for the society "Zokef Kfufim"
200 zł for the Będzin mesivta
and:
100 zł for the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec... To the institution where 90 per cent of the poor patients are Będziners they have tossed a little bone — 100 gulden [złoty]...
— Criticise — whom? Protest — what for?
The best punishment for such people is — "when figures speak"...

A question without an answer?...
— We have come to ask you a hard question [kashe].
— Why don't you go with the question to the rabbinate?
— Because the rabbinate too has a connection with the "kasha" [pun: question / porridge, mess]...
— What connection?
— You have surely heard that at the last meeting of the Będzin kehilla board it was resolved that a "neutral" commission should pronounce on whether a new shochet [ritual slaughterer] is needed in Będzin at all...
— Well, don't you agree?
— What do you mean, we don't agree? One ought to raise heaven and earth! After a year of quarrels, scandals, window-smashing, after so many insults and so much bad blood, they, our dozors, have all at once sobered up, have risen from a deep, sinking sleep, and seeing the ruin of the Będzin kehilla, the bankruptcy along the whole front, only now are they humble[?], shed crocodile tears and say:
— "Gentlemen! Let us elect a commission that shall judge whether another shochet is needed"..
— Could the "neutral" one not have been created earlier?
— Perhaps you, dear readers, know an answer to this hard question?

"Sha, don't make a commotion"...
At the Sosnowiec cemetery.
A well-known doctor has died in Sosnowiec; he comes to burial at the Jewish cemetery; behind the coffin — Jewish mourners, chevra kadisha men, friends, patients, but the main thing — "don't make a commotion", because it may happen that a non-Jew passes by and sees that in the cemetery are the children of the deceased, who, poor things, are obliged — (it wouldn't be proper otherwise...) — to be present at the burial ceremony of their father at the "żydowski cmentarz" [Jewish cemetery].
They, the converts, were careful enough not to show any sign that might cast a stain on their "piety"; in the obituary notices it was, God forbid, not announced that their father would be buried at the cmentarz żydowski; they even guarded themselves against the words "wyznania mojżeszowego" ["of the Mosaic faith"]; and the tahara [ritual washing] too the dead man received not at home but in the tahara room — one cannot, after all, make oneself ridiculous in people's eyes...
— — — — —
A well-known Jewish doctor has died, Jews attended to the dead man, converted children were at the "pogrzeb" [funeral], but — "sha, quiet, don't make a commotion"...

"Żyda zabił"...
In a Będzin cinema, during a revue on the stage.
A dancer comes on, holding a "straszak" [blank-firing pistol] in his hand; he dances, dances and ends — with a shot.
One of the cinema-goers, a non-Jew, who plays no small part in public life, is holding a small child, who is interested in what is happening on the stage.
And this little child asks his father with childish naivety:
— Daddy, whom did he, the dancer, shoot?
— "Żyda zabił" ["He killed a Jew"] — answers the father.
The child asked no further questions, and the father too was pleased with his "successful" answer — "Żyda zabił"...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Vayechi)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Vayechi
The Portion
—o—
a) “Bury me not, I pray thee, in Egypt” (Gen. 48:29) [sic; should be 47:29]
“And because the dead outside the Land come to life only through the pain of rolling through underground passages.” Rashi.
With this the author of “Noda BiYehuda” explains, by way of a jest, in his book “Ahavat Tzion”, the meaning of the Torat Kohanim — that the Exodus from Egypt is mentioned alongside the prohibition of usury, of taking interest, because only by the merit of not taking interest will you go up to the Land of Israel. —
For of usurers it is said that they will not rise at the resurrection of the dead; so what use is it to them to go to the Land of Israel in order to avoid rolling through the underground passages, if in any case they will not rise at the resurrection of the dead...
* * *
And why indeed will the usurers not rise at the resurrection of the dead?
Because they will be told: “Sleep, sleep — your money is growing...” A popular saying.
—o—
b) “And let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers” (ibid., 16)
Seeing how Joseph had brought him his children straight out of school, with the shiny brass buttons, he pleads with them: your clothes you have already changed — at least do not change your names; “let my name be named on them, and the name of my fathers”: Avraham and not Abram, Yitzchak and not Izaak, Yaakov and not Jakub... Kohelet Yitzchak.
—o—
c) “And let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth” (ibid.)
Jews multiply, buy themselves every good thing, but they must hide with it, bury it in the ground, so as not to draw upon themselves the envy of neighbours. The greatest blessing is therefore “let them grow into a multitude in the midst of the earth” — to be able to develop freely, openly, before everyone. Peninim Yekarim.
—o—
d) “And he saw that rest was good” (49:15)
“Menucha” [rest] written without a vav (it ought to be “מנוחה”), because the Torah scholar of whom the verse speaks, Issachar, never has any true rest. “Torah scholars have no rest, neither in this world nor in the world to come”; with Torah one can have no true rest... Siftei Kohen.
* * *
As is known, we rule that “the law of a Torah scholar does not apply in our time” (as regards returning a lost object on the strength of visual recognition, and the like); but as regards this, that Torah scholars have no rest — as regards this, one probably does rule today, too, the law of a Torah scholar... Lachmei Torah.
—o—
e) “Until Shiloh come” (49:10)
“The King Messiah.” Rashi.
A Mitnaged asked the Rav (R' Shneur Zalman [of Liadi]): what will the Messiah be, a Hasid or a Mitnaged?
— A Mitnaged — the Rav answers.
— You, of all people, say so?
— Yes, because if he is a Hasid, the Mitnagdim will not believe in him, even if he be as great as Moses our teacher...
* * *
R' Eliyahu Chaim — the Rabbi of Łódź — was an opponent of Hibbat Zion. He said:
— The Messiah will not be brought; he will come by himself...
* * *
Rav Zalman Posner [?] once went out for a drive in a splendid carriage harnessed to four horses; beside him sits a Hasid, who sees barefoot little gentile urchins running after them and shouting “Żyd!”
The Hasid sighs over the hardship of the Exile.
Rav Zalman smiles:
— Do not sigh so. In return, God willing, when they are in exile, they will ride in the carriages and we shall run after them...
* * *
R' Shmuel Mohilever once came to Petersburg on behalf of Hibbat Zion. He came to Baron Günzburg, asking him to permit, in his home, a meeting of communal activists about Hibbat Zion work. The Baron was an opponent of Hibbat Zion, yet he could not refuse the rabbi, and he quietly sent in Professor Bakst and Dr. Kantor to dispute with the rabbi. The latter held a lengthy conversation with him against Hibbat Zion and in the end set about proving that Zionism is in fact a destruction of the belief in the Messiah.
That Rabbi Mohilever could no longer bear, and he cried out:
— Belief in the Messiah is my affair, mine — of one who believes in it — and not yours, the freethinkers, who deny it; do not you take up the grievance of the belief in the Messiah... HaDat VehaTechiya HaLeumit.
—o—
f) “And Joseph died” (50:26)
He died before all his brothers, although he was younger and richer than they, because “the rabbinate [authority] buries its holders” — leadership shortens one's years... Or Pnei Moshe.
—o—
Haftarah
g) “And he charged Solomon his son, saying” (I Kings 2)
This is what he enjoined upon him: remember that you are my son... Shaar Bat Rabim.
Patents [trade licences].

[Economy — trade and industrial licences.] A shattering piece of news: almost 50 per cent of the patents [the annual trade and industrial licences] have not been taken out! Of course, this does not mean that 50 per cent of the shops and workshops [printed: “געשעפטן אין ווארשטאטן”] have gone under — that would after all have been a catastrophe on a national scale; but it does prove that industry and trade in Poland are struggling convulsively for their existence.
For we know that even those who did take out their patents did not — apart from small exceptions — have the necessary sum ready in the till; rather, they laid down their heads, ploughed the earth with their noses, got themselves out with the help of interest-free loans, so as not to tear the thread; the rest, however, could no longer help themselves and had to leave their businesses in jeopardy, or else they had from the outset already taken leave of their branch of livelihood, which is in any case already ruined...
A part of those who have fallen behind will presumably still exert themselves in the coming 15 days and rescue their enterprises; and in the final reckoning there will be a decrease of some 20 to 25 per cent, and besides that a depressed level among those that remain.
And since the greater part of trade and industry in Poland does after all lie in Jewish hands, we shall incidentally have from this a picture of the Jewish decline in Poland.
Especially sad is the tidings from our neighbouring small towns: not even half the patents were taken out there; there, upon the small towns, the entire Rebuke [the biblical curses] has already been poured out — the shtetl is going under!
This very ruin of the private enterprises in Poland must compel the higher, authoritative powers that be to reflect seriously on the matter. To let things go on like this, by nature's course, is after all not permissible.
P. L.
An Exchange of Letters between the Old Year and the New

[Feuilleton — New Year satire.] Signed: "Yeled" (ילד).
My friend!
Barely a few days have passed since I took over your office, and already I ask you: what did you have against my young year? Why, I have been disappointed ever since I came to life!
What I found here is a panic, a tangle, a chaos. It is downright frightening... Everything is desolate, people wander about as in the world of chaos, everywhere crisis and want, crises in every country. All the banks, etc. Troubles in trade, troubles in the associations, crisis and squabbling even among relatives, parents and children. One would literally tear the morsel out of another's mouth and drown him in a spoonful of water.
Poverty — that fine fellow — lies sprawled on velvet chairs and lords it like a man in his own home. How come you managed things so cleverly? Not for nothing did you run off like a thief, ha!...
Usually, when one leaves a flat, one has to sweep up a little, not leave all the dirt to the next man.
No, that is not how it is done — how can it be? What does it mean, to grab one's bundle on a stick and make a "vayivrach" (and he fled)? Give me at least a piece of advice on how I am to conduct myself here. So that I may know how to behave.
Your friend 1933.

My friend!
Your letter was all I needed on top of my troubles. — As if you had too little? — If you knew what I have suffered, you would not pester me; I came out of it damaged, and I was chased away in shame and disgrace. And you think that is all? [?] All at once they put out all the lamps, so that I should break my back and loins in the dark, and more than one curse was sent after me — that I should not live to come back.
But — apart from the fact that you were welcomed with a broad "vivat" [?] and doused with champagne — I pity you greatly, because you, poor thing, have driven in, shaft first, at a very ugly time. May God help you; may you have more luck than I did.
In truth I was already glad to leave the office, because I was a great shlimazl; whatever I did was no good. I believe I am not an only son. And here is the proof: even — not to be compared — the new committee of the Będzin "Machzikei HaDas" also came a cropper with its koshered little plaques...
You ask me for advice; it is admittedly a hard thing, but since you are still a young pup with fresh strength — so be it.
Know that my whole fault was that I was a great miser, and that is why I was so persecuted; one called me a "bad year", another a "black year". I therefore advise you thus: open the purse and hand out money with a generous hand. Art, morality, science and ethics nobody demands of you...
Money, only money you should hand out, because the public is very needy, and then envy, hatred, impudence and quarrelsomeness will vanish of themselves. Grant moratoriums, as many as you can. Do not act like the foolish shopkeepers who, the moment money is owed to them, come out in anger — and what do you think the customers do? They go to another shopkeeper. Would they not have done better to wipe out the debts, so that they could go on taking in money?
If you obey me, it will go well with you. Everyone will wish himself a year such as you are, and you will bring the world much happiness — not like your unhappy friend
1932.
In the Worldwide Madhouse in Which We Live

[Feuilleton — the crisis; educated men without a living.] A few days ago the following advertisement was printed in a Polish newspaper:
A young man of about 30, who has completed university and possesses a thorough education and many-sided knowledge in various fields, puts forward his candidacy for marriage; he is looking for a bride, and her person is completely indifferent to him; he is interested only in whether she has money and whether she would undertake to maintain him.
She may be 18 years old, she may be a lady of about 30, or she may be an old woman of about 60 — it is all the same to him; for an 18-year-old — he will be a hot, temperamental lover; for a 30-year-old — he will be a good husband; for a 60-year-old — he will be a quiet, modest family man; for a woman of over 60 he will be a good son
It goes without saying that her outward appearance is all the same to him; a man who is ready to marry even a 60-year-old granny will naturally take no interest in the build of her nose — that is almost certain; that such a one will also not be put out if his destined bride turns out to be a cripple — nothing will hold him back from his goal — to get a wife who will maintain him.
Is it worth finishing a university for this, in order to engage publicly in... prostitution?
That the proposal of such an educated man can be regarded as a one-hundred-per-cent act of prostitution is clear: to demand financial reward for "love" has until now been an occupation pursued in such an open form only by pimps ("Alphonses"); they, however, did not finish universities for it, and they had no diplomas other than those issued to them by the courts and the prison administrations.
As openly as in this advertisement male prostitution has never before come forward [?]; but in its concealed form it flourishes all over the world; every diploma has its own fixed market price, which fluctuates like every market price [and] depends on the relation between supply and demand; together with the general fall in prices, a fall has also occurred in this field; a doctor of medicine, who a few years ago was valued at a minimum of 10 thousand dollars, you can now get for two or three thousand, and as for the other faculties, prices have fallen catastrophically; masters of law and philosophy are bought for pennies.
I have heard of a Będzin merchant for whose daughter a match with a doctor was proposed; the merchant asked at once.
— Tell me what he is — a doctor of medicine or of philosophy; if — of philosophy, I will not give even five groszy for him.
It is quite probable that the doctor (or master) who advertised himself in the Polish newspaper belongs to those for whom a solid merchant will not give a grosz; nobody wants to buy him; in vain did he cram, in the hope that the moment would come when this or that rich man would come and buy him for his daughter; it was a false calculation, the curse of our time: many sellers and few buyers — and now in the field of male prostitution, too, one has to place notices in the newspapers — that one is ready to sell oneself to anyone — to a 60-year-old, a 50-year-old, a 40-year-old, an ugly one, a cripple — just to finance the diploma.
Perhaps his idea will help him. Some such woman will turn up who will respond and take him to herself; but of such candidates for selling themselves there is a legion — such as nobody will give even 6 groszy for, although they had counted on thousands of dollars; the golden dream has melted away — what remains? A slump (baisse) in diploma-holding men who want to sell themselves.
The crisis has penetrated into the field of prostitution; on the pavements of the Polish Manchester, Łódź, street-women stroll about who show their clients university diplomas and matriculation certificates; in Wilno the chronicle has recorded a woman who commands three languages and has completed two faculties and engages in prostitution.
If you were to ask our hero, who advertised himself in the Polish newspaper, about it, he would answer you:
— Yes, it does not pay, but neither does it pay to finish university in order afterwards to polish shoes, as is done in Berlin; in order to put forward one's candidacy for a hangman's post, as is done in Czechoslovakia; in order to stand as candidate for a night-watchman, as happened in a Hungarian small town, etc., etc.
What pays and what does not pay — of that one can speak only among normal people — but the question is entirely out of place in the great worldwide madhouse in which we live.
Gemilut Chasadim — the Crown of Jewish Virtues!

[Article — interest-free loan funds (gemilut chasadim); the propaganda month.] By Deputy Rabbi Aharon Lewin. (Sent in connection with the propaganda month.)
In the fine array of the various good qualities by which the Jewish public has always been distinguished, gemilut chesed [the practice of loving-kindness] takes first place. Gemilut chasadim is, so to speak, the outflow of all the noble feelings which the Jewish heart feels and which bear the stamp of our glorious past, of our ancient tradition, covered with the lustre of thousands of years.
And how greatly the Jewish public needs gemilut chasadim precisely now! We live in an especially hard and oppressive time. The Jewish sky is covered with heavy clouds. Thousands of Jewish livelihoods are collapsing, and the „daagat machar“, the worry about tomorrow, the unknown and so uncertain tomorrow, weighs on all spirits literally like a hundredweight load.
It is therefore a sacred duty of all who are at all able to do so to step in here. It is a sacred duty of all who have any possibility of it to help, to support, to raise up the Jewish livelihoods that can still be saved, and that — the sooner, the quicker, the better!
It is not so much charity that is needed today — which is certainly also to be valued very highly — in the present hard time, as gemilut chasadim, which is, as our holy sages say, even greater than charity. It is necessary to create the possibility of granting interest-free loans to the great mass of Jewish small traders and artisans, so that they should not collapse. Today more than ever it is necessary to fulfil the „vehechezakta bo“ [„you shall uphold him“], to help the poor, broken merchant or artisan to remain standing on his feet, before he completely loses the ground beneath him and sinks into the abyss of poverty and despair!
This task has been taken upon themselves by the gemilut-chasadim funds in Poland, also in Zagłębie. Only recently we had the opportunity, at the conference in Warsaw, to get a picture of how great and splendid the achievements of the gemilut-chasadim funds are, how many thousands of people they have already put on their feet and protected from despair and collapse.
The duty of the Jewish public in Zagłębie is therefore to support the gemilut-chasadim funds in their activity. No one may stay behind! Let the present propaganda month give the opportunity for it; let gemilut chasadim, the crown of the Jewish good qualities, celebrate a new triumph in this month!
Do Not Let the Trade Out of the Family!

[Article — Jewish crafts and artisans.] By H. Abramowicz. The danger of extinction threatens Jewish handicraft. But the matter is far sadder still than people imagine.
Compared with earlier years, the new growth (the rising generation) of artisans has now shrunk probably 10—15 times. We already see whole trades that have died out. We come across dozens of trades in which there is not a single apprentice (smiths, shoemakers, tinsmiths), and other trades in which the number of apprentices can now literally be counted on one's fingers. And these apprentices too are threatened by the danger of never becoming artisans, because perhaps only one in 10 or 20 reckons on adapting himself to the Industrial Law with its demands of supplementary education, examinations and so on. It must be said, however, that no small part in this process of destruction — besides dozens of factors that do not lie within the power of Jewish society in general and of the Jewish artisan in particular — is in fact played by the artisans themselves; the blind or short-sighted egoism which aims at not admitting any new artisan forces that would come to replace the old generation is — one must admit — extremely harmful to the interests of Jewish handicraft. Artisans are afraid of competition and therefore often simply do not want to allow „hands to be added“, when the old artisans do not always find employment.
But in our times that is no motive, because whereas in many other livelihoods (for example a shopkeeper's) that kind of occupation disappears for ever and ever, the artisan can always find some work. And then again, the Jewish artisan ought to feel himself a part of the whole people and have a certain sense of responsibility towards the coming generations. What will the people look like when it loses entirely its productive part, the artisan class, in which the new growth is dying off.
Among other European peoples the craft is a kind of established right (chazakah) of whole families. The craft is handed down from great-grandfather to grandfather, father, son and grandson. People take pride in it, because each generation brings in something new, a touch „of its own“, to the art of carrying out the craft.
Among us the craft lasts at most two generations; only rarely will a father find it necessary to put his son into the same trade.
But it must become a commandment of the hour that no Jewish artisan should let his trade out of the family. If there is no possibility of handing the son (or the daughter) over to another master artisan or to a vocational school — then, then the father himself must teach his son the same trade; from the purely practical standpoint it is a relief for the father. The son already helps him, he comes in useful in every case; later he can replace him in case of illness, weakness, old age and so on. The workshop, the tools and machines will not go to waste „after a hundred years“[?] [i.e. after the father's death] — they will remain in the family's own hands. The same surroundings, the same clientele will also remain.
In a word, the Talmudic expression „chayav adam lelamed et beno umanut“ [„a man is obliged to teach his son a trade“] must be broadened in the sense of „umanuto“ (his own trade): the father should teach the son his own trade as well.
H. Abramowicz.
A Little Feuilleton — Peace Letters

[Feuilleton — political satire.] A Little Feuilleton: Peace Letters (written from one state to another). Intercepted by Rebus.

1.
My dear ally.
First, be informed that my business is going in the best of order.
Second — I have lately undertaken an action that is to strengthen peace in the world, namely: I have ordered in my factories machine-guns of a kind with which one can shoot without bullets. They shoot with a sort of compressed air, by which thousands of people are murdered in a single second. If this means does not help against militarism, then it is simply the end of the world.
Respectfully:
Yaponada Shidikita [a mock-Japanese name].

2.
Dear little friend, Japanese!
I have received your peace-loving and friendly letter and simply cannot stop marvelling at your anti-militarist spirit. A wild desire has positively seized me to do as you do, although I hold that one must not be so strongly anti-militarist in mood, for we live in a time when people tolerate no idealism.
At home I too have introduced the same peace methods as you have, namely: they work at my place day and night on arms production, and all this is done in order to make wars impossible, for the more the world is armed, the harder it will be to wage wars.
I hope soon to make use of a kind of gas that will be able to destroy, over a large area, everything in its path, both living creatures and inanimate nature.
In short, we are marching with gigantic strides towards world peace.
With hearty greetings, yours
Jean Français.

3.
To the world-wide bourgeoisie, may its name be blotted out!
Everyone knows very well that we, in Red Russia, want only peace; to this end we have prepared a gigantic army, which is armed terribly, like no other army in the world.
Here hundreds of factories work day and night, and all of it — in order to annihilate the bourgeois world, which wants only wars.
The only means of doing away with bloodshed in the world is, in our opinion, only a strong, class-conscious army, which exists only among us.
We know that the bourgeois states too are preparing hard for peace, but they do not mean it seriously, and the proof: they are arming themselves badly.
Soon we shall let the whole world know what peace and anti-militarism mean.
With friendly greetings:
Ivan Pushkaryov [a mock name, from Russian "pushka", cannon].

4.
Esteemed friends.
Who else, like us Englishmen, stands the whole time on guard over world peace?
We endure roasted torments [i.e. unbearable sufferings] from half the world, from all sorts of nations and peoples; we must, poor things, maintain a colossal army of police and gendarmes — and all in order to secure calm and peace at home and in the whole world.
We therefore have the honour to announce to the public over the entire globe that soon we shall be able to distribute to all our friends a weapon of such a kind as will call forth a revolution in the world of wars.
With brotherly greetings:
John Bull.

The Silesian Righteous Convert — Yosef son of R' Avraham (Józef Steblicki) (2)

Yosef son of R' Avraham (Józef Steblicki).
A historical tale by Y. Aduren[?].
2)
Everyone in the courtroom is waiting in great suspense for what the Jewish witness, the owner of the synagogue, Mr. Avraham Samson, will say about the deed of Józef Steblicki, who in the last years of his life went over to Judaism.
"What do you know about this?" the presiding judge of the court asks him.
"I, Avraham Samson, owner of the synagogue, know that Józef Steblicki, now Avraham, always had a leaning toward Judaism; unnoticed by his family and acquaintances he came to the synagogue from time to time with a book that had a Hebrew text on one side and a Latin one on the other."
"Was he in the synagogue on Yom Kippur?"
"Yes, on Yom Kippur he came to the synagogue holding a kittel. And since he himself related that he had circumcised himself, he was allowed to be in the synagogue. But we made no ceremonies whatsoever with him; our Torah commanded us to draw a convert near, but we Jews are an exception in the matter of persuading someone of another faith to go over to Judaism. As far as I have learned, none of our Jews talked him into leaving Catholicism. The only reason was, as he himself declared, that he was enthusiastic about the Jewish religion and does not want to give it up."
"Did he circumcise himself in Nikolai [Mikołów]?"
"No, in our community there is no such expert who would be capable of circumcising a grown man; only in Amsterdam are there those who know how to do it well. At the same time I also declare here before you, honourable judges, that the opinion is false that when someone is a Jew he must blaspheme Christ.”
After the examination of the witness Avraham Samson, one of the judges read out a declaration sent in by the local magistrate (town council).
The magistrate, to which the accused has long belonged, likewise confirms unanimously, under oath of office, that “Steblicki always led a quiet, peaceful and honest life, and he also behaved well and honestly toward all the inhabitants.
He fulfilled his office as town councillor (Ratmann) faithfully and punctually, and he managed the municipal treasury entrusted to him with the greatest fidelity[?].”
Apart from the above-mentioned testimonies, the inquiry wanted[?] to hear the opinion of the district physician as to whether the accused is mentally normal and physically healthy.
And the district physician, after examining the accused, said that “the defendant looks quite like a melancholic, and therefore he looks thin, dry, pale and yellowish.” Certain defects are also to be noticed in his skull: both main bones are deeply sunken at their junction and look as if pressed in.
There enters the courtroom
The defendant.
Everyone's eyes are turned toward him and every word of his is listened to with bated breath. In a side corner sit the defendant's wife and her close family; their gazes were turned downward, unable to bear the shame they have to endure from the believing Christians who are here in the hall.
"Józef Steblicki has the floor," the judge calls out.
The defendant approaches the green table and begins in a trembling voice.
“My name is Józef Steblicki. After my father, who was a butcher here in Nikolai. Until the age of eleven I was with my parents. Later my father placed me in the Jesuit seminary in Troppau [Opava], where I studied for two years. My further schooling I received in Tarnów [as printed: 'Tarnov'] and in Teschen [Cieszyn]. After I finished rhetoric in the sixth class I came back to my parents. When I came home my father took me into his trade and taught me the profession of a butcher.
"At what age did you marry?"
"I married at 32 my wife, who is still living now."
"Do you have children?"
"My wife bore me four children; only two remained alive, they live in Rybnik. To my son I handed over this year my farm as a recompense. Apart from that I have no property at all."
"How old are you?"
"60 years."
"What causes brought it about that you left the Catholic faith?"
(To be continued).
A “neutral” commission is to decide whether another shochet is needed...

[Będzin — kehilla.] As our readers know, the kehilla council resolved to strike from the new kehilla budget the salaries that the board had fixed for the new “little shochtim” (shochtimlech) Radoszycki and Gerlic.
The board — which has certain obligations towards the young “little shochtim” — was not content with this resolution and sought means so that the council's resolution “should not see the light of day”...
For this purpose an “urgent” board meeting was called last Friday morning, at which the question was dealt with: which budget should be sent for approval, the budget of the board or that of the council?
Also present at the meeting was the Rabbi, who declared that, as he is not well, Mr. Shlomo Yitzhak Ryński would speak on the question.
Mr. Ryński expresses the view that only the board's budget should be sent for approval, because the matter of the shochtim is closely bound up with the kashrut question in our town.
Mr. Buchwajc is against this. It is a lie — says Mr. B. — the claim that the “Aguda” is here after matters of kashrut; these are only ambitions of the “Aguda”.
Mr. A. Liwer takes the floor on the question and turns to the Rabbi with the following words:
“In the course of the few years that I have been a member of the board, I have seen you at a few meetings — precisely when it is a matter of a victory for the “Aguda”; other town affairs do not interest you. You take a salary as rabbi of the whole town, but you are only Shlomo Yitzhak's rabbi.
Our Sages say: “Torah scholars increase peace in the world”, and you are the opposite of that; you help the intriguers in their quarrels. At a time when widows and orphans are dying of hunger, you occupy yourself with a matter of shochtim. In the present crisis the kehilla cannot allow itself any new expenses and fix salaries for the “shochet twins”.
— Rabbi of Będzin! — cries out Mr. Liwer — I am your open opponent, but you should know that all the humiliations you have had in Będzin until now were caused only by the Shlomo-Yitzhaks, because only they drag you into the various intrigues from which you, as rabbi, ought to stand afar; but the moment you raise your hand for the present Aguda proposal, that will be proof that your coming to today's meeting is to pour oil on the fire that has flared up in the town, and public opinion will not tolerate that”...
After Mr. Liwer's speech the secretary, Mr. Frajlich, proposes that, in order that the kehilla's finances should not become more catastrophic than they have been until now, a commission be elected to settle the matter of the shochtim.
Mr. Frajlich's proposal is adopted.
The proposal to send off the budget drawn up by the board falls, and it is resolved that the budget adopted by the council be sent for approval.
The textile (manufaktura) section for the government's proposal concerning the turnover tax.

[Będzin — trade and taxes.] On Tuesday evening a meeting of the textile (manufaktura) section took place at the Merchants' Association, which dealt with the government's proposal that the merchants who pay a fourfold price for their trade licences (“patents”) be exempt from the turnover tax.
After a lengthy discussion of the question the section declared itself in favour of the proposal and resolved to turn to the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce, that it should intervene so that the government's proposal be carried out.
For this purpose a delegation was elected consisting of Messrs. H. Unger, K. Kapłowicz, Jedidja Politański, H. Sztachlic[?] and J. Sandzer[?].
On behalf of the delegation we are asked to draw the attention of the sections in other towns, that they should join in this resolution.

The charge states that by means of terror they extorted large sums from local merchants.
The merchants who did not want to carry out their “orders” were terrorised, and no customers were allowed into their shops.
The trial has aroused great interest in Zagłębie. Because of the crush, only those who hold admission tickets are let into the courtroom.
120 witnesses have been summoned.
Before the start of the trial the defence counsel put forward a motion that, because several principal witnesses were absent, the trial be adjourned.
The court holds a short consultation and decides to reject the motion.
In the further days of the sensational trial a number of witnesses were heard, who uncovered various revelations and “fine” deeds done by the gang of terrorists.
The trial will last several more days.
Terrible death of a young woman under the tram wheels.

On Saturday at 7 in the evening, on Żeromski Street, the 27-year-old Czechowska got caught between the wheels of the tram.
The municipal firemen, who were alerted, lifted the car, but the victim was already dead.

Heavy sentence for the money counterfeiters.

The ringleader sentenced to 7 years in prison.
On Monday the Sosnowiec District Court handed down the verdict on the counterfeiters of the 5-złoty pieces. The leader of the “factory”, Mr. Karbownik of Dąbrowa, was punished with 7 years in prison. Amid tremendous suspense the floor is taken by the guest, Dr. Wdowiński of Bielsko, who speaks at length about the essence of Brit Trumpeldor. The 1½-hour speech of Dr. Wdowiński, rich in content and full of spirit, is received with resounding applause.

The last minutes of the murderer Knapik
On Wednesday at 6 o'clock in the morning, at the murderer's request, the priest came to the Będzin prison and said the confession with the murderer.
At 7 o'clock the prosecutor [was] in the prison cell; he read out the sentence and the decision of the President of the State.

A father dies before his daughter's wedding canopy.

[Pilica — family tragedy.] Last Sunday a terrible family tragedy occurred in the shtetl of Pilica [Yiddish: Pilts].
On that day the local resident Yosl Kerner [Josl Kerner] was celebrating the wedding of his only daughter. The joy at the wedding was very great. The bride's father, who had already been ill for several years, beamed with happiness that he had still been granted the merit of living to see the wedding of his daughter, whom he was marrying off to a respectable bridegroom, a fine Torah scholar.
The klezmer musicians worked wonders, the rooms were full of in-laws and relatives from both sides. Now comes the veiling of the bride [bedekns], the hearts of father and mother are steeped in joy, they bless their daughter before the chuppah, and
— I don't feel well! — the bride's father suddenly cries out.
An alarm, weeping, they try to revive the man who has fainted, but —
— it is too late. Yosl's soul was breathed out as they began to lead his daughter under the chuppah...
One can easily imagine the heart-rending scenes that took place. The wails of the mother, of the bride, of the in-laws and of the guests rose to the very heart of heaven.
After the bridegroom had, in accordance with religious law, betrothed the bride, all the wedding guests left and people set about attending to the dead man...

[Będzin — kehilla; Chevra Kadisha; letter to the editor.] Esteemed Editors!
We ask you to print the following lines in your esteemed newspaper, for which we thank you in advance.
For several months now we have been ceaselessly besieging the kehilla representatives in Będzin to give us back the several thousand złoty which we collected for the purpose of buying a plot for a cemetery. We have also threatened with ultimatums, we have pleaded, but unfortunately without success. Our outcry has remained a voice crying in the wilderness.

An open appeal to the esteemed Dr. T. Melodysta.

[Sosnowiec — health and welfare; open letter.] A short time ago we had the opportunity of being present at the lecture which you, Doctor [Dr. T. Melodysta], delivered in the premises of “Maccabi” on tuberculosis. In that lecture you stressed several times that the main thing is that whoever becomes even slightly ill should turn at once to a doctor, so that he may establish the diagnosis.
We, the listeners, understood the importance of your remarks, but not having the possibility of putting the following proposal to you personally, we have the honour of turning to you through the esteemed newspaper.
We all know that such a medical examination involves expenses, especially at the present time; we therefore propose to you that you set aside for the “Bikur Cholim” society in Old Sosnowiec [Stary Sosnowiec] a fixed hour or two a week for treating the patients who will hold slips from our society. in Old Sosnowiec.
Greetings from the Będzin young men who set out by motor-car for Eretz Israel.

[Będzin — aliyah; a journey by car to Eretz Israel.] Of the group of young men who a few weeks ago set out by motor-car for Eretz Israel, we only now have the possibility of passing on something about their journey.

Because of this they travelled to Salonika, from there by ship to Egypt and then to Eretz Israel.
For a cheap price — to visit the most beautiful winter region in Europe: Zakopane.

What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — short news items.]
The swindlers who defrauded several Polish banks of 21,300 dollars have been arrested.
In the month of October [in the original the Polish październik] of last year several banks in Poland, among them the International Commercial Bank in Poland, were defrauded by American swindlers, who cashed false cheques in the banks for a sum of 31,300 dollars. The International Bank in Katowice alone cashed 83 cheques for 8,300 dollars.
The Katowice authorities applied by telegraph concerning the affair to the Polish consulate in New York, and thanks to its intervention the New York authorities undertook a thorough investigation and the two swindlers were arrested.
It turned out that the swindlers had travelled to Poland with the help of false passports, taking with them 1000 false cheques of the travel company "Cunard".
On Monday the prosecutor of the district court in Katowice received word from New York that the swindlers are already on their way to Katowice.
After their arrival in Katowice the swindlers will be handed over to the disposal of the investigating judge Dr. Szczelczyk[?].
The sensational trial will probably take place at the end of the month of February [luty].

To spite her mother, a 16-year-old girl commits suicide.
An unemployed man came into Schulz's dwelling in Łagiewniki. In the house there happened to be a 16-year-old girl, who made the unemployed man a present of a pair of shoes and a little lard.
When the girl's mother came back and heard that her daughter had given the shoes away, the mother began to abuse her daughter and went off to the police station (the commissariat) to report that the unemployed man had stolen the shoes.
The girl, unable to bear the disgrace, hanged herself. The mother, coming back from the commissariat, already found the dead body of her daughter.
