How We Solve Our Holiest Problems

[Będzin, Sosnowiec — kehilla; Chevra Kadisha; cemetery; opinion article.] (The Chevra Kadisha sends ultimatums and the dozors [kehilla board members] do not want to give any money.) (From the Będzin chronicle.)
(A committee of the magistrate [city administration] declares that the question of buying a plot for a cemetery is an urgent one.) (From the Sosnowiec chronicle.)
Both towns, Sosnowiec as well as Będzin, are in need of cemeteries, and in both towns there is no money for the purpose; here as there the bells are being rung and the alms boxes rattled, and still no money comes in.
In Będzin the Chevra Kadisha sends ultimatums to the Jewish kehilla administration, demanding that the money it paid in for this purpose be returned to it, and in Sosnowiec it was necessary for a magistrate committee to pronounce on the urgency of the future cemetery.
Either way it is no small matter to obtain those bits of field, which may none of us ever need and which today surely cost a trifle. Either way all that is needed is a few thousand in total, which in communal terms ought to be a zero even in the severest crisis, and yet Jewish Zagłębie cannot manage to reach it. One cannot say, after all, that we are penny-pinchers, that people among us are stingy; yet it is a fact that the necessary sum cannot be put together either in Sosnowiec or in Będzin.
Both sisters are frightened neither by the ultimatums nor by the appeals, in which people are persuaded that in a hundred years there will be nowhere to lay [the dead]. Somehow people have frozen and they remain indifferent to the matter. And in truth this is no wonder either, for at a time when people have ceased to love life, there is surely no need to worry about death. And therefore there is no other remedy than to turn to the press, that it may rouse and awaken the petrified hearts, so that they take pity on themselves and provide for their later "well-being". Granted, once, when people led a quiet, comfortable life, they were afraid of death, and then rousing them meant something; but today, when people have become abandoned to their fate, when they see death before their eyes every minute, they have grown used to it, so that people have become refined and have reached the conviction of their own that the devil is not as terrible as he is imagined.
Well then, go and suddenly take upon yourself, in such a lawless time, the mission of agitating the other fellow to provide himself with a better future after life, seeing that life itself is not worth a broken two-groszy piece to him.
But if we wish to be subtle and honest and consistent, all this rousing and agitating makes no sense; it is surely high time that we too became the equals of decent people, and that there should be no grating in people's ears about matters which ought to be settled quietly, modestly and with a certain sanctity. Such questions surely ought not to be carried out into the street, and there is no need to shout and make a din and an uproar about them. Let us learn from decent people how to settle such sensitive matters. Among the nations of the world such things are settled quietly and modestly within their own four cubits; not to speak of ringing the bells and calling the press to one's aid — to help oneself in such a manner would there be an insult, a sign of backwardness and degradation. It would mean that one is not worthy of carrying out this holy mission, which must be conducted with the greatest reverence.
We have Chevra Kadishas, whose task ought to be to safeguard this holy and responsible mission under all circumstances. And as if that were still too little, we have in addition been given kehilla representations, which must likewise see to it that the municipal cemetery is kept in proper order. It is a fact, however, that nobody lifts a finger [literally: nobody puts his hand into cold water]; were it not so, a Chevra Kadisha alone or a kehilla board alone would be capable of seeing to it that a cemetery in the town is kept in proper order.
True, we know that in Będzin, for example, the Chevra Kadisha stands at the proper level, and the gmina [kehilla] even took from them the money they had collected for this purpose — from which, incidentally, they are now demanding the sum — but the Chevra is not in the right in this case: it should on no account have handed such money over into unsafe hands, and if it did do so, it had to be done in such a way that the kehilla bore the obligation that it takes upon itself the task of fully settling the cemetery question; otherwise, by what right was this sum, designated for that purpose, handed over to the gmina?
The question is considerably worse in Sosnowiec. Not enough that Jewish Sosnowiec is altogether terribly apathetic with regard to communal questions, the Chevra Kadisha too is not in a proper state there, and it has no money at all, neither with itself in its cash box nor in the kehilla cash box, so that it has lost nothing and gained nothing.
We are not versed in the income and expenditure of the Chevra Kadishas. We do not know their system, although they ought to have taken pains that it should be no secret to the public; but be that as it may, we do understand that there is income, and quite often very respectable income, so that there could have existed or arisen a procedure whereby so-and-so much, or such-and-such a percentage, of every possible income would be set aside for the purpose of enlarging the cemetery, rather than a money question suddenly being born. Just such a stable provision could have solved the cemetery question in a very modest manner, so that the drumming and the useless bell-ringing would be avoided.
From the communal standpoint we know that every institution has its regular expenses; thus, for example, a Linat HaCholim or a Bikur Cholim or another charitable society has its expenses in providing the helpless with milk, with a doctor, with medicine or other items; the Chevra Kadisha, by contrast — if it is not to have money to buy a morg [Polish land measure] of field, then what expenses does it have and what does it accomplish? All it does is bury a poor man for nothing? For that, after all, it very, very often has larger revenues, which cover those expenses many times over.
In any case we are not out here to determine who is to be blamed, if only[?] because the situation will not improve by that and the question will not be solved by that. What is important, however, is this: that it should become clear once and for all who is responsible for the cemetery question, the Chevra Kadisha or the Jewish kehilla. Let one of them work on autonomous foundations, only let the one that will work, the one that will regard the matter as its ideal, remain responsible for all and everything.
We know: de facto the kehilla representations stand above the Chevra Kadishas; they, that is to say, must supervise them — let alone that they should be the obstructors and the non-implementers. Where is it written that there should be time for everything, that every kind of politics may be conducted in the most harmful and most useless manner "for the good"[?] of the public, while people remain cold towards this problem, which can in no way be avoided?
The set-up of the situation in Będzin is different from that in Sosnowiec. Notwithstanding that in both towns the cemeteries are needed, there must be one rule: that either the Chevra Kadisha or the kehilla representation must be made responsible for what is done. Otherwise both together wash their hands clean, and the public does not know whom to blame for the defects that have arisen.
It is therefore high time that such delicate matters should not be put off until the time when there is no way out left and one has to shout so that it grates on the ears.
Society therefore demands, both from the Chevra Kadishas and from the kehilla representations, first and foremost responsibility in the full sense of the word, and a complete solution of the question within our own four cubits, so that it should never be necessary to call outside elements to our aid, on account of which we lower our honour and prestige.
R. Let[?] [or R. Lem]
A joint celebration of employers and employees

[Będzin — industry; the Fürstenberg family.]
Last Friday night a festive banquet for the hundreds of workers of the factory was prepared on the factory premises of the Polish zinc factory in Będzin.
The banquet was held in connection with the wedding of the director of the factory, Mr. Jerzy Fürstenberg, to Miss Maria Blok [Block] (Czechoslovakia).
On the couple's arrival the workers of the zinc factory had prepared a warm reception, and as an expression of gratitude the couple arranged the banquet.
Around the 2 long tables sit the workers; the Jews, numbering 50—60, sit separately, some of them wearing yarmulkes; the „Jewish“ table is marked with several little signs — kosher.
The tables are laid with various dishes, but the main thing is:
— „And the drinking was according to the law...“ [Esther 1:8]
Director Mr. Jerzy Fürstenberg proposes the first toast and drinks to the health of the workers of the „vaklarn“ [apparently the rolling mills, walcownia; the word is so printed].
The president, Mr. Fürstenberg, gives an overview of the origin of the „Polish zinc vaklarn“ [„Polish zinc rolling mills“?]. Exactly today — he says — it is 10 years since the factory began to develop, and I hope that the former number of workers will be employed again.
For the workers who have been laid off Mr. Fürstenberg donates 500 złoty.
The family, and above all the wife of Mr. Sz. Fürstenberg, sees to it that the guests do not sit „idle“ [with empty glasses], and after the 50 litres of vodka, over 1000 small bottles of beer and the like have been finished, the hall resounds with the incessant cheers in honour of the Fürstenberg family.
Several photographs were taken by „Moderne“, proprietors: Lewiński and Karasek.
On Sunday a film was shown for the workers at the „Światowid“ cinema.
Cheap cigarettes

[Feuilleton — the cheaper cigarettes; the monopoly and the crisis.]
So it means that cigarettes really do cost less now?
Four groszy for a „Grand“?
Two years ago, when I still used to smoke up a whole pack a day, it would have saved me 20 groszy every day and I would have had a pack for nothing every fifth day. Last year, when I used to smoke 10 a day, it would still have been a tidy saving. Today, however, I have already reduced myself to 2 in the morning and 2 in the afternoon, so the cheapness will leave me 4 groszy — just enough to buy one more cigarette before sleep
This too is for the best.
I shall have my pleasure and the government will suffer no loss either: it will take in from me the same 20 groszy a day; only what? It costs it one more pinch of tobacco? Well, let it imagine that somebody stole it.
So here I sit now with the fifth, the „gift“ cigarette in my hand, not yet smoked, and write my feuilleton. Without a cigarette I cannot write, and were it not for the cheapness, who knows whether I would have had a feuilleton.
So you too already have some benefit from the cheapness..
When I am in the middle of writing, I shall smoke the cigarette a puff and a line, a puff and a line — just as in the old days, when a box of cigarettes stood on the table and whoever had God in his heart stuck in two fingers.
Oh, those good old days, when one smoked a „Gracja“ at a kopek apiece! How beautiful was the bluish soft smoke that curled from it above one's head, what a delicious aroma spread from it, and what fine deals one used to conclude between one puff and the next!
In the morning, at breakfast, the maid would bring you in a little box of „Gracja“ to round off the meal. Meanwhile you had to run to the business, your head was in a whirl, so you most likely left the Gracja on the table — who thinks about such trifles? — and on the way you dropped into a little shop and bought a fresh pack.
During the day people kept going in and out, the box was quickly emptied, so one bought a fresh one.
The item „cigarettes“ took up a considerable place in the business ledgers, but never mind, it paid. In the thick fragrant smoke neck-breaking transactions were woven, which covered everything.
The last pack of „Gracja“ of the day was opened and emptied in the private room of the first-class restaurant, where over a rich supper and a good glass of drink one settled accounts with the customer and put through a new order, which sufficed for a good spell of work in the factory.
That is how it was, once upon a time.
As soon as the German came, the „Gracja“ vanished and in its place appeared a „Daj“ [Polish: „give“] and a „Borg“ [Yiddish: credit, loan]; coin had already become scarcer in the pocket; the cigarette now had a symbol, a motto: give or lend!
And from then on it went downhill [„barg arop“ — a pun on „borg“].
When you bought a pack of cigarettes, you pushed it deep into your pocket so that it should lie firmly. When you take the pack out, you are a little careful, lest the evil eye have power over it. The fashion of opening the pack and shoving it under everybody's nose was abolished long ago. If someone stretches out his pair of fingers, one cannot, after all, be a p... [pig, i.e. a miser]. But you have already learned to manipulate the pack of cigarettes in such a way that before the other man has made up his mind, the treasure is already buried back in the pocket...
And when you smoke, do you feel the taste of old, the smell of old? Even the smoke, it seems, is a bedraggled one; it does not curl, it spills out sideways like autumn mud, and a bitterness comes off it, just as it is bitter on the palate, just as it is bitter in your heart.
And tell me, I ask you, what sense is there in simply sitting and puffing at a cigarette when there is no business and the head is empty, nothing to think about and nothing to daydream from?
Once you used to smoke away the fat dinner; today you smoke away the troubles, the poverty. If only one could smoke away the crisis! But it will not let itself be smoked out; with sticks[?] you cannot drive it off.
So you did indeed make one reduction after another, until you got down to „pairs“ — a pair in the morning and a pair in the evening.
And only now has the cheapness come — a little too late, you are already small consumers.
But one thing is good.
Until now we saw that only the peasant and the merchant make things cheap, while the monopoly holds firm, for whom does it have to be afraid of?
But now that the monopoly too has given in, the turn will surely soon come for sugar and for salt and for the railways and for everything that is monopolised and state-run.
And the real cheapness will come, and everything will be bought for groszy.
There remains, then, only one worry: where does one get the groszy?
For that I have a very good piece of advice, but I have already taken the last puff of my cigarette, so I must put off my advice until another time.
Argus[?].
The Outcry for Work.

[Article — the crisis and unemployment; by „Mikri“.] Something must be done for those who are being pushed out of their posts.
The matter we wish to touch upon today is, properly speaking, not a new one; on the contrary — all of us already know it well. It almost belongs by now to the „everyday phenomena“. But from these „daily occurrences“ [Hebrew: ma'asim she-be-khol yom] arises that great number of „quiet catastrophes“ which are felt very keenly!
The extraordinary crisis and the economic collapse of the manufacturing and commercial enterprises have, as is known, dragged along with them an enormous number of white-collar workers [„geistig-arbetnde“, brain-workers], driven them out of their jobs[;] they have been left unemployed and without livelihoods.
One fine morning they all at once ceased to be in the positions they had held until now and stayed at home on a „longer leave“. This is by now almost a collective fate of salaried employees and brain-workers.
The further road in life, too, on which such an „unemployed man“ now begins to walk, is no longer any new discovery.
At first, i.e. under the first and strong impression of the great „change“ in the course of life to which one has been accustomed for a long time, one still conducts, directly or indirectly, negotiations with the employer: „perhaps he will have mercy“? Perhaps he will show understanding and „take one back“ to the former post, even if for a much smaller salary... But the effort was in vain; even the greatest „pull“ [protektsye] did not help. Then begins the trudging to the institutions of „social insurance“ (if only one was insured there!), in order to receive the six — in the best case — monthly payments of support, which barely suffice for dry bread.
One „lives“ in the hope that tomorrow, the day after, in a week, or in a month, or at most after a certain time, work will surely be found. How could it be otherwise? In so large a centre of factories and trade, where one has been working for a long time already, where one has a more or less large circle of acquaintances, should one not be able to find work? Several factories are still in operation, there still exist well-established firms that do big business; trade and commerce have still not died out altogether, — is it possible that brain-workers should no longer be needed?
The term of the „zapomogi“ [Polish: relief benefits] meanwhile runs out, and then one begins to think about a „takhles“ [a practical purpose], i.e. how to earn at least enough for the „miserable bread“ [lechem ha-klokel], dry bread.
And so one takes up various „livelihoods“: one acts as a broker, one acts as a go-between, one sells tea, cocoa, postage and revenue stamps together with bill-of-exchange forms[;] one goes day in, day out, upstairs, downstairs, with graters, little washing machines, rubber aprons and other such „patented“ „articles“, highly important and necessary in the household. Some of these „unemployed“ suddenly become „haberdashery dealers“ and „mobile stores“, carrying neckties, scarves and the like on a stick that is tied to the neck.
But these „businesses“ too have scant success. For lack of any choice one begins to conduct „transactions“ with the pawnshop: from time to time one pawns something else, whatever has any value at all; jewellery, objects of art, even the better clothes, until one is left with only what one wears on one's own back!
What is there left to do now? One waits, one still hopes that „salvation“ may yet come, soon, unexpectedly, from whichever side it may be! That is the psychological mood and the only illusion with which one consoles oneself and strives to maintain one's mental balance!
Those are the unemployed who are, relatively speaking, still fortunate. Others no longer have even such a hope and cannot have any hope; sometimes they have no prospect at all that the crisis will ever end and that they will again get employment. They stand at the edge of their possibility of existence[.] Perhaps they will yet succeed in keeping themselves for a short time on the surface of the abyss, but who knows for how long?...
This category of unemployed feels worst and most wretched. They do not knock on the doors of the charity societies, of the free-loan funds; nor do they hold demonstrations, protest meetings, which might draw to them the attention of the „authoritative spheres“ or of the employers who still remain; they are in their homes — and wait; what are they waiting for? They themselves do not know!...
Thus days, weeks, months go by, — yes, even years, and the help in the form of work still does not appear; utter despair seizes such an unemployed brain-worker, who feels cheated in his hopes and expectations!
The vexation and bitterness of these hopeless brain-workers become still more acute with the awareness that somewhere there is, after all, still work, and that for it the appropriate working hands are needed! Where, then, is that still large number of factory owners, industrialists, producers and plain businessmen, with whom there is indeed still something to do and who are in need of labour? Where are they, where indeed is the Jewish community [kibbutz], socially still strong? Why do they not come, in such a time of trouble, to the aid of the great army of unemployed, of salaried employees?!
A whole social stratum is in despair and is almost going under before their eyes; thousands of more or less intelligent and capable workers are wrestling with life in a desperate struggle — and society does not see it! Only when a catastrophe has already happened and one feels morally guilty, only then does one — and that too merely for a moment — become seeing, but it is already too late.
This article is not an indictment against anyone whatsoever. It is not a matter here of accusations and reproaches against anybody; we merely wished to draw attention to the sad fate of a certain stratum of people, to the great distress of the army of those who are able to work, willing to work, but unemployed, who are looking for employment. Something really must be done to create help in the form of work, productive work for brain-workers!
How "the Girl from the Sky" Unites Two Worlds

The conversation of the famous aviatrix Amy Johnson with her husband Mollison.

The most famous woman in the world is now, without doubt, the heroine of the air Amy Johnson. With her solo flight from London to South Africa and back to London she has proved that she surpasses not only the women but even the men, who until now have not been able to show such a feat in the field of flying.
The greatest defeat of all the men, however, was suffered by none other than Amy Johnson's husband, the famous flyer Mollison. His young wife declared that she must beat her husband's record, and she carried it out.
It is superfluous to point out that, although Mollison has such a heroic wife, he was nonetheless very uneasy during the three days when she was flying over seas and deserts. Day and night he sat without a break at the radio set and waited for news of his wife.
On the fourth day the radio station in Cape Town at last announced that Amy Johnson had just arrived with her aeroplane, in good health but terribly exhausted.
This news spread lightning-fast over all of England, and the joy of the English was beyond measure.
Wishing to give a surprise to the 5 million English radio listeners, the London radio station decided that husband and wife must have a conversation with each other, and all of England would listen in to this conversation of the heroic couple.
But it was not so easy to carry out a conversation over 22,000 kilometres.
Mollison, happy at his wife's victory, did not let himself be asked for long, and just a few minutes later he was at the London radio station.
It went much harder with Amy Johnson, who was then on the other side of the "line without a wire". All the pleas of the South African radio station did not help. "Leave me in peace," she begged, "for four days and nights I have not slept and my strength is giving out."
But Mollison, and together with him all the radio listeners who were listening in to the conversations of the technical directors of the two radio stations, did not want to know anything at all about her tiredness.
At 4.30 in the afternoon Amy, half fainting, was placed at a microphone; but as soon as she heard the voice of her husband — "Hallo Amy" — she became wide awake and began to talk in the true wifely manner and did not let her husband get a word in at all. Husband and wife completely forgot that millions of people were listening to their conversation with bated breath. They sent each other the most heartfelt kisses over the radio waves; she questioned him about what he had eaten today and whether he had enjoyed his dinner, and in the course of this related that a day earlier, because of a defect in the engine, she had had to come down in the wilderness, and the lions had had a mind to make a meal of her. A few revolver shots, however, took away the lions' appetite.
The heartfelt and touching conversation of the heroic couple, during which Amy Johnson recounted exactly all the details of her sensational flight, would never have come to an end, were it not for the sober radio announcer.
He broke into the conversation and declared with regret that husband and wife had already been talking for more than half an hour. At that moment he made himself five million enemies — radio listeners. But the normal radio programme had to begin at its appointed time, and the touching conversation over a distance of tens of thousands of kilometres was cut off.
It is perhaps[?] pure chance that Amy Johnson's second conversation over the radio was also held at 4.30 in the afternoon; as is known, she held her first conversation over the radio in Warsaw, when on her way London—Tokyo she came down not far from Warsaw. Then too she began her conversation over the radio at 4.30 in the afternoon.
Homely Little Letters

[Feuilleton — Będzin, kehilla.] B"H, for the portion "And the children of Israel sighed"...
My friend Reb Shlomo, may his light shine.
After duly inquiring after your well-being: in today's letter I want to give you a little pleasure — and precisely from our kehilla leaders, long may they live. You know, Reb Shlomo, that the Będzin kehilla possesses dozors [board members] who are true geniuses; there is a conjecture that this is why the authorities do not want to release them from their offices — because their deeds must serve as a „model“ for all the other towns in Poland...
But what the Będzin kehilla has lived to see this week, even the greatest fantasist could not have dreamt up. Imagine, Reb Shlomo, that Będzin is the only town on the globe where „the Angel of Death no longer has any dominion... The „He will swallow up death for ever“ has „come true“, and
— „People don't die any more“...
— How did this happen?
— It happened in a simple way, because of a plain money dispute between the Chevra Kadisha and the dozors.
The dispute consists in this: the gabbaim of the Będzin Chevra Kadisha demand that the dozors give them a couple of thousand gulden [złoty] to buy a plot for a cemetery; the gabbaim point out that in these times, when merchants jump out of windows and the whole of mankind is guttering out like a candle, they must have a new plot for a cemetery at their disposal. The dozors, on the other hand, are against it: if there is — they say — no plot for graves, „people will not die“... In general, they say, a Chevra Kadisha is no longer needed. The gmina [the kehilla] is, after all, nothing more than a mortuary chamber, so what does one need a Chevra Kadisha for at all? No difficulty. In the field of „dying off“ the dozors are great experts[?] — and the proof? „Tovar Goda“[?].
If you, Reb Shlomo, saw how the gabbaim of the Będzin Chevra Kadisha stroll about the streets like Chol-HaMoed idlers, how the gravedigger sits in a corner of the gmina premises and... dozes — you would cry out:
— Happy are you, people of Israel, that you possess such „emissaries of the public“...
And now, Reb Shlomo, I want to treat you to a second „sensation“, or rather to the new victory that democracy has won in the town of Będzin.
As is known, for our many sins, it was the custom for long years, the law was observed, that ordination (smicha) for shechita was issued by a rabbi. One rabbi was not even enough — only several rabbis. Well, how long can a system of that kind be allowed to exist? What is said in the Mishnah — that all may slaughter, except a deaf-mute, an imbecile and a minor — in this respect too Będzin is an exception: in Będzin there are no imbeciles, no minors, only pure sages; and for that very reason the order[?] that held until now has been changed according to the version of civilisation...
The cause of the radical change were indeed none other than our kind-hearted dozors. First of all they showed the world that a shochet no longer needs to toil himself black in order to obtain the proper practice. Nor need he be the authority, the God-fearing man; only, if the candidate has the strength to bear the contribution laid upon him... he can be crowned as shochet...
What is more, the matter of shechita has been so reformed among us that it is quite in order to hand the candidate the writ stating that he has been appointed shochet even before he has said the „harei at“... for the main thing is the „kiddushin“ of the American currency... Oy, Ameritshke ganev [America, you thief]! How much longer will you, with the power of your dollars, keep in check all the European states, and among them those who have a say in the matter of the new shochtim...
With the „reforms“, truth to tell, not everyone is content; there are also „conservative“ elements who are against the new order and insist that in Będzin the shochtim be experts, Jews with long beards, with ailments, as in the old „dark“ times...
These very elements had, a few days ago, prepared an attempt on the whole gmina; a plain overturn was to take place; but the danger has passed and it proved possible to settle the dispute between the contented and the discontented, namely: both sides agreed that ordination for shechita shall be given by the former kehilla president Mr. Fürstenberg, the president „without the kehilla portfolio“ Mr. Rubinlicht, and the former dozor Mr. Unger.
According to the agreement between the above-mentioned sides, the ordination examination will take place in the following manner:
Mr. Fürstenberg will test whether the slaughtering knives were „made“ in the Polish steel works; Mr. Rubinlicht, as town councillor, will establish whether the knives bear a stamp of the „rzeczoznawcy“ [experts] of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce; the third member of the commission, Mr. Unger, will, during the shochtim's examinations, write memoirs of the kehilla of old...
I have a third „sensation“ for you. Our Będzin rulers have invented a kashering apparatus. The first trial will be made with the former cantor Zhupazitsh[?]: the more he knocks off his debt with the gmina, the more kosher he becomes... But about the new invention I shall write another time; meanwhile have a good Sabbath, as wishes you your
Ben Amotz.
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Shemot)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Shemot
The Portion
—o—
a) "And Joseph died, and all his brothers, and all that generation... and the children of Israel were fruitful and swarmed" (Ex. 1:6–7)
In our lands of exile it is like this: when the old generation of "children of Israel" dies out, there arises a generation of "children of Poland", "children of Germany"... The coming generation no longer belongs to us; it is assimilated. Only in the first exile, in Egypt, was the coming generation, too, still counted among the children of Israel.
Divrei Sha'arei Chaim.
—o—
b) "And the king of Egypt said to the Hebrew midwives... and he said: When you deliver the Hebrew women" (ibid., 15–16)
Pharaoh used the same methods that all Pharaohs in all ages use with regard to their Jewish subjects: having shameful plans concerning the Jews, and wishing to enlist Jews themselves to help with his shameful plans, he first of all picked out Hebrew midwives, raised them above the people, made "houses" for them, made them great, gave them state posts — "and he said to the Hebrew midwives": he spoke nothing but kind words to them; and only later — "and he said: When you deliver the Hebrew women": only later did he let them in on what he wanted of them...
Rabbi Eliyahu Chaim Meisel.
—o—
c) "Surely the thing is known" (2:14)
"Because he saw wicked men, informers, in Israel." Rashi.
The Gemara says in tractate Sotah that Pharaoh got nothing at all out of the Jews' labour. ("Pithom" — the mouth of the abyss swallowed it; Raamses — one part after another crumbled.) The abyss somehow swallowed up the work. The state treasury even became poorer because of it (as with Jewish labour!...). And yet Pharaoh, disregarding his own loss, worked them with rigour out of sheer wickedness. And that is why Pharaoh is likened to a "tannin" [serpent], for a snake, too, has no enjoyment from its biting.
This caused Moses sorrow: Jews work without bringing anyone any benefit; Jews work simply to torment themselves.
But when he saw that among the Jews there are informers, denouncers, who also bite others without having any benefit from it, he said: they deserve the stick, measure for measure...
Totze'ot Chaim.
—o—
d) "And the king of Egypt died, and the children of Israel sighed because of the labour."
Because with the death of every Egyptian king there began the work of building pyramids and statues in the king's memory. And as can be seen from history, the Jews were mainly employed in erecting the pyramids.
Imrei Chen.
—o—
e) "And behold, the bush burned with fire, and the bush was not consumed" (3:2)
1.
"And was not consumed" — for how many thousands of years has the Jewish soul been burning at the stake, and yet — "it is not consumed". This is what God showed Moses when He spoke to him of the Jews' redemption.
Minchat Shai.
2.
"The bush burns with fire."
That is why Jews are in exile: because each one is to the other a thornbush, a thorn in the eyes — "like a painful thorn and a pricking brier"...
Siftei Da'at.
—o—
f) "Who has made a mouth for man" (4:11)
There is a "man" who is nothing but a "mouth": his whole essence and worth is only his mouth; that is his sole merit...
Alei Zayit.
—o—
g) "He comes out to meet you, and when he sees you he will be glad in his heart" (ibid., 14)
Now that really is a marvel! Two Jewish leaders rejoicing in one another...
Nachalat Yaakov.
* * *
"Torah scholars increase peace in the world."
That means: they stir up so many quarrels that one must constantly be making peace between them...
Imrei Chen.
—o—
h) "And he led the flock to the far side of the wilderness" (3:1)
"...to keep them from robbery — and the Holy One, blessed be He, took him to shepherd His people."
Midrash Rabbah.
The leaders of the generation like to grant themselves a dispensation: if I rob something from the community, what is the sin? After all, I am the community's man, and it is for their good and their benefit that I want to live in grand style; it is, after all, for their sake, so that I can faithfully occupy myself with the needs of the public... so that people may see how handsomely a Jewish leader lives...
But God chooses to shepherd His flock only that shepherd who runs away from robbery, even when the robbery is for the sake of the flock...
Tal LeYisrael.
* * *
In Brody they once caught a synagogue beadle who had polished his shoes with the oil that had been bought for the eternal lamp. R' Ephraim Zalman Margolioth asks him: How can this be? How does one polish one's shoes with such oil? How does one rob this from consecrated property?
— Rabbi — answers the beadle — the shoes, too, were bought with eternal-lamp money... (which the public had thrown into the alms box for the eternal lamp.)
Nachalei Devash.
—o—
i) "And you shall despoil Egypt" (4:24) [sic; the verse is 3:22]
When Dr. Aaron Jellinek was preacher in Vienna, there was a priest there, Klinkstrom, a great Jew-hater, who often organised antisemitic meetings at which he appeared and made use of the most varied quotations from the Torah, twisting them and interpreting them in an antisemitic spirit.
One day Dr. Aaron Jellinek comes to the sermon and hears the priest speaking:
— See what thieves the Jews are. They borrowed vessels of silver and vessels of gold from the Egyptians and stole them, and Moses himself told them to do it.
Dr. A. Jellinek stands up and answers him:
— And what of you, the gentiles, who stole from the Jews their Torah, which is worth more than gold and silver, and you break it over their heads!...
—o—
j) "Why have You done evil to this people" (6:22) [sic; the verse is 5:22]
Moses came to the Jews and said to them: if you live in unity, you will be redeemed. Well, so be it — they gave it a try.
But when they were not redeemed so quickly, they began to storm: why were we talked into unity for nothing? Why were we tricked? This complaint Moses passed on to God in the Jews' name: "Lamah hare'ota" (from the word re'ut, friendship) "to this people"? If they are not redeemed, why did You fool them and make them unhappy by bidding them live for a short while in unity?...
Rashei Besamim
Snow — a poem by Roza Jakubowicz

[Poem.] Roza Jakubowicz.
Snow.
Only yesterday the day was dazzling with thousands of colours,
and purple proclamations reared up sky-high,
and red motor-cars sped swiftly to go strolling in the fall of leaves,
and shop windows cried out that one lives but once in this world!
And overnight a snow fell on roof and gate and doors,
and buried the streets deep in whiteness — all one,
and all is white and all is cold, so that you may lose your way,
in snow that has wrapped, as one, the various colours. —
"If Poland had many citizens like you, things would surely be better in the country"

[Poland — unemployment; a new book.] A book has appeared in Warsaw, "Memoirs of the Unemployed" [Pamiętniki bezrobotnych], written by unemployed Polish workers from every corner of Poland. Altogether the volume contains 57 memoirs.
The book is a true cry of pain of those tormented by unemployment in Poland.
Nevertheless, here and there, out of a mountain of filth and death, cruelty and wickedness, there shine forth the pure, bright sparks of humanity.
Here, for example, an unemployed locksmith-worker from Warsaw tells how, after months without work, after selling almost everything in the house, his wife fell ill. The doctor who was called in declared that the patient needed a long and careful course of treatment.
"I explained to him," writes the unemployed man, "that I am without work, that my wife has no possibility of lying ill at home; it happens more than once that there is also nothing to eat. He heard me out and told me to come to him the next day. I came; he greeted me with extraordinary warmth — it seems that this was the first person in the course of the five months without work who treated me in such a way. He gave her a note to the hospital, I should only take my wife over there — and the rest should not trouble me, because he had already settled matters with the hospital.
During my wife's illness he sent, through the maid, two quarts of milk and baked goods every day, for nearly two months. I stress that this doctor was a Jew. I do not mention his name, because he asked me not to mention it to anyone, but here I thank you once more, unknown doctor, for your truly fatherly deed. If Poland had many such citizens as you, things would be better in the country."
A second unemployed man, from Dąbrowa, tells how he lived for a long time on the money he got from selling the wardrobe, the sideboard and the bed. "Once," the unemployed man's daughter relates, "they boiled the last of the potatoes together with the peelings. Suddenly someone knocked; mother opened the door. A poor man came in, begging for alms; mother pointed to the potatoes with the peelings, explaining that she herself had nothing.
The beggar's heart filled with pity; he poured out of his sack the bread he had collected, pieces of sugar and sausage, gave it to us and went out without a word. Mother wept then for a long, long time."
Such stories, however, are regrettably very, very few...
The Silesian Righteous Proselyte. Joseph son of R' Abraham (Józef Steblicki)

[Historical tale in instalments — Silesia; part 3.] A historical tale by Y. Adwen. (3)
"What causes brought it about," the judge asks Steblicki, "that you went over to Judaism?"
"As to the main cause itself," says Steblicki, "God is my witness, and before you too, gentlemen judges, I shall not deny the truth: it is already more than twenty years that I have been strongly drawn to Judaism. In secret, so that my family and those close to me should not learn of it, I kept Jewish customs and Jewish traditions; even before being circumcised I used to slip into the synagogue and, together with the local Jews, celebrate the Jewish Sabbath; I used to nourish myself only with kosher foods."
"How long is it since you were last in church?"
"For five or six years I have not been to confession, because the clergy, having learned of my conduct, did not want to admit me to confession; but from time to time I did go to church."
"In what year did you circumcise yourself?"
"On the feast of St. James [25 July] I had already separated myself completely from the Church, for I had firmly resolved within myself to become a true Jew.
I informed the Jews in Nikolai [Mikołów] of my resolution, but with them I could not carry out my plan, and every time I pressed them with my plan they put me off with various excuses.
Then I travelled to Oświęcim, and from there to Kraków; in Kraków I turned to several respected Orthodox Jews, whom I asked to help me with the circumcision.
The attitude of the Kraków Jews towards me disappointed me anew: instead of meeting me halfway and helping me to carry out my wish to become a Jew, they talked me out of it. Only, seeing that my wish was a genuine one, that my love for the Jewish religion was a true one, they declared to me that I should go home for the time being, and that they would send me from Kraków a specialist who would perform the circumcision.
This happened with a delay of several months. I was in Kraków at the end of winter, and the Kraków Jew came to me about the matter in the month of August.
The operation, however, he did not want to perform himself; only, following his instructions, I did it myself before his eyes, and he gave me a name: Joseph Abraham.
On Yom Kippur I went to the synagogue and there performed all the prayers and did penance in the Jewish manner, and from that day on I am a Jew, on a par with all Jews. I declare once again that I came to this through no one's fault; none of the Jews persuaded me to it, but I myself chose it of my own good will, and until my last day I shall remain in the Jewish faith. Nor do I deny that before I circumcised myself I kept Jewish laws; I did not shave my beard with a razor, only clipped it. Also, it is already a few years since I separated from my wife, because, first, we are both already old, and secondly, I am after all a Jew, who may not mix with any Christians."
"Have you read the New Testament?"
"The true reasons why I became a Jew I took only from Holy Scripture, where it is said that God remains one, and likewise His laws which He gave to His beloved people Israel. In the Acts of the Apostles in the New Testament we also find that no one can save his soul if he is not circumcised. For more than twenty years I constantly read the Bible, and I became convinced that the Jewish faith is the true faith.
I talked about this with the clergy, who tried to persuade me, but I did not consider their answers right, and it remained settled with me to become a true Jew.
I have no regret that I did this, and since every person must have his freedom of conscience — I have done no harm to anyone here in the country, and I promise that henceforth I shall not sin against the King and those in authority, and I hope that by you, gentlemen judges, I shall be left without punishment."
(To be continued).
Our Gemilut Chesed (free-loan) funds.

[Zagłębie — the Gemilut Chesed free-loan funds; article for the propaganda month.]
By Y. Giterman.
(In connection with the propaganda month in Zagłębie.)
"I simply do not know what the Jewish masses would have done without the immediate help (of the funds)" — that is how Sholem Asch, with his great sense for Jewish reality, felt it, and after him the activists of the funds repeat it at all conferences, in all their appeals and on every other occasion.
Among the appraisals and praises that you can hear from those active on behalf of the funds (or, as they often call themselves, "those engaged in the holy work"), the assertion that the funds are the most important factor in the present economic life of Polish Jews is the smallest of all the praises voiced by the enthusiastic adherents and devotees of the Gemilut Chesed movement.
It would perhaps be hard to find work in any other field that has so many devoted and fanatical adherents as have gathered around the still young Gemilut Chesed movement.
"When I no longer have the strength to occupy myself with communal work, I shall give up all my offices and tasks, but my work in the fund I shall keep up until my last day," the chairman of the Sosnowiec kehilla exclaims at a conference.
And the tremendous attachment to the funds finds expression not only in praises and words of commendation at conferences, but indeed in mighty exertions on every day of the whole year.
One must know the present Jewish situation in order to understand what exertions, what tremendous efforts are required by the constant collecting of money and by seeing to it that not a single grosz of the loans given out should, God forbid, be lost.
It is therefore worthwhile, and even necessary, to make clear to our own people as well as to outsiders what social content the funds have and what the essence of this movement is.
And after all, those who stand far from this work also ought to reflect on the strength that lies in this young movement, which in so short a time has embraced all of Poland and has won in every town and townlet people who are likewise devoted to it heart and soul.
If one wants to understand where the strength of the Gemilut Chesed movement comes from, one must, first, know the present situation of the Jews in Poland and, second, become imbued with the character and spirit that prevail in the greater part of the Gemilut Chesed funds.
As for the situation — alas, a thousand times alas, the situation is such that not only two hundred and one hundred złoty, but even 50, literally fifty złoty, are a matter of saving life, and in countless cases they rescue families from complete ruin and downfall.
This you will hear from every Jew who stands close to the work of the funds, and this will be confirmed by everyone who knows today's sad reality.
Fifty to a hundred złoty as a loan from the fund, and through it a further small credit in goods, is the foundation of the little shop, of buying up goods in the village or for the village, of the artisan's little workshop; it helps the Jew to buy a horse or a cow from which he draws his livelihood, it saves him when he has to take out a trade licence or pay taxes.
Fifty to a hundred złoty are the thin straw to which thousands upon thousands of poor and weak existences cling, saving themselves through it from complete decline, from sinking to doles and alms, from losing their human countenance. Thanks to the loan of 50–100 złoty from the fund, hundreds and thousands of Jewish families in the townlets still lead a gloomy, darkened, but [printed: "or"] independent life, regard themselves and are regarded as householders in the townlet, and perhaps even still give, now and then, 10 groszy in alms.
And what would these Jews have done, were it not for the Gemilut Chesed funds, in the towns where there are no other credit institutions and where, in the best case, the Jew who does manage to get a loan must hand over to the usurer the first and usually also the last few złoty he has earned.
What would these Jews have done, who are already too weak to benefit from normal cooperative credit because of the share payment, the interest and the terms of repayment?
We say 600 towns with funds; we name an almost astronomical figure of over 100,000 families who benefit from them each year.
Very large figures, which nevertheless do not yet create the impression; but try to put living persons behind the figures, and picture to yourselves, for example, the Jew for whom all sources of livelihood have been stopped up. He struggles in despair with his last strength so as not to stretch out his hand, and now, thanks to the loan from the Gemilut Chesed fund, he has again been able to bring home to his family a few earned złoty.
And once more — behind the five-digit numbers mentioned you must picture the living, suffering people whom you can see every Monday and Thursday in each of the 600 funds; let this sink in, and the big numbers will become more alive for you and you will feel the mighty importance of the Gemilut Chesed funds in Zagłębie.
In order to understand the importance of the Gemilut Chesed funds one must, besides the direct task — the help itself which the funds give — also know and understand something else, which is no less important than the help itself. We mean the character and spirit of the funds.
We have tried to show that the funds have a deep social content, that they answer the important needs of the present state of distress. But how did it come about that these social needs really found their partial answer in the founding of the funds?
How did it come about that, for the struggle against the rapidly growing impoverishment, an army of 6000 communal workers was mobilised simultaneously in every corner of Poland?
How did it come about that thousands of people took upon themselves, of their own free will, a dreadfully heavy burden of constant collections for the funds; to endure the greatest anguish in granting a loan to one and refusing another, often to bear the gravest insults when demanding repayment of debts from bad people — and all this without any benefit to themselves, and not for one week or one month but for years?
It is hard to explain; it is truly a wonder, a miracle; it is apparently the miracle that happens in a moment of ruin and destruction, when forces arise of themselves among the masses of the people, forces that stand up against the ruin and strive to lessen its devastations.
Such a wonderful phenomenon we saw in the time of the expulsions and homelessness, when, one may say, the entire Jewish population in Ukraine and Russia took part, with a mighty readiness for sacrifice, in creating a gigantic people's relief to mitigate the consequences of the terrible catastrophe.
Apparently it is to this wonderful strength, which lies in the Jewish masses and comes forth in moments of destruction and danger, that we also owe the spontaneous rise of the Gemilut Chesed funds, and whoever has an open eye and heart will see the wonder of boundless self-sacrifice every day.
Acquaint yourselves, for example, with the touching account by the activists of the excellent Zawiercie fund of how glaziers, carters and other artisans joyfully presented themselves for work on putting up a building for the fund, taking no payment for it; let this spirit that prevails in the funds sink in, and you will understand how right were the words of the delegate from Sławków, that the funds have awakened the sense of responsibility among the Jewish population, and that with the rise of the funds it is no longer possible for a Jew to perish because he does not have the couple of hundred złoty in time, and that "a Jewish townlet is no longer Sodom".
And if you have understood the importance of the measure of rescue that the funds bring in the present unbearable situation, if you have become imbued with the touching popular and Jewish spirit that prevails in the Gemilut Chesed funds, you will no longer ask: "What is this service to you?" — why do serious people occupy themselves with such "lowly", old-fashioned work as the Gemilut Chesed funds. Into the old form a deep, pulsating social content has been put, and as it has turned out, the old form not only did not hinder but actually helped the movement of assistance by interest-free credit to grow so much and to take on such a fine popular character.
Therefore let all this sink in, and you too will surely say together with the writer Asch: I simply do not know what the Jewish masses would have done without the immediate help of the funds.
A Brother Nearly Married His Own Sister...

[From life — a true story.] The F. family sent out hundreds of invitations for the wedding of their daughter Ewa to Mr. Gustaw G.., for which great and eager preparations had been made.
But on the day of the wedding something unexpected happened and the wedding had to be called off.
Some wanted to conclude that it was the bridegroom who had changed his mind, demanding an addition to the dowry; others simply whispered about something „of such and such a kind“; but only the very closest knew the true reason, and they kept silent.
To find out what really happened here, we must go back to the year 1910. Right after Yankl F. married his wife Beyle F., he opened a small ready-made clothing shop, which did not go badly. F. began to go from strength to strength, and in a very short time he bought a house of his own.
Mrs. F. (although from a poor family) let the wealth go very much to her head, and with a passionate ardour took to dancings, balls, the theatre and the like; together with her husband (who was by now called Jakub) she was a frequent guest in the night-spots and bought the best boxes in the theatre. And when father and mother used to come on a visit, Madame F. would twist her mouth and wrinkle her nose and see to it that they went away as quickly as possible, so that she should not, Heaven forbid, be left „shamed“ before the „aristocratic“ guests.
And it came to pass one day that Madame F. got up with severe headaches, with eyes red and swollen from weeping. Jakub, seeing his pretty little wife in such a state, became greatly alarmed.
Mr. F. began to tremble and flutter: perhaps his wife had learned of his former intimate relations with the beautiful Rivka (his parents' maid), who, as became known later, had given birth to a little girl and left it as a foundling.
At last Jakub, frightened to death, learned what had happened: his „better half“ was pregnant and was beside herself, because it would be the end of her „slim line“ and of all the amusements...
Very quickly Madame F., with her husband's consent, freed herself of the „burden“ and went on living with her ardour as before.
At the same time that Madame F. went back to living the good life, Rivka, the former maid, married a young man of respectable family (a dowry she had received at the time from F.'s parents) and entirely forgot what had happened to her. Helena — that was what she was called now — became a respectable housewife, a loving and faithful wife to her husband, and exactly at the nine months gave birth to a boy.
Times ran on, years went by; Madame Bela, standing before the mirror, began to notice little wrinkles on her face; the flaming temperament cooled off, and no trace remained of the former ardour. The girlfriends[?] now come more rarely, a kind of cold wind blows from the rooms, there is no carefree, merry little laughter of a child, the tiny, downy, warm little hands are missing that would embrace, just like this, around the neck and press on a firm, strong, true child's kiss.
What had Madame Bela not already done to have a child. She had been to all the doctors and professors, travelled round all the spas and — not to be mentioned in the same breath — to the „good Jews“ [Hasidic rebbes]; it had already cost a treasure[?] of money, and nothing.
After such days Mr. and Mrs. F. decided to adopt a child, and so that nobody should later be able to take it away from them, what remained was to take a child from the Jewish foundling home.
It did not take long, and in F.'s richly furnished rooms there ran about an 8-year-old blonde little girl with a little head of golden-blonde curls. A special governess was engaged for the child and it was sent to the best gymnasium.
Who is the child? Who are her parents? — That was soon found out.
— The mother is the beautiful Rivka, and the father?... Mr. Jakub, the very same, who has now adopted her. Naturally, he had not the slightest idea of it.
The years ran on. Ewa (that was the child's name) grew up and finished the gymnasium with distinction.
The World War, which had broken out in the meantime, had long since ended; for some the war was a curse, for others a blessing. Many became great rich men; among the latter was also G., Rivka's husband, and from the former small drapery shop he became a big manufacturer.
The manufacturer G. had his eldest son Gustaw educated, and after he finished the gymnasium sent him off to Prague, to the university. As fate would have it, Ewa was already there at the university, in her 2nd semester, and between Ewa and Gustaw (actually between the sister and the brother) an ardent love was woven.
The lovers made no secret of their love and wrote home about it to their parents.
The parents had nothing against it. Gustaw's mother, the beautiful Rivka, at once, from her son's first little letter, recognised in the surname of his beloved the name of her former seducer; having no choice, she kept silent, for several reasons. She did not imagine, however, that her son's beloved was her own illegitimate child, whom she had cast away years before.
When they had finished the university, the date was fixed; Rivka found some excuse, fearing that Jakub might recognise her.
But since there are no secrets in the world, Ewa, being by nature good and honest, did not conceal from her fiancé her stay in the foundling home, and told the fiancé that she was not F.'s real daughter, but had been adopted by them when she was 8 years old.
The fiancé told it to his mother, and here we come to the very thick of it.
Helena, Gustaw's mother, went off to the foundling home, and after a lengthy inquiry and investigation she succeeded in establishing that Ewa, her son's bride, was indeed her own daughter.
The despairing mother, when the day of the wedding ceremony drew near, could bear it no longer; she called her son into her room and revealed the secret.
What went on in G.'s home it is superfluous to tell. Mother and daughter fell on each other's necks and wept bitterly: G. forgave his wife her former sins and even agreed to take Ewa into his home as his own child.
Ewa, however, remained with her father as before, not wishing to cause him pain in return for the kindness he had shown her.
Now one can indeed see, day after day, mother and daughter strolling together.
Lamed-Reysh.
A Death Sentence Carried Out in the Local Prison

The hangman — a brother of the murdered man.
On Monday and Tuesday the summary court („shtand-gerikht“, sąd doraźny) sat in the Sosnowiec district court against the murderer Knapik, who in Kazimierz murdered the policeman Ludwik and the local resident Miguls[?].
The interest in the trial was very great. The courtroom was packed full with a public of every kind.
The hearing of witnesses lasted the whole of Monday; the next day, Tuesday, the prosecutor delivered the speech for the prosecution, and after that, at 12 o'clock, the summary court withdrew to deliberate.
At exactly 3 o'clock the court comes in. An enormous tension reigns in the hall. With bated breath and in dead silence people listen to the words of the presiding judge, who declares that Knapik is sentenced to death by hanging.
The man condemned to death is calm, and when he receives permission to take leave of his family and those close to him, he goes up to his wife and kisses her.
He takes leave of his sister and brother, does not let them weep, and asks them to remember his children.
After the leave-taking the murderer is led away, under a strong police guard, into the local prison [in Będzin].
The defence counsel applied by telephone to the President of the State for a pardon.
A few hours later an answer came that the President of the State had refused the request.
On Wednesday at 7 o'clock in the morning the death sentence was carried out in the yard of the local prison.
The gallows was put up voluntarily by a brother of one of those murdered by the bandit Knapik.
City Council Elections to Take Place in the Spring?

As we are informed from a reliable source, city council elections are to take place this coming spring in the towns that are administered by commissioners.
In connection with this, the magistrates (municipalities) have received a circular (okólnik) from the Ministry of the Interior, saying that sums for the election expenses are to be entered in the new budgets.
33 Per Cent of the Jewish Population Take Loans from the Gemilut Chesed Fund

The public meeting („akademie“) that took place on Monday evening in the „Kapitol“[?], devoted to the campaign of the Gemilut Chesed fund [the interest-free loan fund], was a great moral success.
Even before the meeting began the hall was already overcrowded; the crush at the entrance was so great that the police had to intervene.
The meeting is opened by the president, Mr. Rubinlicht, who proposes Mr. Sz. Fürstenberg as chairman of the meeting. After the „Hakoach“ orchestra has played the Polish and the Jewish anthems, Mr. Rubinlicht gives a report on the Gemilut Chesed fund.
From the report it emerges that 33 per cent of the local Jewish population make use of the interest-free fund.
On the important role of the Gemilut Chesed fund at the present moment speak Messrs. A. Liwer, Kwiatek (Sosnowiec), Wygodzki, Wendel, Giterman, Fürstenberg, Bożykowski and Goldsztajn, and an appropriate resolution is adopted.
The Community-Tax Arrears at the „Urząd Skarbowy“

This week a list of „etat“ debts [arrears of the Jewish community tax] was handed over to the „Urząd Skarbowy“ [the state tax office].
As we are told from the kehilla (gmina), this is only a beginning; several more lists of the unpaid „etat“ debts have already been prepared.
Incidentally we note that the collection of the „etat“ by the sequestrators [tax-office bailiffs] is bound up with considerable enforcement costs.
Memorandum from the Artisans' Association about Relief for Craftsmen

The board of the local Artisans' Association (Handwerker-Verein) has applied to the commissioner with a memorandum describing the bitter situation of the artisans, who are unemployed and are perishing of hunger.
The memorandum demands: 1) that the magistrate (municipality) grant relief from the item for urgent aid which is provided for in the budget, and 2) from the Unemployment Fund.
A Lesson in Thrift...
This week a commission from the voivodeship (województwo) stayed here, which gave the self-government bodies (local authorities) instructions on how to make savings in the new budgets.
Because of the Frosts, Work in the Coal Mines Has Increased

Some coal mines in Zagłębie received larger orders this week.
At the „Paryż“ coal mine the number of workers has been increased. In general the frosts have brought a bit of revival into the coal industry.
Conference on Economy Measures.

[Będzin — authorities.] On Tuesday a conference of representatives of communal (municipal) institutions and of the voivodeship took place at the local starostwo (district office).
The aim of the conference was to adapt to the order of the Minister of the Interior to make the most far-reaching savings in the communal budgets.

Three Days after the Wedding She Regrets the Match... / From the Keren “Torah va-Avodah” Academy. / A Fire in an Aluminium Warehouse. / Silver 1- and 2-Złoty Coins Are Being Withdrawn from Circulation.

[Będzin — from life.] He is 56 years old, she is 48. He came to Będzin to look for a settled future; good and pious people arranged a match for him with a woman, a respectable one, a breadwinner.
But 3 days after the wedding the woman took a dislike to him and said:
— “Nie pojadę” [apparently Polish: “I am not going”]...
The epilogue was played out this week at the local rabbinate, where the divorce (get) took place.

From the Keren “Torah va-Avodah” Academy.
[Będzin — religious Zionism.] The academy (festive gathering) arranged in connection with the founding of the League for Religious Labour Eretz Israel, in the “Kapitol”[?] hall, was a great success. Before a packed hall Mr Mosze Openheim opens the academy; he dwells on the important role of “Ha-Poel ha-Mizrachi” as the only religious workers' party in Eretz Israel.
After the greetings of Messrs Buchweitz, Baum, Turner and others, the floor is given to the representative of “Ha-Poel ha-Mizrachi” in Eretz Israel, Mr Gardi, who delivers a fine lecture on the development of “Ha-Poel ha-Mizrachi” and its prospects for the future.

The second part of the academy too, performed by the Kraków cantor Mr Wszupowicz[?], was a great success.

A Fire in an Aluminium Warehouse.
[Będzin — fire.] On Sunday afternoon a fire broke out in a warehouse of aluminium ware. The fire destroyed the wooden building. The damage is great.

Silver 1- and 2-Złoty Coins Are Being Withdrawn from Circulation.
[Economy — currency.] From the New Year onward the silver 1-złoty coins are being exchanged by Bank Polski; they will be exchanged by the state bank until the end of the year.
The silver 2-złoty coins of the first issue (the larger ones) will remain in circulation until the end of January of this year. After 31 January the silver 2-złoty pieces will be withdrawn from circulation. The old silver 5-złoty pieces, on the other hand, will continue to circulate together with the new ones.
Sosnowiec: Brutal Deeds of the Terrorist Gang

[Sosnowiec — court.] On Friday and Saturday the further witnesses were heard. They brought nothing new at all. Only the deeds of the accused were unfolded before the court, and above all those of the chief ringleader, who was known under the name “Rycerusz”[?].
The merchants trembled at the name “Rycerusz”; even in the courtroom the witnesses are full of fear when they catch sight of the so-called “Rycerusz” in the dock.
The 70-year-old witness Szmul Lampel declares that the “łapacze” (touts who catch customers) and their king, the “Rycerusz”, did not let any customers into his shop, by various means, such as “Lampel has gone to Palestine” or “Lampel has died” and the like — so they lured the customers away; and when I gave them — he goes on — 107 złoty, they beat me and my children all the same.
Why did you not report this to the police? asks the presiding judge.
— I — declares Lampel with tears in his eyes — was afraid of them as of fire; they threatened me with a knife in the belly if I would not give them money.
Witness Józef Cymerman: The “Rycerusz” came into my shop and said to me: “Are you paying or not?” And when I told him that I had no money just now, he cut up my hat with a knife and said: “If I don't give him money, he will do to me the same as he has done to the hat”...
A further series of witnesses is heard, who confirm the same.
An interesting dialogue takes place during the examination of the witness Nuta Tenenbaum, for whom the “Rycerusz” had worked for a considerable time as a “łapacz” (tout).
— Wanting to get rid of him, I gave him 230 zł, borrowed another 150 zł on top of that, and gave him an overcoat. And when he was arrested, his pals came to me and took 50 zł from me for a lawyer.
— Did the gang threaten the witness? — asks the presiding judge.
— No! Only I did not want to have any quarrels with them, because I knew it would cost me more dearly.
Presiding judge: And if you had not given?
Witness: I would have had to flee from Sosnowiec...

Important Provisions of the New Code of Civil Court Procedure

[Law — the new Code of Civil Procedure.]
The right of the poor.
Only those persons whom the court recognises as having the right of the poor can be exempted from court fees; such a right, however, will be recognised only for the absolutely poor, on the strength of appropriate certificates from the magistrates [municipalities].
The claim, together with the certificate of poverty, must be filed in the court where the petitioner (the "petent") lives, even though the trial proper has to take place in another town. In the latter case the petitioner has the right to demand at the same time that an advocate be appointed to conduct the trial for him.
Likewise such a person has the right to demand that an advocate be appointed for him even when the trial has to take place in the very place where he lives, if under the procedure representation by an advocate is required, or if he can invoke other well-founded reasons.
Not only the plaintiff but also the defendant has the right to apply to the court immediately after receiving the notice ("avizatsye") or the claim, asking that the right of the poor be recognised for him and that an advocate be appointed for him.

Regulations concerning auctions (licitations)
The date of an auction may be fixed within 15 to 30 days after the seizure ("zajęcie"). Objects that spoil quickly, or that at once lose a considerable part of their value, may be auctioned before the appointed date. In the latter case the court is not competent to stay the execution on the strength of a complaint lodged by the debtor.
At the demand of the creditor or the debtor the sequestrated objects may be sent to another place or even to another town, if they can be sold there for a higher price; the transport costs must in such a case be covered by the party that makes such a proposal; for objects spoiled or lost on the way the creditor is in any case not responsible.
3 days before the auction the bailiff (komornik) must hang up, in front of the gate where the auction is to take place, an appropriate notice. If the value of the auctioned object exceeds the sum of 500 zł., a proper notice about it must likewise be published in a widely circulated local newspaper.
The auction starts from one half of the appraised sum, below which the object put up may not be sold. Gold, silver and platinum objects are auctioned starting from the full appraised price; they may not be sold more cheaply than they are worth as metal.
The auction may not begin later than 2 hours after the time given in the announcement.
If nobody offers at least the sum called out, it means that the auction has not taken place.
In case the debtor or the creditor observes that the auction has been carried out not in accordance with the regulations, he must demand that the bailiff enter his remark in the minutes. Then the things may not be handed over to the buyer. The rule does not apply to objects that spoil quickly.
The buyer must at once pay in the whole sum, and not, as it was until now, 20 per cent; if he does not at once pay in the sum in question he loses the right to the thing bought, he may no longer take part in the auction, and besides that he can also be sentenced to pay a fine amounting to 1 fifth of the price in question.

[Taxes — turnover tax; guidance for merchants.]
Is a wife obliged to pay her husband's „zaliczki“ [tax advances]?
Because of the many enquiries about the advances on the turnover tax, we consider it necessary to give the following explanations.
1) If a business now has a „ryczałt“ [flat-rate assessment] for the turnover tax and the owner enlarges the business, that is, he takes yet another branch of trade into his shop, he must report that from now on he also deals in another article; in such a case the ryczałt is taken away, because, so it is said, the business has been enlarged.
2) If the present owner liquidates his business and another person, for example a wife, a son, a daughter, begins to trade in the same place, the patent [trade licence] must be transferred to the new name and the advance is „taken off“ (nemt op).
3) If the trade is moved to another place, the flat-rate turnover tax is likewise taken away.
