Small Remarks on Great Matters

[Sosnowiec — public life; opinion column.]
Backwardness and understanding.
At every occasion of communal activity we find ourselves having to state that, as far as Jewish affairs are concerned, Sosnowiec is very backward when compared with her sister Będzin. That we say so more than once, that we prove it and give reasons for it — the Sosnowiec "carp-heads" [blockheads] hold it against us, as if we were blackening their faces before the world. But those who are annoyed by it are a handful of people, a quite small minority; the great majority is not interested in any of this; for the well-to-do Jew, the Sosnowiec Jew, all communal matters lie in his left sidelock [i.e. he could not care less]. "What do I know," they always say, "who has such foolishness on his mind; they think up what Haman never thought up." They keep saying in unison that one man need not worry about another, everyone has his own muddled head; such is the opinion of the Sosnowiec rich men on every question that touches the pocket, and it need not be a matter of large sums — it may even be a matter of złotys or groszy, the situation does not change; such is their view of the problem of communal activity.
As an example, a small characterisation: not long ago at all there lived and worked in Sosnowiec a Jew by the name of Dr. Abraham Perlman. It seems we all still remember him quite well and we all know how energetically and how intensively he was active in communal matters, in the problems of the community at large; everything interested him and everywhere his heart ached, but dearest of all to him was the Jewish hospital, into which he put the marrow of his bones. The Jewish hospital was his ideal, his embodiment.
Well, during the war we had all sorts of times, after all. It was bad and good, and only bad and altogether good; the periods turned like a kind of panorama, and at just such a moment, when days of hunger drew near and people earned nothing and longed for a piece of bread — in just such a period it came about that the Jewish hospital was closed. But Perlman's heart could not bear it; he could not rest, he could not remain indifferent to the wretched, helpless sick; he ran about and turned worlds upside down. Once he comes into our editorial office and pleads with entreaties and commands dictatorially that he will not budge from the spot unless we promise him at once that we will begin to rouse the population to come to the rescue, to take the locks off the hospital and open the gates wide for the poor sick. He got his way; we had to promise him that we would not let the pen out of our hand until the locks were torn off.
Now for several years the hospital administration has wanted to honour his memory by naming one ward after him, but since even this modest work cannot be approached without money, the project could not be realised to this day, and meanwhile a second doctor has also died, who certainly also had merits for the Jewish hospital, so that now two wards are needed to honour the deceased, and the hospital administration has begun to collect donations for that purpose — which, by the way, were listed last week in the columns of our newspaper — and what do we see: of the first five donors one is from Sosnowiec and the other four are Będzin doctors.
This is what characterises how far Sosnowiec lags behind Będzin. One would think the institution is a Sosnowiec one, the deceased doctors lived and worked and achieved in Sosnowiec — and the first donors have to be Będziners, of all people. Nor should it be forgotten that Sosnowiec has more Jewish doctors than Będzin, and the Jewish intelligentsia in Sosnowiec is also a larger one, and last but not least one must also know that the economic conditions, the material situation, are considerably better in Sosnowiec than in Będzin.
On the other hand, when the squire comes, the non-Jew, they will not try at all to be clever and to wriggle out of the business; on the contrary, they will want to play first fiddle and will not even try to take an interest in who is collecting the money and for what purpose, and whether we benefit from it and how much one benefits from it.
Yes, those who so tremble to show their Jewish nose are afraid to tax themselves for Jewish purposes and make light of everything that is done for their brothers and sisters, and they guard their pockets even when it is a matter of a few poor złotys.
Well, the campaign has begun after all, and the Sosnowiec intelligentsia and rich men will surely, surely tax themselves for it — it need not, by the way, swallow any very large sums — and we want to hope that they will certainly respond of their own free will and bring the money for the desired purpose. By all means, let us see how great their "good deeds" will be.
The responsibility of the "TOZ" administrators.
On this occasion we will also touch in passing on the following:
Sosnowiec had a useful institution of its own. An institution that is necessary and ought to be dear to every cultured Jew and intelligent person, an institution that should and could have been served by the local Jewish doctors; the institution watches over hygienic conditions among Jews, heals the sick and brings a little light and air onto the darkened horizon of the poor; the institution is called "TOZ" [Society for Safeguarding the Health of the Jewish Population]. And so, when Sosnowiec did have such a useful institution, people ran about with it over bridges and footpaths and begged: take this burden off us, for which we have neither time nor patience, neither strength nor courage. And besides, Sosnowiec has well-situated Jewish doctors and a whole pleiad of young doctors whose time would still allow them to devote themselves to the institution.
Is it not a disgrace for Sosnowiec to fling out such a useful establishment — and for what? Because they want to be rid of this "hump"? Are you not ashamed, Jewish doctors, to treat such a useful institution this way? Who if not you — you, after all, understand best its usefulness, its practicality, its plain necessity at every step in the smoky, stifling Zagłębie, where the air chokes and oppresses every inhabitant, not to speak of the poor masses!
We can still understand liquidating an institution when there is a deficit, when there are debts over one's head, but not when the institution has a capital of a thousand zł., at a time when its pillars declare that with 1,500 zł. one could simply work wonders.
Is such a kind of tactic understandable and comprehensible? Should such lawlessness be permitted? These persons must surely not forget that a communal mission stands higher than private matters, in which everyone may do as he pleases and no one can tell him what to think; it is quite different, however, when one takes on communal offices — then one must remain answerable to the public. One must give an account, say why one wants to liquidate without cardinal reasons, without proper motives; capricious one may be in private matters, which do not concern the public at all.
Here too a "taker" was sought for the burden, and it was brought into Będzin, so that it gives the impression as if one had said: take the corpse for yourselves, we have neither strength nor time for it; you put a soul into it, cover its bones with skin and flesh and make of it a living creature for yourselves.
This is the high level at which the Sosnowiec Jewish intelligentsia stands, and this is how they understand their communal duties.
Selekt.
Three Little Diplomatic Letters (In the Name of All Israel)

[Feuilleton — political humour; the Jews and the three great powers: the United States, England, Soviet Russia.]
By Pini Baal-Loshn.
My readers give me no peace. They literally swamp me with letters full of questions, and the questions demand answers; they want to know where we stand in the world!...
That is to say, properly speaking, they only want to know about the three greatest world powers: how we stand with them and how they stand with us.
The other states, they say, do not interest them so much, and one really cannot know anything about them anyway: the German, for example, does not himself know where he stands in the world. The Romanian is simply not a human being, he listens to nobody in the world — a state, that is, of „the deaf-mute, the imbecile and the minor“; well, and elsewhere we simply have only a small part of our Jews left.
The main thing, my Jews say, is that they want to know about the three great ones of the world: Uncle Sam, John Bull and Red Fonye [the Jewish nickname for the Russian]!!
The eyes of the whole Jewish people are, after all, turned on them and want a clear answer: are Jews there Jews, or human beings? Are we loved or hated?...
And when the readers demand, nothing helps. What do we not do for the sake of our readers? — so I rolled up my sleeves and wrote three little diplomatic letters to the three states in the name of all Israel.
1.
Dear Uncle Shmuel, called „Uncle Sam“, in the land of America!
First, I come to inform you that all the 4 and a half million little Jews who are to be found in your country are, thank God, healthy and strong and have a good appetite; may the Almighty only grant them something to go with the health and with the appetite! May we hear the same from you!
And secondly, know that I am not writing now in my own name, but in the name of all your Jewish citizens.
True, they do not complain, God forbid, about you, dear Uncle; they have not lost their fathers' fortunes on you. As much as they brought over to you they still possess, and with a surplus, and therefore they truly love you.
And you yourself, good Uncle, have not lost your grandmother's inheritance on them either. They have worked your country up for you — may it be no worse in the future. Just take a deliberate look at New York, at Chicago, at Philadelphia and the other big cities, and you will see a pretty bit of satisfaction, for which the whole world may envy you; and you too ought to have loved the little Jews.
I mean to say, then, that the match was a successful one on both sides.
And yet we do not know how we stand with you in the world: do you love us, or do you hate us? We are muddled [?] in the reckoning!
Here you lock the doors of your universities before the grandchildren of our father Abraham, although you have no official „percentage norm“ or „numerus clausus“; and here your biggest business houses cannot bear to look at a Jewish nose and do not want to employ people with a Jewish name.
In short, dear Uncle, let us know how we stand with you; let us not grope about in the dark. Do you love us or do you hate us?
In the name of the Jews who demand an answer.
Your faithful nephew, Pini.
2.
Dear friend Yochanan Ox, called „John Bull“, in the land of England!
First, I come to inform you that we, the children of the People of the Bible, know that you have loved us very much from time immemorial and that you esteem us and our feelings, and for that we are very grateful to you. Jews have this nature, that they remember a favour that someone does them. The Jewish people is never an „ingrate“!...
And secondly, know that I am indeed writing in the name of the whole People of the Bible. The people knows explicitly that you have your own troubles just now, but then you have such a nature that you like to drag troubles upon yourself. The proof: here you have dragged upon yourself the Palestine trouble as well. You probably enjoy putting a foot in everywhere.
And about this I do want to ask you: we want to know how we stand with you in the world. How does it say there in the „Bible“ (have a look): „Art thou for us, or for our adversaries“? Are you out for our good or, God forbid, for our harm?
With the right hand you give us a „Declaration“, and with the left hand you smear it over with all sorts of colours — with red and with blue and with black?...
With the right hand you make us a present of the Land of Israel, and with the left hand you hang a lock on its gates, so that not a Jewish fingernail should be able to get in there?...
You do know, friend John, that the „People of the Bible“ is no fool; it knows the smell of fumes [?], and it cannot be so easily deceived. Therefore better come out with the whole truth, one way or the other, and do not play hide-and-seek with us; enough of pulling at our bones!
In the name of the Jews who demand an answer,
Yours respectfully, Pini.
3.
Dear Tovarishch Ivan, called „Red Fonye“, in the land of Russia!
Slushai [listen], Ivan, you are, after all, a fellow without diplomatic twists: you say what you mean and mean what you say.
So tell me, how do you stand with your Zhidiklekh [little Jews]? We very much want to know.
We wish you, God forbid, no ill; on the contrary, we want to see you as a decent man, the equal of decent people — chestnoye slovo [word of honour], Tovarishch Ivan!
But you should know that our hearts ache for our little brothers there with you, and we want plain words.
We know that all peoples are equal with you: all of them are, with you, in burning troubles, without distinction of nationality, and all alike are building the new world with you.
But, regrettably, we see that the Zhidiklekh are still not equal to all other people with you.
For all peoples you had enough, only for Jews not? How does that come to you, Tovarishch Ivan? You were supposed to show the world something quite different!
And here you even say that the Jews are, with you, the cream of the cream [?], and that you are going, God willing, to found even a Jewish republic (at the Jews' expense!)
Tell the truth, Ivan: does a „Jewish question“ still exist with you?
In the name of Jews who demand an answer,
Your former resident, Pini.
P. S. Slushai, Tovarishch! Do a man a favour! Perhaps you could make me into a bit of a lord for a while and afterwards send me away somewhere — either to Turkey or to Honolulu? Then I shall be provided with a good fee for my scribbling!...
—
These, then, are the three little letters, my dear readers, and as soon as I get the answers to them, I shall let you know at once.
But I must tell you that before we get the right answers we shall, God willing, I think, live to see grandchildren and great-grandchildren!
Is Cheapening a Remedy?

[Economy — article.] By Engineer Gershon Praszkier [?].

The catastrophic crisis, which has gripped every branch of the economy and from which all circles of the population without exception are suffering, compels the authoritative circles to take energetic steps in order to find a way out of the situation, or at the very least to make it possible to hold out through this bitter time "until the wrath passes" [ad ya'avor za'am], until the hoped-for better times come.

Since the village makes up 65–70 per cent of the country's total population, it is no wonder that the government has first of all taken an interest in the fate of agriculture. The situation of the village is truly tragic. The prices of agricultural products have fallen so enormously that the peasant has absolutely no possibility of providing himself with the most elementary articles he needs; the peasant is not in a position to buy any linen, clothing, footwear, agricultural implements and the like, i.e. all those things without which one can [thus printed; the sense requires "cannot"] manage if one wants to have at least a trace of civilization.

Wishing to ease the situation of the peasants on the one hand and to raise consumption on the other, the government has carried through a series of laws and steps for the benefit of agriculture. On the one hand the peasants were freed from taxes for a year and a half; on the other hand they were given a moratorium on their private debts. Apart from that, the interest of the agricultural credit institutions ("Ziemskie Towarzystwa Kredytowe" — the Land Credit Societies) was reduced by almost half.

With this, however, only one goal was achieved, namely, the situation of the peasants was eased. But in order to make it possible for the peasant population to buy the industrial articles it needs, the government has begun an action to bring about an equilibrium between the prices of industrial and agricultural articles. They want to close the so-called "scissors", i.e. that industrial manufactures should become cheaper in the same proportion as agricultural products.

To this end the government has thrown out a slogan: "Down with prices", and it has begun a fight with the cartels, demanding that they make the prices of their manufactures cheaper.

Is the fight against the cartels justified? Are the cartels harmful or useful at all for the state economy?

Before we give an answer to these questions, we must first make clear to ourselves what the cartels actually aim at and for what purpose they were created.

The cartels have three tasks: 1) to regulate production, i.e. to avoid over-production, 2) to fix prices and 3) to make it possible for the enterprises belonging to the cartels to bring certain profits.

The idea of cartels is therefore in and of itself quite a healthy one. It is better for the economy and for the state that enterprises should bring profits than that they should have deficits. An enterprise that has deficits cannot give the state any income tax, because it has had no such thing [income], and sooner or later it must liquidate itself... It is another matter that the cartels can become harmful and also dangerous if they exploit their privileged position to grow rich at the expense of the consumers. One must therefore control the profits of the cartels, but not abolish them. If only trade too were organized; the unhealthy competition is leading commerce to complete ruin. Free competition, which, especially in times of crisis, leads to the downfall of thousands of enterprises, is far more harmful to the economy than an organized trade and industry that bring profits. We take the standpoint that trade and industry must be stabilized, i.e. that all enterprises must be placed on such a foundation that they bring profits.

Proceeding from this standpoint, we regard the cartels as a healthy phenomenon. One need only, as said, control the profits of the cartels.

The government's slogans about cheapening prices will not only fail to achieve the expected goal, i.e. increasing consumption, but on the contrary: consumption is thereby becoming considerably smaller. The public holds back from buying the most necessary articles because it reckons that they will become cheaper still. For example, the sale of textile goods, especially of white goods (linen), was in January 1933 70[?] per cent smaller than in the year 1932. This came about not merely as a result of the crisis, but of the government action to cheapen prices. The public does not want to buy any goods because it believes that things will become cheaper still.

It is therefore far from a gratifying phenomenon that in the last month the savings in the P.K.O. [the Postal Savings Bank] grew by 115 million złoty. This is no proof that the situation has improved, as government circles want to interpret it; rather it happened because, instead of buying the necessary industrial manufactures, people prefer to put the money away in the bank and wait until prices fall even further.

The action to cheapen prices has thus led to 115 million złoty being withdrawn from circulation.

The upshot: the action to cheapen prices "rescues" [thus printed: "ratevet"[?]; the context calls for a word meaning hampers or ruins] commerce, reduces production and thereby increases unemployment.

The government can of course continue its action against the excessively high prices of cartel articles, but the action must be conducted quietly. Let it be announced after certain results have been achieved. But let them stop the campaign about cheapening prices, because it brings no one any benefit and, on the contrary, causes great damage to commerce.
Towards Intensive Work

(On the premises campaign of the Jewish Singing and Music Society in Będzin)
A year ago a group of lovers of Jewish folk music in Będzin set about founding the Jewish Singing and Music Society.
We knew that this corner of Jewish creativity had been badly neglected for a number of years, especially during the war, and that in the years of panic many treasures of Jewish creation were lost. At a time when, among other cultured nations, a mighty movement has arisen in recent years to go back to the natural, unartificial riches of the people, in which powerful cultural institutions have grown up, on the Jewish street this has remained without an echo. Only very faint signs have carried over to us from the great world.
There are no longer the patrons who would send expeditions into the Jewish shtetl — as An-ski and others did — and the work of the Jewish Scientific Institute [YIVO] meets with great difficulties. And precisely at a time when various pessimists want to see the decline of Jewish culture — when large parts of the Jewish intelligentsia are miles away from Jewish cultural life — when assimilation, in the most varied vulgar, crippled forms, is forcing its way into Jewish life — and the spiritual apathy on the street is great.
In Będzin it has nevertheless proved possible to gather around the Singing Society several hundred members from the most varied strata. It is not singing for the sake of singing. The aim of the society is — to raise the spiritual level of Jewish cultural life in Będzin.
The work, however, is enormously hampered, and without premises of its own — the society has the greatest chances of becoming the cultural centre of Będzin. We know how hard everyone's daily cares are today. The economic crisis is great, and yet we believe that the Jewish working intelligentsia in[?] the broad strata of the friends of Jewish culture will respond warmly to our appeal. Only a very small part of the members of the society have pledged contributions — we call on all members to contribute — a whole series of collection sheets has been issued, to which we ask you to respond warmly.
In today's issue of the „Zagl. Tsayt.“ [Zaglembier Tsaytung] we give the first list of those who have contributed, and we want to believe that the broad public will respond to our appeal as is fitting.
M. B.

Heard and Seen.

[Feuilleton — Będzin. "Heard and Seen".] By Ben Amotz.

They burst into tears...
Sorele is a "round" orphan [bereft of both father and mother], barely 6 years old, yet she has already soaked up a great deal of trouble, pain, want and misery. Having lost her father and mother within a short time, she, the little one, was taken in by an uncle, a brother of her late mother — himself a poor man, burdened with children, unemployed; there is not enough for his own children, and here, if you please, comes an addition as well
— a 6-year-old little orphan girl...
But the Almighty, as it were, is after all a father of orphans, and His emissaries — a few women and men communal workers in Będzin, not pious people, but warm hearts they do have, hearts that absorb the quiet groans of
— helpless little children, little orphans...
And a building — not quite finished yet, it is true — God's emissaries have put up, and into the warm nest of the orphans' home Sorele was received.
And when Sorele saw in her new home that people smile at her, speak a tender word to her, wash her, that she eats good food, and has a bed to sleep in too, she said a quiet prayer:
— "Praised be God that I am here already"...
The children around her, who are being brought up in the "orphans' home", on hearing Sorele's words
— burst into tears...

How much longer?
Many times already we have asked the same question: — "How much longer shall we have no little bit of respect for ourselves? How much longer shall we defile that which among other peoples is like a sanctuary?
After all, we already have a whole pleiad of actors who, with their artistic abilities, can measure themselves against the greatest theatrical geniuses of the non-Jewish world; after all, we possess a Dr. Baratov, a Maurice Schwartz, a Zygmunt Turkow, an Ida Kamińska and many others of whom we ought to be proud — and yet
And yet one's face turns red with shame on hearing and seeing the behaviour of that section of theatre-goers to whom it makes no difference who is playing — Cwilich or Ida Kamińska... and they profane the seriousness with their uncouth shouts, as in the market halls:
— "Kopl, want a biscuit? — Here you are!...
We have artists, friends of Jewish culture, and we also have
— loutish gallery-rowdies.
Other nations, too, possess this class, but among them there is respect. Their common man will not dare to come to a serious performance. For him a sensational cinema film is enough. Among us, on the other hand, among the people of "Thou hast chosen us", it is "all of one piece".
— "They're playing theatre — so I've got to go".
And they are right, the grown-up young men, lovers of Jewish art. With bitterness they ask themselves the aching question:
— How much longer?

A lively report...
Believe me, one commits a grave sin when one permits oneself to utter a bad word about the Będzin kehilla board members. These are people, I tell you, who are as well versed in the laws of economics as a Jew is in "Ashrei"...
In what connection has this come up?
Before us lies the report on the budget for the year 1932. The report contains very interesting figures, figures which prove the "lively" activity of our public representatives, may they live long.
From the report we learn that out of the 43 thousand zł. budgeted for the religious functionaries, no less than 6,864 zł. was paid out. The widows Graubart and Manela did not receive a single grosz of the sums budgeted for them, amounting to 7,500 zł.... and the pensions for the rabbinical judges (moyre-tsedek) Melner[?] and Frydberg remained untouched in the budget...
— Subsidies? Who ever mentions their name? It is enough that they are entered; paying them out is not necessarily required. Even the 100 gulden [złoty] — a fixed allowance of 2 gulden a week — which the public representatives designated for the Jewish hospital in Sosnowiec were not given either...
But be that as it may, recognition they do deserve, our kehilla board members: "whatever they are, they are", but spendthrifts they are not... It is no trick — they say — to prosper with big budgets; the main thing is — "thrift".
— To pay out no pensions and no subsidies; let the officials perish of hunger, let orphans suffer want — those are trifles; the main thing is that the kehilla's assets "grow".
— 155 thousand złoty the kehilla owes.
— A lively report...

Their eyes have been opened...
Young and old, girls, women, people in short [modern] dress and Hasidic Jews too were to be seen last Saturday night at the railway station in Będzin.
The crowd had come to see off the group of girls who were leaving for the Land of Israel.
Of the whole assembled crowd I was interested only in the Jews with the velvet caps on their heads. — What are they doing here at this celebration? Surely these are the ones well known to us for their fanatical hatred of Zionism, of the "heretics"?..
And meanwhile I am reminded of the following little story:
It happened in a cheder where the young generation is brought up to be great mortal enemies of Zionism. A pupil was late in coming to cheder.
— Why were you late? — asks the melamed.
— Rebbe, I couldn't come, our cat "had kittens".
— You rascal, you — the melamed shouts louder — playing with an unkosher cat?
— Rebbe, I performed a "mitzvah". One black kitten I named "Zionist" and the white ones — "Orthodox".
— Upon my life, a fine lad; your holy work ought to be reported to our great man of the generation, the kehilla president; he will surely buy you a little Chumash...
A short time later the cream of the "Agudah" gathered in the cheder.
— Well, Shmuelikl — the melamed turns to the boy — do tell what you did with the kittens?
— It was like this: the black kitten was called "Zionist" and the white ones — Orthodox, but now they are all called "Zionists".
— What? What sort of change is that? What has suddenly happened?
— Their — says Shmuelikl
— little eyes have opened...
That is the story. The moral you will surely understand yourselves...
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Yitro)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Yitro
The Portion
—o—
a) "Who delivered you out of the hand of the Egyptians... who delivered the people from under the hand of the Egyptians" (Ex. 18:10)
The words "out of the hand of the Egyptians" Onkelos renders "mi-yeda de-Mitzra'ei" [from the hand of the Egyptians], and the last words, "from under the hand of the Egyptians", he renders "mi-tehot marvat Mitzra'ei" [from under the dominion of the Egyptians],
because "who delivered the people" — through the redemption the people was freed "from under the dominion of the Egyptians", from Egyptian bondage. By contrast, "who delivered you" — you, the leaders, were saved through the redemption "from the hand of the Egyptians", from the Egyptian hand that is stretched out flatteringly to the leaders in order to enslave the people... After Toldot Adam.
—o—
b) "And there Israel encamped before the mountain" (Ex. 19:3 [as printed])
"As one man, with one heart. But all the other encampments were with grumbling and strife." Mekhilta.
See: before the Torah was given there could still be unity among Jews. After the giving of the Torah there was nothing but grumbling and quarrels. Everyone fought over the Torah: it is mine, it belongs to me alone... Imrei Chen.
• • •
"Vayichan" [and he encamped] — from the word chen (to please, to find favour).
That is what unity means: that one man should find the other's opinion pleasing; not to insist on saying "day" when the other says "night"... Rashei Besamim.
—o—
c) "Hating unjust gain" (Ex. 18:21)
Rabbi Ahrele, the rabbi of Vilkomir [Wiłkomierz / Ukmergė], was a great Torah scholar and an even greater pauper. In his old age the parnasim [community wardens] wanted to add a few more kopecks a week to his salary, so that he should no longer suffer such want; he refused.
— To eat — he answered the parnasim — I have, after all; and to go on taking money from the community and leave it to the children — why, that is robbing the public...
• • •
The "Ibn Ezra" compares Moses' words (in Deuteronomy) with Jethro's:
"Get us [sic] wise and understanding men" corresponds to "God-fearing", because one can be pious only if one is wise and understanding as well. And "and known" corresponds to "hating unjust gain", because a lover of money has to be recognised at first glance...
—o—
d) "Then you shall be My own treasure" (Ex. 19:5)
"You shall be My own treasure", "and you shall be to Me a kingdom of priests" — with Me, at any rate, you will be the chosen ones; but you, among yourselves, do not take yourselves for "Thou-hast-chosen-us"-niks... Rabbi Yitzchakl of Vurke [Warka].
—o—
e) "And Moses [printed: 'asa'] brought back the words of the people to the Lord" (ibid., 8)
Moses had always been so used to "and the people murmured", to constant quarrelling and scuffling — and suddenly "and all the people answered together"? No: "the words of the people to the Lord" — that was brought about by the Divinity alone; the words of the people belong to God alone... Peh Kadosh.
—o—
f) "Visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children" (Ex. 20:5)
On this the well-known tzaddik R. Menachem Nachum of Horodna [Grodno] told the following sharp-witted parable:
A hungry lion meets a fox and wants to devour him. The clever fox says to him:
— What will you get out of me? Look, there stands a man, fat and broad-boned; devour him and you will have pleasure.
The lion answers:
— Don't you know that we are not allowed to eat a man? So God commanded the beasts ("And the fear of you and the dread of you shall be upon every beast of the earth")?
The fox laughs:
— You want to devour and you want to be a righteous one into the bargain? If you want pleasure, you must commit a sin as well.
The lion answers:
— I am not afraid of the sin, only of the punishment.
The fox:
— Eat; as for the punishment, God punishes only the children for the parents' sins ("visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children"), and what do the children matter to you?

The fox laughs at him:

"Rebeka" caused an incident in a public establishment

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism; entertainment.] An incident in a public establishment.
"Tango Rebeka" — in plain Jewish, Rivkele's tango — is the newest hit in the Polish revues, and from there this Jewish-sighing melody has passed over into the public establishments, onto all the dance floors; and it must be noted that even the green-ribboned girl and boy students, coming back from yet another little piece of anti-Jewish work, melt away in a rapturous tango precisely to the melody of "Rebeka".
The "Rebeka" tango finds favour with all the antisemites.
In a public establishment in Sosnowiec they play the "Tango Rebeka", and the gentiles are delighted; later a few Jewish guests gather and ask that the Jewish tango be played in their honour as well.
At one of the tables sits a well-known antisemite; he cannot bear the café (cukiernia) being ruled by "żydowskie" [Jewish] melodies. He is not lazy, and although already an old man, he drags himself over to the orchestra and angrily snatches the "Rebeka" sheet music off the music stands.
From all the tables people look round to see what is going on. The little old man is nearly bursting: he has already taken the music away, and "Rebeka" is still alive. The orchestra plays the melody without the music.
The old man fumes, his legs tremble. But the orchestra does not let itself be terrorised and finishes the tango.
The whole hall applauds.
"Rebeka" has won.
Julian Tuwim — Misery (poem)

[Poetry — translated from the Polish.] Julian Tuwim.
Misery.
The wrong cries out from the very earth,
The black and the withered cry out!
With women — dried-up bitches — beside us
We shall come out as a gang, howling!

It is here, it is here, our misery!
There are children like nightmares [zmory]!
There really are the garret rooms,
Dreary cellars and dens!

There are the wheezing ones, sick with want,
Whose blood pours into the bucket,
It is here — the green damp in the room,
Filth, a foul smell, sour cabbage,

Frozen, raw potatoes,
A cough, a chill that seizes the limbs,
And under the head — a hard board:
These shall be our songs of misery.

It was, it was in cold, hunger and thirst,
There is one who suffers and dies without a plaster [?].
There will be, there will be a dry bone in water,
A piece of black bread with sand, a stinking sausage.

It is here, it is here, the misery: a table frozen to ice,
Rags in the window, the clothes one single patch,
And a cry in the night, an accursed one, a holy [?] one:
Father, my dear father!!
Translated [into Yiddish] by Tuvia Boim.
A Few Complaints of a Będzin Jewess in the Land of Israel (3)

[Feuilleton — Land of Israel; instalment 3.] By J. Stawski, Tel Aviv.
So there I stood with him, poor thing, in court together with the whole bundle of neighbours — with the Yemenites, with the „Frenks“ [Sephardim], with the Bulgarians and with the „radiant“ lady-neighbour — of whom I learned only in court that they live together with me! Well, don't even ask what kind of a comedy that was!
Back home a „sendzia“ [sędzia — judge] is at least something of an „osoba“ [a personage], and here there sits an elderly Jew, with a pair of spectacles on the tip of his nose, who neither hears nor sees! Beside him sits, apparently, another „sendzia“, a younger one this time, but such a wicked Haman that he doesn't let you get two words out! Next to them sits yet a third, with a shaggy head of hair, like a priest's... and he writes without stopping: a word is asked — he writes it down! What for one has to write down all the complaints — I don't know.
In short, we were all told to line up and the „sendzia“ counts us — 17. „No more?“ — he asks — „a fine crowd!“ We are called up to the table, and the one with the „kutshme“ [kuczma — shaggy mop] wrote down our names, how old one is and what one does. I push my way closer and he asks me something in the holy tongue, so I tell him that I am a simple Jewish woman and understand only Yiddish. „Good,“ says he, „you may speak Yiddish.“ After me a young woman tells him that she understands only Polish. „Dobrze“ — he answers — „mówimy po polsku“ [Fine, we'll speak Polish]! Whoever came up, and in whatever language they wanted to speak with him — he spoke them all! I tell you, the young man with the „tshuprine“ [czupryna — mop of hair] really must know all the languages of the world! In short, he now asks me in Yiddish: what is your name?
I tell him. „Pshshsh[?]...“ — goes he — „what a length of a name you people have...“ and writes it down quickly.
— How old are you?
— What do you need to know my years for — am I walking about in your world?
— This is a court, and what you are asked you must answer!
— So I answer him — and add under my breath: a black year upon you!
— What is your occupation?
— Nothing.
— What do you mean, nothing — what do you live on?
— What business is it of your grandmother's, do you give me to eat?... I make counterfeit money — your piastres with the holes!
— If you will not answer what you are asked, we shall...
— What will you do to me? You'll send me back to Będzin — so be it!
— We ask you for the last time, what is your occupation?
— Tfu, may it come to nothing! What did you want an old Jewish woman to do? Isn't it enough for you that my children break stones here on your highways, and you sit here like counts and judge people on top of it!..
Well, I paid them back in full, just as it lay on my heart! Just imagine, I left the dinner on the „mashinke“ [the primus stove], where it will most likely be burnt to coal, and I am supposed to stand here and argue with them!
In short, the „sendzia“ calls up a young man and asks him: do you throw rubbish into the courtyard?
„No“ — he answers — „I don't throw any. All the throwing is only from the second floor. I can give you a sign: that the Jewess“ — he points at me — „once poured a bowl of water over my head...“
The „sendzia“ smiles (a diamond of a Jew — such a year[?] upon him!) and asks: but the bowl she didn't throw down onto your head?
„No“ — he answers — „not the bowl, only the water!“
They call up a second one, an American Jew, who has had himself registered here as 70 years old and still looks like a young lad — and the „sendzia“ asks him: well, and do you throw rubbish?
„I“ — he answers — „want to tell you, first of all, that I have no wife!“
The „sendzia“ tells him that he is no matchmaker and asks him to answer the question he is being asked. The American turns a little red and says: with us in America, it shows[?] — that since I have no wife I am one person — so what sort of rubbish can there be from one person?...
The „sendzia“ asks him again:
— Have you a kitchen?
— Yes.
— You cook in the kitchen.
— Of course one cooks in a kitchen.
Then how do you throw out the rubbish?
Into the bin that stands in the courtyard.
Then why is the courtyard dirty?
— The landlord has a sour-cream business; does he make the mess there himself?
— „Yes,“ answers the landlord, „I keep sour cream there, but what mess can one make with sour cream? I'm surely not going to pour it out onto the street...“
The „sendzhe“ turns to me:
— A neighbour has said here that you pour bowls of water on people's heads; is it true?
— May he have his years as surely as that!
— Shshsh... you are in court, and here one may not curse!
— If lies are told in court, I may curse!
— Quiet! I ask you to answer only the questions I put to you; so then, did you pour water or not?
— How should I know... as if I could remember it... perhaps I once poured out a pot[?] of water; so what are you afraid of, that I made, God forbid, a hole in his head!?...
There is laughter, and the „sendzhe“ rings a little bell and goes on asking me:
— Now tell me this as well: the landlord accuses you of throwing banana peels; is that correct?
— I, banana peels? May he eat as many bananas as I do.
— Then say, who does throw them?
— May a fever be thrown at the landlord; he throws them himself and drags 17 tenants [lokatorzy] into court!
In short, they went on to question all the Yemenites, with the Bulgarians, with the „Frenks“, and what they said I did not understand. The end was that the „sendzhes“ went into another room to deliberate what they should do with us. When they came back in, one of them read out from a paper a whole „haftarah“, and a young man who stood beside me gave me to understand every word.
(End to follow.)
With the Power of Faith and Trust...

[Będzin — Zionism, Keren Hayesod; article.] (On this year's "Keren Hayesod" campaign in Będzin.)
After a year's rest, we, the activists and emissaries of "Keren Hayesod", come once again to you, Jews of Będzin, to claim from you the voluntary Keren Hayesod tax. And more than one of you will surely shake his head with a feeling of dismissal and mockery, look upon us activists as people without sense, idlers, and perhaps also ask: are you Zionists not "mockers of the poor"? Where do you get the courage, the great audacity, at the present time, when all around a terrible distress prevails, when Jewish livelihoods that held out for generations are tottering and are being ruined and laid waste one by one, the arrows strike and aim at every corner of Jewish life, the ranks of the expelled, displaced Jewish masses grow larger and larger from day to day, and the worst, the saddest thing of all is that there is not a single spark of hope that tomorrow will be a better day. And in such circumstances and with such prospects you Zionists come and demand that we give away our few złoty for "Keren Hayesod" — is that not madness, idle foolishness? And we know very well that not only the ordinary everyday Jew will ask this seemingly sharp question; we know that even among the Zionists themselves there will be some who will join that "ordinary questioner". Yes, we take full account of all this. And yet, and yet we come to you with the bold demand to claim from you the truly blood-earned złoty for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel, and let it not sound like a paradox if we say that precisely we Zionists perhaps know better than you how to assess the economic crisis; precisely because we know better than you the sad situation of the whole Jewish public, precisely for that reason we have the courage, even the chutzpah, to come to you and demand sacrifices from you. We come to you with the wonderful magic word that is called Eretz Israel, which is the only balm that can heal other deep pains; armed with this faith and trust, [we] have the strength to come to the broad Jewish masses, to blow into their hearts sparks of hope and belief in a better future, with the striving for national revival and self-liberation; and even when it seems that all the appointed ends have already passed, God forbid, we come with our "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people" and we point to the single bright spark of Eretz Israel as the only lighthouse in our long, dark life of exile.
For fifty years now we have been walking our well-trodden path, and notwithstanding the various "stumbling blocks" we have had in the course of this half century, we have nevertheless, despite all the obstacles, slowly drawn nearer to the goal, and today Eretz Israel is no longer romanticism; Eretz Israel is today already a real factor in Jewish life, and all the "evil angels", from right to left, must say Amen against their will. It is enough to pay a single visit to the central Palestine Office in Warsaw, or to the provincial Zionist organisations, to be convinced of the great surge of the Jewish masses towards Eretz Israel; from the left-wing groupings to the right-wing "Agudah", all keep clinging to the apparatus of upbuilding that we have set up and demand certificates from us, begging that we give them the possibility of travelling to Eretz Israel. Unfortunately we are not in a position to fulfil all these requests, because our financial institutions, Keren Hayesod and Keren Kayemet, are today not strong enough in capital to help all the displaced masses who are straining with all their might towards Eretz Israel as the only plank of rescue. We know very well that the Jewish people will still have to give many sacrifices in people and money before we are privileged to see Eretz Israel built up. But one thing is already certain: no obstructing force is any longer able to hold us back in the process of liberation; it really depends only on our own efforts and achievements, and we do indeed have firm faith in the stiff-neckedness of the Jewish people, which is expressed in "the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied"; to spite all our enemies from without and from within we shall redouble our energy, speed up the tempo of creating and building, and with this firm faith we come to you, donors of Będzin, with our call that you bring your sacrifices — indeed, your złoty, earned with toil and sweat — for the upbuilding of Eretz Israel; and our voice is bolder this year than last year, even though the crisis in the Jewish street is greater this year than a year ago, because then the nightmare was a double one. An impending ruin of Jewish life in the lands of the exile, and in Eretz Israel itself, too, heavy dark clouds hovered, which darkened the beautiful blue sky of Eretz Israel; immigration was almost halted. The spectre of the various Simpson—Passfield—French reports lay in wait for us, and it truly seemed that all the appointed ends had already passed, God forbid. Quite different is the situation in Eretz Israel today.
The Arabs themselves have already become convinced that Jewish colonisation brings with it prosperity for the entire population of Palestine; they are already demanding that they be permitted to sell their land for the purposes of Jewish colonisation. Today Eretz Israel is the only country that knows no unemployment; the government budget shows a surplus in its revenues; all the eyes of the larger Jewish communities are turned to the small corner, Eretz Israel, as the only land of reception for the suffering Jewish masses, and therefore it is not alms that we ask of you, not philanthropy, but self-help for yourselves and your children. Eretz Israel has today become a personal matter for every individual Jew, and no one knows whether a moment will not come when he will need Eretz Israel as the only way out in his life. Still more must we think of our children, our youth, who are in the greatest despair, who see no future whatsoever before them. Therefore every Jew must render account to himself and know that with his contribution to "Keren Hayesod" he is at the same time building a future for himself and his children; and who knows whether his children who are in Eretz Israel are not already now benefiting from the Keren Hayesod institutions. Therefore it is our duty to remember "the more they afflicted them, the more they multiplied and the more they spread": the worse the situation becomes here in exile, the more we must multiply our contributions, in order to speed up the building of the Land, to create a place of refuge, the national home for ourselves and our children. This is the sacred commandment of the present moment.
Nute Londner.
Oh, How Hard It Is to Part with the Carnival!

(A piece of her mind from a respectable girl.)
What shall I tell you, gentlemen and lady colleagues? Long live the carnival! Long live the winter!
What, if you can call it that, does such a choice[?] young lady [panna] as I get out of the sweet, bright summer? What — may I not sin with my words — can a landlord's daughter achieve in summer anyway? Am I to talk myself into the expensive outfits? My father, after all, is no tailor! If my father had at least been a certificated cobbler, I too would have stepped out on a par with the ladies; but may no one ever be born to a father who is a landlord, do you hear! I say: Father, a pair of little galoshes[?] — and the answer I get is: "Crisis!" I beg: Father, a little blouse — let it be without a sleeve, let it be half a metre shorter, just to cover a scrap of body — and he again answers me with the same refrain: "Crisis!"
So it really is as bitter as death; one patches things together all summer long and never stops scheming. I have an old blouse that I had made for myself at the time of the first revolution, with sleeves, wide at the top and narrow at the bottom — I turn it round, a bit of business, "Yokl upside-down": narrow at the top and wide at the bottom — a new fashion! If a hole wears through in my skirt, I set an artificial flower on it. If the collar of my coat wears out, I sew my father's tallit bag round it and I have a modern "fur collar"; and so I torment myself a whole summer without a break.
And taken altogether, what does such a young lady do all summer? Once again in the avenues and once again a ball in the park? What, if you can call it that, can one live to see? A young lady like me is already looking for something substantial in life... Illusions are a business for teenage girls [podlotki]; I am already looking for — deeds!...
And if deeds, where are there deeds more substantial than at carnival time?
When carnival comes, my heart grows lighter. I feel that I am alive; I shun what is stale, what is old. With all the fire of my soul I throw myself into the arms of life, and I live it up by day and by night — and a plague on all the men, and never mind!
What are outfits to me, what are toilettes? What for, little patent-leather shoes with packs of pleats[?]? What the devil for, silk tricotine dresses? I need it "na tysiące" [for thousands of] kapores!
I go up to the wardrobe and steal out a pair of my father's old trousers, which have already been turned to the third side, with a fair number of patches; and if they even have a whopping tear somewhere, that is no great fault either. On top I put on an old satin waistcoat, I work it over "po mistrzowsku" [in masterly fashion]; if I have shoes, well and good, "a ile nie" [and if not] — a pair of slippers is merchandise too — it is more original still! My face I curtain off with a roller blind. The troubles are covered up — and off we go to the masked ball.
It is here that my sweet dreams come true. What I think of and what I long for all year long is realised here. Here nobody fantasises! Everything goes dancing and playing.
Who cares about clothes here? My father's trousers, with the patches and the whopping tear, draw the crowd like a deputy to a concession; father's mouldy satin waistcoat is gazed at like a rare treasure; and since the little blind hangs over my "gęba" [mug], who can tell what is going on "za kulisami" [behind the scenes]?..
In short, father's trousers work wonders, the satin waistcoat rakes in boxes of chocolates — and all this when? — at carnival!
Ah, carnival! Beloved carnival! It is hard to part with you; how I would wish that life were an eternal carnival! That for ever and ever my father's satin waistcoat might be stroked and admired! That for ever the little "parokhet" [ark curtain] might hang over my mug, and the greatest swells [facety] might hop "Kadosh" before me and dance to the jazz band and skip the foxtrot.
"Żegnam cię, kochany karnawale" [Farewell, beloved carnival], vivat!
Honig Foygl ["Honey Bird" — a pen-name].
A King Who Ran Away from the Throne in the Middle of the Night (1)

[Serialized historical tale — Poland, King Henri de Valois (Henryk Walezy); installment 1.]
(A historical tale)
By Al—Be.
1)

It was in the year 1572. The Polish people was wrapped in mourning. The country had been left without a king. The sudden death of Sigismund the 2nd [Zygmunt II August], who had reigned over Poland from 1548 to 1572 — he died suddenly, without children, and he left no will as to who should be his successor. The Poles, who in those days were accustomed to monarchist comedies and games, began to tear at one another. On one side stood the szlachta [the gentry] with the great lords. On the other side — the Catholics with the Protestants. And besides them Poland had yet another trouble on the side: Lithuania — the one-time partner of the Polish state — had its own sympathies and leanings.
The internal frictions among the Polish people grew stronger and greater. It had already come to the point where a civil war was about to break out in the country. Because of the threatening situation the contending sides came to an agreement that a national assembly should be convened, at which a king would be elected.
The national assembly took place in Warsaw in the month of April 1573. Five candidates figured for the Polish throne. Lithuania very much wanted Ivan the Terrible of Russia to be elected king of Poland. The bishops and the majority of the Catholic magnates wanted an Austrian duke as king, but the szlachta had no candidate of its own. The szlachta fought only for this: that the Polish crown should be taken over neither by a German nor by a „Moskal“ (a Russian).
The opportunity was seized by Catherine de' Medici, the widow of Henri the Second and the mother of the then king of France, Charles the Ninth. She, Catherine, wanted precisely that her beloved son Henri, who was then Duke of Anjou, should be elected king of Poland.
As her helper in the matter she took the French ambassador in Poland, whom she empowered to use every means so that her son Henri should obtain the Polish throne.
The ambassador, incidentally a very energetic and cunning man, created by all sorts of means sympathy for the French candidate, and the result was that on the 11th of May 1573, in the turmoil of intrigues, corruption and acts of violence, Henri was indeed chosen as the king of Poland.
Henri himself had scant desire for the Polish throne; he was then 22 years old and was living the wild life, carousing for all he was worth, and here suddenly — become king of Poland. Still worse for him was that, before he was elected king, Poland had adopted a constitution which turned the country into a limited monarchy and a republic, with an elected king as president.
According to the constitution the king had no say and was not allowed to concern himself with the election of his successor; for a wife he must take the one the Senate gives him, and he may never divorce her.
This gnawed at Henri's brain — how would he leave his beloved, the Princess of Condé, with whom he was so much in love; but if mother says[?] go to Poland, he must go.
Henri altogether had no firm character, and more than once he had already submitted to his mother's evil will. Under his mother's influence Henri had had to abandon his Protestant leanings, which he had had in his earliest youth, and went over to the camp of the Catholic fanatics; Henri even helped his mother organize the St. Bartholomew massacre of the Huguenots.
In the year 1574 Henri travelled to Poland to take over the Polish throne. He arrived in Warsaw in the month of January, and already on the 24th of February of that year he was crowned with great pomp in Kraków as king of Poland.
The situation in the country became calmer, the internal frictions gradually ceased, the new king influenced the various factions in various ways to give up their plans.
But it was not fated that the Polish people should have rest. Thirteen months after Henri had taken over the Polish throne, Charles the Ninth, the then king of France, died at the age of 34[?] years. Charles the Ninth, a man weakened by debauchery and persecuted by his own conscience over the terrible Bartholomew massacre, which had been carried out under his rule and with his consent, departed this world still so young.
Charles left no children behind him, and the lawful heir to the French throne after Charles's death was Henri, the third son of Catherine de' Medici, the king of Poland.
As soon as Henri received the news that his brother Charles had died, he thought to himself: „What good is Poland to me, when the French throne has become vacant?“
But this he was afraid to say publicly, for he was certain that the Polish people, among whom he had already won sympathy, would not agree that he should leave them, and would force him to be their king to the end of his life.
The thought gave him no rest; day and night Henri went about lost in thought, pondering how he might leave Poland and take over the French throne.
At last he decided that the only way was to steal out of Poland by night, so that no one should know, and to make his escape.

What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The tax office carted back goods seized from a taxpayer

[Będzin — taxes.] [Page heading: "What's New in Zagłębie?"; date boxes: Friday, 21 Shevat 5693 — piątek 17 lutego 1933 (Friday, 17 February 1933). Section heading: Będzin.]
The tax office carted back goods seized from a taxpayer.
In the month of December Mr. Aba Małach received from the tax office a demand to pay a tax debt amounting to several hundred złoty. And since Mr. M. had already paid the tax several days earlier, he took no notice of it. Some time later, in spite of the fact that Mr. M. proved with receipts that he had already paid the debt, a distraint was carried out at his place, and afterwards 6 bales of paper were taken from him for the tax debt.
The paper was taken in Mr. M.'s absence, and on coming home he went off to the Urząd Skarbowy [tax office], where he demanded that the paper which had been taken from him without justification be given back to him.
The clerk in charge, seeing the mistake that had been made, wanted Mr. M. to take the paper back, but Mr. M. declared that he did not want to bear any expenses; rather, the paper should be sent back to him at the office's cost.
The dispute about carting it back lasted several days, and the end of it was that the office put the paper back where it had been taken from.

Theatre Notes

[Sosnowiec, Będzin — theatre and art.] "Rasputin", staged at the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre, directed by Director Mr. Tański.
Since the October Revolution in Russia, the heroes of the former chief opinion-makers at Tsarskoye Selo have been depicted both in the press and in separate works. Among others, the figure of Rasputin is also revived[?] in black colours — the persecutor of the Jews, a loathsome lecher and at the same time the right hand of the Russian Empress Maria [sic], who believed that "nothing will happen to Russia, because Rasputin's prayers will protect the Tsar's court from all evil"...
"Rasputin" by A. Tolstoy, which is being played on all European stages, is also being performed by the artists of the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre. The premiere, which took place on Sunday afternoon, had an extraordinary moral and also material success.
The artists, with Director Tański in the leading role, have honestly earned the success. Director Tański has created a splendid characterisation, has given a "Rasputin of flesh and blood"; he is above all splendid when he falls from the revolver shots in the apartment of his beloved Irena.
Very successful is the scene of the Gypsy choir and the dancers, with whom Rasputin amuses himself very merrily in a "modest" manner, while at the same time he telephones the Empress, "Mama", that "she should have no fear, because he is praying for her"...
The actress Czenszna[?], as the Empress, contributed to the great success. The role is as if made to measure for her, her manners are in place, her commands — bold, there is a scent of chivalry about it; only in the last scene is she a little weak.
The roles of the priest[?] Yusupov (Wojtecki) and Rubinstein (Orliński) — very good.
In general the whole ensemble is not badly set up, and it is worth seeing the play "Rasputin" in the production of the Sosnowiec Municipal Theatre.
Sz. L—og.[?]

"We Women" (on "Monika's Case") by Morozowicz-Szczepkowska. Performed by Ida Kamińska, Rachel Holzer and R. Lerer.
Psychologically complicated situations — that is the content of the modern play.
In "We Women" the author depicts for us, in contrasting types, the psychological effects upon the betrayed woman.
She has clasped together the highest radiant joy with the deepest pain of a human soul, and has given us a Monika and her antithesis — Anna, who does not break down after her erotic disappointments and finds in fruitful human work her aim and content[?] in life.
Monika, a doctor in a children's hospital, an energetic, active woman, loves Jurek — the elegant, pampered, pleasure-loving young fellow who, although he is the axis around which the whole action turns, is not seen on the stage at all.
The indictment against the "ugly sex" takes place without his participation. Monika is happy and enraptured by her love, and because it seems to her that if she bore Jurek a child he would be happy, she decides to undergo an operation in order to be able to become a mother. Monika tells her friend Anna about the great joy and happiness she experiences in her love for Jurek. She breathes with him, he is the driving force of all her deeds, her thoughts are moved only by him. Anna laughs at her feelings, which take away her independence and make her a spiritual slave; she tries to dissuade Monika from the risky operation, but the radiant and glowing Monika is not in the least impressed by the words of the ice-cold Anna, who knows nothing more than her architectural drawings, and she has herself operated on.
Monika falls ill after the operation, and Anna, running for the doctor, also goes in to Jurek in his apartment, where she finds Jurek in the arms of Antosia, Monika's maid, whom Monika had taken in out of pity because of the illegitimate child Antosia was about to bear.
The greatest blow for Monika is when she learns that the father of Antosia's child is her Jurek. Complete resignation and emptiness take hold of her, she wanders about like a shadow, wants to commit suicide. But when Monika learns that Anna too once loved Jurek and yet did not lose her willpower and lives as a useful person in society, the psychological change takes place in Monika and she goes back to work in the hospital, finding there the content of her life.
The author presents Monika's life with a simplified[?] sentiment that is not free of a very delicate, subtle irony. Simple words fall from Monika's lips, but the simplicity has its effect and grows almost into a symbol.
A finely carved type is Anna, who resembles her profession — architecture, where there is no room for psychological experiences. Cold, "misnagdic", the erotic spell is alien to her and she does not let herself be influenced by it. Clever and decidedly logical are her answers to Monika. But does Monika's tear thereby become whole again, or is it merely patched?
Ida Kamińska, with her great artistry, has shown that she can bring out of herself, as Monika, what is most valuable; simple everydayness, love, disappointment, betrayal she has raised with her artistic interpretation to the level of an epic. Especially splendid were her telephone conversations with Jurek; she carried away the spectator, who lived through with her all the transformations of her soul.
The gifted actress Miss R. Holzer fully succeeded in embodying the type of Anna, towards whom one felt respect and esteem. For her brilliant characterisation and juicy language she was rewarded with stormy applause.
Miss Lerer as Antosia performed her role with understanding and talent.
A. Lrn.

What Happened on Tuesday Night in Berlin?

Torah scrolls torn up. — Jewish homes demolished. — Jewish passers-by beaten.
As this issue goes to press we are informed by a Berlin Jew, who arrived in Sosnowiec yesterday, about the cruel deeds of the Hitlerites on Tuesday night in Berlin, on Grenadierstrasse.
The Hitlerites entered the prayer houses and synagogues located on that street and tore up the Torah scrolls; then they fell upon Jewish homes, dealt cruel blows to those present, and smashed the furniture and whatever else was to be found. They took about 100 Jews away with them, and it is not known where they are.
The wives of the tortured men, mostly Polish Jews, have turned for help to the Polish consul in Berlin.

On Public Collections of Money

[Law — public collections.] In number 22 of the “Dz. Ustaw” [Dziennik Ustaw, the Polish Journal of Laws] a law has appeared on public collections, which are regulated in detail by the administrative authority. Under the provisions of the law one must obtain, for every collection campaign, a permit from the administrative authority.
The permit is given only when the purpose of the campaign is not against the law and is worthy of being supported from the standpoint of the public interest.
Such permits can be granted only to registered associations, organisations that have the rights of legal persons, or specially created committees.
Only members of the associations or of related institutions, as well as persons invited by name, may take part in the campaigns.
It is not permitted to pay for taking part in a collection campaign.
The law provides for very close control of the campaigns by the administrative authority. Thus, for example, the authority has the right to inspect the cash books and documents, to take part in the meetings, and the like.
The result of every campaign and the manner in which the collected money is used must be reported to the authority and published in the press within 1 month of the end of the campaign.
The authority has the right to withdraw the permit at any time in case of failure to conform to the provisions of the law. In that case the authority may transfer the collected money to any social institution whatever or to humanitarian purposes.
Acting against the provisions of the law is severely punished, with arrest of up to 1 month and a fine of a thousand zł., or one of these penalties.
Both the organisers and the participants in the collection campaign may be punished.
Money collected without permits is confiscated and handed over to other institutions.
The law does not apply to collections in closed private premises, synagogue [or: school — “shul”] collections and the like (art. 13).
The law comes into force on the 30th[?] of this month.
It is clear that the law radically changes the system in use until now: a large number of associations and societies which have until now based their budget on the collection campaigns (“flower days”) will from now on not receive the permits. Those, too, who will benefit from the campaigns will have to fulfil various formalities, such as: keeping books, exact minute books in the language of the country, etc.
The above-mentioned law further provides for the issue of an ordinance by the Minister of the Interior, which will regulate in detail the technique of the collection campaigns.
It is therefore important that the associations and societies which must resort to public help should acquaint themselves with the law in good time and adapt themselves to its provisions, in order to be able to benefit from the campaigns.
Dr. R. R.

Exact Details of the Finance Ministry's Circular on the Possibility of Cancelling Tax Arrears

[Taxes — Finance Ministry circular.] In a circular of the Ministry of Finance of 23 March 1933, L. D. V. 11560/1/33, it is stated that, in order to remove from the books the tax arrears that are impossible to collect, the Treasury Chambers [Izby Skarbowe] are empowered to remit the tax arrears from before 1 December 1931: 1) in turnover tax up to 10 thousand zł. 2) in income tax up to 5000 zł. 3) in property tax up to 10 thousand zł. 4) in taxes on capital and annuities up to a thousand zł. 5) in land taxes up to 1,500 zł. 6) in taxes on immovable property up to a thousand zł. 7) in local taxes up to 500 zł.
The enumerated [sums] also include the share of the state tax; apart from that, the Treasury Chambers may also remit all surcharges to communal taxes, among others.
The Treasury Chambers are also empowered to remit all fines from before 31 December 1931.
The tax offices [Urzędy Skarbowe] are empowered 1) to remit taxes up to 100 zł., as well as fines, among others; 2) to spread payment in instalments (except advance payments — “zaliczki”) over 30 months up to a sum of 2,000 zł.; 3) to charge 3 per cent interest annually on taxes from before the year 1927 and 6 per cent from before 1930.
Whoever wishes to benefit from the said reliefs must submit an application, which should be reasoned.
The action of remitting the taxes must be completed by the end of the 6th month of this year.
What's New in Upper Silesia?

[Upper Silesia — news column.]
German newspapers burned and Hitler "hanged" in Katowice.
On Sunday large anti-German demonstrations took place in Katowice, organised by the Polish academic youth.
Before noon 5 motor-cars appeared in Katowice with students sitting in them; the cars stopped at all the newspaper kiosks, from which the students took away all the German newspapers, weeklies and monthly journals.
Part of the newspapers the students tore up and part they burned in front of the building of the Voivodeship office and on the Rynek (market square), where a huge crowd of onlookers had gathered, who greeted the deed with applause.
Then a doll was hung on an electric wire on the Rynek, representing a Hitlerite storm-trooper with a swastika on its belly. The assembled public reacted in lively fashion. After the singing of Konopnicka's "Rota" a demonstration procession formed, which passed through[?] 3 Maja Street. In front of the editorial office of the "Kattowitzer Zeitung" shouts were raised, condemning the provocations of that chauvinist press organ.
Soon police arrived, who did not allow any further demonstrations; the editorial premises of all the German newspapers in Katowice were under police guard.
As is being said, Sunday's anti-German demonstration is the beginning of a broad campaign which will be carried out in all the towns and townlets of Polish Upper Silesia.
In connection with this, the German government has ordered the German consul-general in Katowice to hand the Polish authorities a categorical protest because a doll representing Chancellor Hitler was burned on the Rynek in Katowice.

The Mortgage Moratorium Is Being Introduced.

[Law and economy — mortgages.] In reply to the inquiry of many persons we explain that the moratorium law on mortgage debts has been passed and is valid from the 1st of this month.
The law, however, has not yet been published in the "Dz. Ustaw" (Dziennik Ustaw, the Journal of Laws), and therefore one cannot yet rely on it. But in the coming days it will be published.
One may take steps in court to obtain a stay of auctions (licytacje) on the strength of the law.
The mortgage moratorium applies to all debts that are entered on the mortgage register, urban and rural alike. It also applies to debts with which one has oneself gone onto the mortgage register.
The moratorium applies to mortgage debts and to mortgage guarantees on account of which the house is put up for auction.
