Antisemitism, Antisemitism, Antisemitism!

[Opinion article — antisemitism; Hitler's Germany and the situation of the Jews in Europe.]
Fifteen years have already passed since the war ended. And when one looks around at what has been achieved, one cannot become very enthusiastic.
The world has changed greatly in recent years. Political life in all countries has changed especially greatly. In many of them a complete upheaval has taken place in this time.
Mighty thrones have fallen, and on their ruins republics have been built which were formerly bound as if with chains to larger, stronger states; they were set up, freed themselves from their former dependence and became free, independent.
The whole appearance of Europe has changed in a remarkable way. In place of a handful of great states, which formerly spread out over the length and breadth of Europe, there sprang up after the war, like mushrooms after rain, little statelets with independent governments, their own parliaments and their own presidents.
Some of them are as small as vipers [„pipernoters“], but they put on great airs; in everything they still play the great ones; they have great ambitions, great appetites and big mouths.
Had the great countries behaved decently, the tiny ones, the poor neighbours, would presumably have imitated them too, and they would have been quite respectable little republics. But the trouble is that in the great countries, too, everything somehow lands butter-side down, and from the smaller ones one can no longer expect much. The little one chews what the big one spits out.
We have before us a series of European countries which came to life after the war as free, independent republics — but what do we see in them?
Their economic condition is a wretched one: the people there live in want, in poverty. For years now a bitter crisis has reigned, which chokes the population as if with pincers.
And under the effect of the need, of the crisis, people are disappointed, embittered and in despair. They are ready to give up all the political gains which they barely, with great trouble, won through a hard struggle of many years — if only to be fed, if only to have work and the means of life for themselves and their family.
The disappointment and bitterness have brought it about that many people who were formerly steel and iron for a republic have cooled, have become indifferent to political freedom, to civil rights, for which they formerly fought.
And some of them, the most short-sighted, the most naive, have not only cooled but have even become hostile to the republican idea; they have become ready to sell the birthright for a pot of lentils to every political adventurer, to every political charlatan and demagogue who wants to exploit the citizen's weak nerves, his discontent and bitterness. Such a demagogue promises great good fortune, mountains of gold — and the credulous citizen stretches out his arms to him with a cry of woe:
„Come, take me, rule over me, but give me bread, a dwelling and clothes!“...
The victim is the citizen, and the worst victim is the Jew.
The European Jew now thrashes about as in a net from which it is hard to disentangle oneself. The ground is taken away from under his feet, the dry piece of bread is torn out of his mouth, the doors to all occupations, to all kinds of work, are barred to him; and when he clutches at the only little branch that is left, at trade, fingers are pointed at him angrily and people shout:
„Speculator, huckster! Parasite!“
Just as in the old times, the Jew is now still a stranger, a stepchild, in part of the European countries; whether in the great ones or in the small ones, everywhere he is treated like a stepchild.
The present Hitlerite Germany has now become even worse for the Jews than Tsarist Russia, which became sadly famous for its decrees and persecutions against Jews and for its bloody pogroms. Jews flee from Germany as from a plague. In cultured Germany, in the land of Heine, Goethe, Einstein, a Jew cannot be sure of his life, because a former non-commissioned officer has taken possession of the minds of the Germans. The same German who is enraptured by his Schiller, or who perhaps once also immersed himself in the philosophy of Kant, now bows his head low before the former Austrian soldier and begs him:
„Führer, redeemer, save us!“
And in his idolisation of the new German hero, the German „Michel“ grabs a stick and goes to beat Jews.
This is a picture that can strike terror and can cast the deepest melancholy upon a person. Faith in culture, in human nature and in progress in general is lost.
If in the year 1933, in the age of radio and aeroplanes, in the age of democracy and of socialist ideas, a Jew cannot show himself freely and safely in the heart of Europe, in learned, educated Germany — where, then, do we stand with all our culture, with all our human progress and with man in general?...
The present German reaction is therefore not only a misfortune for the Jews alone; it is also a heavy blow to human progress, to the idealism that lives in the minds and hearts of the better people in the world.
From behind Hitler's figure there looks out at us the ugly face of a cynic, who winks at us with sly little eyes and sniggers with a mocking little laugh: „Aha, you want culture, progress, freedom, brotherhood? Well, here you have them!“...
Hitlerism is the crisis of human faith, of human idealism. It is the sharpest expression of the old cynical philosophy which holds that human beings are by their nature wild beasts, ready to cut one another's throats, and that the only moral right that can rule among men is might, is the fist of the strong and nothing else.
The Jew, as the weakest of the weak, is therefore the first and the worst victim. He is helpless and defenceless. This remains now just as bitter a truth as years ago, as generations earlier.
He is now driven out of Germany, so he runs to France, to Czechoslovakia, wherever his eyes carry him, wherever they will only let him in and wherever they will only let him huddle up. For a while, yes, for no more than a while, for here comes a new wave of Jew-hatred, and he is driven on again and carried again across countries, across seas and borders.
•
And the well-known, the old tragic figure of the „eternal wanderer“ still stands before our eyes like an eternal historical question mark that finds no answer in the world.
Where is he to turn — that is the question which still stands before us, which has still not come off the agenda.
So it has been until now and so it will presumably be now as well; the history of the Jews does, after all, repeat itself so often and in such a scandalous manner.
Even writing about it, talking about it, is by now also becoming a little tiresome, because what one can say about antisemitism has already been said over thousands of times, on the thousands of sad occasions that Jewish life gives us.
All the words have already been said; all the arguments have already been used up; all the cries have already been cried out, and it does not help. And as before, a murky wave runs over the minds, over the hearts and over the conscience of peoples, and they again begin a hunt for Jews.
But history shows us many examples of how sadly all the wild, insane Jew-hunters have ended. They were all finally drowned in the innocent blood which they had shed. They were flooded by a new wave, which wiped away the dark leaders together with their bloody helpers.
No country has blossomed and grown up on Jew-hatred; on the contrary, every power that has smeared the wheels of its chariot with Jewish blood has been condemned to ruin; such a fatal ruin must come. It is unavoidable.
In this lies the inner logic, the inner meaning of history, its hidden justice, which displays its secret power and carries out its verdicts with a merciless hand.
History issues grave warnings to peoples and countries. But, drunk and dazed with narrow-hearted nationalism and with other such base and evil feelings, they do not listen to such warnings.
And later they pay a very heavy price for it.
But until the price is paid, thousands of victims fall.
The Jews have always brought the heaviest sacrifices. And they bring such sacrifices now too, after thrones have fallen and the world has become free for „democracy“.
Instead of a free democracy, there has grown up in great countries an iron dictatorship, which is even worse than the former monarchist power. Instead of freedom, there reigns an even worse lawlessness than before. The cynical philosophy of naked might, of the iron fist, has now seized the minds of millions of people. It is now being justified with brand-new arguments.
The Jew now stands on the ruins of the former hopes and dreams, disappointed, dejected, despairing, and with lost glances he seeks a place where he might be able to save his life.
And he now again asks the old, old question:
Whither?...
L. Fogelman.
"Up to Here One Recites on Shabbat HaGadol"

[Feuilleton — a satire for Shabbat HaGadol.] By Argus.
"Ad kan" — up to here one may recite on Shabbat HaGadol, and further one may not. What kind of lock on the mouth is that? Censorship, it would seem, we do not have, thank God, so why up to here yes and further no?
Is the point that a little further on the "Shulchan Orech" [the meal] already begins, and therefore you need say no more, because you might yet ask to eat?
So it is. Talk you may as much as you like; even if you can be[?] "button to button" [hand in glove] with the government, you may nonetheless complain of the "vaye'anunu" — they torment us — "b'missim", with taxes. You may speak and write, send delegations, write memoranda, hold protest meetings, adopt sharp resolutions — for that, after all, we have freedom of speech; but draw no consequences from it, ask for no food; for a bite of bread there are fitter takers than you.
Well, Passover is, after all, your time. You toss out a phrase: "Kol dichfin" — whoever is hungry, let him come and eat; but everyone knows that you say the Haggadah and mean the kneidlach, kneidlach for yourselves and for others. One would think, what of it? "Lechem oni" — poor man's bread. A fine poor man's bread — matzah with wine, with fish, with meat, with broth, with kneidlach — seasoned with charoset, and afikoman for a bite afterwards! And all Jews must have this, without exception! If a man has none himself, the neighbour gives, and if the neighbour has none either, it is sent from America.
Imagine: today America is no longer flush, she herself has nothing — how [where] is the Zaglembie "Center" [the Zagłębie landsmen's centre in America] with its thousands of dollars for Passover? It has its own bundle [of troubles] there, its own maot chitim [Passover relief], its own "old-age home"; and while we sit here with our families at the Seders and fiery sermons are delivered in honour of Passover, over there our landsmen will sit with silk skullcaps on their heads and they will deliver the sermons, melting into sweet memories of the dear old home...
But never mind, "Będzin is not yet widowed"; money there is none, but the town has honour: it will share its last, it will not abandon a brother, it will not break the tradition — on Passover a Jew must not be hungry.
So be it, Passover is your time — but Shabbat HaGadol as well? We in Poland cannot[?] live on so grand a scale. Shabbat HaGadol is no aristocrat; one still eats chametz, and for chametz all the laws are in force — I mean the lawlessness of the land, that "Yehudi b'lo" [the Jew — without]: for the Jew there is none.
The bit of reciting we do not begrudge you, with all our heart. On the contrary, talk away your troubles, your hunger; whom can it bother? And know, by the way, that Poland is after all not Egypt: see, Pharaoh did not want to let you out of Egypt, while as far as we are concerned you may go in good health. Ah, they don't let you in? And did they ever? Why indeed should you not obey Jabotinsky and organize an army? For us it is even better: as long as you are here, you will strengthen the militarist spirit among us; when we need it, you will help us eagerly, you will even march in front, like[?] the "chalutz" [vanguard] of old. And later, when you want to set out on your way, we shall send you off with timbrels and dances, we shall even give you our heartfelt blessing for the road — why not?
"Reciting" is altogether a precious gift for all the oppressed and tormented. The "voice, the voice of Jacob" we do not begrudge you, with all our heart; first of all, when the mouth is busy talking, one cannot eat. You surely remember the story of those two beggars who sat at one bowl: one of them felt like talking, and he talked so long, telling stories, until the other had emptied the whole bowl. We too, after all, have a "Pascha" [Easter], but of a Haggadah we know nothing — we go straight to the "Shulchan Orech".
You like to talk — talk in good health! Once you used to spend days on praying and studying; today you soak in speeches: before the elections — speeches, after the elections — speeches, in parliament — speeches; first — promises, afterwards — protests; on Passover, at the Seder — Haggadah. Before eating, Haggadah after eating; every bite of yours is dipped in a quart of reciting, and even Shabbat HaGadol — reciting too, Haggadah too...
So it is "ad kan", little brothers! Before the kneidlach you must stop — no kneidlach will be given.
Passover is your chance, but Shabbat HaGadol is chametz-like, weekday-like, hungry — no privileges whatsoever.
Up to here one recites on Shabbat HaGadol...
Our Balance Sheet

[Zagłębie — society and culture; article.] By Dr. P. Widerman.
(After the meeting of the Jewish Society for Landkentenish [knowledge of the land; Żydowskie Towarzystwo Krajoznawcze] in Zagłębie.)
When we turn our gaze to the activity so far of our Society, which is entering the fourth year of its existence, we can state with pleasure that in this respect it has been — intensive.
Figures will convince us of this best of all[?]. From the last general meeting until now, i.e. in the course of 1 year, the number of members has increased by 152 persons, and the branch now counts 302 members. It is worth noting here that, in admitting members, many declarations [applications] were rejected without any appeal, so that elements having no connection whatsoever with tourism and knowledge of the land should not be brought into the Society. And it is indeed thanks to this that a negligible number of members leave our ranks.
The largest item in the balance sheet of our activity in the past year is the number of outings carried out, which reaches 72, with the participation of 1631 participants. Some of the outings had an almost mass character. There were excursions in which the number of participants reached 100. The above-mentioned figures are the best proof that the idea of knowing the land has found the proper echo in the Jewish society of Zagłębie.
The outings mostly had a local character: 1) because Zagłębie, together with neighbouring Silesia, contain within them inexhaustible treasures for knowledge of the land; it is therefore no wonder that we set ourselves, in the first place, the aim of getting to know what is nearest to us; 2) the economic crisis, growing from day to day, did not allow distant excursions to be arranged; nevertheless their number reached 7.
This is not the place to give an exact survey of all the excursions. It is, however, worth mentioning 2 of them because of their special character.
A great mass of participants, which reached as many as 100 persons, was attracted by the excursion on the surface of the „Paryż“ ["Paris"] mine, led by Dr. Piwowar. The great mass of excursionists, despite the rain, listened in the open air for a couple of hours to the interesting exposition of Mr. [ג׳] lecturer on the subject of the geological properties of the Zagłębie soil and its natural riches.
No less important was the excursion around Będzin, led by Mr. [ג׳] editor Kantor-Mirski, the brilliant expert on the antiquities of Zagłębie. The excursion gathered over 50 excursionists and left the highest impression on them. Before our eyes were revealed objects of high historical value, past which we had walked dozens of times with indifference.
Our greatest undertaking carried out in the past year is without question the tourist and landkentenish exhibition, arranged for the first time in Zagłębie. The large number of diagrams, precisely executed, gave a clear picture of our activity so far.
The exhibition of the photographic section was imposing with its large number of artistically executed amateur photographs. Besides this, various firms that have a connection with tourism exhibited their exhibits. The organisation of the exhibition demanded very much toil and work, but its moral success fully satisfied us.
Besides this, the rest of the work is carried out by the sections: the photographic section, the ski section and the lectures section. The first possesses a properly equipped laboratory for amateur photography, and arranges special outings and courses for its members.
The ski section spreads the so useful sport of skiing by arranging courses and ski outings, which gives us the possibility of penetrating into the depths of the mountains in winter and thus getting to know their splendour.
The lectures section arranges from time to time lectures on various tourist and landkentenish subjects.
From this short survey we see that we can be satisfied with our activity so far. This gives us courage for further fruitful activity.
Dr. P. Widerman
An Inheritance!...

[Satirical poem — a motif of the times.] By Leyzer Shikman [Lejzer Szykman], Sosnowiec.
(A motif of the times.)
A rumour: a Jew is to get an inheritance;
a bagel-seller, a pauper of a Jew, —
and one gets a somehow peculiar[?] feeling in the heart,
among poor people and among the rich alike.

A poor man winks with one little eye;
pretends he hasn't the faintest idea
how much, for instance, a bagel costs,
he pretends he hasn't the faintest idea...

Another, a rich man, asks just like that,
out into the world at large, like a simpleton:
"Dear uncle, have you any fresh bagels?
Well then, what do you think of doing when you get rich?"

Rascals choke with laughter,
joke and eat the bagels with their eyes:
"A millionaire — a bagel-seller in the street!...
Reb Jew, make us a gift of a bagel and don't be angry!"

The heir waves his hand dismissively:
"To the devil with you [lit. 'to all the good years'], you rascals, you „drabes“ [louts],
let the customers come up and leave me in peace —
I swear I don't know where one gets enough for the Sabbath"...

A rumour: a Jew is to get an inheritance;
a bagel-seller, a pauper of a Jew, —
and one gets a somehow peculiar[?] feeling in the heart,
among poor people and among the rich alike...
Leyzer Shikman (Sosnowiec).
A Little Hitler Tale

[Feuilleton — a parable; Hitler's Germany.] By L. M.
I do not remember exactly where I once read it.
Perhaps[?] it is Tolstoy's "Barbara".
The story goes like this:
Barbara Libshitskaya[?] comes into a village and hires herself out as a servant to a well-to-do peasant.
There things go very badly for her; she works hard and must suffer harsh torments. The peasant and the peasant's wife beat her, slap her almost every day — and the poor servant girl weeps, sheds tears.
Opposite lives a rich man, a nobleman. He sees through his window how the poor girl Barbara is beaten and tormented. He decides to take her into his house as a maid, to free her from the hands of her tormentors and beaters.
Here at the rich man's things are better for her, easier; she is not tormented and not beaten, neither by him nor by the members of his household. So a long time passes.
Once it happened.
Barbara caused some damage. The wife of the rich and noble master gave Barbara a slap.
And Barbara actually fell ill from that slap; she could not be consoled at all.
And when the rich master says to her:
— Barbara! Why, there at the peasant's they tormented and beat you every day. Why then is the outcry here greater than anywhere?
Barbara answers:
— As long as simple, ignorant peasant hands beat me, it did hurt, to be sure, but — it was the peasant who beat...
When hands of culture beat, it hurts more, and the suffering is not to be borne at all...
L. M.
Some Clarifications on Housing Matters.

Grounds for an eviction.

Under the laws in force, the court may order an eviction for an important reason.

The law does not, however, draw any precise limits as to which reasons may be regarded as important. True, the Tenant Protection Act and the Civil Code do enumerate a series of reasons that must be recognised as important. But this list is not an exhaustive one, and so in each separate case the court is called upon to decide whether the reason given is so important that it justifies an eviction.

In any case, the circumstance that the landlord himself has nowhere to live and therefore needs the dwelling in question for himself cannot be qualified as such an important reason, nor even the circumstance that the tenant being sued owns a house himself and can therefore move into his own house.

Rights of the tenant and the subtenant.

The Tenant Protection Act makes, in general, no distinction between a tenant and a subtenant. The same rights that a tenant enjoys on the part of the landlord, a subtenant enjoys on the part of a tenant.

In one particular, however, there is a difference between a tenant and a subtenant, namely: if a landlord demands, for example, of a tenant that he vacate the dwelling for him and move to another suitable dwelling which he places at his disposal, the tenant is obliged to do so in certain cases. By contrast, if a tenant demands of a subtenant that he move into the dwelling which he gives him, he must always agree to it; otherwise he is threatened with eviction.

Y. A.
Matchmaking, Heaven Help It!

(A monologue of a matchmaker.) Passed on by Y. Marshelik [“the Jester”, a pen name].

If you think that Y O U have it bad, then go, if you please, and put yourselves in the position of the poor matchmaker.

Him the crisis has really done to death.

A fashion has come in: love. A girl needs to get married, so she waits for someone to fall in love with her. She has a face like a grater. But she waits.

And what do you think the end is? Ask me, Yosele, the famous matchmaker, and I will tell you what the end is.

— The end is that when she comes to me, she no longer has the few gulden; crisis-shmisis — you know the excuses already. Love is what she fancied.

— But love — I argue — is surely nothing new. I remember, after all, that when I was still a boy, young people were already marrying “po lyubvi” [Russian: for love]...

— Well, so it was indeed bitter, one really did plough with one's nose before one caught sight of a few gulden from matchmaking. But it has never yet been as bad as now. Quite simply: people lie on their few gulden like a cat on the kneading-trough. The girls themselves are like that, and father and mother — like that too; they will not hand over the few gulden, do what you will. I have lying with me, do you hear, young men — one need only say a blessing over them. I have a doctor lying with me, he can be had for two thousand dollars; do you hear what it has come to? Two thousand dollars with a consulting-room — for a doctor! And when, tell me, did you ever hear that one could get a lawyer for two thousand dollars? As long as I have lived I have never heard the like. And what do you think is the case with engineers? Of pharmacists I do not even speak. I have pharmacists lying with me, they can be had for — for how much do you think? It is a disgrace and a shame for me to say it... And girls — girls like blocks of wood — girls who only two years ago would not have dared even to ask for more than a cobbler's apprentice, such girls, when I propose a lawyer or a doctor to them, still turn up their noses. Do you hear who is turning up her nose? T H E Y still turn up their noses! It is beneath them! “Why on earth” — they say — “do you keep throwing nothing but lawyers and doctors at my head? What use is a lawyer to me, what? Better give me some fine dancing-master”... Do you hear such talk? I must be made of iron, I must, that I can stand it...

I must, of course, admit that the situation is truly a critical one.

— But never mind, — I console him — the crisis will surely not last for ever. It is a crisis, no business is being done, so people lie on their few gulden.

— Well, and if there is a crisis — he flares up — what of it? Does one not need to get married? Must one, on account of money, let a poor girl be left on the shelf? I have a Rabiner [a modern, university-trained rabbi] lying with me — may I only have such a year, what a jewel of a man he is — and I cannot get even 15 hundred dollars for him. A girl is swooning over him, do you hear, so that her eyes are fairly crawling out of her head; but her father says that more than five hundred dollars he will not give. Five hundred dollars, he says, is enough for a male person with spectacles. I argue with him: “For pity's sake, Mr. Letshik, where have you ever heard of getting a Rabiner for five hundred dollars?” And he has piercing[?] eyes too, the swine. “Never mind,” he says, “let the crisis only, with God's help, last another two or three years, and the Rabiner will be had — do you know for how much? For a thousand gulden.” I spit in his eyes and ask him further, I say: “Do you know, Mr. Letshik, how many medals the man received from the two universities he completed? Three of them! Medals this big!” He laughs at me. “Medals?”, he says, “medals, my friend, are nowadays bought by the pound.” Did you hear such talk? Well, go Y O U and argue with them. I cannot any more.

The man, I see, is angry, so I do not want to ask him much, and I put to him just one more question.

— And how do things stand — I ask him — nowadays, for example, with a writer? Can a writer still get a few dollars of dowry?

— About writers — he answers me — I do not know. With writers I do not bother at all. With writers I want nothing to do. Writers should be killed. It is they, after all, who stirred up the whole commotion with love-shmove; when did a Jewish daughter ever know anything of love? They read about love in the storybooks. So they took a fancy to love. Well, what can one do, when it is so cheap?..
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: A Delegation of Respected Householders

What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 11 Nisan 5693 — piątek 7 kwietnia 1933 [Friday, 7 April 1933].)
Będzin
A Delegation of Respected Householders
They report to the starosta [district governor] on the sad state of our kehilla.
Last Sunday a meeting took place in the kehilla premises at which the sad state of the Będzin kehilla was strikingly reflected.
The meeting was in fact called on the initiative of a group of well-to-do citizens, in order to put an end to the conflict between the Chevra Kadisha and the present rulers of the kehilla.
As is known, the Chevra Kadisha in Będzin has not been active for several months, because the gmina [the kehilla administration] obstructs the Chevra Kadisha in carrying out its demand to buy a plot for a cemetery.
The policy of the kehilla president has led to the gabbaim of the Chevra Kadisha going on strike.
A larger number of householders began to take an interest in the matter, and they gathered on Sunday at the gmina in order [to put] an end to the dispute between the Ch.K. [Chevra Kadisha] and the kehilla.
The president, however, was not impressed at all and declared innocently that „this is not a meeting“...
Such conduct on the part of the president outraged those assembled, and a resolution was adopted expressing recognition and thanks to the Chevra Kadisha for its conduct; at the same time the kehilla president is called upon to hand over to the Ch.K. within a few days the deposited sum, with which — together with the sum promised by Mr. Fürstenberg [printed here: Firstenberg] — a plot for a cemetery is to be bought.
Meanwhile the kimcha [Passover flour relief] campaign was also brought up at the meeting. In the discussion around the question the whole sad management of the gmina came to light. And when Mr. Fürstenberg proposed that those assembled lend the kehilla several thousand złoty for the benefit of this year's kimcha campaign, stormy protests were heard:
— „What? To such a rotten gmina we should lend money? Let the poor people react to the fact that the president, with his management, has ruined the gmina“!
Then the proposal of Mr. Fürstenberg was adopted, that a delegation of 6 persons should present itself to the starosta and hand him a report on the sad situation of the kehilla's finances, and ask the starosta to put an end to the abnormal situation and to make it possible for the dozors [kehilla board members], who were elected as long as 2 years ago, to take over the power over the kehilla.
On Sunday the Shops Will Be Open.

This coming Sunday, on account of the Polish [Christian Easter] holidays, the shops will be open from 1 in the afternoon until 6 in the evening.
On the following days the shops may be open until 9 in the evening.
A Scandal in the Synagogue — Over the Proclaiming of a Ban on the „Foreign“ Matzot.

As every year, the synagogue beadle (shammes) last Sabbath proclaimed, in the name of the rabbinate, a ban on „foreign“ [baked out of town] and machine-made matzot.
The result of the proclaimed ban was that a scandal broke out in the synagogue on the part of the worshippers, and sharp outcries were heard directed at our rabbinate, which has apparently this time too forgotten the saying „Better that they sin unwittingly than that they sin deliberately“...
The Tax Authority and Members of the Assessment Commission on an Inspection Visit to the Taxpayers.

As is known, the assessments of turnover [turnover tax] for the year 1932 are now taking place.
During the assessments disputes often arise between the members of the commission and the tax authority, which relies on the „mesires“ [denunciations] that reach it.
For this reason an on-site inspection (wizja) was carried out last Tuesday at several taxpayers', to become acquainted with their actual situation.
Taking part in the inspection were the head (naczelnik) of the tax authority, the inspector and 7 members of the assessment commission.
The „Chad Gadya“ Game at the Slaughterhouse. — The Young Shochtim Strike and the Old Ones Take Away the Income Money from the Slaughtering.

Because the shochtim [ritual slaughterers] are not being paid their salaries by the gmina [the kehilla], last Monday they took away the slaughtering money from the slaughterhouse.
The young junior shochtim, too, have gone on strike for the same reason.
In connection with this, a meeting of the kehilla board took place on Tuesday evening, which adopted a resolution to call upon the shochtim to pay back in the money they took, and that such a thing should not be repeated any more. If not, the kehilla will draw the appropriate consequences from it.

German Merchants Reassure Jewish Firms in Zagłębie That No Harm Befalls Jews in Germany..

[Sosnowiec — Germany: the persecution of the Jews and its denial.]
In the last few days letters from the German firms have been arriving by the hundreds at the Jewish merchants in Zagłębie, in which the atrocities that are being committed[?] against the defenceless Jewish population are denied[?].
From the wording of these letters one sees plainly that one is dealing here with a systematic counter-campaign, which is being directed by some hand. They resort to the very simple method that is known to all enemies of Israel: one denies everything flatly. Jews are being beaten? Defenceless Jewish women and children are being murdered? A wild libel! All is hush and quiet. Not a fly on the wall is being touched..
The national and human consciousness of the Zagłębie Jewish merchant is, however, developed to such a degree that he knows his way around all these treacherous tricks and knows how to give the proper, fitting answer.
Among the many letters that have reached Jewish merchants of Zagłębie it is worth recording the following characteristic case:
A certain Sosnowiec merchant suddenly received, the day before yesterday, a letter from a German firm in Duisburg, in which the firm denies all the reports about persecutions of Jews and asks the merchant, as its "business friend", to communicate this to all his acquaintances and, as far as possible, to endeavour to inform the Zagłębie press about it as well.
On receiving such a letter the merchant was greatly astonished. He had never done business with this firm in Germany, and he could not understand from where his name is known to the firm.
It is worth pointing out here that the letter was a hectographed one and was presumably sent out in many thousands of copies.
After long reflection the merchant recalled that years ago he had once been in Duisburg and had bought from the said firm a magnifying glass...
And so a copy of an old invoice had presumably been lying about at the firm, and it remembered to hand it in, as one should, in order to send the hectographed letter with the denial and the "clarification"...
Need one add anything more about these sly little tricks?

On the Charge for Water.

Recently the question of the charge for water has become topical because of the new ordinance of the Minister of the Interior of 24 December („grudzień“) 1932, in the form of regulations on the water and sewerage installations in Będzin.
§ 17 of the ordinance says that the water consumed in every house, as well as the use of the water apparatus (meters — „zeygers“), must be paid for by the house-owners. This has caused a stir in the interested circles, and each side wants to interpret the regulations one-sidedly.
It is therefore necessary to clarify the matter objectively. The Tenant Protection Act of 1924 laid down in Art. 6 what percentage of the pre-war rent must be paid, as well as the gradual increase of the rent.
Art. 7 of that Act gave landlords the right to demand, besides the rent, also a separate charge for water and other house expenses.
Under point 2 of Art. 7 the supplementary charges ceased once the rent paid exceeded 75 per cent of the pre-war norm; tenants would then have been freed from paying for water and sewerage.
The ordinance of the President of the Republic of 14 March[?] 1928, which forms an amendment („novella“) to the Tenant Protection Act (point 3 of Art. 7), changed the situation, because under the amendment the charge for water and sewerage remains binding in towns that had no municipal waterworks on the day the Tenant Protection Act came into force.
House-owners therefore had the right to go on demanding that tenants pay for water.
The above-mentioned ordinance of the Minister of the Interior, which is based on the resolution of the Będzin provisional administration, does not mention the tenants' obligations at all and says clearly that the house-owner must pay for the water.
Since, however, the provisions of Art. 7 of the Tenant Protection Act remain binding, the landlord is entitled to demand that each tenant cover proportionally the bill for the water consumed.
Under the same ordinance every water bill must be paid within 14 days of delivery of the bill (Art. 23); otherwise the debts are collected administratively, like all municipal taxes.
Also important is § 15 of the said ordinance, under which the lump-sum („ryczałt“) charge for water may not be levied for longer than 3 years from the moment a given house is connected to the municipal water-supply network.
After that term the lump-sum system must be changed and the charge levied according to actual consumption, i.e. according to the readings of the water meters.
This change will undoubtedly reduce the charge for water in a large number of houses.
Dr. R. Rechtman.
Do Not Let Our Children Be Demoralised! (An Appeal to School Managements and Parents)

(An appeal to school managements and parents)
Sport, which is highly developed nowadays, has lately drawn in our school youth as well, who, incidentally, ought not yet to take part in various branches of sport.
Despite the fact that every school today has gymnastics in its programme, in which various sports games are played, our school youth nevertheless take part in various sports that are undesirable for them.
We mean the new gambling („hazard“) game of ping-pong, into which our youth has been drawn to such a great extent.
Day after day one can see whole groups of pupils going into various cellars to play ping-pong. In these premises the children listen to all kinds of obscene talk from the lowest elements, and how this can affect our children is easy to imagine...
It has already gone so far that, instead of going to school, they go into the cellars to play ping-pong. In the afternoon, too, instead of doing their lessons, they occupy themselves with this gamble. And all this at a time when every school has ping-pong on its own premises.
But I want to ask the parents of these children: do you know that your children spend their best time on a gambling game in dark premises among all sorts of persons?
Do you know that at 2 o'clock at night your children can still be found at the ping-pong tables?
Do you know that your children, instead of going to school or doing their lessons, are soaking up demoralisation?
And if you do know it, have you tried to react?
True, no single person can achieve anything alone, but why should a joint action not be undertaken in this matter?
As far as I know, the management of Public (Folks-) School No. 2 in Będzin has already begun to act on it. But it has been left without support from the other schools and from the parents.
A joint action must therefore be undertaken by the school managements together with the parents, so as once and for all not to allow any demoralisation among our children.
Let the school managements begin a strong campaign among the children against this gambling, not stopping even at expulsion from school.
Once and for all there must be an end to the demoralisation among our children!
Emer.

Ben-Zvi Baratov

[Będzin — theatre.] (On the holiday guest performances of the great Jewish actor in Będzin.)
He is the greatest Jewish actor we have seen in Poland so far. Some nine years ago Vienna discovered him. He became the sensation of literary and artistic Vienna. A master. He was compared to the very greatest.
Only later did it become known that the man who hid under the pseudonym Ben-Zvi is — Dr. Baratov. A doctor of medicine by profession, who had played in Stanislavsky's Art Theatre. His Yiddish was at that time, in Vienna, still halting. But in his every movement and his every word one sensed the great Russian actor.
He played in a melodramatic story by Gordin, “The Stranger” (“Der fremder”), but with Baratov it grew into a King Oedipus figure, into a Sophoclean shape, into a Michelangelo figure.
In the meantime he has played in Berlin, on the Piscator stage, and in New York with Maurice Schwartz. He has already settled in and become naturalised in Jewish cultural life, and yet: a “stranger”. He stands sky-high, set apart, on a pedestal; he has a good Russian schooling and European fame.
It is to be hoped that the Jewish theatre public will receive the outstanding actor warmly and that the performances will have the success they deserve.
The Great Obligation

(The difficult situation in which we find ourselves. — May we remain indifferent to these hardships?)

When people sometimes come to us from Galicia or from the Kresy [Poland's eastern borderlands] or from other, quite neighbouring places, they simply envy us, the inhabitants of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia. They admire everything here[?] — that people still live here, that people still trade here, that there is still traffic here as in the good old days. And by the way, it is no wonder that travellers passing through think so, when they observe the situation like that. After all, the trains and trams still disgorge hundreds of people here; after all, the movement, the traffic, is still a living nerve[?], which elsewhere has long since died, long since frozen stiff.

And yet we see ourselves as unfortunate; and yet thousands upon thousands of people go hungry here. Unemployment is growing, trade has almost vanished, and so have the artisans. The broad masses have long not seen a scrap of work before their eyes. If people from other places still see a bit of life here, for which they envy us, we are nevertheless sliding down the same mountain, [?] a great deal; a fairly large percentage has already reached this most abject state, which one does not yet see in the street, but which, on the other hand, occupies a place of honour inside the homes.

Yes, poverty is growing and advancing at a colossal pace, and it is no wonder: our corner lives off the coal mines and the ironworks [huty], which shut down work more and more, and the workers are being cut back; and we, as is known, live only off the workers. When the factories prosper well, when the workers and clerks are employed, the surroundings and the towns, the merchant and the artisan all live off them; but as soon as the workers' ranks[?] in the factories begin to thin and one begins[?] to manage without [—][?], it immediately leaves marks on our economic field, and then the horizon is veiled with dark clouds that cast terror on our inhabitants.

It goes without saying that it is the Jewish population that suffers first, because then no more[?] cash comes[?] into town, and the clerks and workers cannot go on paying their monthly instalments, which are so badly needed in order to keep the existing businesses going.

Taking all this into account, making a reckoning of all of it, we arrive at the conviction that it is no wonder at all that business conditions are so weak and that we are becoming ever more broken, ever more disintegrated.

The whole luck, or misfortune, is that the process of disintegration takes place systematically, which is why the misfortune does not hurt so much. And to the pains, however strong they may be, one gets used easily in this way. But when we look around and begin to draw[?] a parallel, only then do we see the deep abyss, the long way [we have come].

It gives the impression that we have before us a person, a body, which begins little by little, little by little, to grow weaker, to grow sicker, to grow more endangered, until it reaches a hopeless state; the family, the bystanders, do not always notice that stage; they see it only when it is already too late, when there is no more hope.

So it is with our economic situation: we do not see the continually flowing tragedy only because it arises systematically, because it moves at a slow pace. De facto, however, our situation is dangerous, unbearable, so that the burden becomes so heavy, the body so overloaded, that it can no longer hold out, it cannot carry all this on its shoulders. At such a moment a catastrophe threatens, and then one must stop for a moment and consider this situation calmly, in order to find a way out to save ourselves, not to let ourselves be drawn ever deeper into this dangerous vicious circle [lit. "witchcraft wheel"]. We are ruined and broken to the highest degree. Jewish society sinks ever deeper and deeper; the artisans' workshops are rusted and run down; the shops are opened out of habit — "upon my life, we would suffer no loss at all if we did not open them at all," so the merchants and artisans complain; our communal credit institutions have almost completely vanished from the Jewish street — so how is a Jewish artisan or merchant to run his business? How can they accept bills of exchange for their goods? To whom will they give them, since the last one has nowhere to discount[?] them.

The professional institutions, both for the merchants and petty traders and for the artisans and small manufacturing, have fallen apart, and at best they exist in such a way that they bring no benefit to anyone; they do not take care to raise their members to a higher position, to a better existence. True, earlier they did their members more harm than now, because once the members believed in their association with perfect faith and relied on it, so that it cost them dearly and they were economically ruined; now at least the sanctity of the association has vanished, and they know that they must not rely on it. That means that nowadays the members cannot weep[?] that the institution brings them harm. But is the matter thereby settled? Will the Jewish situation be improved this way — the Jewish situation [thus duplicated in print], which finds itself in such a sad state?

Yes, it is high time no longer to let ourselves be fooled; we must look reality, true reality, straight in the face; we must create the institutions we need, if they do not exist, and on the other hand we must liquidate the associations that bring us no benefit but only weigh on our body like a superfluous swelling. Our times are too hard for us to allow ourselves any luxuries; our situation is too serious and too responsible for us to allow ourselves to value lightly our most cardinal problems, our ideas of existence.

———

Each of us knows how hard our situation is, how unbearable it is to drag on our existence, our being here. Yom Tov, Chol HaMoed, is the time when Jews rest and when one can form an idea of how hard life comes to us. Let us in these days make an exact reckoning; let these days be used with full awareness of how we are to continue our hard, stubborn life.

Let us in these Chol HaMoed days deliberate on our existential matters; it must be established once and for all whether our institutions, our administrations, care for our affairs or not. As soon as we hand the affairs over to them, they must bear full responsibility; if not, let them not take public responsibilities upon themselves, for only in that way do they help to break even further the already weak public institutions, which ought to bring so much light and health into desolate Jewish life.

Let us in these Passover days remember what state we are in and who is entitled to seek means to improve it, because to go on letting the ship float without a helmsman, without a leader, is too risky, too dangerous. At the same time one must not forget one thing: those who take it upon themselves to solve public problems must be responsible for all their deeds; otherwise they must not take upon themselves this great obligation.

R. Let.
With Consideration

[Editorial notice — the paper's own advertisement.] Everything must be done (with consideration), and therefore, if you give it some thought, you will come to the conviction that you cannot manage without a local newspaper. So remember to buy the "Zaglembier Tsaytung" every time — it tells you what is happening in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia.
The Wheels Don't Turn...

[Satirical feuilleton — the economic crisis.] The crisis penetrates ever deeper into our life — it is growing organically into us, and no one will have the power to stop the wheel of history: not the Magistrat [city council], not the starosta [district head], and not even the voivode [provincial governor].

Here, you see [?] — conferences of the big industrialists keep taking place, at which people want to prevail on them to set the wheels of more factories turning; but the conferences end with a decision to call a second conference, and the second conference will decide..

You understand? Together with the wheel of history, various other wheels will also turn: a wheel of conferences, a wheel of bankruptcies, a wheel of relief campaigns for hungry unemployed — but not the wheels of the factories, because the manufacturers have no one to work for, unless [?] — orders for the military, and there are no orders. So what will the end be? We can already see the future as through a glass — it won't be so bad at all.

It is only we who are badly off; we feel as if an abscess, a plague, a scar [?] had grown on us. But the generation being born in this crisis, which will later take our place — it will definitely not be badly off. It will have as much notion of better times as a man born blind has of light...

What is light for, if it is fine in the dark too?

We are indeed badly off, because "we still remember the fish which we ate in Egypt"; but our children will know only of such "fish" and "meat" as are prepared from various plants..

And should someone ever happen to taste a genuine piece of fish of [?] meat (which, by the way, will be very cheap, since there will be no takers for it), he will make a wry face — it is indeed similar [?] in taste to "fish" and to "meat", but still it's not the real thing...

The coming generation will also not know the worry — where does one get the rent money?

Because after we have, little by little, one after another, been evicted and left under the open sky, the landlords will beg us to occupy the empty flats, even without money...

Our children will also have no yoke [?] of dressing [?], because holed and patched clothes will then be very much in fashion, and a pair of whole trousers will be put on only a bridegroom on his wedding night, just as today he is dressed in a kittel — a kind of symbol...

People who make a living will then be legendary figures (though they almost are already today). One will tell that he heard from a second, who spoke with a third, who himself heard [?] from a fourth, that he saw a fifth, who told him of a sixth, who knows of a seventh who has a living.

But the world will be so enlightened that nobody will believe such legends...

Nor will people seek posts as in our time, because that will be a "noble pursuit", engaged in only by great men, just as today they occupy themselves with seeking a way to Mars or to the Moon...

There will be no petty bankrupts in that epoch — no one will trust another with even a pencil or a box of matches; and should anyone manage to get such an "object" on loan and then return it, he will at once be sent to Rybnik or Kobierzyn [psychiatric hospitals]..

And since there will be no rent to pay, food too will cost almost nothing, people will dress in rags and there will be nothing to do, the public will constantly be busy marrying and divorcing — simply divorcing, so as to be able to marry again, and marrying, so as to be able to divorce...

For man is by character a restless creature — he hates to go about idle; he must do something and make a "to-do".

Yes, this question, you see [?], is a hard one.

Today's tax system will then be "music of the past" — who will pay taxes, and out of what will they pay?

And since in that epoch no one will hold with thrift — there will be nothing to save from — instead of today's "one-child system", people will have children without any system, and...

Instead of helping the state maintain the military, they will rather supply it with the military itself — the army will grow!

Then the voivode (a grandson of the present voivode) will invite the big industrialists (grandsons of the present big industrialists) and tell them thus: "Our army is great and mighty, only it has no clothes. So set your factories going, and we will give you orders to clothe it!"

The manufacturers will smile and reply: "A pity, salvation has come a little too late; we cannot set our factories going, because the machines have rusted and the wheels do not turn"...

Y. G. Shteynsapir.
Passover Delight (Oneg Pesach)

Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes around the Passover Haggadah.
By Yehuda Yafet.

a) One wise and one wicked.
All the commentators ask about the difference between the questions of the wise son and of the wicked son. The first asks: "What are the testimonies, the statutes and the ordinances which the Lord our God has commanded you?" and the second: "What is this service to you?" What is the great difference here — why is the first entitled wise and the latter wicked, when the sense of their questions is, on the face of it, the same?
But of the wise son the Torah says "And it shall be when your son asks you tomorrow" — that is, only the next day will he ask; first he does what he is told, and afterwards he asks for the reason.
The wicked son, however, asks before he does anything; he has not yet done a thing and already has questions and objections... Imrei Yaakov.
* *
Another answer:
Of the wise son the Torah speaks in the singular, "And it shall be when he asks you," because he asks alone, wishing to know the reason.
Of the wicked son, on the other hand, it says "And it shall be when your children say to you," in the plural, because he does not come to ask alone, but rounds up a crowd, preaches to them and mocks. Mesharet Moshe.

b) "He went down to Egypt — compelled by the word."
A Hasidic teaching from the Rebbe R' Ber:
"By the word" — with the mouth, with impure talk — "he went down to Egypt": one can be brought down into the deepest abyss. Rashei Besamim.

c) "And we cried out."
The verse says: "I have surely seen the affliction of My people in Egypt and have heard their cry because of their taskmasters." "The affliction of My people," the poor in spirit — "I have seen": God had to see this Himself, because about them the Jews did not cry out. "And I have heard their cry because of their taskmasters" — they cried out only when the taskmasters began to torment them. If you do not lash with the rod, the Jew does not cry out... Zikhron Efrayim.

d) The mixed swarm.
All the beasts and animals tormented the wicked Pharaoh. Strange was only the attitude of the dogs. They did not know what to do at the Exodus. At that time Elijah was in Egypt, so they ought to have shouted (see Bava Kamma 60b); and the Angel of Death was also in town, so they ought to have barked. They did not know whom to help, Elijah or the Angel of Death. So they stayed neutral — did not bark and did not howl, helped neither the one side nor the other: a fine way out for the dogs... Hegyonot el Ami.

e) "And afterwards they shall go out with great wealth."
God's intention in having the Jews borrow money from the Egyptians was that they should never again have any desire to go back. For a runaway debtor never returns... Beit Aharon.

f) "Who passed over the houses of the Children of Israel."
In Płońsk there was a Jew who particularly liked to buy in Christian shops. Once the rabbi, R' Yechezkel Michelson, met him coming out of a gentile's shop and said to him:
— Good morning, R' Pesach.
— What, Rebbe? [?] My name is actually Moshe.
— But you should be called Pesach, "because He passed over" — for you pass over Jewish shops in order to buy from the gentile...
* *
The sign that God ordered to be put on Jewish houses was a sign of blood. "And the blood shall be a sign" — forever has the Jewish sign been a sign of blood... Divrei Yitzchak.

g) "And we shall eat there of the Passover offerings and of the sacrifices."
A freethinking Jew once asked R' Mordechai Busker:
— What will happen when we already have a rebuilt Land of Israel with a rebuilt Temple — will we really offer sacrifices there?
— Ah — answers R' Mordechai — if you knew how many worries we still have until then, you would wait a little with your question...

h) Elijah's cup.
Why is the fifth cup called "the cup of Elijah"? Because the fifth cup corresponds to "And I will bring you into the land" — so it is Elijah's cup: him we are waiting for. Metziat Yitzchak.
A Quiet Funeral. A Eulogy for the „Obóz Wielkiej Polski“

[Satire — Polish politics and antisemitism.] A. Cincinnatus [pen name].
A Quiet Funeral.
A eulogy for the „Obóz Wielkiej Polski“ [the Camp of Great Poland — the nationalist Endek organisation, dissolved by the authorities in March 1933].
Last Tuesday a quiet funeral took place throughout Poland. The coffin was drawn by a pair of black-draped horses, and hundreds of wreaths lay upon it.
What was carried from the world of falsehood to the world of truth was a very young deceased, who had not yet lived even seven years. The deceased — it was the „Obóz Wielkiej Polski“. The hundreds of wreaths adorning the coffin came from the professors of the Polish universities, from the academic organisations, the corporations [student fraternities], and among them all stood out the wreath sent from Poznań to Warsaw by „the father“ Roman Dmowski himself.
Only a very small crowd followed the coffin, because the police did not permit the funeral to be held with a great parade. There was not even time to form a „funeral committee“, because the authorities ordered the „deceased“ to be buried at once. Roman Dmowski fired off telegrams to Warsaw asking to postpone the funeral by at least a few days, so that he might be able to attend the funeral of his „child“, whom he had raised and pampered, but the authorities were merciless. The Minister of the Interior ordered that the matter not be delayed.
Hence only the Endek deputies [of the National Democratic party], who happened to be in Warsaw, took part in the funeral.
The eulogy was delivered by the well-known Endek deputy Wierczak, and one must say that his speech moved people to tears.
„His mother went into labour — began Dep. Wierczak — not quite seven years ago, after the „Dziadek“ [„Grandpa“ — Piłsudski] had in the month of May [the May 1926 coup] driven out his grandfathers[?] and great-grandfathers, who only then held sway[?] in the ministerial palaces. It seemed then that his mother would remain a barren woman forever, and that not even a single „potomek“ [descendant] would remain of the great and famous family. But dear Romek (Roman Dmowski) took pity on his mother, and together they brought you[?] into the world. You, however, were not a full-term child: it began in mid-May and you were born in mid-December [the OWP was founded in December 1926]; you were a „seven-month baby“, and therefore your constitution[?] was a weak one throughout your short life.
O dear and precious „Obóz Wielkiej Polski“ — we placed so many hopes in you; we believed that when you grew up into a decent lad, you would provide well for your family, you would supply everyone who helped raise you with good fat posts for ever and ever. We believed that you would grow up a „chwacki[?] boy“ [a dashing lad] and drive out of our dear country all the „Żydzi [a slur for Jews], Masons, socialists, communists and plain honest people. You were born in the seventh month and died in the seventh year — is this not some fatal coincidence?“
And it seemed that, to our great satisfaction and joy, our „most humane“ and „ethical“ upbringing which we gave you would not go to waste; but the cruel Angel of Death tore you away from us precisely at a time when the sun warms so pleasantly, when your best and finest friends are making merry in the streets of Berlin, Munich, Leipzig, Magdeburg, when under the intoxicating influence of the sun's rays they show the whole world what „Aryan culture“ means.
Dep. Wierczak's speech made a strong impression, and some deputies were so moved that they fainted.
A no less moving speech was given by a representative of the academic youth.
„We — said the young academic — always gazed in admiration at you and at your father Roman Dmowski. We were always obedient children; we were taught that the „Żydzi“ make Poland unhappy, so we did not think much and decided to settle the matter. Instead of studying we took sticks in our hands and tried to sort things out [make a „talk“] with the „Żydzi“. Our professors helped us a great deal in this; they stroked and pampered us and always took us under their protection. And so we truly grew up into decent children. By day we strolled with the Żydzi, by night we used to visit the cabarets, the dancings, and let ourselves have a good time with street-women.
And all this we owed to you — „Obóz Wielkiej Polski“; now you have left us lonely. You have left us at God's mercy[?], and the „Żydzi“ with their „pachołki“ [henchmen] — the Sanators [the Piłsudskiite „Sanacja“ camp] will go on ruling against the will of the „national patriots“ and suck out the „soki“ [juices] of the poor, downtrodden Polish people“.
Tears began to choke the young academic, and he had to break off his eulogy.
With a Kaddish by Dep. Stypułkowski the funeral was ended.
The universities, together with the professors and academics, decided to sit shiva.
Condolence telegrams reached the deeply mourning family from Hitler, Göring, Goebbels, from the Latvian National Socialists, from Russian émigré „black mahnikes“[?] [Black Hundreds?], and from a whole row of other intimates and friends.
In the antisemitic International the sudden death of the „Obóz Wielkiej Polski“ made a strong impression.
A Queen Who Dies for Her Sins

The tragic story of Queen Mary of Scotland. Her loves and political intrigues.

When we begin to speak of the Queen of Scotland, Mary of Stuart, and of her tragic end on the scaffold, readers must bear in mind that the queen was brought up at a French royal court of that time, and moreover in a circle such as that of [Catherine] de' Medici — already known to our readers — the Italian wife of Henri II. Fornication and all kinds of debauched pranks, murder, all manner of crimes and killings were the everyday pastime of the circle that gathered around Queen Catherine de' Medici.
After her father's untimely death Mary Stuart became Queen of Scotland. And when she was about ten months old she was formally crowned.
Mary was six years old when she was betrothed to the French crown prince; afterwards she was sent to France, where she was brought up under the supervision of her bridegroom's mother, Catherine de' Medici.
For ten years Mary studied under Catherine's supervision, with the woman who deliberately, for the sake of her political aims, corrupted [?] and made dissolute her own children; in this respect Mary too was no exception, and when she had finished the "course" in Catherine de' Medici's school she was — being already fifteen years and five months old — led to the wedding canopy with the crown prince, who was the sickliest and the weakest of all the children of Henri II and Catherine de' Medici.
After the wedding Mary Stuart decided to return to her own home, to her subjects, and to make peace with the Protestants; her passage had to take place through England. The situation was exploited by the English Queen Elizabeth, who firmly resolved that she would not let Mary pass unless she ratified the Edinburgh [?] agreement, which had been concluded earlier (without Mary's knowledge) between England and Scotland.
Under that agreement Elizabeth's right to the English throne is recognised.
Mary rejected the demand, because signing the agreement would have meant renouncing her own claim to the English throne.
Mary's ambitions were very great; she did not accept Elizabeth's condition to sign the agreement in return for free passage through England, and on her own responsibility, accompanied by three of her French uncles, she set off straight home.
After a journey of several days Mary arrived safely in the town of Leith, the port town of Scotland.
The Puritan burghers of the Scottish port town had not known Queen Mary before; for them Mary existed under the name "the terrible whore of Babylon". In their pious fantasies they had pictured the queen in the darkest colours, and when they saw her arriving at the port they were surprised: before them they saw a youngish [?] woman, graceful and naive-looking, who received everyone with a kind word and bestowed friendly glances on the pious Puritans.
The queen's friendly attitude aroused tremendous enthusiasm for their queen. As mutual gratitude to the queen, the Puritan trumpeters [?] gathered around Holyrood Palace, in which Mary lived, and for a whole night they sang chapters of Psalms in honour of Mary in the Puritan manner.
———
The continuation of this most interesting historical tale our readers will find in the next issue, which appears on Friday the 21st of this month.
Lahle, the Prague Rabbi's Daughter

Moshe Feinkind.
(A Passover tragedy.)
Jewish Prague has long had such bitter luck that the Jews' beautiful spring festival was always just ruined.
The dark priests used to preach poison and gall against the Jews, that they need Christian blood for Passover, and the naive[?] mob, as always, believed what the priests sang and said, and then set about settling accounts with the Jews in its cruel fashion...
Therefore the Jews of Prague used to shut themselves into their "ghetto" under lock and bolt on the nights of "Leil Shimurim" [the night of watching], hoping thereby to protect themselves from the bloody attacks that mostly took place on those holy nights.
About one such attack the Prague martyrology tells us; it took place there on the first Seder night in the year 5149 (1389) and ended very tragically for the local Jews...
On that holy night the rabble, led by priests, stormed the ghetto with axes and pitchforks and burst into the Jewish houses, plundering and pogroming whatever came to their hands, and whoever merely dared to stand up to those dark savages paid for it at once with his life...
• • •
The old[?] Prague rabbi, R' Shlomo Prag, had on that tragic night invited to the Seder the bridegroom of his only daughter, Lahle.
Of all the young men who studied with R' Shlomo in his house, he had chosen him as the destined husband of his only, orphaned daughter...
Lahle, in truth, had long since cast an eye on this fine young man, who also excelled in great virtues, but she had to suppress within herself her warm feelings for him and hide them from people's eyes, since she was, after all, the rabbi's daughter...
But as a bride she could no longer contain herself, and she prevailed upon her father, the rabbi, to invite the bridegroom to the Seder. Lahle wanted to have her intended at her side on the beautiful spring festival...
The bridegroom did this for his bride, and they celebrated together the festival of "freedom". Lahle took great joy in her radiant bridegroom, who graced the Seder table with his presence, and in a singing voice everyone recited the Haggadah with great relish, and on reaching[?] the verse "In every generation they rise against us to destroy us, and the Holy One, blessed be He, saves us" — at all times the enemies want to destroy us, but God saves us from their hands — an unusual tumult is heard from the street, mixed with Jewish weeping and cries of lament...
R' Shlomo Prag does not hesitate at all and runs out in his socks and kittel to see what has happened. But hardly had he managed to cross the threshold of his house when he fell dead. A murderous hand had killed him.
But in Lahle's tender heart the holy fire of vengeance against her father's murderers was kindled, and tearing herself from the arms of her ardently beloved bridegroom, she too went out into the street, risking her young life. But, alas, she too met the same fate as her father, the rabbi: she perished for the sanctification of God's name.
But even with this the Passover tragedy of 1389 in Prague did not end; the bloody epilogue played out only on the last day of Passover...
The "burghers of Prague", taking advantage of the favourable moment when all the Jews were in the Altneu synagogue pouring out their embittered hearts at the memorial prayer (Yizkor), again attacked the synagogue with axes and other irons and set it on fire from all four sides, not letting out a single living soul[?], and all of them perished there, "from children and women to men", amid the flames of fire...
And all this took place before the [—][?] eyes of the cruel King Wenceslas, who watched this fire-execution with great indifference, as thousands of people wrestled with death and had to breathe out their innocent souls so horribly...
• • •
This dreadful Passover tragedy of Prague found an echo in Selicha no. 144. It begins with the words "Et kol ha-tela'ah asher metza'atnu" [All the hardship that has befallen us] and is printed in the Prague festival prayer books.
This selicha is still recited today in Prague on Yom Kippur at Musaf. Its author is R' Avigdor Kara of Prague, a great kabbalist and liturgical poet (died in 1439).
Recounting there all the details of this tragedy, R' Avigdor Kara sheds a sea of tears over the fiery death of those countless martyrs who perished on that tragic last day of Passover in Prague, crowning them with the name "Passover sacrifice"...
He also laments the dead, whose bones the Prague "heroes" dug out of the graves in the cemetery, smashing their tombstones, etc.
In that cemetery the memory of Lahle was then made eternal.
On the large white tombstone standing at her head is engraved a beautiful female figure, holding in her right hand a rose as a symbol of loyalty and love for her people.
Lahle's grave is covered with small field stones. Since time immemorial there has been a custom there that all who come to visit the cemetery place on it a small stone in remembrance, which is gathered there.
And when the guide who leads you out to the graves there comes to this "heap of stones", he explains to you with a bitter mouth that here was brought to burial the holy martyr Lahle, the rabbi's daughter, who died a hero's death for the honour of her people in that tragic Passover.
And when at the memorial prayer in the Prague synagogue the rabbis, the community leaders and the other martyrs are remembered, one also remembers our heroic Jewish daughter who perished for the sanctification of God's name on the first Seder night of 1389.
Anything Yes, Just Not That

(A short feuilleton).
Her first words to me were few:
"I love you, I want to marry you, I want to be your wife and the mother of your future children."
To that I answered her, also in few words:
Anything yes, just not that.
But she got her way. Women always get the very thing we men do not want them to get.
We became husband and wife — and here the trouble begins.
In the third week after the wedding she says to me: "Motl Rud [sic, for Motl-Dovid], I want to have my mother with me; she has nowhere to be in her old age, let us give her food and a bed."
I answered all in all five counted words: "Anything yes, just not that."
But she opened her mouth and let out more than 5 words, more than five hundred words, and — she got her way, not I!
Women with big mouths always get what they want, and not what we men want.
So my mother-in-law was already in my house, with everything, the whole lot.
She even brought along the wart on the tip of her mug.
Then my little wife again dropped a few hot words:
"Motl-Dovid! I need and I must have for Passover two coats and two pairs of shoes and a new hat and two pairs of stockings."
I answered in my own way, short and sharp:
"Anything yes, just[?] not that!"
She listened to me as one listens to the tomcat, and egged on her mother. And the two together went for me and —
I had to give in; I could not hold out any longer.
When she, my little wife, was already clothed and sewn and shod and hatted, she demanded something new of me:
"Motl-Dovid! Right after the holiday I want to go to Zakopane for two weeks; two weeks is not much; other women go for 4 and 6 and for 10 weeks."
Having heard out her demand, I answered her again in my own way!
"Anything yes, just not that!"
She again put her heads together with her mother — and both together began to cry murder.
I stopped up my ears and answered:
"Good, good, you will go!"
"When?"
"Right away on Isru Chag if you like!"
"If so, you are a fine husband, a good soul, a faithful one."
That is what my pretty little wife says to me with a little smile, and she insists on giving me a kiss, and I barely, barely tear myself out of her hands:
"Anything yes, just not that!"
And this time I did get my way...
B. Kowner.
