The Red Shadow.

[Literature — poetry. Passover supplement.]
(A Passover legend) by L. Malach [Leib Malach].

Night.
Now the windows of the shul go dark,
the last light has gone out,
not a single Jew has stayed behind,
and the old grey shammes
has hung a lock upon the door
and with shuffling steps
has gone off home.

Night.
Lights flare up in the windows,
break out through the shutters,
glitter [?] as if with bands of rays,
pierce — as if with bright spears —
the darkness of the lanes,
and the crooked little houses
straighten up like palaces.

Night.
Melodies ring out
from the [—] [?], sweet, ever higher,
and the eyes light up,
words glow on the lips,
drops sparkle in the goblet
and from all, all the corners
joy rises up, a white joy.

Night.
Now the hour of midnight has come,
children sharpen their gazes;
any moment now he will appear, the old
grey guest, Elijah the Prophet..
At the threshold he stands, he holds
his hand stretched out to the goblet,
brings the goblet to his lips.

Night..
And hark: a tiny drumming,
like drops of rainwater
on the windowpane in late autumn...
Could these be Elijah's steps
treading the road to the shtetl?
No! Something rings hollow [?] in the heart,
as if a barrel had rolled.

Night.
Louder and louder grows the drumming,
as if with hammers at the temples —
higher, higher, higher, higher! [last word misprinted]
as though a horde of wild demons
had broken into a dance on the roofs... [misprint "rekher" for "dekher", roofs]
lips remain torn open,
in the hands the goblet has frozen.
* * *
The Haggadahs left unfinished,
the Song of Songs not sung to the end...
Over all the roads there flood
hordes of drunken gentiles
and the monastery bells ring out
and incite them, incite, incite!

Night.
Torches flare up
and with red light they illuminate
the shtetl like a conflagration...
On the monastery a shadow dances,
like a dark witch
it dances out an evil tiding,
it dances out a wild announcement.
* * *
The Chad Gadya's left unfinished,
the last cup of wine not drunk to the end...
Stones fall upon houses,
shutters are broken open
with murderousness, with raging,
and now the fists ring out
over heads and over necks
in the name of the "Redeemer"...

Night.
By the town hall, by the old one,
the horde presses ever tighter,
wrath rises up to the tower
and murder hangs over the throng [?]...
Soon the shtetl will be wiped out...
murder goes dancing in the alleys.

Night.
Like sheep in a storm,
huddled together, hunched over,
the congregation stands pressed together,
just now still "kings".
Are these not the birth pangs
of a light being born
in the desolate night of freedom?
* * *
And in the whisper of quiet words
meanwhile rumours flutter in,
evil rumours full of unrest —
on the old cemetery
lies a Christian child, slaughtered.
* * *
Night.
The walls grow redder,
and the torches blaze ever more...
At the call of the monastery bells
new hordes come nearer,
new flame in their eyes,
new foam on their lips.
* * *
And the whisper of quiet words
is like drops of rainwater
on a windowpane in late autumn.
And the dark herald
beats annihilation on the drums.

Night.
And now they drive children, old men
from the reclining-couches, in their kittels,
to the old cemetery.
Gentiles take off their hats,
cross themselves beside the slain one...
the tombstones grow paler.
* * *
And the priest's voice resounds
as though it had braided a lightning bolt:
"Confess! Which Jew has
slaughtered our Christian child?!"
* * *
As the tombstones keep silent,
as the dead in the graves,
shoulder pressed to shoulder,
arm pressed to arm,
the crowd stands pale, terrified.
And the priest's black words
are caught up by the monastery bells:
"Once more: if no one confesses,
all the Jews will be..." Suddenly,
see, how a shadow rises
from around the body of the slain,
like a heavy red cloud,
as though it stepped out before them.

And the red shadow-cloud
draws forward over the graves,
over [?] paths — to the monastery lane
and reaches the priest's little house.
It lowers itself into the cellar
and drowns in a small cask.

And the people and the hordes
follow the shadow, trembling,
look at the mute sign.
And they see: the cask is full of blood
and the blood surges upward
as if it wants to reach the rim.

And the people and the horde
stand as if frozen in terror,
look at the secret sign
and the priest, full of dread,
confesses...
he is the murderer.
* * *
Night.
* * *
And the sky begins to pale,
18 Years Since the Death of I. L. Peretz

[Article — literature; anniversary of the death of I. L. Peretz.]
Peretz died during the intermediate days of Passover [Isaac Leib Peretz, d. 3 April 1915, Chol HaMoed Pesach].
Who remembers it? All in all 18 years have passed, and nobody is surprised any more that the anniversary has been forgotten: on the contrary, others will be surprised that someone suddenly remembered it...
And not only Peretz — Sholem Aleichem too, Mendele, Spektor, Rosenfeld — the whole Pleiad of our classics: who remembers their anniversaries? Who mentions them with a warm word.
And that is not the misfortune, that one does not observe anniversaries; Jews are no fetishists, they make no fuss over people, however great they may be — otherwise we would, like them, need a full calendar of departed great men, several on every single leaf!...
Worse is that their works, too, are already almost like forgotten tombstones! And Peretz, who only 18 years ago stormed Jewish hearts, lifted and carried them off to higher worlds, is now no longer "topical"...
There are no eternities at all. It has already been established that the greatest older writers, whose names are still [?] carried today with holy trembling on the lips, are in truth hardly read at all — only their name has remained.
But the "sudden death" that our literary-classical generation suffered is a grave tragedy for us.
If one does not read Smolenskin, Kalman Schulman, A. M. Dik, Abraham Mapu, Adam HaKohen [printed "Aram HaKohen"] and others, it is because they are shallow, naive, primitive with regard to the form and content of our present-day thinking.
But Peretz, that giant of thought and image, that revolutionary of the ghetto, that brilliant talent who marched with giant strides toward progress and dragged the masses after him — is his face too already covered with a shroud of oblivion?!
Where are the new great talents who have eclipsed him?!
Among us, his younger comrades and disciples, there still hovers the breath of his glory, the longing for his rabbi-like literary influence — yet for the broad public he is already dead; has his word already died away?!
This is without doubt a sign of our decline, of our spiritual degeneration.
First of all [printed "kurem kol", misprint] it simply proves our ignorance. Peretz was steeped in Talmudic learning and in Jewish and secular scholarship; his style is soaked [?] with scholarly imagery, his thoughts soar in heavenly heights, and his striving is toward beauty of soul, toward nobility. Thus he idealised Hasidism. His social motifs, too, are interwoven with idealism, with a chase after the wholeness and elevation of the human race. Who understands that today? Who needs it today — today, in an age of brutal struggle between human vilenesses and coarsenesses?!
In these 18 years the average Jew has moved so far away from the book that he has simply stopped understanding it — to understand Peretz (and Mendele too) the masses now lack the former preparation. A generation of ignoramuses cannot appreciate Peretz, and the handful of intellectuals is, after all, enslaved to the mob — that is why people have stopped mentioning Peretz.
And the second reason is our fragmentation.
The greatness of our classics consisted in their non-partisanship, and today that is a defect, a disgrace — backwardness!
A writer today must buy himself a party patent and stick a label on himself; otherwise he is boycotted, excommunicated on all sides.
Were Peretz alive, he could at most have been honorary president of the Jewish PEN Club; but had he kept to his non-partisanship — though [printed "chagam" for "hagam"] with a strong leaning toward the Yiddishism of those days — no one would envy him.
Let this be recalled on the day of his yahrzeit.
P. K.
The Women's Seder...

[Humour — a Passover sketch.]
A comedy-caricature (charge) in 1 act.
By Pesach-Shin.

Characters:
Pola Abramowiczówna (Feygl daughter of R' Avraham), a lady between 30 and 50 years old.
Zosza Szepikówna (Zlate daughter of R' Yosef), a lady at a dangerous age.
Lola Naumówna (Leah daughter of R' Nachum), years undetermined.
Genia Grinówna (Gitl daughter of R' Netzl), entirely without a birth certificate (metryka)...
The seder table is set with various feminine dainties[?].

Instead of the shank-bone with the egg — an eyebrow tweezer; instead of charoset — a box of Coty powder; instead of bitter herbs — a bottle of eau de cologne. All sit around the set table, open their little purses (sakiewki), look at themselves in mirrors, powder themselves and smear their lips with red lipstick (pomadka).

1st Lady: Well, honoured lady (szanowna pani), let us proceed to conduct the seder. On the first nights of Passover the men (mężczyźni) ruled over us. A teraz [and now] it is our holiday (święto), so let us have fun (bawić się)...

2nd Lady: Very good (bardzo dobrze). But there must be order — porządek musi być. At the seder the man presides; here a woman (kobieta) must preside too... I propose that we choose as our chairwoman Genia Grinówna, as the oldest of us...

4th Lady (jumps up from her place like a scalded woman).
That is impudence (nachalstwo)! Insolence (bezczelność)! Where do you get the idea that I am the oldest? It seems to me, Pola Abramowiczówna, if I am not mistaken, that your wedding took place during the great Boxer Uprising in China... quite a few years, eh?

1st Lady: (turns red) A lie (kłamstwo)! The things a person dreams up. On the contrary, let Lola Naumówna say — she still remembers me as a child.

3rd Lady: jumps up as if scalded) I don't want to know (ja nie chcę znać). God be with you, Polia[?] Abramówna, how can I remember you as a child when I was not yet even in the world (na biały świat) then... Zosza Szepikówna can testify (świadczyć) to that — she was my mother's nanny (niańka)...

2nd Lady: (bangs her fist on the table) What a curse (co za przekleństwo)! A Sore-Heve from some boorish woman (chamka), to insult me like that — how do you like the mademoiselle? You are already a grandmother... Just because you dye your hair?...

3rd Lady (beats her breast) I — a grandmother? May you not live to see it... There is no one to laugh — why, I still go on dates (randki)...

1st Lady (squeals and wants to outshout everybody) Well, ladies, calm down (uspokójcie się), soothe your nerves. Feh, not nice, as I live. Is this how one conducts (prowadzi) a seder? If our husbands heard this, that would be a laugh (to by była śmiech)... (All sit down at the table, heated, inflamed.)

1st Lady: Well, ladies, I have found[?] a way out of our difficult situation.

2nd Lady: For example (na przykład)?

4th Lady: Without jabs?

1st Lady: I propose that we choose as chairwoman of tonight's seder the very youngest of us... Teraz [now], understood (rozumiem)[?] — no more quarrels (kłótnie) will break out among us, and since you all know that I am younger than you, all of 30 years old, I take the place at the head.

(An uproar, shouting, banging on the table, squealing, yelling, everyone speaks at once.)

2nd Lady: You are younger? A thing of yesterday!

3rd Lady: 30 years? Not counting Sabbaths and holidays.

4th Lady: It seems to me you could already be celebrating your golden wedding...

1st Lady: I can show you documents, a Russian passport and an identity card (dowód osobisty).

2nd Lady: I know that one (ja znam tego) — you must have a dozen such passports...

3rd Lady: That is insolence (bezczelność). To take people one knows and spit in their faces like that.

4th Lady: Tfu, boorishness (chamstwo)!

All: Tfu, tfu, I don't want to know you (nie chcę was znać)...

1st Lady: Listen (słuchajcie), Genia Grinówna, never mind who is who, but you must keep entirely silent (milczeć) — after all you have no birth certificate (metryka) at all...

4th Lady — Ach! (faints) All rush to her, rub her temples with eau de cologne, sprinkle her with water, but it doesn't help. All run to the telephone to call the ambulance (the "quick help").

4th Lady — (opens her eyes and squeaks) No need (nie trzeba)... no need, I hate doctors, I hate their questions.

1st Lady — Well, peace (zgoda), Geniusza, you are young, you are fresh, you are still a young girl — only don't faint... Oh my heart (moje serce), see how it pounds as if with hammers; what would I do if you, God forbid (broń Boże), died on us... it could have spoiled the women's seder... Please be seated (proszę siadać)!...
(Curtain)
Jewish Anecdotes about Passover

[Passover — folk humour.]
Collected and rendered by A. Litwin.
Every Jewish holiday, besides the religious melodies with which all our exalted days are interwoven, is also embroidered with a fine wreath of secular Jewish folk songs. Jewish humour, too, likes to adorn every Jewish holiday in its own way. Passover, despite the deep seriousness that permeates this most festive, most poetic Jewish holiday, still has its comic sides, which Jewish humour picks up good-naturedly.
Passover beer.
A village Jew (yishuvnik) once wanted to bring the rabbi a gift, so that the rabbi would remember him. He thought and thought: what could he make that the rabbi would value? He hit upon an idea: to make the rabbi beer for Passover. Since he knew that the rabbi was a very scrupulous Jew who would not drink just any beer, he saw to everything himself, from beginning to end. He let nobody touch it, until genuine kosher-for-Passover beer came out...
On the eve of Passover, at midday, he drives into town, goes straight to the rabbi and carries in the little keg of Passover beer that he had made himself.
When the rabbi saw it, he began to shout:
— Help! Take it out of my house! It is chametz!
The villager was deeply offended:
— How so, Rabbi, I made it myself; guarded it like the apple of my eye, just so that you, Rabbi, would have Passover beer.
The rabbi's arguments, showing him from the "Shulchan Aruch" and "Orach Chayim" that beer is chametz, did not help at all, until the rabbi took an ordinary "Haggadah", opened the first page and showed him that even in the "Haggadah" it says explicitly: "ale bir iz chametz" ("all beer is chametz") (al bi'ur chametz).
Now the villager understood and let the beer be poured out.
"Rabbis" and "plagues".
On Passover, at the Seder night, sits Reb Yisroel — no villager, but actually a learned Jew — with his wife Sarah, the afflicted one: already ten years after the wedding and they have no child. Reb Yisroel recites the "Haggadah" and Sarah listens. When he began "Ma'aseh be-Rabbi Eliezer" with the same tune with which one says "blood, frogs"..., Sarah began to dip her finger into the cup.
— No, my wife — her husband says to her — you are making a mistake, these are great rabbis.
And he continues the Haggadah until he reaches the real "blood, frogs"; his wife Sarah thinks these too are probably among the rabbis, and cries out:
— Oh, Master of the Universe, bless me at least with one of them!...
— No, my wife — her husband explains — you are mistaken again; the earlier ones really were rabbis; but the present ones are "plagues".
An increase[?] in the "plagues".
A villager and his son were conducting the Seder. When they came to the "Ten Plagues", blood, frogs etc., a page of Selichot had strayed in there: "Ashamnu, bagadnu, gazalnu" etc. — and they recited them in sequence...
The son wonders and asks:
— Father, how come there are more plagues this year than last year?
— Understand me, my son, this year is a leap year...
"Selichot" and "plagues".
A villager gave a Haggadah to be bound, and the bookbinder mistakenly inserted a page of Selichot into the villager's Haggadah, so that in place of the Ten Plagues came out "Ashamnu, bagadnu, gazalnu".
When the Seder came, the villager stood there not knowing what to do. But soon he hit on a plan. Coming to the words in the Haggadah: "These are the ten plagues which the Holy One, blessed be He, brought upon the Egyptians in Egypt, and these are: ashamnu, bagadnu, gazalnu"... he beat his breast with one hand and with the other dipped into the cup and poured off the plagues...
Why he weeps over the "Haggadah".
A villager was conducting the Seder, and when he came to the verse in the Haggadah "And the children of Israel were fruitful and swarmed and multiplied and grew exceedingly mighty", he burst into bitter tears. At the table sat a kloyznik (study-house scholar) whom he had brought from town on the eve of Passover to help him conduct the Seder. The kloyznik was astonished, seeing how the villager had suddenly broken into wailing. He asks him: "Dear master of the house, what is the matter, why are you crying?"
— How can I not cry — answered the villager — after all, the end was "and the land was filled with them" — the earth was filled with them! They all died out!
The plague of sons.
A carter sat down to the Seder with his wife and big strapping lads. The sons did not think much of "honouring one's father". They used to embitter their father's years. The carter himself, poor man, limped on one side ("evri"), as the verse says — "ha-makeh be-evrato": there was a sore in his side. His Haggadah was already very old; it had served its time. Many letters, which had once shone and glittered at the Seders, had lost their shape — a gimel looked like a nun; a kaf — like a bet. The vowel points had suffered even more; they had entirely lost their true face: a "tsere" looked like a "chirik"; a "melupum" had become a "shva". In such a Haggadah it is hard to find one's way even for scholars, let alone a carter. Nevertheless, up to the "Ten Plagues" he somehow "stumbled through"; but when he got into the middle of the Haggadah and met the "Ten Plagues" on the way, he started to flounder like a blind horse, and instead of saying "dam, tsfardea, kinim" (blood, frogs, lice) he said "dam, tsfardea, banim" (blood, frogs, sons)...
"Father!" one of the lads cried out, "in our Haggadah it says differently!"
"Shut up, you bastards!" the carter answered angrily. "They are going to teach me! 'Sons' are a plague too"...
Pharaoh and Haman.
Pharaoh and Haman once met in the next world.
"Listen, Pharaoh!" — says Haman — "everyone says you were a mighty king and a great sage. And I say you were a great fool. You wanted to wipe out the Jews, and I wanted to do the same. You gave them hard labour, tormented, oppressed, choked them... and what did you achieve? The work did them no harm; they became even much stronger: they got healthy, powerful bones. You see, my plan was excellent: I wanted to hang them all at once; the only flaw was that my king, Ahasuerus, was a great dolt, and he wrecked my whole plan; but you were, after all, a 'king in his own domain', a great ruler: had you only given me a free hand[?], not a single Jew would have remained in the world."
"Oh, you are a real fool!" answers Pharaoh. "I achieved more than you. You gave them a Purim — they revel and dance, and you get your bones beaten to the very foundations[?] of the world. But I provided them with a Passover — they suffer before Passover, during Passover and after Passover"...
The Hammer of the Tower Clock

[Literature — poetry; the "Zangen" section.] (Page heading: "Zangen" [Ears of Grain] — a section for literature, theatre and cultural matters.)
Efraim Klajman (Katowice)

Hammer, hammer, strike the hours,
drive the clock upon the tower;
drive the waves along the air,
without mercy chase time on!
Without mercy tell life:
that time is above everything,
that it is always in motion
like the clock upon the tower.

And the time that you crumble away:
(whole, half, quarter hours)
are pieces, pieces of palaces
torn out of the infinite —
you announce to the child his hope
that he is growing into life;
with your strokes you forge for him
the prospect of a future, to grow great.

In the young man now grown up
you hammer out the road to old age,
tear out the green leaves
from the garden of joys of his existence;
heavy as lead you are — on the backs
of the heads strewn with snow —
every knock of yours is a finger
that points the way to the grave.

Over gardens, over halls,
where only lamp-eyes flash,
where people whisper or dance
in black tailcoats and white little dresses —
the cruel tones draw out
from the tower like a cobweb
stretched out, ringing far away
over gardens, over halls.

And the time that you doze through,
hammer, hammer on the tower:
the minutes between the whole hours;
the minutes between the halves,
the minutes between the quarters —
lives of forgetting resound,
voices ring out above everything,
lips kiss the time away
between halves, between wholes.

But you keep watch, hammer-guardian,
like the sharp sword of Damocles
over heads and over little heads,
over mind and brain —
you screech out angrily
over moments of forgetting
and remind that you are cruel,
hammer, hammer on the tower.
A Stormy Night in Zagłębie.

[Literature — poetry; Zagłębie.] Tobiasz Bojm/Baum (Sosnowiec)

All day long the clouds drew across the sky,
covered it one by one with a thick layer of mould,
until they covered it entirely, and toward evening
it was already dark, as deep down in a mine shaft.
It was quiet — no buzz of a fly, no worm crawling —
it was the stillness before a storm.
And suddenly:
as through a door burst open, the wind rushed in
head first. As with a battering ram it hurled itself "blindly"
among the street lamps, put out their light and flashed
into the forest of chimneys, and there danced itself out,
wildly, madly danced itself out
an unbridled wreath of laughter [?],
and forced itself into a cancan dance,
a dance of lust.
The factory sirens began to whistle and to sing,
the chimneys [?] began to bend like tongs,
red, to climb to the sky like copper snakes,
on two split, poisonous, thrust-out tongues
choking and spitting rings of smoke,
with fumes tearing apart the lungs of the sky
in time with the song of the factory sirens.
The heavens took fright,
began to roar,
["ferkheste" — unclear word] to spray sparks,
to hurl thunder, to shoot lightning;
heads of clouds — knocking hard together,
and not letting themselves be caught,
began to scream,
the clouds, and even to spit blood,
from the thunder and from the lightning,
to sweat round drops,
until smashed and broken
with a clatter [?] — they burst out...
[—] stood and lurked [?] in the black, deep night,
[—] from [—], blasted [?] with a thunder from the shaft.
From the Book Table

[Literature — book reviews.]
"Di shpayzerns in step" ["The Pantries (?) in the Steppe"]. An idyllic novel by S. L. Blank [Shmuel Leib Blank]. Translated from Hebrew by G. Sh. [?]
This is a book of quiet beauty and of colour-rich playfulness. A song to nature, to man and to the wide, beautiful world that lies beyond our narrow big-city walls and small, half-collapsed little houses — in the quiet kingdom of the sun-drenched blossoming field, the green, adorned, song-filled forest, and the wide, spacious steppe poured out in wilderness [?].
After a few counted pages we find ourselves in the lap of nature, where the dawn of the field blooms upon us, the daytime sun glows through us, and we thirstily drink the cool, gentle breeze that seems spiced with perfumes. We find ourselves in the fragrant summer steppe at dusk.
It is an idyllic pioneer novel of soil and labour. A song of physical building and fruitful creation in the lap of nature.
It is the story of a young, simple man — Boaz, who dared, all on his own, with his own strength [misprinted "pukhes" for "koykhes"], to build up a settlement in the uninhabited steppe. Starting from a barrack for himself and his five sheep, where he could lay down his head, until he arrived later, through hard toil and trouble, at a house of his own and a whole village farmstead. And just like Isak in Hamsun's [Knut Hamsun] "The Blessing of the Earth" [Growth of the Soil], though on a much smaller scale, we see Boaz from early dawn until late at night, how he digs and builds, ploughs, creates and acquires; only the boundless love for the soil, the joy of building and creating by himself a new life in the lap of nature, could [?] make it possible that one man should be able to achieve so much. To endure: snow, cold, darkness, storm and many other obstacles — by tearing with his teeth, by biting and winning. And with quiet steps we follow Boaz and rejoice in his zest for work, his stubbornness, seeing how he transforms stony ground into a blossoming field, a wild steppe — into a blossoming settlement. Naturally, when his young wife Rachel comes to live with him in the steppe, she helps him. But it is clear that this man, who seems cast of steel, is capable on his own of overcoming all difficulties.
"Di shpayzerns in step" is distinguished by a quiet, laborious, productive creativity and above all by a great deal of natural beauty, because in places [?], as we read the book, we find ourselves together with Boaz, with his flock of sheep, with the dog Primusi, with his young wife Rachel in the sun-field [?], and delight in the quiet sunset, the clear blue skies, and we bathe in a world of sun, greenery and beauty. As far as descriptions of nature are concerned, S. L. Blank is lavishly rich. Here S. L. Blank shows us an evening in the steppe:
"Boaz lights [?] his pipe and gazes at the sunset, which glows towards and onto the clouds, red as blood, wandering aimlessly under the distant skies of the steppe. On high the stars come out one after another, and a light cloud paints the river with the bloody redness of its last glowing glance. From somewhere a quiet [?] breeze arrives, and with gentle calm it brings with it sharp smells of freshly ploughed earth, the good fat smell of sheep and cattle. But [printed "gur" for "nur"] now clouds draw over the clear skies, the stars vanish one by one, and a thin warm [?] rain begins to drip. The earth soaks up into itself the fertilization from above, it opens its hidden treasure and smells of fragrant freshness. The air becomes spiced with the heavy scents of intoxication. Everything awakens to soak up into itself the blessing of heaven."
S. L. Blank can excellently [depict] nature with all its treasures. In depicting nature he is a master through and through. He can also excellently [depict] the life of the cattle, beasts and birds; he understands their life and their language (if one may express oneself so). In this respect he strongly recalls Moshe Stavsky [Moshe Stavi]. With quite special sharpness and full-bloodedness [?] S. L. Blank draws human portraits and figures.
S. L. Blank possesses a sense of delicate, fine humour. When Shmuel Nachum, Boaz's father-in-law, comes to Boaz while the latter is building the house, and showers [?] him meanwhile with countless plans, advice and projects on how to build the house, and meanwhile boasts to Boaz how much honour is paid him — the priest himself consults him, the uriadnik [Tsarist rural policeman] himself drinks l'chaim with him — suddenly his wife Zlate pops up beside him and tells him, if you please, [?] cheerfully [?], not to muddle anyone's head and rather to put a pot of potatoes on the fire...
With this novel Jewish literature has become richer by a beautiful, colour-rich and juicily artistic work, written by a poet, an artist. We are refreshed and thank the author gratefully for the true enjoyment we had while reading. This book brings joy and refreshment.
N. Shternberg. Warsaw.
———
"Gerangl" ["Struggle"]. Poems and long poems by: Efraim Klayman, Tuvia Boim and Leyzer Shikman. Sosnowiec 1933.
A collective anthology — a "mezumen" [?] [a quorum of three, as for grace after meals] of three young poets who declare in the preface to the book — "We have no line and no [?] bench, our way is a wayless one, our voice — the street, our hearth — the Jewish human heart!"
Each has his own "page", and for each "page" a matching linoleum cut (by Zalman Sh. Boim).
The "head of the table" is occupied by Efraim Klayman; his "Shlogn-tants" ["Beating-dance"] is a spring of gall, and he pours it on the makers of riots:
"Students with shouts and with / noise march / and each time another one takes / it higher with a [?] / Jews start slamming the shutters / of the shops / running like the ḥvv (?) with / outstretched hands / kupkes (?) start chasing / after everyone / laughing with a beating drunken / laughter."
Klayman's second piece is the long poem "Poyln" ["Poland"] (1863–1919); a rich gallery of types and pictures passes through it. But it must be said that the author only took pains that the poem should be as large as possible..
———
"Di gas" ["The Street"] by Tuvia Boim is a reflection of the abandoned life of streetwalkers, pimps and heroes of the underworld. The language — juicy, pithy, only in some places it sounds like a wedding-jester's.
"I [sit?] on my step / everything dances around me like a goat / a coarse bass sings to me / with a [?] voice of the street / hoppy hop! hoppy hop!"
Tuvia Boim can also laugh, and he laughs
"at everyone and everything / at judgments, commandments, / at human poverty / at his own shadow."
Among his most successful things are [?] "Der bister" [?]? and the dedication to Shikman.
———
Leyzer Shikman is no new face to our readers. His stories too appear from time to time in the columns of our newspaper. His genre: lyric (hospital songs), a prominent expression of his human vision [?]; his whole being, his sufferings and hopes are the melodies of his despairing poems:
"A life and light" [as printed; perhaps "a life without light"]. / "Without shine" / full of shadow / adorned with an abyss-wreath / always only pain / oh, you life / why must this be? / [?] life — ptui! / bitter tears choke / "See, mother" / who will redeem? / ah, ptui...
This same [printed "velber" for "zelber"] thought of despair one feels while reading Shikman's 28 poems and [printed "in"] ballads, from which there emerges the "better never to have been created"...
The book, printed on fine paper, ought to be bought. It will be the best stimulus [?] for the young poets, children of Zagłębie.
Finally — a reproach for the bad proofreading.
Sha-El.
Theatre Notes

[Będzin — Theatre.] (On Dr. Paul Baratoff's guest performances in Będzin.)
We live in a time when everyday life grows ever more cruel, truly unbearable; slowly the festive spirit is vanishing from our lives. Gone is the time when the glow of the romanticism of old still shimmered; the struggle for existence devours all of man's spiritual needs.
And when this toil-worn person comes to a theatre in which Dr. Baratoff plays, he receives an artistic tikkun [repair]; through Dr. Baratoff's artistic achievement a person is lifted above the worries of daily life.
With Paul Baratoff's two guest performances at the "Szwitowid" [Światowid?], the belief in the development of a good Jewish theatre that would enrich our cultural treasures has grown stronger among the Jewish theatre-going public.
Baratoff works with his acting, his movements, his rhythm, like a pious, guileless prayer-leader (ba'al tefilla).
For his first appearance Baratoff staged Némirovsky's novel "David Golder". For the degenerate French-Jewish bourgeoisie the play might have produced an unexpected impression, because Golder's tragedy can in no way be our tragedy; the problem of David Golder is too far from us, far from our Jewish essence. But Baratoff raised the piece up to himself and poured into it his many-branched talent, so that it might grow into a tangible theatrical reality.
The second play, "Hinkemann" [by Ernst Toller], is a good weapon against those who lead people onto the battlefields, and the result: — cripples, maimed men, and they cease to be — men...
Baratoff in the role of "Hinkemann" was a splendid figure: although the war has made him incapable of being a husband to his wife, the true love and loyalty to her still smoulder in him, and for a living he is ready to be the circus hero, to gnaw live mice... But when the good and faithful "Hinkemann" learns that those close to him, and his wife too, are laughing at him, he roars like a lion and pushes them away from himself.
Baratoff's acting is calculated in every detail; Baratoff carries [the audience] along and compels it to laugh with him and to suffer with him.
The whole ensemble contributed to the great moral success of both performances.
The well-known actress [printed "artists"] Sonia Altbaum (Glara.) [?], who strove to stay at the level of Baratoff's partner.
The actors Hart, Melman, Brakarz [?], Domb and others create distinctive types.
S. L—tsh
The Modern Haggadah

[Satirical feuilleton — a Passover Haggadah for 1933; Będzin, Sosnowiec, Hitler.]
Cleaned, koshered[?] and translated by Ben Amotz.
The Kehilla Seder.
Around the table sit all the Zagłębie "cooking-spoons" [busybodies], stool-twirlers, bench-holders, bell-ringers and charity-box rattlers; at the head sits a merchant who keeps account books, and he begins:
Kadesh — Praised be Thou, O God, that I find myself[?] here with you and am not a "kadosh"[?] [martyr]...
U-rechatz — You may be washed, clean; but if you happen to be a Jew you remain a smeared one...
Karpas — Take one issue each of the "Zaglembier Yudisher Kurier", "Ostatnie Wiadomości" and "Nasz Głos", dip them in salt water and say "Borei pri ha-adama"...
Yachatz — Split the Revisionist organization. Give one half to "Haynt" and the other half to "Moment"...
Maggid — People keep on telling at which Jew there is still a złoty to be found...
Rachtzah — Wash as much as you can; the landlord will pay for the water anyway...
Motzi — If you can "extract" a couple of gulden from somebody, you are a clever one[?].
Matzah — [matzah = strife] People quarrel incessantly, even at a meeting about organizing a protest rally against Hitler..
Maror — If you have a newspaper, the news from Germany will do you for bitter herbs...
Korech — One lies buried nine ells deep in the earth...
Tzafun — One hides from the distraint-runs[?].
Hallel — If there is still anything left to praise, it is "not unto us" — not for us...
Ha Lachma Anya...
Place on the seder plate the new ordinance on local self-government and say: "Ha lachma anya" — it is a poor man's bread to be a public worker; "this year here" — here one has to attend at the Commissioner's, here one has to run into the [mayor's?][?] kitchen; but "next year" — a year from now there may already be a town council, and we shall be free men, no longer dependent on the nasty magistrate "inquiries" [wywiady]...
Ma Nishtana?
Why do the Będzin dozór members [kehilla board] do everything the other way round? On all other nights, in all towns and townlets, when a shochet [ritual slaughterer] is to be hired, a competition is announced and afterwards money is taken; on this night — only in Będzin — it is all matzah: only money is taken, without a competition.
On all other nights — almost all municipal magistrates also have Jewish officials; on this night — the exception is the Sosnowiec magistrate, where there is not a single Jewish official.
Avadim Hayinu... We were, and still are, citizens of the second category; even if we are all wise, all understanding, even if we are the greatest geniuses and men of science — you will not find a Jewish conductor on the tram or on the railway; therefore it is our duty to tell — we must at least tell, hold protest meetings, so that the great world learns of our sad plight...
Ma'aseh — The story happened in the land of Germany, in the twentieth century. The "Jews" there always sang songs of praise and told and recounted their "freedom and equal rights", until there came — until Hitler's gang came and said — and they said: gentlemen, Jews, the time has come, the hour has arrived when "you must leave the country"...
Said Rabbi Simon[?]: I am like a man of seventy — "I have indeed become seventy years old" [in mock German] — and I never merited, nor do I remember, that the Exodus should be told at night — "that the Jews should flee Germany by night" — until he expounded it: until Hitler made a speech that "all the days of your life — nights": "as long as I am chancellor your life will be dark". And the Sages say — and the wise say that Hitler's government too will suffer a downfall...
(Cover the matzot, take Hitler's plans in your hand and say:)
For not one alone — not Hitler alone has risen against us to destroy us, wants to annihilate us; but in every generation and in every land there are Hamans who want to exterminate us; but the enemy plots and, as it were, laughs...
These Ten Plagues...
Blood — in "cultured" Germany Jewish blood is being shed.
Frogs — Jews all over the world lie in the mud like frogs.
Lice — the enemies of the Jews multiply like...
Wild beasts — [arov, read as arev = guarantor] the epidemic of protested bills of exchange (guarantee concerns a bill)...
Pestilence — Jewish families are murdered under Hitler's government.
Boils — a [mere?][?] house-painter becomes chancellor.
Hail — a hail of protests from the whole world.
Locusts — like wild locusts they pounce on Jewish businesses.
Darkness — the Jewish horizon is covered by a dark cloud.
Slaying of the firstborn — it is a "plague of countries": everywhere we are beaten...
How Many Good Things...
If only — without the German pogroms — dayenu.
If only — without the new government tax — dayenu.
If only — without the ping-pong matches — dayenu.
If only — the Sosnowiec gmina [kehilla] had not created any "Chesed shel Emet" [burial society] — dayenu.
If only — no "Revizye"[?] had been born in Sosnowiec — dayenu.
If only — the League came to Jabotinsky's lecture only with white doves[?] — dayenu.
How Much More So...
That in Germany pogroms take place, the government imposes new taxes, in every cellar ping-pong is played, the Sosnowiec gmina possesses a "Chesed shel Emet", there is in Sosnowiec a "Revizye" with "lapel-vests"[?], and the League came with white doves[?], sneezing powders and tear-gas bombs — to atone for all our sins...
—
Take together the old and new "wymiary" [tax assessments] and the new tax laws, and make the blessing:
Baruch — Blessed be the assessment commissions with the assessors [rzeczoznawcy][?], "who redeemed us and redeemed" — who flayed, and again flay, the skin off us; "who brought their blood" — to the last drop of blood; "and we shall thank Thee" — and people keep singing the old ditty:
— "Że mogą płacić" ["that they can pay"]...
And So It Came to Pass at Midnight.
Jewish merchants who still have a couple of gulden are clapped into the "Chad Gadya" — at midnight..
The Sosnowiec "Revizye" looked for a hall for the Purim ball — at midnight.
Bailiffs carry out searches — at midnight.
Jewish young men and girls make a racket in the streets — at midnight...
At Kowalska 2 in Sosnowiec people [—][?] until — midnight...
Jewish informers "tell the truth" — by day and by night...
Who Knows One?
One I know: that the whole world are our enemies.
Who knows two? Two I know: on 20 May it is the second yahrzeit of the Zagłębie kehilla elections...
Who knows three? Three I know: three dozór members run the Będzin kehilla.
Who knows four? Four I know: four 10-złoty notes it cost to kasher an oven...
Who knows five? Five I know: five boxes of sneezing powder the "League" bought for Jabotinsky's lecture.
Who knows six? Six I know: six little shochtim — four studied and two paid[?]...
Who knows seven? Seven I know: seven times a week "mass meetings" take place among the Sosnowiec artisans...
The Exodus According to a New Interpretation.
When the children of Jacob came into Egypt, the land was in trouble. Poverty whistled in every corner. Only cabbage and potatoes. Of industry, of commerce there was no trace; ragged and worn out were they, the Egyptians — "naked as a Turkish saint" [goły jak święty turecki].
As soon as the children of Jacob entered the land, they developed industry, manufacture, commerce — established trade relations with every corner of the world; they built Pithom and Raamses: splendid buildings and huge factory premises.
"Now there arose a new king over Egypt, who knew not Joseph" — a new king arose in Egypt...
"And it came to pass" — it was at the time when the "third plague" [lice] had seized the land, when the "tenth plague" reigned in the royal treasuries of Egypt, and like a minister in Egypt, like a big shot — he was clad in the "sixth plague" [boils]...
"And Pharaoh called for the wise men and the sorcerers" — a plenary session of the magicians of Egypt was convened; they thought and thought until they thought up a new statute[?]: "and they set over him taskmasters" — every second Egyptian was made a sequestrator.
"And they cried out" — the children of Israel began to shout: "We want to — but we can't"... They were answered: "Speak unto Pharaoh" — talk to the wall! — in Egyptian that means: file an appeal..
"And Moses kept the flock" — Moses was a shepherd of the people, a provider for the people.
"And the officers of the people came and cried" — delegations came to him with a cry. Go speak unto Pharaoh! Go talk to Pharaoh! — the children of Israel clamoured.
"And Moses said" — Reb Moshe answered: "Behold, I am of uncircumcised lips" — I don't know any goyish [Polish], I am only in the middle of "Chcę czytać" ["I want to read", a primer], "and how shall Pharaoh hear me" — they won't understand what "dekamri rebitzin"[?] [what I am saying]?
"And it came to pass" — when the eleventh plague had already arrived: there was darkness in Egypt, "and there was a great cry in Egypt" — the outcry was great — "for there was not a house where there was not one dead" — there was no longer a single Jewish door without public auction notices pasted on it, not a single merchant without a bankruptcy [upadłość]; "and I came down to deliver them out of the hand of the Egyptians unto a land flowing with milk and honey" — they began to run to the Land of Israel.
The old story of the Exodus according to a new interpretation... Honig-Foygl [Honey-bird].
After the Seder.
Wife: Why were you groaning like that in your sleep?
Husband: (president of an institution) I had a bad dream: I dreamt that they audited the books.
From Egypt until now
Dmowski, Hitler, Nowaczyński,
Jew-devourers great and small —
ah, we keep them up our sleeve [i.e. we don't care a fig for them],
from Egypt until now...

One more devourer, one more little dog,
and many vile blood-libels —
let them snap, let them bark,
from Egypt until now...

Jews always remain Jews,
wrapped in lovely dreams,
and the little dogs remain little dogs,
from Egypt until now..

What is exile to us? What is suffering to us?
And the enemy's sharp teeth?
Ah, we keep them up our... sleeve,
from Egypt until now..

The "Kokh-Lefl" [Cooking Ladle] burns the chametz.

The promises of the Minister of Commerce.
The salvations of the Disarmament [?] Conference in Geneva.

Incidents and acts of revenge on the protest day in Zagłębie.
As we are informed, the protest day had an effect on some Zagłębie rich men, especially on the well-known rich man and "philanthropist" on the Będzin Old Market [Stary Rynek], who — as an eyewitness relates — let out a groan during the protest demonstration.
But as it turned out later, he had just been told that a close relative of his had arrived from Chmielnik seeking support for Passover.
— It is also reported that several Zagłębie rich men burned last Monday the German "grige" [?] (Marks in the vernacular), which they had taken at the beginning of the war for the houses they sold...

Protest of the Endeks against Hitler.
Rumour has it that the Zagłębie Endeks [National Democrats] are preparing to send a protest to Germany, to Hitler: why does he beat and boycott Polish Jews? All that — they say — belongs to them.

Once and today.
Once, when Jews came to the seashore, the sea was split for them and they crossed over with the gold and silver of the Egyptians. Today they take from the Jew his goods, and his head gets split, before he even lives to reach the seashore...
Leib Shmabinski [?].

The German Republic, may she rest in Eden
After heavy and short suffering, at the blooming age of 15 years, there breathed out her kosher soul
THE GERMAN REPUBLIC, may she rest in Eden,
of which notice is given by the Social Democrats and friends, left behind in deep mourning.
What's new in Zagłębie? — The "new" kehilla administration is to be confirmed within 8–10 days. So the Starosta assures.

A delegation consisting of Messrs. Jakub Gutman, S. Fürstenberg, Chaiml Szejn and Marek Szejn presented themselves to the Starosta [district governor] and gave him a picture of the sad situation of the Będzin [Jewish] community (gmina).
Having heard the report, the Starosta declared that within 8–10 days the new administration (zarząd) and the council will be confirmed.
— If only!
Which prohibition is graver — on machine matzot or on shmura flour from outside?

[Będzin — religion and Passover.] This year, before Passover, the Będzin rabbinate issued 2 prohibitions: 1) on machine matzot and 2) on shmura flour bought from outside.
The prohibition on shmura flour is in fact issued year in, year out, because the profit from the flour goes to the benefit of the Talmud Torah, where[?] hundreds of Jewish children, among them a large number of orphans, receive their religious and also secular education.
The "chukah" [sic; read: chazakah, established custom] of buying shmura flour at the Talmud Torah was observed every year by every religious Jew, who by buying flour at the T.T. indirectly supported the institution.
This year the custom was broken precisely by "those who fight for strengthening the Torah", those who preach that the whole Torah is found only in the hands of the "Agudah" in general and in the cheder "Yesodei HaTorah" in particular... From precisely that camp came a few "sharp" young men, the actual leaders of the Agudah cheder, who exploited the strict prohibition of the Będzin rabbinate and brought shmura flour from outside, in order to harm the T.T. directly.
The breaking of the prohibition by some Ger Hasidim has aroused bitterness in Hasidic circles.
In this connection we have before us a letter from a group of Hasidim who ask: which prohibition is graver — the one on machine matzot, or the one on the outside shmura flour, which caused damage to the T.T.?...

A father's suit against his children before the Sosnowiec court
The Sosnowiec court saw the epilogue of [the affair of] R' Shmuel Grynbaum, a house-owner on Kowalska Street in Sosnowiec, who threw his daughter and son-in-law Elimelech Welgrin out of the flat.
At the time we reported "benoy" [sic, for genoy — exactly] all the details of the eviction, which took place before the eyes of hundreds of people. No intervention whatsoever helped with Mr. Grynbaum to make him hold back the eviction of his children, who were ruined thanks to him.
That was not enough. After the eviction Mr. Grynbaum accused in court his son-in-law Elimelech Welgrin, Chaim Epsztajn, Mordechai Kiwer and Elimelech Kinderlerer, who were charged with having threatened Grynbaum and his family, as a result of which they [the family] did not leave the flat for 5 whole days.
On behalf of the accused twenty-odd witnesses were called, who described the "fine deeds" of Mr. Grynbaum towards his children and denied the whole accusation.
The court acquitted the accused.

Opening of the "Linat HaCholim" outpatient clinic in Sosnowiec postponed
In the previous number of our paper we wrote that the board of the Sosnowiec "Linat HaCholim" had decided that the opening of the outpatient clinic would take place during Chol HaMoed.
All the technical preparations for the opening were carried out, but for unforeseen reasons the ceremony was postponed.
As we are informed, the board of "Linat HaCholim" has undertaken a broad intervention so that the clinic, which is a vital necessity for the poor population, may begin its important activity as soon as possible.

"Jews in Liberated Poland"
Staying in Zagłębie is Mr. Epsztajn, representative of the famous work entitled "Jews in Liberated Poland" [Żydzi w Polsce Odrodzonej], published under the editorship of Dr. Schiper, Dr. Tartakower and city councillor "Maftki" [sic; read Hafftka].

The Minister of Communications, Eng. Butkiewicz, is conducting an inspection in the area of the Kielce voivodeship. The minister, accompanied by Deputy Minister Galas, will also visit Zagłębie in connection with the planned public works.

A Polish recruit departed from Strzemieszyce. When the train began to move, the recruit [fell?, doubtful word "staran"] down under the wheels, which cut off his foot.

This Saturday a session of the Dąbrowa town council takes place. At the session Dr. Madejski, who has been appointed director of the Labour Fund, will lay down[?] his mandate as President [mayor] of Dąbrowa.

On Friday towards evening a young Christian, a former tailor ("krawczyk") from Grojec[?] [Grodziec?], threw himself onto the railway line between Dąbrowa and Będzin.

Extraordinary general meeting of "Hakoach" in Będzin
On Saturday evening an extraordinary general meeting took place at "Hakoach"; on its agenda stood only the single question of the minority rights of the members.
The motion of Mr. Podliński was adopted, not to give the members of "Hakoach" any minority rights.

Jewish councillors of the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce call for a boycott of German goods
In Sosnowiec a meeting took place of the Jewish councillors of the Chamber of Commerce, which represents all Jewish merchants' organisations in the area of the Kielce voivodeship.
At the meeting, after the speeches on the sad Jewish situation in Germany, the following resolutions were adopted:
1) As a protest against the German cruelty a boycott is undertaken of German goods and of German firms. 2) An unconditional boycott of the German firms in Danzig, through whom Polish goods are being boycotted. And 3) to avoid German ports, and all shipments are to go through the port of Gdynia.

Supreme Court rejects the claim of former director Grynberg
The former director of the Jewish gymnasium in Będzin, Mr. Grynberg, when he was dismissed from his post, came forward with a large monetary claim against the school board. Although the claim had already been rejected by several court instances, Mr. G. brought his case to the Supreme Court, which confirmed the verdict of the first instances.

The thieves of the Goldman theft before the Sosnowiec district court
The Katowice thieves Kubik and Szelig worked out a plan to rob Goldman's flat on Kowalska Street in Sosnowiec.
The plan was a strategic one: so that it would be easier to carry out the theft, their girlfriend, a certain Musiałek, hired herself out as a maid at the Goldmans', and at the first opportunity, when none of the Goldmans was in the flat, the thieves made themselves at home and took various valuables and money.
The trio[?] received the following sentences from the district court: Kubik 2 years, Szelig 1 year and the maid one and a half years' prison.

A rich beggar dies of hunger
In Olkusz a Christian beggar suddenly died in the street; on him were found promissory notes (weksle) for 1,300 zł. The doctor established that the beggar had died of hunger.

Performance by Rachel Holzer in Sosnowiec
On Thursday, Chol HaMoed, a recitation evening will take place in the Sosnowiec municipal theatre with the participation of the gifted artist Rachel Holzer. This artist made a name for herself in the guest tours of the "Jewish Troupe" ("Yidishe Bande") in Zagłębie.
On the programme: Yiddish and Polish recitations from her best repertoire.

Endek protest against the Jews coming from Germany to Poland
In Dąbrowa a meeting of Endeks took place with the participation of the Endek deputy Rymar.
After the speeches a series of resolutions were adopted, among others that "the Endecja expresses a sharp protest against the Jewish immigration from Germany, who will settle here in Poland at the expense of the Poles"...
Funny that the Endeks quite forget that Rymar[?] earned[?] his greatest income only from Jewish goods...
Horrifying Deeds of the Inquisition in Germany

A few days ago a Będzin house-owner returned from Berlin, and we turned to him to inform us about the present situation of the Jews in Germany.
"The Jews in Germany," says the informant, "are without any protection. Day after day the most terrible tortures are inflicted on the Jews, and the worst of all is that one does not know of the other's troubles.
As an illustration of the German Inquisition, the horrifying facts that took place last Saturday towards evening in Wolf Miller's shtibl in Berlin are enough.
At the third Sabbath meal (shalosh seudos) 12 Jews and 2 boys aged 10 were sitting in the shtibl. Suddenly 8 Hitlerites entered the shtibl, 3 of them with revolvers in their hands and 5 with rubber truncheons.
'Hands up!' one of them commanded, and after that everyone was searched. One of them, a young man from Kalisz, had 300 marks on him and a small gold watch; they took these from him.
Then the barbarians tore open the Holy Ark, dragged out the sacred ornaments of the Torah scrolls and hurled them on the ground. They did the same with the tefillin and tallitot that were in the shtibl.
The most horrifying and gruesome thing happened only later. The Jews were stood against the wall and ordered not to move from their places. Then a bench was set up in the middle of the shtibl, on which the Jews were flogged until they bled, and whoever cried out from the great suffering had his punishment doubled.
One Jew begged the robbers: 'Shoot me! Don't torture me bit by bit, give me a quicker death...' For this 'insolence' he was made to lick the blood off another Jew's face and swallow it...
Together with the quiet groans of the tormented and beaten Jews, the little boys too, with tears in their eyes, quietly said 'Shema Yisrael!'...
Among the 12 Jews was an elderly Jew who, in his suffering, gave a hiccup. The bandits, thinking that the Jew was giving signals, beat him with rubber truncheons so hard that his whole face became swollen.
After these gruesome cruelties the Jews had to shout 'Heil Hitler!' and declare that they had deserved the punishment and that the Hitlerite deeds were justified..."

An Interesting Book
About Present-Day Germany.
These days a new book by Zygmunt Nowakowski appears, entitled[?] „Germany at the Present Moment“ (Niemcy à la minute). The author stayed in Germany in the period from the last parliamentary elections up to the festive opening of the Reichstag in the Potsdam Garrison Church.
The book consists of a series of last year's[?] articles, such as „Crescendo“[?], „The Land of Human Fear“ (Kraj bojaźni ludzkiej), „Haman“, „The Vampire of Düsseldorf“ etc. Mr. Nowakowski, who has travelled the German territory far and wide, is a great connoisseur of the mentality, literature and history of post-war Germany.
His impressions, although written lightning-fast „à la minute“, nevertheless have great value, even for the reader who would like to become acquainted with the new Germany thoroughly, not in a dilettantish-superficial way.
Mr. Nowakowski devoted special attention in his book to the painful „Jewish problem“, which is one of the most important in the general „Nazi“ programme.
The author spent a certain time in the main centres of German revolutionary life — in Berlin, Munich, Leipzig and Essen — everywhere getting in contact with the leaders of political, economic and cultural life. The impressions he gathered so[?] thoroughly the author shares with the reader in the above-mentioned book, which, like all the works of this popular publicist, stands out everywhere for its light and gripping[?] style.
It is the first Polish book that touches on this so topical and burning subject.
We therefore hope that the broader reading masses, wishing to know about everything that is happening in the new Germany, will appreciate it properly.

In 1918, when Poland became independent, a meeting of house-owners [?] and tenants was called at the Będzin magistrate to fix the level of rents, and it was decided that in the houses that had running water, another 15 roubles per room was to be added for water. A stroll through the past Passover

[Będzin — Passover, community and culture.] By S. Libas Zun.

The past Passover, the "season of our freedom", passed under the impression of the persecutions of the Jews in Germany. Every single Jew was permeated and pained by the sufferings, torment and insults that our brothers must endure in such a land of culture, which in one Hitlerist leap has fallen into such barbarism.
• • •
The seders in the "Beit Yetomim" [orphanage] looked festive. The children's blessing "who has kept us alive and brought us [to this season]" sounded different than it once did, in their own splendid building...
The cheerful children, in holiday clothes, around the long decorated tables, also enjoyed the pleasant scents of living flowers, brought by those who take care that the children of the "Beit Yetomim" be provided with everything. Even — "silver" cutlery...
And it only remains to wish that "next year" the children of the institution celebrate the seders in — the front halls...
• • •
The gmina [municipal] provisions for the prisoners and the Jewish soldiers had the same "face" as the gmina itself... It was done "as if compelled by a demon", just to discharge the duty. As the Polish proverb says: "Tak krawiec kraje" [the tailor cuts as far as the cloth goes]...
• • •
Our magistrate apparently has plenty of worries too; that was surely the only reason why the magistrate's management completely "forgot" that Jews may not eat leavened bread on Passover, and the same challahs that the magistrate gave to non-Jewish poor people — were also allotted to Jews.
And a large number of Jews were found who took the challahs, precisely on the holiday.... Some of the challah-takers figure on the lists of the "Kimcha [de-Pischa]" and the "Beit Lechem"... These are of the gang for whom our charity societies make sure they lack nothing...
• • •
Of secular events there was an abundance. First and foremost the guest performances of the undoubtedly great talent Dr. Baratoff. At every performance the "Światowid" hall was overfilled with a varied public, which left the performances elevated in mood and purified in spirit. Every show is a new recognition for Jewish dramatic art.
And the art — that is Baratoff. Baratoff conquered the audience with his high, unaffected artistic culture, and influenced the public with the charm of his acting personality.
Baratoff presented himself especially in Strindberg's "The Father", a well-known play. Baratoff brought his "Father" to life — himself, with his artistic self; his "Rittmeister" and a tragic figure dominated, steal into your soul. That is how an actor plays who possesses a great, flaming soul.
— Will he come to us again?...
— Would that he did!...
• • •
The old-new "Muza" presented itself with Leivick's "Chains". We cannot say whether the "chains" were of straw or of iron. We only know that for our editorial office the "chains" were strong — there was no possibility of getting into the "temple of art" of the "Muza"...
• • •
The Jewish public schools held a series of performances. At the performance of the pupils of "Powszechna" [public school] No. 4 (directed by Mrs. Marlińska) the spectators were delighted by the children's talents, their free stage bearing, and the main thing — the appearance of the mandolin orchestra under Simcha Lustig's direction. It is a commendable achievement to set up such a children's orchestra that plays so beautifully. Also successful was "The Children's Paradise", a fantastic legend, especially the rhythmic exercises and dances rehearsed by the well-known gymnastics teacher Icchak Bauszykowski [?]. The school's management deserves a special "yasher koach" for breaking the "tradition" that "whatever is Jewish is treif". The first song number was "Hatikvah", which sounded a little goyish, but "in a time of need" one can be satisfied...
Nor do we want to "tear ourselves apart" [with praise] over the little band of "actresses"; we give them a hearty bravo! Above all the best of them: the brook — Malkale Goldsztajn, the "queen" of the dolls — Gutsze Perlsfater, and the natural doll — Pepesze Buchszrajber.
The decorative side, carried out by Berl Fridler — good.
To the children's parents — a sharp reproach for their slight interest. They did not find it necessary to come and see their children's abilities.
• • •
The intermediate days ["the second days"] — rain, snow, cold; the public huddled in winter garments and spent the time talking about today's livelihoods, which are harder than the splitting of the Red Sea, and about the "good tidings" from Germany...
Income Tax.

[Taxes — income tax; article.]
On the agenda of every taxpayer now stands the matter of income tax.
By the 30th of this month, declarations must be submitted on the income of every taxpayer for the past year 1932.
It should be noted that, apart from the fact that the law imposes a duty to submit a declaration on the amount of income, it is in the interest of the taxpayers themselves to declare their income accurately.
If until this year the centre of gravity, both for the tax authority and for the taxpayers, was the turnover tax — the tax organs applied all their diligence so that turnover should not slip away untaxed, and the taxpayer's whole worry was that his turnover should not be assessed too high — the situation has now changed fundamentally.
The turnover tax is receding into second place; this tax is being reduced step by step and partly shifted onto the first source.
The centre of gravity of all taxes will remain, as in all Western countries, the income tax (podatek dochodowy), and it [printed "der"] remains the key to all kinds of taxes. According to the income tax go the crisis tax, the military tax, the newly introduced property tax, and even the budget of the Jewish community will, from next year, go according to income tax.
The regulation of so important a tax lies in the hands of the taxpayer, and the key — in the declaration he submits.
For a long time, however, it has unfortunately been a habit among a large part of merchants and taxpayers — almost exclusively Jews — to dispose of the declaration with expressions that say nothing: to state a ridiculously small sum of earnings, or, to a great extent, to write: "did not earn," "had a loss." Knowing in advance that such a declaration is not taken into account, many dismiss the formality with a wave of the hand: "they won't believe it anyway."
But it is not so!
With such conduct one only brings harm upon oneself. One hands oneself over to the tax organs for better or for worse, and as a result one blocks one's own way to set things right in the second instance, in case one is wronged by the commission with too high a tax.
In recent years, as the basis for calculating the profits of trade and crafts, an average table has been introduced of the profit on every kind of merchandise in every branch. The table of profits is compiled every year by the Treasury Chambers [izby skarbowe] with the participation of merchants' organisations.
The average profit table establishes how much earning remains on each kind of merchandise after deducting all expenses, such as trading costs, taxes, shortages (manko), losses from falling prices, etc. The table serves as a guide for the assessment commission in determining the amount of every taxpayer's income.
It is therefore quite understandable: when the average table shows, for example, that in haberdashery (galanteria) a net profit of 15 per cent remains, then declaring an income of 500 or 800 zl. a year on a turnover of 15–20,000 zl. is an absurdity, because it does not stand up to any measure [?] of income assessment — especially in a case where, besides trade or craft, the declarant also owns a n[—]h [property, i.e. a house?] or another source of profit, as for instance when members of the household earn separately. When the taxpayer allows himself to state such an unfounded sum in order to reduce his profits, he must have no complaints when the commission makes an assessment and increases his profit out of all proportion.
Such an appeal is already lost in advance [?]; it will be lost also on the ground that the taxpayer deliberately did not want to state his income, and his arguments in the appeal (odwołanie) are in any case unfounded, since, understandably [?], the profit sum stated in the appeal is already much larger than in the declaration, and the taxpayer's two entries contradict each other regarding the amount of profits.
Even less tenable is the bare declaration "did not earn" [misprinted "ferdigt"], "had a loss," because the tax organs demand clear proofs for such claims, with figures and calculations of purchase and sale prices that would justify the loss, or the submission of an extract with proofs, for example protested bills of exchange or other documents establishing that there was a loss. After all, it will be taken into account that one does not live on air, and that keeping a household, paying rent for the dwelling and the shop, heating, lighting, clothing, schooling, etc. amount to a certain sum according to the size of the family and the local way of life, and that to cover the expenses one must, after all, earn something.
To believe further that all these declarants are eating up capital — their own or someone else's — as some claim, one needs exact proofs with a calculation in figures of what the state of their capital was a year ago and what it was in the year in question.
The tax authority keeps everyone on record (ewidencja), with all details of way of life, number of family members, etc., so that concealing the account is not possible at all, and to get off with mere phrases: "did not earn," "had a loss," or to state a ridiculously small sum, such as a few hundred zl. of profit, is an absurdity.
Some taxpayers harm themselves by listing a large number of family members whom they support, thinking that a large number of people in the house proves that one is unable to pay any taxes; this is a cardinal error. For according to the view of the tax organs, when one supports a large family one surely earns more, which must suffice for them, and the tax is therefore larger.
One must remember that children from the age of 16 on are not deducted as a relief in the assessment, on the ground that grown-up children earn their own living. True, the present crisis time is an exception. But as a rule this standpoint cannot be adopted. It is therefore more expedient not to mention in the declaration that the older children are supported by the taxpayer.
Some also think that if one has a property (house) in which one occupies a dwelling for oneself, or in which a relative lives who pays no rent, it means that one has no profit from the property. In truth it is not so: the rent value of one's own dwelling and of the dwellings occupied [?] by relatives is counted as profit, and one must declare it.
It is advisable that the declaration be accurately calculated and well drawn up, which is to the benefit of the taxpayer himself.
In order that the tax assessment be a moderate one, it is absolutely necessary to give all sources of income, because the tax office possesses information about everything anyway, and in many cases to a greater extent than in reality.
A well drawn-up declaration gives chances of winning an appeal when the assessment is too large.
The declarations should not be given, as is customary, to the children who go to school to fill in; rather, one should study them carefully oneself and fill them in, or turn to people who have an idea how to fill them in. By waving them away or dismissing the declarations with contempt, one neglects one's own interests and causes oneself harm and, later, running around after advice, which is for the most part already too late.
In today's bitter times, when taxes occupy a large place in life, one must remember not to neglect the matter of income tax and by no means to forget to file proper declarations by the deadline.
Efraim Celnik.
