[Article — education.] (In the hardest times, in the most dangerous moments, we must see to it that our children are brought up.)
The grave situation in which we find ourselves, our economic circumstances, which make the condition of the average Jew ever harder, and finally the dark 'Hitleriad' — all this has begun to throw Jewry as a whole off balance. People have forgotten all their interests and have become beside themselves.
On the one hand people toil, and it has become almost impossible to carry on the struggle for existence, for the possibility of being. On the other hand, every Jewish heart has been shaken by the horrific events being perpetrated upon our brethren in black, 'cultured' Germany. It is no wonder, then, that we have lost our heads here and do not know which way to turn — the Jews have not lived through such troubles for a long, long time.
But come what may, however gloomy the prospects for the future may be, we must adapt; we must not forget the old rule 'Israel is not widowed' (lo alman Yisrael). We have a durable hide and an elastic back. Since the most ancient times we have been accustomed to bearing the worst blows and wounds, and we are not frightened by the most terrible storm-catastrophes. We can endure and overcome [?] everything. We are patient and stubborn; the force that could annihilate the Jewish people has not yet been born. All the wicked, all the Hamans vanish with the same force with which they surfaced, and the Jewish people remains an eternal people with its own traditions and folk customs, among whatever nations we may find ourselves and to whatever lands we may be cast.
And therefore, therefore we must first of all be conscious and keep ourselves within the frame. We must see to it that all functions continue to be carried out properly among us; we must make sure that everything goes on normally, that all the details of our life are in their place, at the proper level.
We have always known, for example, that the Jewish father, that our parents did everything in the world to bring up their children better and more decently. In former times, when the bein ha-zmanim (the inter-term break) came, the father racked his brains [?] over the question of what to do with his son or with the children who went to heder; day and night he was occupied only with how to make decent people of them.
A long way has been travelled since that time. Other times have come, with other worries, with other duties and responsibilities. Today, even though we find ourselves in quite different conditions, incomparably harder than in the past, we nonetheless care much, much more about the future of our children. We devote more time, more work, more strength and more money to them than in the past, and nonetheless one cannot say that the upbringing is a better, a more fruitful one. True, the conditions in which we live are different, the world is open, everything strives more towards life, more towards developing.
Here a father stands up and asks the school managements to take more interest in the schoolchildren, who are being corrupted by frequenting undesirable venues, going to the cinemas to see films unsuitable for them, or who are drawn to the matches (metshn) where games of chance and entertainments not at all suitable for them take place.
Yes, these 'entertainments' bring immeasurable poison into the little hearts of our little ones. Nobody stops them from going to see racy and detective films and supporting programmes [?], which are distinguished by coarse jokes — coarse even for adults — and half or even completely naked women. The same goes for the matches, when the lust for murder flares up, that one should knock the other down, that one should kill the other; the same goes for ping-pong and other games, which tear the children away from the book and from school, from refined feeling and from idealistic thinking about a better future, a brighter and finer tomorrow.
The cinema, sport — these are all useful things, which can give our children a great deal; they can help them develop and educate them spiritually and morally, but all this is said [?] on condition that one takes an interest in it. Are there so few films from which children can derive spiritual enjoyment, and has sport so few branches suited to the various periods of childhood? And does gymnastics give so little to the upbringing of children?
Children and adults. Does one need to tell anyone that these are two separate worlds, two separate levels? For that very reason they need to be under the supervision of qualified educators, who supposedly take this under their protection — at a time when it is being completely neglected from A to Z (from alef to tav).
If, for example, a mother comes into the school, they will even have complaints against her, as if she does not pay attention to this or that defect [?]. They quite forget that this belongs to them, as soon as the child is in their charge. The school takes no interest at all in what the children do when they are not at school, in what they fill their time with then.
Yes, they can have complaints against the parents that they take no interest in their children, but they forget one thing: that both the lower strata and the middle class find themselves in such conditions that, on the one hand, they do not have the possibility to occupy themselves with their children, being less [qualified for it] than their educators, and on the other hand they lack the routine, the clear head, the simplest possibilities. The average people are, after all, harried and tormented, so that even with the best will they cannot afford to take care of their children's upbringing; besides, this is a speciality which demands much refinement, much awareness and a great deal of intelligence.
There are even parents' committees everywhere, which are supposed to see to it that these functions are carried out, but who takes an interest in these matters, whom do these questions concern, which bring in no profits? Insofar as attention is paid at all, it is only as is still the custom in the elementary (folk) schools; in our secondary schools, on the other hand (printed 'ragegn' — misprint for 'dakegn'), where tuition is quite expensive, nobody takes any interest in it at all, and if such parents' committees exist there, the question arises what their work consists of and why they come there? They could after all for once give a report of their activity; if they are engaged in public work, why should nobody know about it? Perhaps one should for once take counsel with the parents of any child at all, with whom one nevertheless needed (printed 'geboykht', misprint) to be in contact.
Our present-day schools are therefore by no means educational institutions; they are nothing more than schools, where one must come to find out which lessons are being set, so that by the next day they should have been learnt. But we need the schools to be at the same time educational institutions in the true sense of the word.
If, therefore, the schools want to be this not merely pro forma, they must then get in touch both with the parents' committee and with the children's parents. In that case an investigation must be carried out into the conditions in which the children live at home and the conditions in which their parents find themselves. Otherwise we cannot imagine in what way the children can be educated in the schools.
It is high time that our schools became educational institutions not just on paper but in reality. Present-day parents of relatively average standing are not in a position to give their children an upbringing at home. They can do no more than keep in contact with the schools, inquire, study the development and the intelligence of the child and the results, report to the educators and hold consultations with them.
In bringing up children, on the other hand, one must be fully aware. Parents must not forget that very often the head is not on it; time does not stand still, the children grow and their development moves on with them systematically; therefore one must not let time go to waste, because every neglect is a delay, and a delay must not occur in any element that is growing, that is in the midst of developing.
Those who are good observers, those who research and study the problem of education, see that in the last ten years countless mistakes have been made in this field, which must not be made any more. We must therefore take proper interest in correcting the mistakes that have been made until now. We must not allow our children to be continually brought up in a defective way.
For all parents their children are the apple of their eye; in their children they picture to themselves a blossoming future, a glorious tomorrow, but even with the best will they are not in a position to give them what they would wish. They do not have the strength for it, the times do not allow them, and not everyone is qualified for this delicate mission; therefore there is no other way out than that the schools should do it — the principals, to whom we entrust our children from their earliest years, and who are also qualified for it, and of whom it turns out that they fulfil the mission in the proper way.
However sad the Jewish situation may be, however hard our forms of life may come to us, we must not let our children be neglected — our future, who must carry on our ancient stock, which has been bound up with so much self-sacrifice (mesires nefesh) from its day of birth.
R. Les [?].
Who Needs an Old Piano?

[Feuilleton / story — a letter; Z. Libin.]
Z. Libin.

Dear Rivkele!

I have not written to you for such a long time. If you ask "why" — I will not know what to answer. That's just how it is: somehow the writing didn't happen, and so the days and the years ran by. So. long a time has gone by, and now I catch myself realising that I have not written to you for so long; it vexes me and my heart aches over it.

But why does one hear nothing about you? Why have you forgotten me so? I heard that you know what is happening to me now. Why then have you left me like this in my hard, tormented situation? Why don't you show yourself, why does one hear nothing at all from you?

My friend, I shall tell you many things in this present letter of mine. But so as not to forget a small matter, I want to ask you right away: perhaps you know of someone who needs to have a piano in the house? I want to give away my old piano. I am not asking for money — that is, if someone did give me a few zlotys, perhaps I would not refuse to take them. But I know that nobody will give a broken[?] groschen, so why should I make a fool of myself and ask for money? I am giving the piano away for nothing. All I want is that someone come and carry it down, and then they can do with it whatever the heart desires.

My piano occupies the finest spot in my flat, but it stays quiet and mute. Not because it cannot be played, only because there is no one to play it. Sometimes it happens that I myself touch the silenced keys, and my piano lets out such a piercing, slow groan that the heaviness on my heart grows heavier still. My piano throws a fright into me and I run out of the house.

I want to give the piano away because I am moving out of my present flat. Should I take the piano with me — I neither need it nor want it. So what does one do with it? I would leave it behind and let my landlord do with it what he likes, but somehow it is hard for me to do such a thing. When I walk past my piano, it seems to me as if it understood my thoughts. It seems to me as if the piano were speaking to me reproachfully:

— Simply abandon me like this, ownerless? What have I done to deserve this?

No, I cannot do it. And on top of that people frightened me and told me that the landlord can legally compel me to clear out the flat and take away the piano. Others even say that I may indeed move out, but as long as I have left the piano behind I am still counted as a tenant and rent can be demanded of me, even though I will already be living in another flat. Then I would have two landlords to deal with. That's all I need! So I beg you, Rikele — perhaps after all you know of someone who wants a piano?

I have already offered the piano to all the neighbours. They don't need it; pardon me, they won't take it even for free. Some neighbours even put me through a cross-examination:

— How old is the piano?

Well, go and tell them stories about how old my piano is! When I answer that it is not brand-new, they ask further:

— Can one play on it?

— If there is someone to play, one can.

They pull a face and answer that a new radio they would take from me, but a piano, and an old one at that — they don't want.

Well, Rivkele? You surely remember how much joy, how much happiness we lived through when the piano was bought and when the piano was brought into the house! I think you even went with us to buy the piano. As far as I remember, you and my wife kissed each other for joy and happiness that we had lived to buy a piano for our Dorele, our little daughter.

And when the piano was brought into the house — how bright, how joyful it became in every little corner! The flat seemed to receive a new soul. And when little Dorele came home from school and saw the piano — how she started dancing for joy! And when Dorele sat down at the piano and played through her lesson, Rivke, dear — you were at our house then, you remember how the house was filled with magic and rapture, do you remember? I will never forget that day.

That same piano stood there new, more beautiful, radiant, proud — the queen of the whole house. And the little children, young, merry, crowded around the piano as if bewitched[?]. Their little eyes burned with curiosity, and the whole home was filled with children's joy.

Gone, gone are those years! The children grew up, they married, they moved into homes of their own. The prophecies about Dorele, the predictions of the piano teachers who taught Dorele that she would grow up to be a great pianist, did not come true.

Dorele now lies ill in hospital. In the house it is quiet, agonisingly quiet. Who knows what will become of Dorele? A heavy, gnawing gloom stifles the house, the walls throw a fright into one, one longs to run away from the home, in every corner tears are shed.

So we are moving to a smaller flat; we no longer need a big flat. But Rivke, what does one do after all with the old piano?

There is no room for the piano in the new flat. Who needs a piano? One needs nothing any more. One thinks: perhaps this is already the last flat?

But perhaps you know, Rivke, who needs an old piano? Skilled, practised fingers and a warm heart can still draw wonderful tones out of the piano even now. But there is no one to caress the old, lonely keys with even a little warmth of soul. And one still wonders: perhaps someone will take an old piano into their home?...

Z. Libin.
A Historical Warning

[Article — Hitler, antisemitism and the Jewish future.] By Dep.[uty?] Dr. Y. Rozenblat.
It would be a great mistake to regard Hitler as an episode, as an accident. When the revolution broke out in Russia in 1917 and the handful of Bolsheviks seized power, everyone hoped that now, any moment now, they would be driven out and everything would go back to the old ways. Experience has shown that this was a great error. Whatever one's attitude to the Soviets, the fact remains that they are here, they exist, and will probably go on existing for a very long time. Hitler is not an individual phenomenon, and one cannot dismiss[?] him with the word "adventurer". 17 million Germans voted for him at the elections, and the rest have today capitulated to him.
How long this system will last is very hard to say. What it will develop into, no one can know; and precisely for us Jews, who received a terrible blow with the upheaval in Germany and who are threatened with being robbed even of the few rights we acquired in bitter struggles over whole generations, it is very important to consider the situation that has arisen with full seriousness.
Now we are forced to fight bitterly and to damage the enemy in every way, to wound him in his most sensitive spot, in order to paralyse the attacks that have already done us such great harm.
We must not have any illusions. The assaults, the atrocities[?] against Jews may perhaps cease in Germany in time, but one thing has already happened — German Jewry has been eliminated from the whole of public life, it has been thrown out of all the free professions, out of all offices, the economic existence of the Jews has been destroyed, and this will not be improved in the near future.
Hitler is a phenomenon of a historical process as old as the world: from time to time, in various forms, there occur outbreaks of antisemitism, which dominates the non-Jewish world. In the perspective of centuries or of millennia these outbreaks look quite different from what they were in reality. The Megillah [the Book of Esther] tells us in epic form about a Hitlerism that bore a different name then; in the light of the epic, Haman within a short time made a plan to destroy the whole of Persian Jewry at one blow, within a few days obtained a corresponding decree from Ahasuerus, and in the course of the following few days the matter was turned upside down, Haman and his sons were killed, and a great joy came over the Jews.
It may be that after thousands of years — and would that it be so — the Hitlerite epoch too will be described in such an innocent way. In reality the events no doubt unfolded quite differently.
From time to time, in every generation, here or there, a violent outbreak of antisemitism comes to the surface. Just as from time to time a period of calm sets in, and the Jews then think that antisemitism and the dangers threatening from it have entirely disappeared. The same psychology ruled the German Jews, who for decades firmly believed that for them the exile was over, that they had already attained everything they wanted and would live forever in the same situation.
Hitler is a warning example that antisemitism lives among the nations among whom we live, and that there is no certainty it will not prevail again in other places. The sympathy we have found in our struggle almost all over the world must not deceive us. Other factors, purely selfish ones, play a role here too. Already the debate in the English Parliament, by which the English people has obliged us to eternal gratitude, showed the sober reader the situation in all its clarity.
In no country does the government listen as attentively to public opinion as in England. In no other country is Parliament so strongly the expression of public opinion as in England. And although all the speakers of all tendencies demanded that the government intervene on behalf of the Jews, the English government diplomatically wriggled out of the intervention and answered that it cannot do so because English citizens had not suffered, and the other matters are internal affairs of Germany. When it was demanded that the persecutions of the Jews be put on the agenda of the League of Nations, the same government answered that the proposal must be submitted by the injured parties themselves. The Jews are not a member of the League of Nations, and nobody else may do it in their name. In other words, in plain Yiddish this means that there is no one to lay the paper with the "proshenie" [petition, Polish prośba] on the table of the League of Nations.
At the very same time, when all countries condemn the Hitlerite regime, people gather in Washington to conclude new treaties, although he, Hitler, does not fulfil the old ones. All this would be quite incomprehensible to the mind of a simple person, if one did not know that states and nations let themselves be guided by an ice-cold egoism. Of sentiments one only talks; but in reality they play no role whatsoever.
The ice-cold truth is that the Jewish people does not yet have the possibility of carrying the paper onto the table of the League of Nations by itself, and here lies the deep cause of our terrible situation.
For hundreds and thousands of years we have been forced to defend ourselves, to wage a defensive struggle. Even a sergeant knows that the hardest thing is to wage a defensive. He who is on the defence must constantly reckon with the blow — when, who and where will attack him. He who is on the offensive chooses for himself the moment, the place and the means of attack. Constant defence and the fear of unexpected attacks dry out the brains and draw the marrow from the bones; they demoralise, because they kill energy. All military books, just like all military authors, from the smallest to the most famous, agree on this: victory is possible only through attack; through defence no radical change can be achieved.
Quite independently of this, we must now continue the struggle that has been forced upon us. In order to resist annihilation it is very necessary to enlighten the Jewish masses about the seriousness of the situation. One must point out that one must think about [printed "ממון", probably for "מען מוז"] not always being dependent on the sympathy and pity of others, but becoming a factor equal to others, having the right and the possibility to demand — not to beg — what is due to us.
If the Hitlerite attack ends merely in[?] our managing, for one reason or another, to weaken the attack a little, we have lost, because everywhere there are a great number of sympathisers of Hitler who say openly that it is necessary to imitate what he has done in Germany. Such political conjunctures favourable to us will not always be found as now. But if the Hitlerite regime opens the eyes of the broadest strata of the Jewish people in all countries where Jews live, and they understand that one must strive for a radical solution of the Jewish problem, in order to make the periodic outbreaks of antisemitism impossible — then we shall be able to say that we have learned from the recurring historical phenomena.

Saved Thanks to Radio
The Expedition to the Highest Mountain in the World — Mount Everest.

The English newspapers are now reporting details of how three members of the expedition to the highest mountain in the world, Mount Everest, were saved literally by a miracle.
At the foot of the Himalaya mountains, in the town of Darjeeling (printed "Dariyeling"), the English expedition moved its headquarters, and from there three daring young men set out to climb the mountain higher and higher. The whole time they stayed in contact with headquarters thanks to the radio set they had taken along.
The radio station in Darjeeling constantly informed them about the weather conditions in the mountains and gave them instructions on how they should proceed.
When the three heroic Englishmen were already at a height of 7 kilometres, they suddenly lost contact with Darjeeling.
For an unknown reason the radio waves did not reach the explorers, and all the efforts of the radio-telegraphist remained without success.
The situation of the three lonely heroic explorers became more dangerous with every hour. The evil forces of nature raged ever more strongly. A terrible snowstorm was raging, and every moment there was the threat that they would be buried by the snow avalanches.
The radio-telegraphist in Darjeeling, however, did not lose his head, and he hit upon a truly brilliant idea. He reasoned thus: since the radio waves of his own station are too weak and cannot reach the scientists, perhaps the powerful radio signals of... London will reach them. The radio-telegraphist got in touch by telephone with London, and from there the signals were immediately sent out to the three heroic scientists who were wrestling with the elements.
Strange as it may sound, the three men did hear the signals of the London radio station and received the necessary instructions as to which side of the mountain they could descend without any fear.
True, this communication of the radio-telegraphist made a small detour of 20 thousand kilometres, from Darjeeling to London and from there back to the Himalayas. The cloud hovering over the peak of the mountain had not yet managed to change its shape, but the news, which had been passed by telephone to London, had already reached the ears of the explorers of Mount Everest.

M. Goldman.
What Jews Make a Living From
(Impressions of the Sosnowiec Exchange).

Even the Sambatyon rests once a week, but the corner of Modrzejowska and Targowa boils and seethes the full seven days. Here is the Sosnowiec "Wall Street", the black exchange, where Jews are blackened before they slave out a couple of gulden for a livelihood.
Just like all branches of industry and trade, the exchange too is now going through a severe crisis, and here too there are now quite a few "unemployed" – simply put, Menachem-Mendels, who wander around with sticks in their hands, hoping to draw a livelihood out of thin air...
And there was a time, not long ago at all, when Jews made a fine living on this street corner. To earn 20–30 zł. a day, and sometimes even a whole half-hundred, was a mere trifle.
That was in the days of inflation, when people played on "hausse" and "baisse", speculated on the exchange-rate differences, and spent whole hours sitting at the long-distance telephone just chasing the Warsaw rates. There were even some who had their branches in the capital and used to trade on a really large scale.
And not only in foreign-currency trading: big discount deals were also done on our homely Wall Street. A few years ago the banks were still great aristocrats; they would accept for discount only "prima-shmima" bills, and if, God forbid, there was some ink blot on a paper, it was already treyf. The exchange, however, looked at that blot through its fingers: so what if a bill is a little soiled? So what if the signer is perhaps also a little "blotted" – in the great hubbub it will work out. Everything is merchandise! And all the [?] and third-rate papers found their final resting place on the exchange, where, by the way, people relished "groping" this trade.
And were the American cheques some trifle to speak of? What turnovers were made with them, how much scheming was done with them!
And not to mention before a holiday – the exchange was literally flooded with these "Yankee" cheques that were sent across the sea to dear fathers and mothers, sisters, brothers and relatives.
And not only cheques – real dollars too used to arrive, and "all rivers run into the sea": both the cheques and the cash dollars first had to receive their "tikkun" on the exchange, and from every transaction nice [?] profits remained with the Sosnowiec exchange people.
But how does the situation look now? All business has fizzled out. Even if a certain moment of "hausse" and "baisse" occasionally comes along, one can hardly take advantage of it, because there is simply no [?currency] to play "up" and "down".
The discount business is nowadays almost defunct. Firstly, the great crisis and stagnation in the commercial world are at work here, so there are few bills. And secondly, confidence in this kind of bill has collapsed altogether: the paper that appears on the exchange is mostly (printed "srov") such as finds no taker, and if there is a taker, the safe bill (misprint "ziberer" for "zikherer") is lacking...
Incidentally, the banks too are no longer such aristocrats as before, and they are now quite willing to discount bills not necessarily from the choicest firms.
The coal trade, which was one of the liveliest nerves in the organism of the exchange, has been completely written off (printed "amra-tirt"), and as for the transactions in American cheques, which were also a sizeable item in the exchange's budget – they too are almost out of the market.
Firstly the crisis in America has had its effect, because of which the relatives on the other side have reduced, or even stopped entirely, their support for their dear relatives; and secondly – the latest dollar crash, which has quite strangled the cheque trade that was barely breathing [?] anyway, and if one now brings a cheque to the exchange, it is not so easy to dispose of, unless it carries a good endorsement (żyro).
And the bottom line is that apart from two or three "carp-heads" who have larger sums at their disposal and are financially strong, all the remaining small fry (płotki) wander around and flounder like little fish thrown out onto dry land...
So what does one actually do all day on the exchange?
It so happens that a merchant needs a few dollars to cover a purchase; a fellow [?] sidles up [?] with some greasy "dollars" (printed "sollars") warmed up in a sack: there is a bit of a commotion over the dollar and a demand for gold dollars begins; one also deals [?] in a dollar bond [? printed "ra-larvike", probably dolarówka]; on the eve of the draw one takes a couple of zlotys for it as "play money" for the day; one speculates on a few "Dillon bonds" [? printed "rilanovkes"], brokers an apartment – and from all these trades, in short [?], a few dozen Sosnowiec Jews draw their "livelihood".
And truly, heaven forbid [?], there is nothing to envy in the eternally toiling and worn-out exchange men. –
Their livelihood hangs [?] on [—].
Oneg Shabbat — Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's portion (Tazria-Metzora)

[Oneg Shabbat — the weekly portion.] Torah sayings, remarks and anecdotes on this week's Torah portion.
Collected and styled by Yehuda.
Parashat Tazria-Metzora
The Portion
—o—
a) "And on the eighth day the flesh of his foreskin shall be circumcised" (Lev. 12:3)
To the Radomsk Rebbe [Radomsko], author of "Tiferet Shlomo", there once came a simple householder, a habitual sinner, to honour the Rebbe with the office of sandek.
"I have come to honour you with a mitzvah, dear Rebbe," he says.
The Rebbe laughs:
"Me you come to honour with a mitzvah, and the sins you keep for yourself — perhaps you might for once do it the other way round?.."
The young man grows angry:
"The Rebbe will be committing a sin by refusing to accept the mitzvah of being sandek."
The clever Rebbe laughs on:
"You begrudger! You revel in all those sins, and you won't grant me even such a tiny little sin?.."
Nifla'ot of the "Tiferet Shlomo".
• • •
Yehoshua Steinberg, director of the Vilna [Vilnius] teachers' seminary, once had a conversation with the Russian censor, a hater of Israel. The conversation came round to the foreign press.
"The entire foreign press," says the censor, "is Judaized."
"Indeed, and that is why," answers Steinberg, "it reaches us circumcised..."
(As is known, the Russian censorship cut out of the foreign press arriving in Russia all suspicious passages.)
—o—
b) "When a man [adam] shall have in the skin of his flesh" (Lev. 13:1)
Hebrew has various terms for a human being: ish, gever, enosh and adam. According to the "Zohar", adam is a higher concept of man.
And therefore in the portion on plagues only "adam" is said, because the causes for which plagues come are, according to the Sages: anger, evil talk — and all this is more common among great people. Mi Shalah.
• • •
Rabbi Hirsch Auerbach, rabbi of Kunig[?], fell ill. The doctor comes, tells the patient to show his tongue and says:
"Rabbi, your tongue is not clean."
"Of course[?]," he says, "and who, for our many sins, has a clean tongue?.."
—o—
c) "And the hair in the plague is turned white" (ibid., 3)
This means those who carry their plague "deeper than the skin of his flesh", deep beneath the skin, while outwardly everything is "turned white" — smoothed over, whitewashed; this is counted as the first plague, because it is the most dangerous... Ma'or va-Shemesh.
—o—
d) "And cedar wood, and scarlet, and hyssop" (Lev. 14:4)
There must be a balance[?]: lower than grass (hyssop) and higher than a cedar tree (cedar wood). Sometimes one must be great in one's own eyes, and sometimes small. One need only know where and when... Menorat ha-Tehorah.
• • •
The Rebbe Reb Bunem used to say: a person must have two pockets; in one he must have "I am but dust and ashes", and in the other "who can deceive me" [mi yirmeh li]. One need only know when to use the one pocket and when the other...
—o—
e) "That they empty the house" (ibid., 36)
For the Gemara says that plagues of houses come upon the stingy, who possess much and do not want to lend anything; therefore their punishment is that they must carry out their household goods, and even take the neighbours to help, so as to clear out quickly before the priest comes — so that the neighbours should see all the things of which he said he did not have them, not wanting to lend them... Tzeror ha-Mor.
Haftarah
—o—
f) "And there were four leprous men" (II Kings 7)
God announced the tidings of redemption through lepers, because with a leper we find a remarkable thing: white hair in leprosy is a sign of impurity, but when "it is all turned white", he is pure. So too the Jews: when they become "wholly guilty", they are redeemed... Therefore, to hint at this, the tidings of redemption were announced through lepers. Ahavat Yehonatan.
Anti-Shmadism (Opposition to the Baptism of Jews)

[Article — Nazi antisemitism in Germany and the assimilated Jews.]
New times — new antisemites. New antisemites — new decrees against Jews. The Nazi power in Germany [Deutschland] has prohibited by law mixed marriages between Jews and non-Jews. Perhaps they will also carry out the "revolution" [read: resolution] that Hitlerite clergymen had adopted against the conversion of Jews. Converted Jews, say the pious Hitlerite clergymen, merely defile German blood and the German nation. Therefore: down with converts — converts are even worse than Jews.
So argue the Hitlerite bishops and priests.
And since Hitler himself in person now holds power, he can surely issue an order that no more Jews are to be baptised.
In short, as we say in our Yiddish: "a scandal in town" — Jews will no longer be able to convert, Jews will no longer be able to run away from Jews; and even more: Jews will have to remain Jews, because converts will be persecuted even worse than the Jews themselves.
Bad and bitter times are approaching even for "our" converts: the bitter yoke of Jewishness will press on their baptised shoulders even more than on the real Jews, who did not run away from Jews.
And it may even come to this, that they, our converts, will have to feel the whole bitter poison of exile, and they will, God forbid, begin to think that they, the converts, are the true "Thou-hast-chosen-us-niks" [the "chosen ones", mockingly], and the proof: they are persecuted even worse than the real Jews, than the unconverted Jews.
For we know to what mysticisms and abstract spiritual self-delusions troubles, pressing [?] troubles can lead.
———
A Jew hates a convert. Well, indeed, why should we love those who run away, or used to run away, from us because things went badly for us — traitors and cowards; those who desert the camp no people loves. We Jews have perhaps even more right to hate our converts and deserters [?], and not only because they ran away from us, from the weak, but also because the greatest enemies of the Jews came precisely from among our traitors and converts: many of the great inquisitors were converts; among Isabella's Christian counsellors there were Jews; and we Jews will not be at all surprised if among the Hitlerite leaders, too, there turn out to be such as have, by all accounts, no reason to love converts.
But nevertheless we may soon have to reckon with their situation too, simply because they are becoming a part — and a very characteristic part — of the Jewish question in general.
———
How will fully and half-assimilated Jewry react to these decrees?
What effect will this new kind of antisemitism — or, as we ought to call it, anti-"shmadism" [opposition to the baptism of Jews] — have on conscious Jewish assimilation and on unconscious Jewish assimilation; on the tens of thousands of Jews who deliberately seek to assimilate with the surrounding peoples, and on the hundreds of thousands of Jews who assimilate, so to speak, unwittingly, because they liked to go with the stream, and because the abnormal national Jewish life gives them no content?
These questions are already interesting and perhaps also necessary to discuss, because the new Hitlerite antisemitism in Germany is only a strong, exaggerated expression of a tendency that has long existed in Europe — and in America.
Neither the modern bourgeoisie nor the modern proletariat is Christian enough, nor religious enough at all, to have a special love for converts and for Jews who run away from Jews.
It may look like a paradox, but it is nevertheless a truth that today's educated Christian, i.e. the model of the average person of tomorrow, much prefers Zionism, the outspoken Jewish nationalist, to the assimilated Jew:
the former he regards instinctively, perhaps, as his equal in standing ["patent"?]; the assimilated Jew, or one who hides his Jewishness, he regards at best with suspicion.
Zionism negates [?] assimilation entirely, both because it is national suicide and because assimilation does not solve the Jewish question.
The great non-Jewish world, for its part, regards Jewish assimilation with suspicion.
And this suspicion — which, incidentally, can find a place even in a proletarian ideology — is the main motive of modern antisemitism.
Its most brutal and savage expression is anti-"shmadism": the strong modern opposition to assimilated Jews.
———
How, then, will assimilated Jewry react to the new antisemitism, which is directed mainly against it?
There can be no doubt that a mighty new stream of "returnees" will soon fertilize the whole of Jewish life in general.
"Those who leave and come back" is a chronic phenomenon in Jewish history. The Spanish Inquisition, together with the returning Marranos, brought back many creative forces to the Jewish people.
There can therefore be no doubt that in the next few decades many creative forces that had gone away [?] will come back to us, not to speak of masses of converts who will "become Jews again" under the cutting whip of the new economic and ideological [printed "ireaishn", misprint] antisemitism.
Some German-Jewish writers are already very much interested in the Jewish question from the midst of Jewish life.
Some Yiddishists already hope that the present new wave of antisemitism will help the Yiddish language and literature.
But whatever changes and reactions this new wave of antisemitism — and not only in Germany — may call forth in Jewish life, neither the world nor the Jewish people will be freed of the Jewish question as long as the great world is "Zionistically" disposed only negatively — as it is now — and does not help us to build positively a healthy and our own Jewish life!
Leo Koenig.
A Queen Who Dies for Her Sins

The tragic story of Queen Mary of Scotland, her loves and political intrigues.

3.
Summary of the previous chapters:
Queen Mary of Scotland was crowned after her father's death, when she was about ten months old. At 6 she was betrothed, and at 15 she married the crown prince, son of Henri II and Catherine de Médicis.
Mary's ambitions were great. The proposal of the English queen Elizabeth to sign the Treaty of Edinburgh, so that she would have free passage through England — she rejected. Travelling home, she was received at the Scottish port with great honour. The Scottish burghers, who had been told [?] that the queen was a dissolute woman, saw before them a young, graceful, naive woman, and in great enthusiasm the Puritan preachers [?] sang chapters of Psalms in her honour.
On arriving in her capital, Mary nominated chief [?] advisers from the Protestant camp. This provoked great [—] issued a ban on Catholic demonstrations.
At that time people began to talk of matches for the queen, who was a widow. Meanwhile the Chastelard affair took place.
Now read on:
Chastelard was a young French poet and musician who was terribly in love with Queen Mary Stuart, and she with him — a little, too. When Mary left France, Chastelard also sailed on the same ship. Mary, knowing that Chastelard was in love with her, sent him back to France, but he could not stay there without Mary, and he came back.
Mary received him quite warmly, often invited him to her and spent time with him, and even allowed herself in public to lean on his shoulder and to caress him. To the courtiers this was a surprise, because Queen Mary was proud by nature, and no strange man whatsoever dared to have any access to her.
[—] was sure that the queen was in love with him, prepared a "surprise" for her. He hid in Mary's bedroom. The ladies-in-waiting, putting the queen's bedroom in order, found the enamoured Frenchman hidden under the queen's dressing-table.
The queen was greatly incensed by this and banished the poet Chastelard from her court. But he did not give up his plans and began to bombard the queen with love letters written in a poetic tone. Mary was greatly moved by the love letters, answered that she forgave him and allowed him to come back to court.
A few days passed; the queen again received him, conversed with him in friendly talks, so that Chastelard regarded himself as the queen's only beloved.
One night, before the queen went to sleep, he again hid in her bed[room] [—] undress, he came out of his hiding place and threw himself upon her with bestial passion.
At the queen's screams her half-brother came running and tore Chastelard away from the hysterical queen, who could not calm down after the sudden assault.
Chastelard was put in prison, where he was severely tortured.
A few weeks later Chastelard stood before a court, which sentenced him to death.
When he was led to the scaffold, he sang love songs in Mary's honour, and so, singing, he died a terrible death.
This was the first true victim of Mary Stuart's love games.
Her second victim was the Italian David Rizzio, who at first was Mary's secretary in charge of her correspondence with the Pope and with France, but later became her close counsellor in place of Moray and Maitland, and also — her lover.
At the time when Rizzio became Mary's close counsellor, she was not content with that [—] cousin Lord Darnley [printed "Dargli"], who was a pretender to the English throne, and she fell in love with him.
The new lover too happened to be a Catholic, and since Queen Elizabeth, for her own reasons, protested and would not permit the match, the wedding between Mary and the lord took place secretly in Rizzio's lodgings, but according to all the rules of the Catholic Church.
Later, when the "secret" was discovered and all the obstacles to the match had not the slightest effect, the wedding took place again with great pomp and full ceremonial in the splendid Holyrood Palace.
The love between Mary and her husband, Lord Darnley, did not last long. Darnley, who moreover was not a pleasant person, used to make himself many enemies. Between him and Mary a sharp quarrel also arose because she would not let him govern together with her. He demanded it of her many times, and when she refused him, he became estranged from her and prepared a conspiracy against her.

[Page head, in a frame:] "The Cooking Ladle" — in honour of the 1st of May. — by Ben Amotz.

May Eve.
Thoughts of a Sosnowiec [Sosnowiec] merchant.

May Eve has come —
welcome!
May refreshes,
psh-psh—psh,
May revives —
and I am delighted!

I am already a Jew past thirty
and still I cannot grasp
how a person gets enraptured
by a little hill, by a valley,
by a sky,
by a little flower
and other such nonsense!

And if the sun pours out its rays,
must one at once fall on one's knees?
And if little flowers give off scent,
must one at once leap into the air?
And if a little river winds along,
must one at once lose one's mind?
And if the grass is already green —
so what?
Big deal, on my grandmother! [mocking idiom]
Will I make a living from it?!...
Let us not fool ourselves:
a piece of cheviot, worsted,
has more substance —
there is something to take hold of,
there is something to feel,
and the rest is "junk" [łamus], faintness;
not worth anything
is whatever lives on the earth...
And in general, and in general,
what is poetry good for, [people?][?]
when in your head buzz and spin —
protested bills.

And in general, what has the poet got to do with it,
what does he need [?], what is he chattering about
["ban!"][?] — if he would at least raise
the price of "manufaktura" [textiles]!
— — — — — — — — — — —
The bottom line:
I consider very foolish
just what they call — literary.
Kibitzer.
The Only Remedy.

[Humour — "The Cooking Ladle"; Zagłębie — taxes, satirical proclamation.]
(Proclamation for the First of May)
To all the clever inhabitants of Zagłębie!
Since the sequestrators want to thrust their hands deep into your pockets and drag out of you your last few groszy, and since, moreover, our city administrators want to do nothing for you — the only remedy left is to abolish pockets!
Citizens of Zagłębie! Abolish your pockets.
Down with pockets!
An end to pockets!
Let no pockets exist any more — not in trousers, not in jackets, not in overcoats, and not even in pyjamas.
When there are no pockets, the bailiffs [egzekutorzy] will have nowhere to thrust their hands.
All who accept our proposal we call upon to come to the mass meeting that will take place next Monday, the 1st of May.
Sefirah [the Counting of the Omer].

[Humour — "The Cooking Ladle"; parody of the Counting of the Omer.]
Within a few days I have to pay the landlord for the flat.
So, starting from the first [of the month], with a headache, in good time, I count Sefirah:
"Today is one day to the rent money"[?]...
The bridegroom says: well, fine, she is clever, she is rich, how splendid — but what about her years?
The poor matchmaker wrinkles his nose and counts Sefirah:
"Today is forty-one days in years"...
A girl tells her parents a secret (there was no good watch kept over her).
The mother sits "in chopped wounds" [= in deep trouble] and counts her daughter's dismal Sefirah:
"Today is nine months to the misfortune"...
Polygamy is disgusting and vulgar and stands in contradiction to the holy law; nevertheless I know a communal worker, a fine Jew, who in this respect must count Sefirah:
"Today there are three wives in the house"...
More than one of you has been a fool and given his friend an endorsement [żyro][?].
And when the friend went bankrupt, you counted Sefirah for him:
"Today thousands of złoty to pay [zapłacić]"...
One shudders at the cruel pogrom raging in Germany's capital.
The Jewish victims already outnumber the days of the Sefirah:
"Today fifty killed in Berlin"...
A. Liber.
Redemption Is Coming.

[Humour — "The Cooking Ladle"; Zagłębie — taxes and merchants, satirical poem.]
(Dedicated to the freshly flogged.)

Little merchants, tiny ones,
poor, plain little ones,
you are, poor things, as clean
as if just out of the bathhouse.

The little assessment commission,
oh dear, has brought you
to your little death-throes —
you'll soon be done for.

It has, without any difficulty,
assessed your livelihood
and your income
at thousands of złoty.

From the "abratn"[?] one will
soon hear of bankruptcies,
and of brand-new little refugees
one will hear in town.

Mountains of summonses [wezwania],
in "Iuba"[?] "paranies"[?],
dead appeals[?] [odwołania]
will pour down in plenty.

You'll pawn, pardon me, your underpants
for the taxes [podatki],
and slowly you'll sit down
on the "fleshy chair" [= your bare behind]...

And now the bailiffs
will make your life a misery,
and dozens of times
come to visit you...

A chair and a little table,
the little pillow from under your head —
this for a tax,
and that for a protested bill.

Merchants, manufacturers,
plain speculators
will shake hands with one another.
One will hear no more of the rich.

Time will make them
into ordinary folk,
and make the little world
equal for everyone.

And no "pule"[?] at all
will remain until the Redemption,
and the Messiah will come
soon, for sure.

For the Gemara says, after all,
that the Messiah, so it is reasoned,
will come only then,
"when the last penny is gone from the purse"...
Helmantshik.
Hitler at Wilhelm's.

[Humour — "The Cooking Ladle"; Germany — Hitler, satirical sketch.]
A conference in Doorn [Wilhelm II's place of exile].
Hitler (raising his hand): Hoch! How are you doing, old man?
Wilhelm (holding out his hand): I am not used to such impudence; with me one first kisses the hand.
Hitler: Don't bang on the kettle [= stop talking nonsense]. That was a business for Bismarck. How do you feel without the throne?
Wilhelm: Better not ask. The royal seat, the throne — give it to me!
Hitler: I've got it in my breast pocket.
Wilhelm: Then why don't you seat me on it?
Hitler: You see, Wilusz, if there is to be a new Kaiser in Germany after all, why should I seat on it such an old shoe-polish tin [gutalina] as you, when for the same money one can get a healthy young fellow?
Wilhelm: Whom do you mean by that healthy young fellow?
Hitler (smiling): "Look at me, Herr Ex-Kaiser" [in German]. The healthy candidate for the German throne, pardon the expression [z przeproszeniem], is me.
Wilusz faints, Hitler laughs, the curtain falls.

That's How One Lives...

[Będzin — satirical feuilleton; economic crisis and charity.]
(A monologue by a Będzin Jew).
You ask me, my friend, what I do for a living and what I live on? Actually I could have answered you: what business is it of yours? Is it your grandmother's worry? But since I see that you are "interested in me and very curious, I will do you the favour and say: next to nothing. That is, I go around idle — and yet I live...
What, you stare at me? You can't imagine it at all? But that is how it is after all: "against your will you live." One gets used to all troubles. On the contrary, be so kind and show me what, for instance, one can make a living from in today's critical times? From work? Or can one get anything out of trade even? For firstly, one is unemployed more of the time than one works, and likewise in business — your eyes can pop out of your head before you get a customer... And secondly you have to deal with "craftsmen's cards" [karty rzemieślnicze], exams, diplomas, the sick fund, "ZUSU" [?], trade licences, keeping books, dealings with bills of exchange: prolonging, protesting, settling, going bankrupt, auctioning and more such things... And above all — t a x e s [podatki]; do you know what the taxes have made of me? They have sucked the whole marrow out of my bones... Everything I had has already been taken from me, they didn't even leave me a pillow to put under my head... Well, I ask you, tell me, on the contrary, who has a head with a brain to drag such a heavy yoke on his shoulders... So I really do nothing, and as you "see — one lives...
You still want to know further what I live on after all? Then listen:
My main source of income is the committees for the unemployed. Since I was, after all, once a Jewish householder and something of a merchant, they have more pity on me and support me — may it be said of all poor Jews. Secondly my neighbours take pity on me, and a few women, very fine Jewish women, go around the town every week and they already bring me even bird's milk [?].. At first my face would flush with shame that I have to depend on a dole, but troubles harden a person and "one gets used to everything.
When I see that the stock of food is running out, I don't think long and get into bed. That is, I become supposedly ill for a few weeks (doctors and prescriptions cost me nothing, because they send to me from "Linas ha-Kholim") and the gain from it is very [?] large. Neighbours, friends, good friends, acquaintances and even strangers come running and bring into the house of all good things: preserves, compote, sugar, sweets, biscuits, chocolate, oranges, lemons, grapes and more such appetising things, so that it already suffices for my family to refresh the heart for quite a long time.
Further you should know that there exist in our town a fair number of societies that care for me. Here Reb Mendel Rozenuost [?] sent me a couple of korzec [a dry measure] of coal; before Passover I got from the "Maos Khitim" [Passover relief]; my little children go to school free of charge and there they even get a free roll with milk. For the summer I send the children off to the Magistrate's [municipal] colony in Sławków, and that also doesn't cost me a penny; they come back from there well-fed and refreshed, so that it's a real pleasure to look at them. Besides that, this winter, thanks to "Balimovsin" [?], I received from the Magistrate a few foodstuffs and things. One way or another I occasionally get a few guldens [złoty] sent to my home as "secret charity", and, not to sin, I have nothing to complain about; for the time being I lack nothing, may it not get worse.. Jews are after all compassionate sons of compassionate ones and do not let their own brother fall.
You ask me what I do about the rent — I pay [?]. Of course I pay, how else? Can I demand of my landlord that he keep me for free? It costs him something after all — taxes, repairs, etc. So where do I take the money to pay from? Quite simple. I paid my landlord in advance, on moving in, for a whole year. The money I took from my previous landlord as key-money for vacating [optret-gelt], and only when my present landlord will want me to move out will he too, of course, have to give me such a sum that it will suffice me to pay for "a new flat for at least a year.
So, as you see, troubles have taught me to find a way out everywhere, and though from next to nothing, I make quite a fine living. I would already have pushed through my few years like this, but the trouble is that lately such "idlers" as I are springing up in our little town like mushrooms after rain: workshops are closing, shops are closing, and an enormous competition is arising...
Only now, you see, the situation is turning bitter and one must already start thinking about a solution. Not always, you should know, is it good to have many brothers in misfortune...
Well, I'll give in [?] to you, since you already want to know what I reckon to do next? I must reveal a secret to you which I am for the time being keeping hidden even from my own family: I have quite decided to pack up and move to the Land of Israel. As I have heard, it is very good there and everyone has work, so something will probably be found for me too. The only obstacle is just — where does one get the travel expenses for now? But I hope that here too I will find a way. There will surely be good people who will help me out. What, did I do little for Zionism? Did it cost me little? When I could, I always gave: to Keren Hayesod, Keren Kayemet and other funds, perhaps more than another rich man. I was indeed always drawn to the Land of Israel. As if I had felt that I would end up there in the end. Our local Zionists know quite well about it..
Well, now you know everything and you see what troubles can make of a person. But our dear Jews are a precious people, and never mind — among them one doesn't get lost...
Z.-G.
What's New in Zagłębie? — Będzin: The Shammes Proclaims a Rabbinate Notice about Treyf, and from the Women's Gallery They Shout 'Kosher, Kosher'...

[Head of the local page; Będzin — Rabbinate and ritual slaughter.]
What's New in Zagłębie?
(Date boxes: Friday, 2 Iyar 5693 — piątek 28 kwietnia 1933 [Friday, 28 April 1933].)
Będzin
The shammes proclaims a rabbinate notice about treyf, and from the women's gallery they shout "kosher, kosher"...
Last Sabbath, after the Torah reading in the town synagogue (Shtot-shul), another scene took place in the matter of prohibitions being proclaimed by the rabbinate.
This time the scandal arose in the following circumstances.
The shammes, Mr. M. Kaplan, proclaimed in the name of the rabbinate a ban on the slaughtering of Yechezkele the shochet-and-bodek. But hardly had the shammes uttered the shochet's name when a scandal broke out in the synagogue; protests and cries were heard:
— Lies! Bribery! Young little shochets! and so on.
The scandal went on for quite a while, because hardly had it grown a little quieter in the men's synagogue when the very same scene began upstairs in the women's gallery, from where a young woman, a relative of the "banned" shochet, shouted down to the men:
— "Mazel tov, Yechezkele is already kosher"...
Paid for the Fowl and for the 'Khutsife' (Impudent Woman)...

[Będzin — Rabbinate and ritual slaughter.]
On the eve of the "second days" (the closing days) of Passover, one of the young little shochets slaughtered a fowl of the Jaskel family in a way that made it treyf. The little shochet, seeing[?] that he had made the fowl treyf, told the Christian servant that the "pani" (the lady) should come herself. When Mrs. Jaskel came to the slaughterhouse, the little shochets were no longer there. After inquiry and investigation the woman found out that the fowl had been slaughtered by the "nachibraniec"[?] (a nickname of unclear meaning) Gerlik, from whom she demanded that he give back 4.50, as much as she had paid for the fowl; but for this "impudence"[?] the little shochet began to curse and used the word "khutsife" ("impudent woman").
The epilogue of the story took place last Sunday at the rabbinate's office: the husband of the insulted woman summoned the young shochet to judgement.
The accused did not present himself at the din Torah; instead his father defended him.
After the pleas of both sides, the rabbinate issued the following ruling: to pay for the fowl as much as it cost, and for shouting "khutsife" — 5 gulden (złoty) for the Talmud Torah.
Unveiling of a Banner at Public School No. 2

[Będzin — Education.]
On Sunday, 14 May (Lag ba-Omer), the unveiling of the banner of Public School No. 2 will take place.
The day promises to be a very festive one, and the programme is a rich one.
Invited will be almost all the "notables" of the town, representatives of the authorities, representatives of the higher school administration, municipal institutions, the press, cultural and social institutions, etc.
Anti-German Demonstrations

[Będzin and Sosnowiec — Against Hitler's Germany.]
On Sunday anti-German demonstrations took place in Będzin and in Sosnowiec, organised by the Association of Reserve Officers.
Taking part in the demonstrations were Jewish representatives of the magistrate (town council), house-owners[?], Betar, Jewish reservists, and the Będzin "Hakoach" with its orchestra at the head.
On the "Sokół" square speeches were delivered. About the persecutions and massacres of the Jews in Germany not a single word was mentioned.
The Board of 'Linat ha-Cholim' Decides to Open an Out-Patient Clinic

[Będzin — Medical aid and welfare.]
At the last meeting of the board of "Linat ha-Cholim" the question was discussed of widening the relief action in the medical field in the present hard times.
A resolution was adopted to open an out-patient clinic (ambulatorium). For this purpose several doctors are being invited to a consultation, which will take place next Sunday, with the aim of becoming acquainted with the technical side of the clinic.
A Theft

[Będzin — Crime.]
In the night from Saturday to Sunday, when nobody was in the flat of Mr. Arish Radzinski, thieves cut through a lock and took from the flat everything that had any value at all.
Artisans must hurry to file appeals — in case of excessive assessments of the 1932 turnover tax

[Będzin — artisans and taxes.] The branch of the Central Artisans' Organisation in Będzin is conducting a registration of all members who were wronged in the assessment of the turnover tax (obrotowy) for the year 1932, so as to be able to make interventions at the tax office as well as at the Tax Chamber, and if need be at the Ministry of Finance, through the Central Artisans' Union.
All members who feel wronged by the assessment of the turnover tax for 1932 may report for registration at the association's office, Kołłątaja 45, during office hours 10–1 and 8–10 in the evening.
Since the deadline for submitting appeals ends on 15 May of this year, the deadline for registering the wronged members has been set for 8 May of this year; therefore all interested members are asked to report as soon as possible to the office of the Artisans' Association.
The above is handled by the Artisans' Association without any special payment from the members.

This Saturday Poale Zion is organising a mass meeting dedicated to the 1st of May, in the premises of „Hapoel-Kraft“.
Sosnowiec — Sunday: the festive opening of the outpatient clinic of the „Linat haCholim“ society

[Sosnowiec — charity and health.] Barely a few months since the „Linat haCholim“ society passed into the hands of capable, active people, and already we are able to record an important deed of the board. We mean the creation of the outpatient clinic for poor patients, which will begin operating as early as next Tuesday.
The festive opening of so important an institution will take place on Sunday morning in the „Sala Angielski“. After the speeches and greetings the assembled public will proceed to the premises of „Linat haCholim“, where the clinic has been installed, and there the official opening proper will take place.

It is also worth noting the board's decision that no monetary donations whatsoever shall be demanded of those present.
Candlesticks may not be seized for tax debts

[Sosnowiec — taxes.] Last week a conference on tax matters took place at the Sosnowiec Chamber of Commerce.
Among others, the inspector for tax matters at the „Izba Skarbowa“ (Treasury Chamber) also took part in the conference.
At the conference councillor Mr. Aliner touched on a very important matter, which to this day has not yet been clarified by the competent tax authorities.
Mr. Aliner turned, in the form of an interpellation, with the question whether the tax bailiffs have the right to seize candlesticks that are used in honour of Sabbaths and festivals. On this occasion Mr. Aliner reported a case in which a bailiff had seized from a Sosnowiec taxpayer a pair of candlesticks, which were all that remained to the family of their entire fortune — a fortune, incidentally, that had been valued in the tens of thousands of złoty.
The inspector to whom the interpellation was addressed gave no definitive answer, but the result is that the next day the person concerned got the candlesticks back; that means, then, that for seized candlesticks one can file for an exemption (wyłączenie).
„All Jews must be driven out of Poland“ — a „commandment“ of the Polish Hitlerites

[Sosnowiec — antisemitism.] This week a Polish publication called „Jedna Karta“, issued by the Polish National Socialists, was distributed throughout the town.
The publication, which contains venomous and inflammatory articles against Jews, also includes 10 „commandments“. The 8th commandment of the Jew-devouring gang says:
„Jews in Poland are becoming ever richer, at a time when the Polish people is becoming poorer. Jews demoralise Polish society and the state; all of trade, industry, the liberal professions and the press are in Jewish hands and are dominated by Jewish capital“.
Well, what is to be done against this? To this comes the following answer:
„If it is not possible to drive out all the Jews to Palestine, they should be dispersed among the other states of the world. For those who will nevertheless remain here, a percentage quota should be introduced in the schools, and there must be no Jews in any government office“.
The hate leaflets were pasted up on the busy streets of Sosnowiec.
According to the „Będzin version“... — the shochtim seize the slaughter revenue

[Sosnowiec — community and shechita.] On Sunday the kehilla board held a meeting at which a resolution was adopted that the shochtim (ritual slaughterers) are to receive 50 percent of the slaughter revenue, and the rest is to be given to other officials.

Katowice carters want to introduce a new „border“, to begin at the Szopienice bridge

[Zagłębie — antisemitism and carting.] Carters from Katowice, probably graduates of Hitler's „cheder“, have resolved among themselves not to let in any Jewish carters from Zagłębie who bring or carry out goods from Katowice to Zagłębie.
They carried out this hooligan resolution by force: they lay in wait for the carts, fell upon the carters and beat them savagely. The „border“ was to be at the Szopienice bridge, up to which the people of Zagłębie had permission to bring goods.
In connection with this decree, a group of injured Jewish carters from Sosnowiec turned with a cry of woe to Mr. Aliner, who turned about it by telephone to the starosta.

What Taxpayers Must Be Told About the Assessment Principles
Because in the offices (urzędy) they are reluctant to disclose the assessment principles ("zasady wymiaru") of the turnover tax, we therefore point out that under Article 80 of the law on the turnover tax, the tax offices are obliged to disclose — only orally — the assessment principles to every taxpayer who requests it.
This therefore does not depend on the official; he is obliged to do so by law.
The official is not obliged to show the assessment sheet; he reads out the principles. He is not obliged to give the names of persons who supplied information, but he must say from which sources the size of the turnover was compiled, and the amount of turnover from each source separately, as well as at what turnover the experts (rzeczoznawcy) assessed it.

The Extraordinary Levy (Danina)

The "Dz. Ustaw" [Journal of Laws] No. 20 has published the law on the extraordinary levy (danina), which is to replace the annulled property tax.
The levy will be in force for 5 years, from 1933 to 1937 inclusive, and is to yield 24 million zł. a year; of this, payers of the land tax will pay 10 million, payers of the turnover tax — 10 and a half million, and payers of the tax on real estate — 3 and a half million zł.
Exempt from the tax are: state and municipal institutions and enterprises, professional associations if they have no profit-making enterprises, pension funds and the like.
Also exempt from the tax are the assets of scientific and cultural institutions, schools, seminaries and the like; new and thoroughly rebuilt buildings completed after 1 January [styczeń] 1923; smaller agricultural holdings; commercial enterprises and free professions whose turnover does not exceed 20 thousand zł. a year, and under the lump-sum (ryczałt) system 27 thousand zł.; urban real estate (houses etc.) with an income of up to 1000 zł. a year.
The levy is calculated as a percentage of turnover. The payment dates and details of the assessment and collection of the levy will be fixed by an ordinance of the Minister of the Treasury, who is also entitled [?] to reduce it, grant individual relief and even annul the tax entirely for individuals.
The 10 per cent surcharge will not be collected on the levy, nor any additional payment for the municipal institutions.
The law came into force on 29 April and applies already from 1 January 1933.

What Does the Dollar Turmoil Mean?

[World economy — article; the USA and the dollar.]
I.
The latest fall of the American dollar has provoked great turmoil and disappointment. In fact, the financial experts are still not unanimous whether this is an inflation or a depreciation (a reduction in the gold value) of the dollar. If the first concept — inflation — means a surplus of money and means of credit relative to a country's general need for cash or credit, the second term, "depreciation", means the reduction of the currency's value in gold. It happens that a country has 100 per cent gold cover and is nevertheless in a state of inflation, having more money and means of credit than the general need, as a result of economic life, requires. This interesting phenomenon could be observed during the war in the neutral countries such as Spain, Norway, Holland, Switzerland and others. On the other hand, a bank of issue may have a very small gold cover and still be able to keep the currency on a stabilised basis. The case of post-war Germany, where the gold cover at certain moments did not exceed 10 per cent of the circulating banknotes, is characteristic enough.
"Inflation" therefore does not coincide with "depreciation"; but neither do they contradict each other — on the contrary, quite often the two phenomena come together.
The American dollar is falling. It would be ridiculous to claim that the cause lies in a small gold cover: the United States is at this moment, with its 4 billion 272 million gold dollars, the country richest in gold in the whole world. The causes of the dollar's latest fall are therefore not monetary but purely political and economic. First, it is a matter of balancing this year's state budget, which for some years has been closing with a large deficit. Issuing fresh dollars will thus enable the Roosevelt government to balance the budget. We in Poland, who remember Grabski's monetary experiments, know quite well how such a budget policy can end. Secondly, the Roosevelt government wants, by lowering the gold value of the dollar, to raise prices artificially, first and foremost the prices of foodstuffs, which still show a tendency to fall. It should, however, be noted at once that as far as prices are concerned it is quite probable that they will rise, but to a smaller extent than the dollar will fall; so instead of the desired "hausse" in prices, the result will be a "baisse".
Thirdly, Roosevelt intends, by reducing the gold value of the dollar, to reduce in practice the large debts weighing on commercial and industrial enterprises. He thus hopes in this way to make the various enterprises more viable and competitive (once the real debts and interest have become smaller). This should in turn lead to a rise in prices. The other side of the medal, however, is that since most of the large enterprises came into being thanks to share and bond issues subscribed by the broad public, even of the lower strata, the reduction of the real value of the debts will also reduce to a certain extent the purchasing power of that great mass which has placed its "savings" in the industrial, commercial and agricultural enterprises. Thereby the planned price rise will meet serious obstacles, because the consuming power of the freshly impoverished population has clearly diminished. And finally it should be stressed that Roosevelt means by inflation to strengthen American exports; this is the so-called currency dumping. In this case Roosevelt wants to follow England's paths. One would, however, like to remark that unemployment in England has not diminished significantly — which is what the English actually expected when they abandoned the "gold standard".
Besides, if we are indeed heading for currency dumping, it is, from a purely business standpoint, not to be recommended because of its bad psychological effect. The other states, wishing to protect their domestic products, will defend themselves with high prohibitive tariffs or with the same currency dumping. Instead of the present tariff war we shall have a currency-dumping war — but the results will be the same.
Inflation in the United States can, apart from the momentary benefit, bring no great good to the world economy.
Ch. Ish.

But if these same elements are sharpening their teeth here in Poland, then one must stand on guard and not allow this sickness-psychosis to penetrate. They are bent, by all means of violence, on provoking an abnormal situation in the country, and then [?] they will seek revenge — and it is clear that the first "kapparah-hen" [scapegoat] will then be the Jew, he who is guilty of everything. Naturally, the Jew, as a weak element, can at the first moment become the scapegoat.
Here in Zagłębie and in Upper Silesia the antisemites are toiling, sprawling, so to speak, at full length and breadth, if only to provoke hatred and enmity between the workers and the Jewish population. They agitate everywhere, they call meetings and distribute hate-leaflets full of poison and hatred. So they prepare for the "holy" work with the greatest self-sacrifice. They give no account to anyone or for anything, and want only to reach the single goal: to make the masses a blind tool that will obey [?] like a machine and carry out every order without knowing why or when. The model and the system they will take from the Germans, and imitate them in the wildest deeds, the most terrible atrocities, at which the world shuddered and from which the finest personalities dissociated themselves.
Our antisemites, who crave blood, want to know nothing; they do not want to give themselves any account at all; they do not even want to wait and see how the German savage deeds will end. That they have no time, that they are sick, that they set out on the wildest, most lawless paths only to bring the country to an abnormal state, only so that people should murder and beat and incite like nobody's business [lit. "on what the world stands"], that they have only the one aim of learning from the "Hitlerowcy" — that goes without saying.
But we, we Jews, must look with open eyes; we must not take this problem lightly; we must not forget that those who want to see our blood are multiplying, those who want to destroy the Jewish name and the Jewish honour in Poland.
We see [printed "are"] how preparations are being made; we see how the dark elements want to burst, with every act of violence, into the Polish masses, and incite them and inflame them and poison the human hearts of the broad strata of the Polish population. We feel it in the air, the atmosphere tells us so, and we must see to helping ourselves; we must explain in all sorts of ways that the agitators want nothing more than to fish in troubled waters.
We must intervene in good time and see to it that it does not come to catastrophes which could lead still [?] further, for we know very well what the antisemitic clique is after — Jewish excesses [pogroms].
The Jews of Zagłębie and Upper Silesia must remember in this case in what circumstances we find ourselves and how grave our situation can become if the working elements are made into blind tools and persuaded that the Jew is guilty of everything and that their only salvation can be the driving of the Jew out of Poland.
Why should we fool ourselves? We see, after all, that human minds are completely reshaped with the help of provocation and incitement and agitation, and simply by throwing salt in the eyes. The unfortunate catastrophe in Germany has given us a good lesson: that we must not remain indifferent when we see that, day in, day out, pitch and brimstone are poured upon the Jewish citizens. Let us therefore confer in good time, in order to avert what is a catastrophe, what is a misfortune.
The antisemites are already at work on deeds; they are preparing. They want the sky to be clouded over already; they want their swords to be waving already over Jewish heads. They thirst for blood and keep on recruiting followers and members.
It must not be allowed that the country should fall into a sickness-psychosis that could destroy everything that has been built with so much toil and torment for the good of the Polish state, for the good of the free, independent Polish Republic.
Be that as it may, and whatever turn these deeds may take, the Jewish representation must stand on guard and protect our most pressing [?] interests. At this present moment we must not let pass even a single small thing. Everything for the good of the Jewish population must be considered and analysed from all sides, positively and with deliberation, so that it should be for the good of the Jewish citizens in Poland.
